Lessons Learned: Transitioning From Cadaveric Dissection to Virtual Anatomy and Point-of-Care Ultrasound in Physician Assistant Education

Author: Stone, Joshua D1; McNeal, Patrick11 Joshua D. Stone, PhD, Assistant Program Director, Division of PA Studies, College of Health Professions, Medical University of South Carolina, Charleston SC; Patrick McNeal, DMSc, PA-C, Division of PA Studies, College of Health Professions, Medical University of South Carolina, Charleston SC

Publication info: Stone, Joshua D; McNeal, Patrick. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/lessons-learned-transitioning-cadaveric/docview/3272735455/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: The traditional use of cadaveric dissection in Human Anatomy education for Physician Assistant students has been increasingly challenged by the need for greater clinical relevance, flexibility, and cost efficiency. In response, our program transitioned to a modernized anatomy curriculum incorporating virtual anatomy tools and point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) to enhance learning and better prepare students for clinical practice. INTRODUCTION The traditional use of cadaveric dissection in Human Anatomy education for Physician Assistant students has been increasingly challenged by the need for greater clinical relevance, flexibility, and cost efficiency. In response, our program transitioned to a modernized anatomy curriculum incorporating virtual anatomy tools and point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) to enhance learning and better prepare students for clinical practice.We replaced cadaveric dissection with a combination of the Virtual Human Dissector, Sectra Anatomy Table, and POCUS. Implementation strategies included structured faculty development workshops, hands-on training sessions, and early communication with incoming students. Anatomy instruction was redesigned to integrate clinical imaging and real-time ultrasound scanning to promote active learning and application of anatomical knowledge. METHODS We replaced cadaveric dissection with a combination of the Virtual Human Dissector, Sectra Anatomy Table, and POCUS. Implementation strategies included structured faculty development workshops, hands-on training sessions, and early communication with incoming students. Anatomy instruction was redesigned to integrate clinical imaging and real-time ultrasound scanning to promote active learning and application of anatomical knowledge.Initial feedback from students indicated high levels of engagement, satisfaction, and perceived relevance to clinical practice. Challenges included faculty adaptation to new technologies and student expectations regarding traditional anatomy instruction. These were mitigated through deliberate onboarding processes and early exposure to the new curriculum model. A longitudinal evaluation is currently underway to assess knowledge retention and clinical application outcomes over time. RESULTS Initial feedback from students indicated high levels of engagement, satisfaction, and perceived relevance to clinical practice. Challenges included faculty adaptation to new technologies and student expectations regarding traditional anatomy instruction. These were mitigated through deliberate onboarding processes and early exposure to the new curriculum model. A longitudinal evaluation is currently underway to assess knowledge retention and clinical application outcomes over time.Transitioning to virtual anatomy and POCUS-based instruction offers a clinically meaningful, flexible, and sustainable alternative to cadaveric dissection. Our experience demonstrates that such curricular innovations can enhance, rather than diminish, basic science education, better aligning anatomy instruction with the competencies required in modern clinical settings. DISCUSSION Transitioning to virtual anatomy and POCUS-based instruction offers a clinically meaningful, flexible, and sustainable alternative to cadaveric dissection. Our experience demonstrates that such curricular innovations can enhance, rather than diminish, basic science education, better aligning anatomy instruction with the competencies required in modern clinical settings.

The important thing neglected: integrating bloom's taxonomy into VR safety training model development

Author: Ji, Zuzhen1; Hu, Chaojie1; Luo, Zhanni2; Wang, Yuchen3; Zhang, Shuai1; Yang, Shuanghua3; Pons, Dirk4; Chen, Yong11 Zhejiang University of Technology, Department of Mechanical Engineering, Hang Zhou, China (GRID:grid.469325.f) (ISNI:0000 0004 1761 325X)2 Chongqing Normal University, School of Foreign Languages and Literatures, Chongqing, China (GRID:grid.411575.3) (ISNI:0000 0001 0345 927X)3 Zhejiang University, Department of Chemical Engineering and Biological Engineering, Hang Zhou, China (GRID:grid.13402.34) (ISNI:0000 0004 1759 700X)4 University of Canterbury, Department of Mechanical Engineering, Canterbury, New Zealand (GRID:grid.21006.35) (ISNI:0000 0001 2179 4063)

Publication info: Ji, Zuzhen; Hu, Chaojie; Luo, Zhanni; Wang, Yuchen; Zhang, Shuai; et al. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/important-thing-neglected-integrating-blooms/docview/3268921534/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: As an emerging technology, virtual reality (VR) is being widely used in the field of safety training. However, a potential drawback arises when the learning theory is weakly considered during the development of safety training models. This oversight may result in several defects, such as a lack of alignment with training priorities and needs, ultimately affecting trainees' learning outcomes and diminishing safety awareness. To address this issue, this study introduces a systematic framework that integrates Bloom's learning taxonomy with VR safety training model development, named the VR Safety Training Goal Taxonomy Framework (VR-Safety-TGT). VR-Safety-TGT provides a comprehensive method for safety trainers and VR model developers to communicate and understand each other's perspectives. Specifically, it assists VR model developers in better-aligning safety training learning objectives. The efficacy of VR-Safety-TGT is examined through a pilot study involving a sample of 91 university students. The students were divided into three groups, each subjected to one of the following training modalities: slideshow-based training, traditional VR training, and VR-Safety-TGT training. The experimental results reveal that the VR-Safety-TGT group exhibits a significant advantage compared to the other two groups. VR-Safety-TGT demonstrates superior outcomes in terms of knowledge acquisition, knowledge retention, self-efficacy, and users’ acceptance of technology.

Full text: Introduction
Safety training is extensively implemented across organizations to equip practitioners with the requisite knowledge and skills for accident prevention and the promotion of a secure working environment (Barati Jozan et al. 2023). Poor safety training would cause weak safety awareness of practitioners and then lead to a poor safety culture, which may further enhance the occurrence of safety incidents (Albert & Routh 2021). Many recent studies used Virtual Reality (VR) technology for safety training development, as VR provides opportunities for trainees to learn in a risk-free environment (Rey-Becerra et al. 2023) (Stefan et al. 2023). It also allows trainees to participate repetitively in an immersive environment, which would benefit worker’s safety knowledge acquisition (Adami, et al. 2021). Studies have indicated that VR safety training can increase the learning efficiency of trainees, which would further benefit their safety behavior (Popov, et al. 2021) (Jenson & Forsyth 2012).
Although VR training focuses on teaching procedural-practical knowledge, declarative knowledge, and problem-solving skills, most studies pay little attention to learning theory while VR training model development, which may negative to trainees’ learning efficiency (Scorgie, et al. 2024). The absence of a theoretical foundation in VR model development has hindered users from comprehending how and why VR could impact trainees’ learning outcomes (Reeves & Crippen 2021). Additionally, poor design in VR models may also lead to an increase in extraneous cognitive loads, which can negatively impact learning effectiveness (Lui et al. 2023). Consequently, there is a need to develop a systematic method for VR safety training model development with the consideration of learning theory. In this paper, a harmonizing framework for VR model development has been proposed with the integration of Bloom’s Taxonomy theory, namely the VR safety training goal taxonomy framework (VR-Safety-TGT). A pilot study is then conducted to demonstrate the reliability and efficiency of the VR-Safety-TGT.
The primary goal of this work is to incorporate learning theories into the development process of VR safety training models. This approach seeks to facilitate effective communication between model developers and training stakeholders, with the goal of achieving alignment between training objectives and requirements. Through this integration, we aim to explore potential improvements in both the development process efficiency and the training’s overall effectiveness. This paper is structured as follows. Section 2 presents the literature on existing VR safety training and also the Bloom’s learning theory. Section 3 delivers the conceptual framework of VR-Safety-TGT. Section 4 delivers a pilot study for examining the efficiency of VR-Safety-TGT and a comparison between traditional safety training. Section 5 illustrates the comparative experimental results. Section 6 concludes the overall work.
Literature review
The conventional safety training methods and recent innovations
For decades, safety training has been primarily conducted in classrooms through lecture-based instruction (Stefan, et al. 2023). Trainees typically learn by attending lectures, viewing slides shows, and watching videos. The safety training curriculum usually includes multiple content such as standard work procedures, hazards management, and risk measures. However, this traditional safety training method is typically unidirectional, leading to low levels of trainee engagement and a deficiency in both interaction and timely feedback (Tong, et al. 2023). Previous studies criticized that the conventional safety training methods are weak in engaging trainees and promoting knowledge retention (Ji, et al. 2023). Hands-on training, another recognized approach to safety training (Serpa et al. 2020) which involves task-oriented learning, where individuals learn by observation and practice. Typically, experienced technicians deliver hands-on training directly on site. This approach significantly enhances participants' knowledge acquisition and engagement in the learning process (Ekwueme et al. 2015). However, hands-on training is hindered by cost inefficiencies, limited capacity, and potential hazards exposure (Dhalmahapatra et al. 2021). Among the challenges faced by hands-on training, the potential exposure for both trainees and trainers to hazardous environments is a significant concern (Calandra et al. 2023), especially in high-risk industries, for example, chemical industry, nuclear power industry, and construction industry. Moreover, practical hands-on training for emergency operations is often restricted due to security concerns, resulting in a deficiency in trainees' knowledge and skills when dealing with actual emergencies.
In the 1990s, computer-aided training is developed for safety training applications (Yang et al. 2001). Computer-aided safety training refers to safety courses delivered by computer-aided technologies. Trainees can access computer-based training when and where it suits their working schedule, which increases the flexibility of training. Nowadays, with the development of technology, Virtual Reality, Augmented Reality (AR), Mixed Reality (MR) technologies have significantly enhanced the effectiveness of computer-aided safety training (Gao et al. 2019). VR applications achieve realism by immersing users within computer-generated environments (Jung & Lindeman 2021). This immersion is facilitated through the use of interactive devices, including head-mounted displays, gloves, and multiple screens (Buttussi & Chittaro 2020). AR is an enhanced version of the real physical world that is achieved through the use of digital visual elements, sound, or other sensory stimuli (Eswaran & Bahubalendruni 2023). One of AR’s primary goals is to highlight specific features of the physical world, and further use the integration of immersive sensations to increase users’ understanding of those features (Pérez-Pachón, et al. 2024). MR is a form that enables the user to experience the seamless transition between VR and AR (Verhey et al. 2020) (Liu et al. 2023). MR is now been applied in multiple industries including construction (Moore & Gheisari 2019), Vehicles design (Wallmyr, Kade, & Holstein 2018), tourism (Mkwizu 2023), and medical applications (Hu, et al. 2019).
Previous studies show that integrating VR into safety training sessions is an effective means for enhancing training efficiency and training outcome (Buttussi & Chittaro 2020; Ji, et al. 2023). Studies utilizing VR for training purposes have demonstrated numerous benefits, including reduced training time, improved learning effectiveness, and decreased training costs (Neyem, et al. 2025; Yang & Fan 2025). Recent VR safety training initiatives have focused on hazards identification, emergency response training, and standard operation of equipment (Pedro et al. 2016). Rokooei et al. presented a VR module that aims to enhance safety training for roofing sectors, which can present essential safety knowledge to new employees and refresh the comprehension of current employees (Rokooei et al. 2023). Rey-Becerra et al. developed VR-based safety training for work at heights and compared its efficacy with lecture-based training. Results have shown that participants using VR-based training acquired better knowledge of safety and risk perception (Rey-Becerra, et al. 2023). Hong et al. developed a fire escape VR training program that focused on responses under stress. The results show the program sufficiently increased user’s self-efficacy in emergency responses (Hong et al. 2023). Ji et al. developed a systematic VR training method using shared VR and integrating diminished quality of life for long-term occupational health and safety risk assessment (Ji, et al. 2023). Makransky and Petersen examined the emotional and cognitive elements that influenced learning within desktop virtual reality simulations, concluded that factors such as presence, intrinsic motivation, self-efficacy, usability, and cognitive benefits significantly contributed to enhanced learning outcomes (Makransky & Petersen 2019).
Bloom’s Taxonomy theory and its application in safety training
Various technologies are emerging, leading to significant changes in the forms of safety training (Buttussi & Chittaro 2018). However, there is still an obvious gap: a lack of effective instructional design that integrates validated educational theories. Lacking educational theories in safety training designs leads to obvious problems. First, it results in a disconnect between the training content and the principles of effective learning (Charlton et al. 2025). Without a solid grounding in educational theories, training programs may fail to engage learners effectively or facilitate long-term knowledge retention. Additionally, the absence of educational theories can lead to ineffective instructional strategies, such as a lack of scaffolding or failure to cater to diverse learning styles (Bader, Abotaleb, Hosny, & Nassar 2023). Furthermore, it hinders the ability to assess the effectiveness of training interventions accurately (Burke et al. 2006). Overall, the absence of educational theories in safety training designs undermines the efficacy and impact of such programs.
In the field of safety training, one educational theory that can be utilized is the Revised Bloom’s Taxonomy (Anderson & Sosniak 1994). The Revised Bloom's Taxonomy is a framework developed by educational psychologist Benjamin Bloom in the 1950s, which was later revised by a team led by Anderson and Krathwohl in 2002 (Krathwohl 2002). The comparison of the two versions is illustrated in Fig. 1. [See PDF for image]
Fig. 1 Original bloom's taxonomy vs revised bloom's taxonomy


The Revised Bloom's Taxonomy categorizes different levels of cognitive skills that students use in learning. The taxonomy consists of six levels, arranged in a hierarchical order from lower to higher order thinking skills:
- Remembering: recalling facts, information, or concepts without necessarily understanding them (Airasian & Miranda 2002).

- Understanding: grasping the meaning of information, being able to explain it in one's own words, and interpreting its significance (Cochran & Conklin 2007).

- Applying: using learned knowledge or concepts in new situations, contexts, or problems (Cochran & Conklin 2007).

- Analyzing: breaking down complex information into simpler components, identifying patterns, relationships, or connections, and drawing conclusions (Brabrand & Dahl 2009).

- Evaluating: making judgments about the quality, value, or importance of information, ideas, or arguments based on certain criteria or standards (Huitt 2011).

- Creating: synthesizing information from various sources to generate new ideas, designs, or products (Husain 2021).



Studies have indicated that the Revised Bloom’s Taxonomy provides a systematic classification of the processes of thinking and learning, which can be used as a measurement tool for education (Febrina et al. 2019). In recent years, the Revised Bloom's Taxonomy has emerged as an effective resource for enhancing learning, particularly within the educational domain (Barari et al. 2022). It has found practical applications in various areas, such as test item design (Köksal & Ulum 2018) and the development of experiential learning (Cannon & Feinstein 2005).
Compared to the education area, the applications of using Bloom’s Taxonomy in engineering are relatively few. Applications can be found in, for example, Khairuddin and Hashim utilized Bloom’s Taxonomy to enhance software engineering education by designing assessment questions that evaluates students’ learning outcomes (Khairuddin & Hashim 2008). Jayakodi et al. combined Bloom’s Taxonomy with engineering exam question design to enable evaluators to analyze and design question papers that measure student knowledge from various aspects and levels (Jayakodi, Bandara, & Perera 2015).
Previous VR safety training studies focused on model fidelity development (Luo, et al. 2023), usability of the VR applications (Radianti et al. 2020), and operational procedure teaching (Li, et al. 2017). Few studies have discussed how to develop efficient VR models for safety training with consideration of learning theory. Lui et al. first pointed out that VR learning studies in the engineering area often lack the consideration of learning theories in research design and VR development to promote students’ learning (Lui, et al. 2023). Radianti et al. pointed out that immersive VR has mostly been part of experimental and development work rather than being regularly applied in actual teaching. This reflects the fact that the introduction of learning theory into VR is still under-appreciated (Radianti, et al. 2020). Niu et al. embedded VR technology with Bloom’s taxonomy in the application of 3D design teaching, however, they treated VR model development and teaching content in a disjoint way (Niu et al. 2021). Marougkas et al. indicated that the application of VR in teaching aligns with various existing teaching theories, including constructive learning, experiential learning, gamification of learning, and the learning by doing theory (Marougkas et al. 2023). While previous VR applications have significantly improved safety training capabilities, the lack of consideration for learning theories in VR model development would negatively impact trainees' learning outcomes. How should VR safety training be better designed to optimize trainees’ learning? This is an urgent question for VR safety training area.
To solve this issue, a solid framework for VR safety training development has been proposed in this paper. The integration with Bloom’s Taxonomy would provide theoretically informed suggestions for future VR training cases. A better harmonization between learning theory towards safety VR model development would improve the trainees’ learning efficacy, knowledge acquisition, and knowledge retention. Integrating learning theory towards VR safety training would have the potential to increase trainees’ learning efficiency and decrease the training costs, which would also assist hazard control, prevention development, and risk assessment.
The VR-safety-TGT framework
The development of VR-based safety training models require collaboration between safety trainers and VR model developers. However, significant knowledge boundaries frequently exist between these two professional domains, potentially hindering effective communication and collaboration. In the VR safety model development process, VR model developers primarily focus on technical implementation aspects, including algorithm design, coding, and system optimization using programming languages and development platforms. Conversely, safety trainers are responsible for defining pedagogical objectives, establishing training requirements, and evaluating the educational effectiveness of the developed VR models through systematic feedback mechanisms.
This interdisciplinary collaboration often encounters communication challenges due to the inherent knowledge gap between domains. While safety trainers possess specific training objectives and scenario requirements, they may lack the technical vocabulary to effectively convey these specifications to developers. Similarly, developers' technical expertise in VR implementation may not always align with pedagogical best practices. To address these challenges, in the conventional model development process, a structured knowledge transfer process is implemented. Initially, safety trainers communicate training objectives and requirements to developers; subsequently, developers provide detailed information regarding VR system capabilities and constraints to trainers. This bidirectional knowledge exchange facilitates the alignment of technical feasibility with pedagogical requirements. Following the initial phase, the VR model undergoes a comprehensive evaluation process conducted by safety trainers. This evaluation encompasses both qualitative and quantitative assessments of the model's effectiveness in meeting predefined training objectives. Subsequently, based on the trainers' evaluation results and feedback, VR developers implement systematic optimizations to enhance the model's performance. This iterative process of evaluation and optimization continues until the VR training model achieves optimal alignment with both pedagogical requirements and technical specifications, as illustrated in Fig. 2, which depicts the collaborative development process between safety trainers and VR model developers. [See PDF for image]
Fig. 2 The conventional VR safety training model development


The conventional development process exhibits several significant limitations. Firstly, the lack of familiarity with VR on the part of trainers often results in an overestimation or underestimation of the capabilities of VR models when articulating their requirements. This lack of understanding may impede the optimal utilization of VR training capabilities. Alternatively, VR model developers might prioritize technical accuracy, realism, and system optimization in the VR development process. This might not align perfectly with the training priorities and learning objectives set by trainers. It would potentially result in a VR training model that doesn't fully meet safety training needs. Safety trainers often possess domain-specific expertise related to safety protocols, industry regulations, and specific job tasks, in contrast, VR model developers often lack this domain knowledge, and it may lead to inaccuracies in the simulation. The absence of consideration for learning theory in the traditional development of VR safety training models would often lead to gaps in the real training application, resulting in poor learning outcomes, and further diminished trainees’ safety awareness and operation ability.
The proposed VR-Safety-TGT addresses the above weaknesses in VR studies by providing a systematic framework for developers to design models that take into account various learning taxonomies comprehensively. With a robust development strategy introduced by VR-Safety-TGT, the training capacity of VR safety models can be significantly enhanced. VR-Safety-TGT functions as an intermediary between VR model developers and safety trainers. It facilitates the transfer of training goals and requirement from safety trainers to VR model developers in a progressive manner. This approach improves VR developers' understanding of safety training and enhances safety trainers' understanding of VR systematically. By implementing VR-Safety-TGT in the development of safety training models, it is anticipated that the existing gaps between safety training goals and VR training capabilities can be reduced. Figure 3 explains how the VR-Safety-TGT serves safety trainers and VR model developers. [See PDF for image]
Fig. 3 VR safety training model development using VR-Safety-TGT


The VR-Safety-TGT is developed based on the integration of the Revised Bloom’s Taxonomy theory and VR model development. The VR-Safety-TGT contains four domains, including operation knowledge training, environment knowledge training, risk knowledge training, and prevention and recovery knowledge training. Each domain consists of six layers, including remember, understand, apply, analyze, evaluate and create. Figure 4 illustrates the conceptual VR-Safety-TGT framework. [See PDF for image]
Fig. 4 The conceptual VR safety training goal taxonomy framework


Part A: The operation domain
The operation domain delivers safety operation knowledge through progressive learning layers. Layer Remember associates with procedural familiarization which focuses on foundational protocol retention through step-by-step recall of standard operation procedures (SOPs), establishing operational muscle memory via repetitive VR drills. Layer Understand relates to mechanistic demonstration which develops system comprehension through interactive models requiring trainees to describe protocol rationales and operational cause-effect relationships. Layer Apply focuses on practical implementation which simulates equipment manipulation scenarios demanding real-time application of memorized procedures, bridging theory–practice gaps through VR interactions. Layer Analyze associates with operational priority management which trains critical assessment of task urgency through different scenarios, requiring prioritization decisions under simulated pressure. Layer Evaluate aims to teach strategic reflection which engages trainees in evaluating alternative solutions within complex simulations, comparing outcomes to optimize operational strategies. Layer Create tends to train protocol innovation skills which enables experimental design of custom solutions in open VR environments, fostering creation of safety-enhanced workflows through iterative testing.
Part B: The environment domain
The environment domain delivers plant/facility knowledge through structured learning layers. Layer Remember focuses on element recognition which trains identification of critical components, including emergency exits, safety equipment positions, and core facility layouts through guided VR exploration. Layer Understand advances to spatial articulation which enables trainees to describe relationships between facilities and pathways using interactive 3D models, building mental maps of production zones. Layer Apply introduces operational navigation which challenges users to locate specific tools/facilities in the VR scenarios, reinforcing wayfinding skills within authentic production contexts. Layer Analyze requires layout appraisal which demands trainees appraise environmental arrangements, assessing component interactions and layout suitability for operational workflows. Layer Evaluate enhances compliance assessment which simulates complex environments where trainees evaluate facility layouts against safety standards, ergonomic principles, and hazard mitigation requirements. Layer Create fosters layout innovation which empowers experimental design of optimized configurations, testing creative solutions to improve safety/efficiency through VR prototyping.
Part C: The risk domain
The risk domain cultivates hazard awareness through progressive learning layers. Layer Remember focuses on hazard naming which trains trainees to name workplace-specific risks (chemical, radiation, mechanical) through VR simulations. Layer Understand emphasizes hazard differentiation which uses multi-sensory cues (thermal visuals, noise audio) to teach differentiating between hazard types and their unique exposure consequences. Layer Apply establishes risk correlation which challenges users to correlate specific hazards with equipment vulnerabilities and operational impacts. Layer Analyze sharpens risk identification which requires trainees to identify and categorize emerging risks during virtual inspections of hazardous operations, enhancing situational analysis skills. Layer Evaluate trains risk examination, this involves examining the likelihood/severity of risks, and assessing mitigation priorities using industry-standard evaluation matrices. Layer Create enables proactive discovery, empowering trainees to conduct self-guided VR explorations that uncover overlooked risks, fostering predictive risk identification capabilities that extend beyond conventional training protocols.
Part D: The prevention and recovery domain
The prevention and recovery domain delivers risk mitigation knowledge through structured learning layers. Layer Remember focuses on foundational memorization which trains trainees to memorize basic safety principles, such as PPE usage protocols and maintenance fundamentals. Layer Understand advances to preventive indication which teaches trainees to indicate specific preventive measures (e.g., pipe rust identification/removal) via interactive VR demonstrations tailored to operational contexts. Layer Apply emphasizes practical selection which simulates scenarios that requiring trainees to select appropriate self-protection methods and execute maintenance tasks. Layer Analyze sharpens strategy assessment which challenges trainees to assess the effectiveness of various prevention/recovery measures, comparing outcomes to optimize safety strategies. Layer Evaluate trains predictive foresight which exposes trainees to scenarios where they must predict consequences of preventive actions, fostering forward-thinking risk management skills. Layer Create fosters innovative solutions which empowers trainees to implement innovative self-protection and risk-prevention measures for specific tasks.
The overall illustrations of VR-Safety-TGT in different domains are concluded in Fig. 5. In the application of Bloom's Taxonomy theory to industrial safety training, the stages of "Remember", "Understand", and "Apply" are correlated with junior-level training. These stages address the training needs of basic level operators, with an emphasis on acquiring standard knowledge without necessitating innovative thinking. The primary goal for training at this level is to instill proficiency in established safety protocols and procedures. Conversely, the stages of "Analyze", "Evaluate", and "Create" are aligned with the senior level of training. Specifically designed for engineers and managers, these stages focus on developing innovation skills and critical thinking capabilities. The primary goal of training at the senior level is to empower participants to assess existing safety measures critically and develop the ability to examine the effectiveness. Moreover, the "Create" encourages senior level trainees to generate innovative safety solutions and the capacity to address overlooked risks. [See PDF for image]
Fig. 5 VR model development in different knowledge domain underpinning with the conceptual VR-Safety-TGT framework


The pilot study
The aim of this pilot study is to evaluate the efficacy of VR-Safety-TGT by comparing it with traditional VR training and traditional slideshow-based training, which both without considering the bloom’s learning theory. The experimental scenario chosen is the spent fuel cooling system of a nuclear power plant (NPP), a setting that presents typical onsite safety hazards and procedural operations. The primary goal of this NPP safety training is to impart essential safety operational knowledge to trainees and enhance their safety awareness, thereby inherently reducing their exposure to operational risks. This necessitates the development of efficient VR safety training models. In this paper, the efficiency of VR-Safety-TGT is assessed from multiple perspectives, including knowledge acquisition, knowledge retention, self-efficacy, and user acceptance of the technology.
Participants and resources
The study was conducted with a sample of 91 students, all of whom reported no physical or visual health problems. The study is obtained at Zhejiang University. The sample consisted of 56% male students (n = 51) and 44% female students (n = 40), with a mean age of 22.3 years. Participants were randomly assigned to one of three groups: 33.0% (n = 30) attended in slideshow-based training (Group 1), with 46.7% undergraduate students, and 53.3% postgraduate students, 56.7% male and 43.3% female; 33.0% (n = 30) attended in traditional VR training (Group 2) with 43.3% undergraduate students, and 56.7% postgraduate students, 56.7% male and 43.3% female; and the remaining 34.0% (n = 31) attended VR-Safety-TGT training (Group 3) with 43.3% undergraduate students, and 56.7% postgraduate students, 54.8% male and 45.2% female. Statistical power was assessed using G*Power 3.1 (Faul et al. 2007). A Post-Hoc power analysis for a one-way ANOVA with three groups (N = 91, =0.05) indicated a 96% power to detect a medium-to-large effect (f = 0.40), surpassing the commonly recommended 80% threshold (Cohen 1992). Sensitivity analysis indicated a minimum detectable effect size of f = 0.33 for 80% power.
The training is associated with daily operations in the spent fuel pool cooling system of NPP. The teaching content and the trainer of three groups are the same. However, the experimental environment differed for Group 1 compared to the other two groups, see Fig. 6. Specifically, Group 1 employed a slide-based instructional approach where knowledge was delivered to trainees through instructor-led explanations. In contrast, both Group 2 and Group 3 adopted a self-directed learning paradigm, where trainees acquired knowledge through independent exploration of the virtual environment without instructor intervention. The primary distinction between Group 2 and Group 3 lies in their pedagogical approaches. Group 2 merely delivered training information within a virtual environment, presenting knowledge in textual/auditory format. Group 3's experimental teaching strategy and model development were designed based on VR-Safety-TGT, which progressively guides learners through annotation, thereby enabling them to achieve higher-order cognitive mastery as defined by Bloom's taxonomy. All participants received instruction in operational knowledge, environmental knowledge, risk knowledge, and prevention and recovery knowledge. Each training lecture lasted approximately 30 min. Ethics approval for data collection and interviews was granted by the Committee of the College of Biomedical Engineering and Instrument Science, Zhejiang University, China, for the data collection and interviews (Reference number: [2024]-No.15). Figure 7 shows a photograph of the VR-Safety-TGT experiment. [See PDF for image]
Fig. 6 Illustration of different training groups in the pilot study

[See PDF for image]
Fig. 7 The VR-Safety-TGT experiment photo


The comprehensive experimental procedure is outlined as follows, and illustrated in Fig. 8. Before the start of the training, participants were presented with a series of preliminary questions pertaining to safety, designed to assess their pre-knowledge. Following this, the participants underwent training in three distinct groups. Upon completion of the training, they were subjected to an evaluative test to determine the efficacy of the training. Subsequently, participants were interviewed regarding their user experience. Two weeks after the conclusion of the training, a follow-up session was conducted wherein participants were posed the same questions to assess their knowledge retention. [See PDF for image]
Fig. 8 The workflow of the pilot study


Model development of the training scenario
The spent fuel pool cooling system in an NPP is designed to remove residual heat from spent fuel, preventing the system from overheating. Regular monitoring and maintenance are key factors to ensure the reliability of the spent fuel pool cooling system in an NPP. VR-Safety-TGT for the Spent Fuel Pool cooling system would require trainees to learn four domains of knowledge, including operational knowledge, environmental knowledge, risk knowledge, prevention and recovery knowledge. For instance, in the risk domain, trainees would be educated on (1) what is a typical risk in the working area, such as noise and heat. (2) where and what equipment would cause the harm. (3) how much level of harm would the risk bring. And (4) how to prevent them. Figure 9 illustrates examples of VR training content development in different domains. [See PDF for image]
Fig. 9 Extracted VR-Safety-TGT teaching content examples in Spent fuel pool cooling system


The development of the VR model for the spent fuel pool cooling system also considers the VR-Safety-TGT. An example of model development based on the VR-Safety-TGT method, progressing from the "Understand" to the "Create" level in the risk domain, is introduced in Fig. 10. In the "Remember" layer of the training program, the focus is on introducing trainees to typical hazards they may encounter in the workplace, particularly within the spent fuel pool cooling system. These hazards include noise, heat, radiation, awkward working positions, among others. To enhance memory retention of these hazards within the VR environment, interactive models are proposed. Here, the incorporation of a collision detection module and a distance detection module is crucial. These modules will facilitate the detection of a trainee's proximity to specific hazards and display related teaching content accordingly. Moving on to the "Understand" layer, risk differentiation becomes the key teaching content. This involves educating trainees on the distinctions among hazards, including their causes and consequences. To achieve this, multisensory sources such as pictures, annotations, and audios should be integrated into the VR model. This immersive approach will enable trainees to experience and internalize the training content more effectively. In the "Apply" layer, the emphasis shifts to linking risks with daily operations. For instance, when maintaining a compressor, trainees must recognize noise as a primary hazard. To facilitate this learning, interactive VR models utilizing controllers for tool manipulation and active operations should be developed. Additionally, environmental hazards like noise and radiation should be modeled using audio and dynamic numerical annotations, respectively. [See PDF for image]
Fig. 10 Examples of using VR-Safety-TGT in risk domain VR mode development


The "Analyze" layer focuses on self-identification of risks. Here, the interactive models are similar to those in the "Apply" layer but without risk information hints. This approach encourages trainees to develop their risk identification skills independently. The "Evaluate" layer involves teaching trainees how to assess hazard-related risks, including the likelihood of exposure and the severity of potential consequences. In this stage, risk matrices should be developed within the VR modeling process. Depending on the nature of the risk, different risk matrices may be utilized. For example, a dynamic risk like radiation requires a time-lag detection model to monitor exposure duration and compute risk dynamically, whereas a static risk like slips or trips can be annotated with simple text. Finally, in the "Create" layer, trainees are encouraged to self-explore within the VR scenario. This allows them to identify overlooked risks that may not have been covered by the training system and to apply their customized risk solutions. For instance, trainees might suggest adding isolation to a compressor to reduce noise levels. To accommodate this exploratory learning, extra integrative models should be developed within the VR environment.
The VR model used in the pilot study is developed using Unity 3D. The VR Head-mounted display used in this study was the HTC VIVE Pro Eye (Resolution: 1080 × 1200 pixels per eye; Refresh Rate: 90 Hz; Field of View: horizontal, vertical). The computer used to control the devices is an assembled computer (CPU: Intel i7–12700F; GPU: NVIDIA GTX3070 16 GB).
An efficient VR model should contain little sickness during the operation, general VR sickness is associated with nausea, dizziness, vertigo, and sweating. To examine the efficiency of the VR model in VR-Safety-TGT, a Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) is used (Kennedy et al. 1993). SSQ evaluates 16 domains of VR sickness, such as fatigue, headache, and eyestrain. A low score on the SSQ suggests that the examined VR model is likely to induce minimal discomfort or sickness among users. In the study, the SSQ is 3.55 on a scale ranging from 0 to 64 for the VR model under evaluation. This result signifies that the developed VR model demonstrated a relatively low susceptibility to causing discomfort or sickness among users.

Self-efficacy
Self-efficacy here in the current context represents the trainee's belief in their ability to successfully perform a specific NPP task or identify safety risks. In terms of measuring self-efficacy, two items proposed in (Lovreglio et al. 2021) were used, see Table 2. The participants were asked to rate their level of agreement using the Likert scale, where 1 represents strongly disagree to 7 represents strongly agree with the following statements. The self-efficacy outcome is computed using the mean rate of the two questions. Table 2. Self-efficacy examining questionnaire (Lovreglio, et al. 2021)

Question content

User acceptance of technology
Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) in the current content refers to the willingness and readiness of trainees to adopt and use VR-Safety-TGT, traditional VR or slideshow lecturing in safety training. To investigate the user’s acceptance of the VR-Safety-TGT, the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) is used (Sagnier et al. 2020), shown in Table 3. In this work, three items are discussed, hence perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, and intention to use (Davis 1989) (Lovreglio, et al. 2021). The participants were asked to rate their level of agreement using a Likert scale from 1 to 7, where 1 represents strongly disagree and 7 represents strongly agree with the following statements. The user acceptance of technology outcome in each domain is computed using the sum of the scores for the following questions. Table 3. UTAUT questionnaire of VR-Safety-TGT group

Hypothesis of the work
VR-Safety-TGT provides a special focus on developing VR safety training models with a consideration of learning taxonomy, hence it theoretically would be efficient for trainees to learn safety context. Alternatively, the application of VR in safety training would also benefit teaching and learning in multiple aspects, such as increasing training engagement, attracting trainee’s attention, knowledge equitation, self-efficacy, and users’ acceptance. Due to the above reasons, there are three hypotheses proposed.
Hypothesis 1
The knowledge acquisition of VR-Safety-TGT training would be greater than traditional VR training and slideshow-based training;
Hypothesis 2
The self-efficacy of VR-Safety-TGT would be greater than traditional VR training and slideshow-based training;
Hypothesis 3
The trainees’ acceptance of VR-Safety-TGT would be greater than traditional VR training and slideshow-based training;
Result of the comparison
Knowledge acquisition comparison
In this section, we analyzed the knowledge scores obtained by participants at different stages of the experiment, including before the training (Pre), after the training (Post), and after 2 weeks (Ret). The Ret data was collected by telephone interview and all of the participants responded.
Data distributions were acceptably normal (absolute skewness < 3 and kurtosis < 8), meeting analysis of variance (ANOVA) prerequisites (Kline 2023). The homogeneity of variance tests showed significant results for the three experimental groups in both the Pre-session (F = 4.747, p  = 0.011* < 0.05) and Post-phase (F = 5.677, p  = 0.005** < 0.05). Consequently, Welch ANOVA was applied to account for heteroscedasticity. In contrast, the Ret-session exhibited no significant variance heterogeneity (F = 1.198, p  = 0.307 > 0.05), permitting the use of standard one-way ANOVA for group comparisons. In case of a statistically significant effect of group, we proceeded with pairwise comparisons using Bonferroni (Bland & Altman 1995). Pre-knowledge of safety in each training group is without significant difference ( p  = 0.994 > 0.05), see Table 4. ANOVA revealed that the training had a significant effect on the participants’ knowledge for each group ( p  = 0.001** < 0.01), as their scores increased significantly from pre-test to post-test (MD < 0, Mean Deviation). Based on the results of the analysis of variance and the subsequent Post-Hoc Test, the following conclusions can be drawn for the Post-session: Group 1, compared to Group 2, has a significantly lower mean difference (MD = − 1.667 < 0, p  = 0.032* < 0.05), however, after Bonferroni correction (adjusted α = 0.05/3 = 0.0167), the difference was no longer statistically significant ( p  = 0.032* > 0.0167). Group 1, compared to Group 3, also has a lower mean difference (MD = − 2.802 < 0), with a highly significant difference ( p  = 0.001** < 0.01). Group 2, compared to Group 3, exhibits a lower mean difference (MD = − 1.135 < 0), which is statistically significant ( p  = 0.002** < 0.01). For Ret-session, Group 1, compared to Group 2, has a significantly lower mean difference (MD = − 1.267 < 0, p  = 0.047* < 0.05), however, difference was no longer statistically significant ( p  = 0.047* > 0.0167) after Bonferroni correction. Group 1, compared to Group 3, also has a lower mean difference (MD = − 2.401 < 0), with a highly significant difference ( p  = 0.001** < 0.01). Group 2, compared to Group 3, exhibits a lower mean difference (MD = − 1.134 < 0), which is statistically significant ( p  = 0.003** < 0.01). Table 4. ANOVA for training outcomes comparisons

For a more detailed analysis of the advantages of VR-Safety-TGT, box-plot analysis was also employed, illustrated in Fig. 11. No observable difference in the reserves of safety knowledge was found among the three groups in the pre-training. Significant differences were observed in both the Post-session and Ret-session when comparing Groups 1 and 2 with Group 3. In terms of knowledge acquisition, the increased median and average scores of the assessment suggest that the use of VR-Safety-TGT had enhanced the learning effectiveness of the trainees. From a reliability perspective, the IQR within Group 3 displayed less variability, indicating that the training outcome data was less susceptible to fluctuations. Consequently, the utilization of the VR-Safety-TGT enhances training stability in comparison to slideshow-based training and traditional VR training. [See PDF for image]
Fig. 11 Participants’ learning scores before the training (Pre), after the training (Post), and after 2 weeks (Ret)


In safety training studies, individuals with poor safety knowledge are considered more prone to commit errors than those who have rich safety knowledge. The lower quartile of the box chart can be used as an indicator to reflect the status of poor knowledge acquisition trainees. Compared to Group 1 and Group 2, Group 3 has a significantly greater lower quartile in both Post-session and Ret-session, see Fig. 11. This indicated that VR-Safety-TGT can enhance training efficiency.
Three metrics, the knowledge growth (KG), the knowledge growth rate (KGR), and the knowledge forgetting rate (KFR) are used to assess training efficacy. The KG represents the knowledge acquired after training. The KGR represents the knowledge-acquiring ratio after training. KFR represents the knowledge loss ratio after a period of time. This observation indicates that the incorporation of VR-Safety-TGT enhances training efficacy in both knowledge acquisition and knowledge retention. In the operation domain, the KGR and KFR of Group 1 are 382.35% and 19.50%. Similarly, the KGR and KFR of Group 2 are 387.50 and 17.95%, while the KGR and KFR of Group 3 are 388.23 and 16.87%. This result indicated that Group 3 outperformed the other groups in both knowledge acquisition and retention.
In the risk domain, the KG and KFR of Group 1 are 3.17 and 25.26%. The KG and KFR of Group 2 are 4.20 and 25.40%, while the KG and KFR of Group 3 are 4.61 and 23.67%. This indicates that the participants of Group 3 learned more risk knowledge using VR-Safety-TGT, and the knowledge forgetting also decreased.
In the environment domain, the KG and KFR of Group 1 are 1.63 and 34.69%. The KG and KFR of Group 2 are 2.20 and 33.33%, while the KG and KFR of Group 3 are 2.68 and 32.53%. VR-Safety-TGT surpasses the other two groups in both the acquisition and retention of knowledge related to the environment.
In the prevention and recovery domain, the KG and KFR of Group 1 are 3.60 and 18.52%. Similarly, the KG and KFR of Group 2 are 3.67 and 16.36%, while the KG and KFR of Group 3 are 3.97 and 8.13%. Group 3 outperformed the other two groups in acquiring knowledge. Specifically, in terms of knowledge retention, Group 3 significantly surpassed the other two groups.
The above findings support Hypothesis 1, hence the knowledge acquisition of VR-Safety-TGT would be greater than the slideshow-based training and traditional VR training method.
Self-efficacy comparison
Self-efficacy represents the participants’ belief in their ability to successfully perform an operation task and risk identification. Self-efficacy results for different groups are shown in Fig. 13. Group 1 has a median score of 8.5 with an IQR of 4. Similarly, Group 2 displays a median score of 9 and an IQR of 4. In contrast, Group 3 shows a higher median score of 11 with a smaller IQR of 2. The smaller IQR and higher median score of Group 3 indicate that the VR-Safety-TGT has a more positive impact on their self-efficacy than the slideshow-based training and traditional VR training groups. The comparison results support Hypothesis 2, hence the self-efficacy of VR-Safety-TGT would be greater than the slideshow-based training and traditional VR training. [See PDF for image]
Fig. 13 Participants’ self-efficacy for different groups


The findings of this study are consistent with previous studies associated with the impacts of VR on trainees’ self-efficacy. For instance, Ding et al. reported that a VR-based negotiation training program improved participants’ knowledge and confidence in negotiation skills (Ding et al. 2020). Srinivasa et al. demonstrated that VR could be used effectively in engineering education to enhance students’ self-efficacy toward manufacturing tasks (Srinivasa et al. 2021). Meanwhile, these results demonstrated that VR-Safety-TGT instills greater self-confidence in trainees compared to traditional training methods, thereby enabling them to effectively accomplish the various tasks mandated by the training program.
Users’ acceptance of technology comparison
Users’ acceptance of technology is measured directly after the training, the result is illustrated in Fig. 14. The IQR for Group 1 is 12, with a median score of 49.5. Group 2 has an IQR of 12, with a median score of 50.5. In contrast, Group 3 has a smaller IQR of 10 and a higher median score of 56. The VR-Safety-TGT group exhibited a smaller IQR and a larger mean score, indicating a more positive effect on users’ acceptance of technology improvement compared to both the slideshow-based training group and the traditional VR training group. [See PDF for image]
Fig. 14 Users’ acceptance of technology for different groups (The total UTAUT value equals to the sum of the different sub-domains)


The questionnaire measured three sub-domains of participants’ attitudes toward the training, including perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, and intention to use. Results for different domains are shown in Fig. 15. The results showed that the mean value of Group 3 scored higher than Group 1 and Group 2 in the first two domains, indicating that participants preferred VR-Safety-TGT training over slideshow-based training and traditional VR training in terms of perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness. The median value of intention of use in Group 3 is with no significant difference compared to Group 1 and Group 2. We propose that this can be attributed to the fact that both traditional training methods, such as slideshow-based lecturing, and the emerging VR training technology have been demonstrated to be effective training tools. The above results are consistent with previous studies that examined the effects of VR on learners’ perceptions and intentions. For example, Fagan et al. investigated how nursing students perceived VR as a tool to learn how to use a medical emergency crash cart and found that VR had higher ratings of ease of use and usefulness than traditional methods (Fagan et al. 2012). Shen reported that VR enhanced users’ intention to use VR for learning purposes (Shen et al. 2019). [See PDF for image]
Fig. 15 Scores in different domains of users’ acceptance of technology


The above findings support Hypothesis 3, hence the users’ acceptance of the technology of VR-Safety-TGT would be greater than the slideshow-based training and traditional VR training.
User experience analysis
We then employed a semi-structured interview to gather personal responses related to different training groups associated with user experience. Participants’ responses were stored via voice record, subsequently transcribed into written text, and finally annotated with relevant features.
Most trainees (n = 20, n represents the number of participants) who received VR-Safety-TGT and traditional VR reported that the immersive and realistic environment makes them feel as if they are physically present on site. The interactive actions and realistic feedback in the VR scene improve the sense of presence. The sense of presence plays an important role in learning and would further benefit trainees’ learning efficacy (Pantelidis 2009). Some trainees (n = 18) pointed out that the VR-Safety-TGT and traditional VR training method is safer than training on-site, especially for high-risk environments like a nuclear power plant. In addition, the novelty of VR technology and its unique training methods make it an attractive option for potential users who are willing to participate.
Several trainees (n = 8) mentioned that, while traditional VR training offers interactive content capable of enhancing retention, the knowledge is often lacks a logical order for learning. Consequently, this makes it hard for trainees to figure out what to learn first and what to learn next. In contrast, some trainees (n = 12) who received VR-Safety-TGT pointed that the training knowledge is acquired through a systematic, step-by-step process. For instance, they first learn about the types of risks, then the origins of those risks, and subsequently, the methods to prevent them. This structured approach enhances the efficiency of knowledge acquisition and helps mitigate the rapid forgetting of information.
There are also several weaknesses of VR-Safety-TGT and traditional VR have been mentioned. The first is fidelity (n = 10), which is due to the hardware and software technology not being advanced enough to fully reproduce the real environment. This can lead to blurry picture quality or lack of frames of action, which can have a greater impact on the immersion experience of the trainees. Additionally, the interaction such as motion and virtual equipment operation are achieved through the HTC Vive controller in this experiment. Some trainees (n = 14) reported that difficulties are found in using such a way to control movement in VR practice. Some trainees (n = 8) are also concerned that dizziness may also occur during the training and decrease the quality of learning. Some others (n = 15) also suggest that the high cost of VR devices and training model development may be a critical issue for the popularization of VR training.
Slideshow-based training also has its strengths in several aspects. For instance, some participants (n = 10) indicated that the knowledge provided by traditional training is often presented directly in outline or highlight, which is clear and efficient. Additionally, there is no need for participants to learn special technical operation skills like VR, which is easier for participation (n = 5). However, most participants (n = 20) reported that they were easily getting bored and lost attention during traditional training.
Conclusion and discussion
VR-safety-TGT vs traditional training methods
Regarding knowledge acquisition and retention, both the VR-Safety-TGT group and the traditional VR training group demonstrated significantly better performance than the slideshow-based training group, as evidenced by higher mean and median scores. This disparity can be attributed to the immersive and interactive nature of VR simulations, which foster a heightened sense of presence through multi-sensory inputs e.g., auditory stimuli. These sensory experiences enhance participant engagement, thereby facilitating memory encoding and consolidation. Conversely, the slideshow-based training, reliant primarily on oral narration and using static or dynamic visual aids e.g., pictures and videos, inherently lacked comparable levels of interactivity and engagement to the VR approaches.
However, after applying Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons, the traditional VR group did not exhibit statistically significant differences from the slide-based group in either the immediate post-test (Post-session) or the delayed retention test (Ret-session) (all p  > 0.167). This indicates that any advantage in knowledge acquisition and retention observed for traditional VR training over slide-based instruction was not statistically significant. This finding aligns with prior research (Leder et al. 2019), which posits that compared to traditional slideshow-based training, traditional VR training demonstrates no substantive advantage in training effectiveness.
The VR-Safety-TGT group demonstrated superior performance in knowledge acquisition and retention compared to the traditional VR group. This can be attributed to the implementation of a hierarchical memory model for risk knowledge within the VR-Safety-TGT approach. This method adopts a sequential framework for comprehending and addressing risks, exemplified by queries such as "What is the origin of the noise risk?"— "What is the severity of the noise risk?"—"How can the noise risk be mitigated?". This structured, step-by-step memory technique proves more efficacious in embedding knowledge in trainees' memories in comparison to the traditional VR method, which merely presents risks without such a systematic approach. Following Bonferroni correction, VR-Safety-TGT maintained statistically significant differences compared to both the slide-based and traditional VR groups. These results suggest that future VR safety training programs could leverage this framework to achieve deeper improvements in safety training effectiveness.
Summary of the contribution
The research makes several contributions. Firstly, the development of VR-Safety-TGT stands out as a noteworthy achievement. This framework introduces a systematic approach for VR developers to design safety training models and provides guidelines for safety trainers to efficiently define model requirements, considering a comprehensive Bloom’s learning taxonomy. By incorporating this structured methodology, VR-Safety-TGT enhances the training capacity of VR models, ensuring a more effective alignment with the objectives set by safety trainers. Moreover, the framework facilitates trainers in evaluating trainees' learning outcomes based on specific cognitive levels. This feature not only provides valuable insights but also serves as a foundation for continuous improvement in future training programs.
Secondly, the efficacy of VR-Safety-TGT is validated through a pilot study. Comparative analysis with traditional VR training and slideshow-based training, highlights the superior knowledge acquisition ability, knowledge retention, trainees' self-efficacy, and users’ acceptance of technology. A user experience analysis further explores the advantages and disadvantages associated with VR-Safety-TGT, traditional VR training and slideshow-based training.
In conclusion, the contributions of this work extend beyond the development of VR-Safety-TGT to its practical application in safety training. The research not only introduces an innovative framework but also substantiates its effectiveness through an empirical study.
Limitation and further opportunities
The scenario for this pilot study is a nuclear power plant, the reliance on college students in the pilot study presents a limitation, considering that the VR training is specifically designed for NPP workers. College students have different level of knowledge, experience, and learning objectives when compared to NPP workers. Given that the training needs of NPP workers are highly specialized, the applicability of results from college students may be limited. College students might not share the same learning priorities as NPP workers, potentially impacting the effectiveness of the VR training. Efforts were made to mitigate this limitation in Sect. 4.1. The study ensured that the three observed groups had similar baseline knowledge, thereby providing a more controlled comparison. The evaluation focused on assessing improvements after the training intervention between VR-Safety-TGT, traditional VR training and slideshow-based training. The results indicated that VR-Safety-TGT outperformed the alternative in terms of knowledge acquisition, knowledge retention, self-efficacy, and users’ acceptance of technology. While these findings are promising, the generalizability of these positive outcomes across other VR safety training scenarios remains further investigation. Additionally, due to the complexity and breadth of the VR-Safety-TGT, conducting a single experiment to verify its entirety is relatively challenging. This indeed constitutes a limitation but also indicates a direction for future work. We aspire to further refine this theory in subsequent endeavors. Nevertheless, the primary goal of this article is to demonstrate the effectiveness of this theory in comparison with traditional VR methods and slideshow-based methods.
Implication of the work
The development of VR safety models often encounters challenges characterized by boundaries, particularly due to a lack of specialized safety training expertise among VR developers. The disconnect results in a misalignment with the objectives set by safety trainers and leads to the creation of inefficient VR training models. This critical issue underscores the need for a systematic approach to VR safety training model development, which can serve as a bridge between VR developers and safety trainers. The VR-Safety-TGT offers a solution to addressing the aforementioned issue. The VR-Safety-TGT not only provides a systematic structure for VR safety training model development but also establishes a crucial communication channel between VR developers and safety trainers. It ensures that the development of VR safety models aligns seamlessly with the teaching objectives set by safety trainers, thus enhancing the overall effectiveness of safety training programs conducted through virtual reality platforms.

Certainty-based marking in multiple-choice assessments in physiology: a web-based implementation using an AI assistant

Author: Suryavanshi, Chinmay1    ; Nayak, Kirtana Raghurama2    1 Department of Physiology, Kasturba Medical College Manipal, Manipal Academy of Higher Education, Manipal, India2 Department of Physiology, Kasturba Medical College Manipal, Manipal Academy of Higher Education, Manipal, India; Department of Medical Education, Kasturba Medical College Manipal, Manipal Academy of Higher Education, Manipal, India

Publication info: Suryavanshi, Chinmay; Nayak, Kirtana Raghurama. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/certainty-based-marking-multiple-choice/docview/3262720315/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: Certainty-based marking (CBM) requires students to indicate their certainty levels alongside their answers. CBM has been shown to enhance self-assessment and metacognitive awareness. This study aimed to explore the implementation of CBM in multiple-choice assessments in physiology. The CBM assessment tool was developed with an artificial intelligence (AI) assistant, Claude 3.5, with prompts focused on functional rather than technical requirements. The assessment consisted of 15 multiple-choice questions (MCQs), which were administered as a pretest and posttest during a small group teaching session to first-year medical students. Following the assessment, students completed a survey to evaluate their perceptions regarding the format, knowledge-gap identification, and overall acceptability. Answers from 195 students were analyzed, and significant improvements were observed in performance measures and certainty indices from the pretest to the posttest. Most students (80.9%) found the certainty scale beneficial, and 78.3% changed their answers after reflecting on their certainty. CBM demonstrated metacognitive benefits, with 86.4% of students better recognizing their knowledge gaps and 85.8% feeling more aware of their learning progress. About 73% of students preferred the CBM format and expressed greater engagement (82.8%) than traditional MCQs. CBM implemented through a web-based platform functioned as an assessment tool and an instructional intervention that enhanced students' metacognitive awareness and self-monitoring skills in physiology education. Our study focused on a single physiology topic and showed improvements in knowledge retention and certainty calibration. However, further longitudinal studies across multiple topics are needed to determine whether students maintain these self-assessment skills over time. NEW & NOTEWORTHY To introduce certainty-based marking (CBM) to novice students, a custom web-based multiple-choice question (MCQ) test was developed with assistance from an artificial intelligence (AI) tool. This enhanced accessibility and allowed for data collection to evaluate and analyze student performance. The integration of AI in creating this assessment tool highlights the potential of technology to improve educational practices, especially in designing various assessment strategies.Certainty-based marking (CBM) requires students to indicate their certainty levels alongside their answers. Clicking one dot opens a whole new world: a qualitative study on using knowledge graphs in surgical nursing education

Author: Liu, Fangchi1; Shen, Mingyan2; Shen, Yanping2; Wan, Pengxia2; He, Tian21 Shulan (Hangzhou) Hospital, Shulan International Medical College,, Zhejiang Shuren University, No.8 Shuren street, Gongshu district, Hangzhou, Zhejiang, China; Hangzhou Normal University, Hangzhou, China2 Shulan (Hangzhou) Hospital, Shulan International Medical College,, Zhejiang Shuren University, No.8 Shuren street, Gongshu district, Hangzhou, Zhejiang, China 289155169@qq.com

Publication info: Liu, Fangchi; Shen, Mingyan; Shen, Yanping; Wan, Pengxia; He, Tian. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/clicking-one-dot-opens-whole-new-world/docview/3272738452/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: The integration of intelligent technologies in surgical nursing education offers opportunities to enhance learning outcomes and address challenges in mastering complex topics. Knowledge graphs serve as a visual and interactive learning tool. It represents a novel approach to improving systematic thinking and enhancing knowledge retention in blended teaching models. BACKGROUND The integration of intelligent technologies in surgical nursing education offers opportunities to enhance learning outcomes and address challenges in mastering complex topics. Knowledge graphs serve as a visual and interactive learning tool. It represents a novel approach to improving systematic thinking and enhancing knowledge retention in blended teaching models.This study explored nursing undergraduates' experiences with a knowledge graph platform in surgical nursing education, focusing on perceptions of its usefulness and ease of use, factors influencing engagement, and suggestions for improvement. AIM This study explored nursing undergraduates' experiences with a knowledge graph platform in surgical nursing education, focusing on perceptions of its usefulness and ease of use, factors influencing engagement, and suggestions for improvement.A qualitative descriptive study approach was employed to investigate the experiences of 13 nursing students. Semi-structured interviews were conducted after completing a surgical nursing course. The interviews were guided by the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology 2 (UTAUT2). Data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis to identify key themes related to knowledge graph use. METHODS A qualitative descriptive study approach was employed to investigate the experiences of 13 nursing students. Semi-structured interviews were conducted after completing a surgical nursing course. The interviews were guided by the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology 2 (UTAUT2). Data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis to identify key themes related to knowledge graph use.The analysis identified three main themes: (1) Developing conceptual clarity through knowledge integration, where knowledge graphs helped students build systematic thinking, discover learning pathways, and enhance post-class review efficiency; (2) Stimulating interest through enriched content, where enriched and well-organized content increased students' interest and enthusiasm for independent study; and (3) Navigating challenges and envisioning opportunities, where participants reported technical and access limitations, a need for richer content, and requests for clearer usage guidance. RESULTS The analysis identified three main themes: (1) Developing conceptual clarity through knowledge integration, where knowledge graphs helped students build systematic thinking, discover learning pathways, and enhance post-class review efficiency; (2) Stimulating interest through enriched content, where enriched and well-organized content increased students' interest and enthusiasm for independent study; and (3) Navigating challenges and envisioning opportunities, where participants reported technical and access limitations, a need for richer content, and requests for clearer usage guidance.Knowledge graphs offer innovative intelligent technology integration within blended nursing education. These tools cultivate systematic thinking, enhance surgical nursing knowledge and skill development, and enrich the comprehensive learning experience. Future studies should explore sustained educational outcomes, broaden technological capabilities, and examine cross-contextual adaptability. CONCLUSION Knowledge graphs offer innovative intelligent technology integration within blended nursing education. These tools cultivate systematic thinking, enhance surgical nursing knowledge and skill development, and enrich the comprehensive learning experience. Future studies should explore sustained educational outcomes, broaden technological capabilities, and examine cross-contextual adaptability.

Immersive virtual reality based on head-mounted display in medical education: a systematic review

Author: Zhang, Wei1; Ding, Ziyun1; Bakaev, Maxim2; Razumnikova, Olga3; Kludacz-Alessandri, Magdalena4; Wu, Jianjie51 School of Medicine and Health Management, Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Wuhan, China; Tongji Institute of Medical Education Research, Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Wuhan, China2 Department of Data Collection and Processing Systems, Novosibirsk State Technical University, Novosibirsk, Russia3 Department of Psychology and Pedagogy, Novosibirsk State Technical University, Novosibirsk, Russia4 College of Economics and Socia l Sciences, Warsaw University of Technology, Plock, Poland5 School of Software Engineering, Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Wuhan, China wujianjie@hust.edu.cn

Publication info: Zhang, Wei; Ding, Ziyun; Bakaev, Maxim; Razumnikova, Olga; Kludacz-Alessandri, Magdalena; et al. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/immersive-virtual-reality-based-on-head-mounted/docview/3271936488/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: Immersive virtual reality (IVR) based on head-mounted displays (HMD), can construct virtual learning environments for medical education. This study aims to explore the application and effectiveness of IVR in medical education. INTRODUCTION Immersive virtual reality (IVR) based on head-mounted displays (HMD), can construct virtual learning environments for medical education. This study aims to explore the application and effectiveness of IVR in medical education.This review followed the PRISMA guidelines and searched the databases of Web of Science, Springer Link, PubMed, IEEE Xplore, and Science Direct for controlled experimental studies published between January 1 2017 and October 1, 2025 on the application of IVR to medical education. METHODS This review followed the PRISMA guidelines and searched the databases of Web of Science, Springer Link, PubMed, IEEE Xplore, and Science Direct for controlled experimental studies published between January 1 2017 and October 1, 2025 on the application of IVR to medical education.36 studies satisfied the inclusion criteria. Among them 34 reported significantly better objective learning outcomes and 29 showed more positive subjective feedback. The findings suggest that IVR is particularly effective in areas such as clinical surgery training, anatomy education, medical skill development, and nursing education. IVR demonstrates long-term effects in medical knowledge acquirement. RESULTS 36 studies satisfied the inclusion criteria. Among them 34 reported significantly better objective learning outcomes and 29 showed more positive subjective feedback. The findings suggest that IVR is particularly effective in areas such as clinical surgery training, anatomy education, medical skill development, and nursing education. IVR demonstrates long-term effects in medical knowledge acquirement.The systematic review reveals that IVR is particularly effective in practice-based medical education. It highlights that VR demonstrates superior long-term knowledge retention and knowledge enhancement. A comprehensive evaluation of IVR use in medical education requires additional perspectives from teachers, and consideration from the dark side of IVR, i.e., technology-induced stress and time. Future IVR implementation in medical education calls for more efforts to address challenges in user adaptability, cost, privacy and regulatory compliance. CONCLUSIONS The systematic review reveals that IVR is particularly effective in practice-based medical education. It highlights that VR demonstrates superior long-term knowledge retention and knowledge enhancement. A comprehensive evaluation of IVR use in medical education requires additional perspectives from teachers, and consideration from the dark side of IVR, i.e., technology-induced stress and time. Future IVR implementation in medical education calls for more efforts to address challenges in user adaptability, cost, privacy and regulatory compliance.

Enhancing STEM Learning Through AI‐Driven Mind Mapping: A Study on the Educational Impact of Napkin AI on Student Outcomes and Knowledge Retention

Author: Truong, Vi Loi1    ; Nguyen, Thuong Hong Thi21 Department of Artificial Intelligence, FPT University, Can Tho, Vietnam2 Department of Software Engineering, FPT University, Can Tho, Vietnam

Publication info: Truong, Vi Loi; Nguyen, Thuong Hong Thi. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/enhancing-stem-learning-through-ai-driven-mind/docview/3275347516/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: This study examines the impact of Napkin AI, a generative artificial intelligence tool, on student learning outcomes and knowledge retention via creative mind mapping. The research model, which combines the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology 2 (UTAUT2) with the Information Adoption Model (IAM), comprises six principal independent variables: Social Influence, Learning Support Environment, Ease of Use, Perceived Benefit, Information Quality of Mind Mapping, and Usefulness of Mind Mapping. Mediating variables comprise Behavioral Intention to Use, Actual Use of Mind Mapping, and Cognitive Engagement in Mind Mapping, while Knowledge Retention and Learning Outcome serve as dependent variables. The study employed a quantitative approach with a sample of 570 Vietnamese university students majoring in STEM. Data analysis was conducted using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) with IBM SPSS 25 and AMOS 24. The model exhibited a satisfactory fit ( χ ²/ df  = 1.906, GFI = 0.889, CFI = 0.935, TLI = 0.929, RMSEA = 0.040, PCLOSE = 1.000), with all direct routes being statistically significant ( p  < 0.001 to p  = 0.037). The findings underscore the significance of user perception and involvement in improving the educational efficacy of AI‐driven mind mapping tools, providing practical implications for technology integration in higher education.
