1 INTRODUCTION
Serious digital games present a strong potential in raising awareness about sustainability and climate change. The consumption of digital games is part of popular culture in various countries. Currently, the digital gaming industry ranks second among entertainment businesses worldwide (ABRAGAMES, 2023). In Brazil, recent years have seen a shift in the percentage of game production by category. In 2020, entertainment games occupied the top spot with 36%, followed by educational games in second place with 35%. By 2022, this gap widened significantly, with the entertainment category rising to 58%, overshadowing the others. On the other hand, the educational category experienced a 50% decline, dropping to 17.5% (ABRAGAMES, 2023). This highlights the need to expand and deepen studies in the field of educational digital games to ensure this category grows again. Wals (2012) notes that introducing and developing new learning approaches focused on sustainability has proven to be a significant challenge for schools, universities, and businesses. In this context, serious digital games play a crucial role in education, integrating gaming elements with technical knowledge and entertainment simultaneously.
Climate change is considered the greatest global challenge today. The increasing concentration of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere has caused negative effects not only on the environment but also economically and socially. Rising sea levels and the growing frequency and intensity of extreme events such as hurricanes, floods, and prolonged droughts have resulted in deaths, population displacement, economic losses, and irreversible damage to biodiversity. This phenomenon tends to reduce water and food availability, among various other effects. Climate change affects all sectors of the economy, potentially reducing global GDP by around 14%. In poorer tropical regions, the losses may be even greater, possibly exceeding 20% (Wenz & Kuil, 2024).
Given this scenario, it is essential to develop effective methods to educate younger generations about environmental issues and encourage pro-environmental behaviors. Younger children are more receptive to new scientifically accurate models than older children (Kelemen & Diyanni, 2005), and their thinking is less constrained by worldview and cultural values (Stevenson et al., 2014). Lee et al. (2020) analyzed several studies and highlighted that younger children expressed greater concern about climate change and were more willing to act than older adolescents. Hence, there is a need to devise strategies to teach children and young people the importance of environmental issues.
Game-based learning is an increasingly popular approach in classrooms. Serious games can serve as effective and persuasive pedagogical tools to encourage pro-environmental behaviors among young people (Janakiman et al., 2021). One of the main characteristics of digital learning is interactivity (Zumbach et al., 2020). Games create a learning culture that incorporates specific interests students have, adaptive challenges, and continuous feedback to sustain ideal engagement and learning (Xu et al., 2022), alongside educational knowledge and awareness (Mattsson & Laike, 2022).
Serious games are designed to achieve a specific learning objective beyond entertainment. The game can be a powerful knowledge tool about urgent environmental issues, promoting education and raising awareness among younger generations (Lombada et al., 2021). According to Hamdan et al. (2023), teaching pro-environmental behaviors in the classroom through digital games promotes knowledge about sustainability issues and makes young people highly motivated to think about sustainable development strategies. Similarly, Mylonas et al. (2023) highlight the acute need to improve awareness at both individual and societal levels, especially among younger populations, about global climate change and sustainable development, addressing today's needs without compromising future generations.
2 METHODOLOGY
This Systematic Literature Review (SLR) aims to provide an updated overview of research and practical experiences involving serious digital games in formal education for youth up to 18 years old, and to identify gaps in their application in the context of sustainability and climate change from 2020 to 2024. To assist in conducting the study, research questions were defined. Thus, the main question is: How are serious digital games applied in formal education for youth up to 18 years old to promote sustainability and climate change learning, and what educational outcomes or gaps are reported? The secondary questions (SQ) were divided into two categories: gamification (SQ) and sustainability/climate change (SQ). These include SQ:G1: Do the studies describe game elements (objective, rules, challenges, and rewards)? SQ:G2: How many of these elements are present in each study? Sustainability and Climate Change (SQ:S): SQ:S1: How are the studies classified within environmental fields (sustainability, climate change, ecology)? SQ:S2: What environmental actions (e.g., prevention, adaptation, mitigation, preservation) are addressed? The choice of the age limit of 18 years aligns with the classification adopted by UNESCO and national education systems, which typically define formal basic education as encompassing early childhood through to secondary education. Furthermore, studies such as Lee et al. (2020) and Kelemen and Diyanni (2005) suggest that learners within this age group demonstrate heightened receptivity to environmental education and behavioral change.
2.1 SEARCH STRATEGY AND STUDY SELECTION
The literature search was conducted between May 20 and 24, 2024, using the following databases: Web of Science, Scopus, Science Direct - Elsevier, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, SciELO. These platforms were selected for their relevance to interdisciplinary research in education, digital technologies, and sustainability. Web of Science and Scopus offer broad coverage of peer-reviewed journals. IEEE and ACM specialize in computing and engineering education. Science Direct contains numerous education and sustainability publications, while SciELO ensures inclusion of Latin American research.
A predefined search string was applied to the Title, Abstract, and Keywords fields: ("serious game" OR "digital game") AND ("environmental education" OR "climate change" OR "sustainability"). Filters applied included: Document type articles and publication years 2020-2024. A total of 928 articles were retrieved. Duplicate entries were removed, and the remaining records were screened in two phases: title and abstract review and full-text evaluation. Each article was reviewed independently by two researchers using the Rayyan platform. Cohen's Kappa coefficient was calculated to assess inter-rater reliability, yielding a score of 0.82, indicating substantial agreement. Disagreements were resolved through discussion and consensus.
The first screening phase evaluated the titles and abstracts of the studies according to inclusion and exclusion criteria listed in Table 1. After this stage, 154 studies were selected for the next phase, which involved a full-text review. In both stages, each study was analyzed by two independent reviewers on the Rayyan platform (Ouzzani et al., 2016). Additionally, comments were added to facilitate transparency in decision-making, and studies classified as "maybe" were evaluated jointly by the reviewers.
In addition to content analysis, the methodological quality of the selected studies was assessed using PRISMA 2020 criteria, focusing on transparency in reporting systematic reviews. Although PRISMA is typically applied to medical research, its structured checklist is applicable to environmental education reviews, ensuring clarity and replicability.
2.2 DATA COLLECTION AND STUDY EVALUATION
The database comprised 40 studies, from which the following information was extracted: platform, inclusion criteria, year, author, title, publication language, journal, study objective, application location, educational level (age of youth), hypothesis or research question, type of game applied, relation to sustainability and/or climate change. In a second phase, specific information was extracted to answer the research questions of this review, according to the categories: gamification (SQ) and sustainability/climate change (SQ).
3 RESULTS
This section presents the results of the systematic literature review based on the 40 selected articles. The data are organized into five categories: database/platform use, geographical distribution, presence of game elements, classification by environmental theme, and type of environmental action addressed.
3.1 DATABASE UTILIZATION RATE
Concerning scientific studies on digital games in education and the sustainability and climate change axis, 40 studies were selected. In terms of the effective number of studies used in the database relative to the initial number retained from the platform, this is referred to as "utilization rate," i.e., the number included after the second stage divided by the number inserted (e.g., Science Direct: (13/500)·100 = 3%). The database was composed of six platforms, totaling 928 studies inserted in Rayyan (Figure 1).
The lowest percentages were for the Science Direct and Web of Science platforms, both at 3%. The highest utilization rate was from IEEE Xplore, with 29%. Thus, we can infer that either the topic may be too specific or niche, resulting in fewer published studies on Science Direct, or the platform may have limited coverage of certain fields or disciplines, not reflecting the full range of available research globally. A third possibility is that the academic audience publishing on this platform has little interest in the topic. A total of 100 studies were excluded due to duplication, with 38 from Science Direct, 59 from Web of Science, two from ACM Digital Library, and one from IEEE Xplore. The remaining excluded and included studies are subdivided into two stages - title and abstract evaluation, and full-text analysis (Figure 1).
3.2 GEOGRAPHICAL DISTRIBUTION OF STUDIES
In this review, we identified the locations where serious digital games described in the scientific studies on education, sustainability, and climate change were evaluated. These studies were classified by continent, as many applied the game in more than one country. In relation to the total (40 scientific studies), 43% of the studies were conducted in Europe, standing out from the rest (Figure 2A). This result is linked to the concern that European countries have with climate change and the financial incentives available through programs, such as the Support Fund for Videogames, financed by France. In South America, 18% of the studies were found, with six studies conducted in Brazil and one in Chile. Among the studies found in Brazil (Figure 2B), two were applied in schools in Santa Catarina (Florianópolis and Itajaí).
3.3 GAME ELEMENTS IN THE SELECTED STUDIES
Gamification has gained prominence as an effective tool in education, promoting student engagement and motivation. This concept involves applying game elements in nongaming contexts, making activities more attractive and engaging. According to Kapp (2012), gamification is defined as "the use of game mechanics, aesthetics, and game-based thinking to engage people, motivate actions, promote learning, and solve problems." This process involves creating challenges and rewards that encourage students to actively participate in the learning process.
Deterding et al. (2011) discuss how gamification, through game elements such as rules and rewards, can transform monotonous activities into engaging experiences, promoting greater participation and persistence among students. Other scholars also corroborate the effectiveness of gamification in education. Perrota et al. (2013) point out that gamification can foster students' intrinsic motivation, as games are voluntary activities that are particularly motivating.
The Flow Theory, proposed by Csikszentmihalyi and discussed by authors such as Saraiva (2021), highlights that games with certain elements can provide a state of complete concentration and absorption, facilitating deeper and more meaningful learning. Thus, we analyzed whether the studies presented game elements such as objectives, rules, challenges, and rewards described throughout the text (SQ), which are present in games that promote this state of flow.
In the context of gamification in digital games for sustainability education, Janakiraman et al. (2021) applied gamification to teach sustainability. This study examined how digital games, when played collaboratively or individually, can encourage pro-environmental behaviors among students. The game Enercities was used, where players had to build a sustainable city, balancing economic, social, and environmental aspects, making decisions about building locations, types of energy to use, and policies to implement to improve the city's sustainability, with well-defined rules.
In games like Climate Connected by Galeote et al. (2023) and EbA craft by Sena et al. (2023), clear rules and rewards play a crucial role in teaching sustainability, as these elements increase student engagement and reinforce learning through immediate feedback. While welldefined rules guide players in their actions, rewards provide a sense of progress and achievement. Therefore, we analyzed the number of game elements (objectives, rules, challenges, and rewards) presented in each study (SQ). These elements are essential for promoting motivation, engagement, and effectively encouraging pro-environmental behaviors. According to Figure 3, out of the 40 scientific articles in the database, 17 studies (42.5%) described four elements, meaning they presented the game's objective, rules, challenges, and rewards. Of the remaining 57.5%, 30% presented three elements, 15% one element, 7.5% two elements, and 5% did not describe any elements in the study text. It is worth noting that the analysis was based on the information present in the studies, which does not rule out the possibility that the game elements are described in other scientific articles and/or the platform where the games are found.
The application of typical game elements in educational contexts has proven effective in transforming learning activities that could be monotonous into dynamic and engaging experiences. This engagement is possible through mechanics that encourage student participation, not only through rewards but also to achieve deeper involvement, characterized by the state of Flow, where there is total immersion in the activity. The reviewed studies, including the games Enercities and Climate Connected, illustrate how clear rules and specific rewards can guide and motivate students, reinforcing pro-environmental behaviors and fostering meaningful learning about sustainability. The integration of such gamified elements proves to be a valuable tool for educators, aiming to promote a deeper and more lasting understanding of critical environmental issues.
3.4 ENVIRONMENTAL THEMES CLASSIFICATION
Among the 40 studies included in this review, 21 (52.5%) explicitly addressed environmental themes such as climate change, sustainability, and ecology. Studies related to climate change were the most prevalent (55%), reflecting its global relevance and alignment with the scientific and political agendas shaped by international frameworks such as the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC). This prevalence also corresponds with growing concern over the intensification of extreme climate events-including droughts, biodiversity loss, floods, and food insecurity-directly linked to anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions.
The second most represented category was sustainability (27%), a theme that has gained considerable visibility since the launch of the 2030 Agenda and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Sustainability is anchored in three interconnected pillars-environmental integrity, social equity, and economic viability-and is defined by the UN (1987) as meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations. Given this framing, it is not surprising that educational research increasingly investigates whether and how these global goals are being effectively integrated into learning environments.
Ecology accounted for 18% of the sample. Although definitions of ecology vary, it is broadly understood as the study of interactions between living organisms and their environments (PINTO-COELHO, 2009). The reviewed studies in this category primarily focused on biological relationships, particularly concerning fauna, and revealed persistent gaps in understanding these interactions under environmental stress. These gaps highlight the critical need to reinforce ecological literacy in basic education.
3.5 ENVIRONMENTAL ACTIONS ADDRESSED
To better understand how environmental themes were operationalized within the selected studies, each was also classified by the type of pro-environmental action it promoted- namely: prevention, preservation, adaptation, and mitigation (Figure 4).
* Prevention (25%): Focused on avoiding environmental degradation, these studies typically involved simulations requiring strategic decisions for energy conservation or waste reduction. For example, Enercities (Janakiraman et al., 2021) enabled players to design sustainable cities using green technologies and energy-efficient buildings.
* Preservation (15%): These games emphasized protecting natural ecosystems and raising awareness about biodiversity, such as marine and freshwater environments (Lombada et al., 2021; Veronica & Calvano, 2020).
* Mitigation (20%): Centered on reducing human environmental impact, this category included games like Climate Connected: Outbreak (Galeote et al., 2023), which linked climate mechanisms with human and animal health. Other games, like Sustainability at Play (Sá et al., 2023), invited users to reflect on the ecological footprint of daily decisions.
* Adaptation (17%): Addressed the capacity to build resilience to climate change, particularly in vulnerable territories. EbAcraft (Sena et al., 2023) and Climate Smart (Hügel & Davies, 2024) are notable examples, engaging students and communities in scenario planning and ecosystem-based strategies.
* Combined Actions (20%): A significant portion of the studies integrated multiple environmental actions into a single experience. These multidimensional approaches- seen in games like Climate Adaptation Game-are particularly promising for fostering systems thinking, long-term environmental awareness, and behavioral change.
The classification of environmental actions revealed a predominance of studies focused on preventive and mitigation strategies, with a growing number integrating multiple approaches. This diversity of actions indicates that serious digital games are not only conveying environmental content but are also being designed with the intent to foster behavioral change and critical thinking in young learners. The concentration of studies on climate change and sustainability, in particular, underscores the relevance of these themes within educational research agendas. These findings form the basis for the discussion that follows, where we critically examine how such games contribute to environmental education outcomes, the gaps that persist, and the opportunities for enhancing their pedagogical impact.
Notably, studies categorized as "combined actions" addressed multiple sustainability strategies simultaneously. Games like Climate Adaptation Game and Sustainability at Play exemplify the integration of environmental actions in holistic learning experiences. These multidimensional approaches are particularly promising for promoting systems thinking and behavioral change.
4 DISCUSSION
This review highlights the growing relevance of serious digital games as pedagogical tools for sustainability and climate change education among youth. The findings suggest that while climate change and sustainability are well represented in the reviewed studies, the overall methodological and analytical depth of these investigations remains uneven. In particular, although many studies address relevant environmental actions (e.g., prevention, mitigation), a smaller subset applies rigorous frameworks to assess learning outcomes or long-term behavioral change.
One of the most significant contributions of this review is the identification of how game elements-such as objectives, rules, challenges, and rewards-are inconsistently reported across studies. This inconsistency hinders the replication of game-based interventions and complicates comparative analysis. The absence of clear descriptions of game mechanics also weakens the evaluation of pedagogical effectiveness. It is therefore recommended that future studies adopt standardized reporting practices, such as integrating PRISMA guidelines or gamebased learning frameworks, to enhance transparency and replicability.
The dominance of studies focused on climate change aligns with global scientific consensus and urgency. However, despite the high frequency of climate-themed games, many of them do not explore the complexity of climate systems or foster systems thinking. Games that incorporate multi-layered decision-making and simulate real-world trade-offs, such as those promoting combined environmental actions, appear to hold the greatest potential for impactful learning. These games not only convey knowledge but engage learners in developing critical thinking and ecological reasoning.
Ecology and biodiversity, while underrepresented, offer fertile ground for future research-especially considering the increasing need to understand human-nature interactions. Similarly, the integration of indigenous knowledge systems and local cultural narratives in game content remains an open opportunity for enriching both content relevance and learner engagement.
From a policy and curriculum perspective, the findings support the inclusion of gamebased methodologies in environmental education at all school levels. National education policies, such as Brazil's National Environmental Education Policy (Law 9.795/1999), and global initiatives like the 2030 Agenda, provide fertile institutional ground for such innovation. Yet, institutional support must be matched with teacher training, digital infrastructure, and research investment.
5 FINAL CONSIDERATIONS
Serious digital games represent a promising pedagogical innovation for environmental education. When well-designed and critically implemented, they have the potential not only to transmit knowledge but to cultivate ecological awareness, decision-making skills, and longterm pro-environmental behavior. For these reasons, educational policymakers, researchers, and practitioners should consider serious games not as peripheral tools, but as central components of sustainability education strategies for the next generation.
Future research should prioritize longitudinal studies assessing long-term behavioral impacts, comparative studies between traditional and game-based learning, and evaluations of learner engagement across diverse sociocultural contexts. Integrating mixed methods approaches can also enhance the robustness of findings.

Transforming education through artificial intelligence and immersive technologies: enhancing learning experiences

Author: Wang, Dan1; Huang, Xi2    1 School of Foreign Studies, East China University of Political Science and Law, Shanghai, People’s Republic of China2 School of Education, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, People’s Republic of China

Publication info: Wang, Dan; Huang, Xi. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/transforming-education-through-artificial/docview/3258005730/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and immersive technologies, such as virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR), is reshaping the educational landscape by offering personalized, interactive, and engaging learning experiences. This systematic literature review aims to examine the transformative effects of AI and immersive technologies on educational practices. The review encompasses 42 peer-reviewed articles published between 2011 and 2023, employing a rigorous search and screening process using the Scopus database, following PRISMA guidelines. The findings highlight how AI enhances learning environments by tailoring educational content to individual student needs, thereby improving motivation, engagement, and knowledge retention. Additionally, VR and AR technologies enable educators to create immersive learning experiences that simulate real-world scenarios, fostering the development of practical skills and deeper understanding of complex concepts. However, challenges such as digital literacy, data privacy, and the need for significant infrastructure and training investments remain critical barriers. This review underscores the potential of AI and immersive technologies to revolutionize education, while emphasizing the importance of addressing these challenges to maximize their positive impact on learning outcomes.

Edge‐AI Driven Gamification in Engineering Education for Improving Student Engagement

Author: Singh, Kiran Deep1    ; Singh, Prabh Deep2    1 Chitkara University Institute of Engineering and Technology, Chitkara University, Rajpura, Punjab, India2 Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Graphic Era (Deemed to be University), Dehradun, Uttarakhand, India

Publication info: Singh, Kiran Deep; Singh, Prabh Deep. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/edge-ai-driven-gamification-engineering-education/docview/3254342710/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: Improving student engagement in engineering education is crucial for better learning outcomes. Engineering education integrates the latest technologies with gamification that fosters student engagement in innovative learning. Gamification involves incorporating game design elements, making learning more interactive and motivating. This paper explores gamification to transform engineering education, improving students' participation, understanding, and overall learning outcomes. Combining Edge computing with artificial intelligence will enhance the gamification of education by addressing two primary challenges: real‐time interaction and personalized service. An Edge‐AI‐driven gamification framework is proposed for improving student engagement through interactive tools like educational games, quizzes, and competitive learning environments. An algorithm related to the Edge‐AI Gamification Optimizer is proposed to improve the overall performance. Results show that the proposed framework improves student engagement by nearly 51%, performance by 30.7% and reduces cognitive load by 57%. A comparative study with traditional learning approaches shows that AI‐based gamification significantly enhances knowledge retention, boosts collaborative learning, increases student motivation, and, through statistical analysis, demonstrates a validated increase in student engagement over conventional methods. Future studies will investigate the extendability of this framework to different fields of engineering and learning environments. The proposed framework has the potential to transform educational practices by providing personalized, interactive, and motivating learning experiences, leading to better educational outcomes. Future research could explore broader applications and long‐term impacts of Edge‐AI‐driven gamification.

Teacher Perceptions of Gamification's Influence on Student Engagement and Learning in Nigerian Primary Schools

Author: Ikpat, Ngeri Anita1    1 Management Information System, National Open University, Lagos, Nigeria

Publication info: Ikpat, Ngeri Anita. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/teacher-perceptions-gamifications-influence-on/docview/3243266691/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: This study investigated teachers' perceptions on the impact of gamification on student engagement and learning outcomes in Nigerian primary schools, aiming to bridge the gap between traditional teaching methods and contemporary learner needs. A mixed‐methods approach was utilised, involving quantitative and qualitative data collection through an online survey distributed to 82 primary school teachers. The results revealed that most of the respondents incorporated gamification techniques weekly, with badges and points being the most frequently used elements. Gamification was most commonly applied in Maths, followed by English, Science and other subjects. Teachers perceived significant positive impacts on academic achievement, student participation and knowledge retention, though challenges such as lack of technological resources, curriculum alignment, scepticism from stakeholders, and insufficient teacher training were highlighted. Thematic analysis of qualitative data identified themes related to enhancing problem‐solving abilities, catering to diverse learning styles and fostering healthy competition. Despite challenges, the study found unanimous support for gamification, with teachers willing to undergo further professional development. The findings suggest that gamification holds promise for transforming educational environments in Nigerian primary schools by promoting active engagement, motivation, and improved academic performance, although addressing technological and training barriers remains crucial.

Evaluation of virtual training delivery for health information systems implementation in Canada: A qualitative study

Author: Karsan, Inaara1    ; Hasan, Hafsa1    ; Jeyakumar, Tharshini1    ; Ambata-Villaneuva, Sharon1; Fur, Katharine1; Hanley, Ivanka1; McClure, Sarah1; Omar, Maram1; Sheriff, Tamee1; Wiljer, David2    1 University Health Network, Canada2 University Health Network, Canada; University of Toronto, Canada

Publication info: Karsan, Inaara; Hasan, Hafsa; Jeyakumar, Tharshini; Ambata-Villaneuva, Sharon; Fur, Katharine; et al. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/evaluation-virtual-training-delivery-health/docview/3131499407/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: As health information systems (HIS) become a critical part of patient care, it is crucial to build an effective education strategy that facilitates the adoption and sustained use of these systems. The COVID-19 pandemic (2019-2023) has contributed to the rapid shift in virtual education and training for healthcare staff. INTRODUCTION As health information systems (HIS) become a critical part of patient care, it is crucial to build an effective education strategy that facilitates the adoption and sustained use of these systems. The COVID-19 pandemic (2019-2023) has contributed to the rapid shift in virtual education and training for healthcare staff.We sought to evaluate the efficacy and long-term sustainability of virtual training for using a HIS by examining opportunities and challenges. OBJECTIVE We sought to evaluate the efficacy and long-term sustainability of virtual training for using a HIS by examining opportunities and challenges.An exploratory, multimethods study was conducted with staff who had taken part in a virtual HIS training program as part of the clinical transformation journey at a large academic health science center in Canada. The study was guided by the Accelerating the Learning Cycle framework. Data were collected through pre- and post-training surveys, as well as semi-structured interviews. An iterative, inductive, constant comparative analysis approach, outlined by Braun and Clarke, was taken to thematically analyse the data. METHOD An exploratory, multimethods study was conducted with staff who had taken part in a virtual HIS training program as part of the clinical transformation journey at a large academic health science center in Canada. The study was guided by the Accelerating the Learning Cycle framework. Data were collected through pre- and post-training surveys, as well as semi-structured interviews. An iterative, inductive, constant comparative analysis approach, outlined by Braun and Clarke, was taken to thematically analyse the data.Of the 33 participants in this study, 13 were educational champions, and 20 were end-users. The pre- and post-training surveys yielded a total of 1479 responses in both groups. Three prominent themes emerged from this study: (1) fostering dynamic facilitation techniques to cultivate an inclusive culture and adapt to diverse learning needs; (2) integrating practical learning activities that contribute to knowledge retention; and (3) ensuring training resources are accessible and consistent for an optimal training experience. RESULTS Of the 33 participants in this study, 13 were educational champions, and 20 were end-users. The pre- and post-training surveys yielded a total of 1479 responses in both groups. Three prominent themes emerged from this study: (1) fostering dynamic facilitation techniques to cultivate an inclusive culture and adapt to diverse learning needs; (2) integrating practical learning activities that contribute to knowledge retention; and (3) ensuring training resources are accessible and consistent for an optimal training experience.As HIS continue to be part of the transformation of the healthcare ecosystem, education is vital in preparing healthcare providers to perform their clinical tasks and effectively use these technologies. Findings from this study can be used to inform the development of virtual training that is inclusive and addresses the needs of care providers. CONCLUSION As HIS continue to be part of the transformation of the healthcare ecosystem, education is vital in preparing healthcare providers to perform their clinical tasks and effectively use these technologies. Findings from this study can be used to inform the development of virtual training that is inclusive and addresses the needs of care providers.

Application of Artificial Intelligence and Virtual Reality in Soft Skills Training with Modeled Personality

Author: Budnarows ki Dawid1    ; Jereczek Dawid2; Detka Kalina3; Wieczorek Iwona41 Department of Marine Telecommunications, Gdynia Maritime University, 81-225 Gdynia, Poland2 Department of Business Informatics, University of Gdansk, 81-864 Sopot, Poland; dawid.jereczek@ug.edu.pl3 Department of Power Electronics, Gdynia Maritime University, 81-225 Gdynia, Poland; k.detka@we.umg.edu.pl4 E-learning.pl, Konsorcjum Doradczo-Szkoleniowe S.A., 02-235 Warsaw, Poland; iwona.wieczorek@e-learning.pl

Publication info: Budnarowski Dawid; Jereczek Dawid; Detka Kalina; Wieczorek Iwona. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/application-artificial-intelligence-virtual/docview/3243982209/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: Across the world, people are exploring fields where AI (Artificial Intelligence) and VR (Virtual Reality) can be harnessed to unlock new possibilities and drive innovation. The aim of this article was to review the potential and assess the feasibility of using virtual reality technology in soft skills training (including people management, stress management, communication, conflict resolution, and sales). A project was developed featuring an application that utilizes virtual reality and artificial intelligence to facilitate communication with a virtual coach. The application operates on Meta Quest 3 virtual reality goggles (Meta Platforms, Inc., Menlo Park, CA, USA). Tests of the presented solution confirm market trends, highlighting the potential for achieving positive training outcomes through immersive technologies. The conclusions outline opportunities for improvement and further development of such solutions. This study applied a quasi-experimental model with pretest, posttest, and four-week follow-up measurements. The effectiveness of VR training was evaluated using a knowledge test (0–100%), a self-assessment scale of soft skills (Likert 1–5), expert behavior observation (0–10 scale), and posttraining surveys. The VR group demonstrated significantly higher gains in knowledge, soft skills, and behavioral performance with knowledge retention reaching 89% after four weeks. These results confirm the effectiveness of immersive VR training and its alignment with current market trends in innovative professional development.
