1 INTRODUCTION
In recent years, educational innovation has been increasingly driven by the integration of digital tools and playful strategies, particularly in higher education. This shift reflects the need to adapt teaching methodologies to the preferences and learning styles of a new generation of students, characterized by their familiarity with technology and preference for interactive, engaging experiences. Chemistry education, especially in foundational courses like General Chemistry I, often presents unique challenges, including abstract concepts, complex problem-solving requirements, and the need to relate theoretical knowledge to practical applications. These challenges frequently result in low student motivation, high dropout rates, and suboptimal academic performance.
The potential of playful learning and gamification to address these challenges has been well-documented in the literature. Playful learning leverages enjoyment, interaction, and curiosity to foster engagement, while gamification applies game design elements-such as rewards, competition, and progression mechanics-to non-game contexts, including education (Calderón et al., 2024; Czakóová, 2019). Together, these approaches provide a framework for creating immersive, motivational learning environments that not only enhance cognitive outcomes but also promote positive emotional and attitudinal changes in learners.
Mobile devices, which are integral to students' daily lives, offer a versatile platform for implementing playful learning strategies that promote dynamic and personalized learning experiences. Their accessibility and interactivity provide an opportunity to meet the evolving demands of higher education. This study examines whether playful strategies, delivered through mobile devices, can significantly improve academic performance in General Chemistry I, a course known for its abstract concepts and complex problem-solving, which many STEM students find challenging.
Although research on the use of playful learning in chemistry remains limited, this study aims to fill two key gaps: first, the effectiveness of playful strategies in chemistry education, and second, the role of mobile devices in supporting these strategies. By exploring these aspects, the research seeks to offer actionable insights into enhancing student outcomes in STEM disciplines.
The general objective of this study is to analyze whether the use of playful strategies via mobile devices positively impacts the academic performance of students in General Chemistry I. Specifically, the study aims to design, implement, and evaluate a didactic intervention for chemistry learning based on playful strategies using mobile devices. Additionally, the study will assess the effectiveness of these playful strategies in improving students' academic performance in the course.
The general hypothesis posits that the use of playful strategies through mobile devices will significantly enhance students' academic performance in General Chemistry I. More specifically, it is hypothesized that a didactic intervention incorporating playful strategies and mobile devices can be successfully designed, implemented, and evaluated. Furthermore, it is expected that students in the experimental group will show a significant improvement in their academic performance compared to those in the control group.
Through these objectives and hypotheses, the study aims to provide empirical evidence on how innovative teaching methods can address the challenges faced in STEM education. The findings will contribute to educational innovation, offering valuable insights and resources for designing effective teaching interventions in higher education.
2 THEORETICAL FRAMEWORK
The theoretical framework in a study comprises a critical and organized analysis of the literature relevant to the topic, providing a theoretical contextualization and defining the key concepts. It must comprehensively contain theories, models and previous research, identifying gaps, contradictions and consensuses in the literature that are important for the focus of the work being developed.
The use of playful strategies and digital tools in education is supported by various theories and models that emphasize the importance of engagement, motivation, and interaction in the learning process (Ballatore & Tabacco, 2024; Playfoot, 2016; Playfoot et al., 2017). This section provides a critical and organized review of the literature, highlighting the theoretical foundations, relevant models, and previous research that underpin the focus of this study.
2.1 PLAYFUL LEARNING AND GAMIFICATION IN EDUCATION
Playful learning is grounded in constructivist and experiential learning theories (Ahmed & Sutton, 2017; Despeisse, 2018; Tsang et al., 2024; Usman et al., 2023) which emphasize the active role of learners in constructing knowledge through meaningful and engaging experiences. Playful learning incorporates game-like elements into educational contexts, promoting curiosity, exploration, and enjoyment as central components of the learning process. It aligns with recent literature research (Ilbeigi et al., 2024; Massad, 2024; Putra & Suhaimi, 2024; Zhang, 2024), which underscores the importance of interaction and social dynamics in fostering cognitive development.
Gamification, a specific application of playful learning, refers to the use of game design elements-such as points, badges, leaderboards, and challenges-in non-game contexts, including education (Alcaraz et al., 2019; Behl et al., 2024; Salleh et al., 2024; Stadnicka & Deif, 2019). This approach seeks to harness the motivational aspects of games to increase student engagement and participation. Gamification positively influences learning outcomes by enhancing motivation, satisfaction, and performance, particularly in STEM disciplines (Flores-Nicolás & Reyes, 2022; Forndran & Zacharias, 2019; Halvorsen et al., 2019; Indriasari et al., 2020).
2.2 MOBILE DEVICES AND DIGITAL TOOLS IN EDUCATION
The integration of mobile devices into educational practices is supported by the theory of mobile learning (m-learning), which emphasizes the flexibility, accessibility, and contextual relevance of mobile technology. Mobile devices enable personalized, on-the-go learning experiences, fostering autonomy and adaptability in students (Candel & Colmenero, 2022; Choi-Lundberg et al., 2023; Maev & Zhiltsov, 2021; Martínez et al., 2016). It highlights that m-learning enhances interaction, collaboration, and real-time feedback, making it a valuable tool for addressing diverse learning needs.
Previous research has demonstrated the effectiveness of mobile-based learning in improving academic performance across various disciplines. In this context, the scientific literature underscores the potential of mobile devices to transform traditional educational practices, particularly when integrated with gamified and playful strategies (Elsherbiny & Al Maamari, 2021; Jacobs et al., 2023; Lytvynov et al., 2022; Terzieva, 2019).
2.3 CHEMISTRY EDUCATION AND INNOVATIVE METHODOLOGIES
Chemistry education often presents unique challenges, including abstract concepts, complex problem-solving, and the need for practical application of theoretical knowledge. Traditional teaching methods, such as lectures and rote memorization, are often insufficient to address these challenges (Alberto et al., 2024; Alwassil et al., 2024; Marín et al., 2020). Instead, innovative methodologies that incorporate interactive and immersive elements have been shown to enhance student engagement and understanding.
Playful and gamified strategies have gained prominence in chemistry education as effective tools for improving student motivation and learning outcomes (Guerrero et al., 2012; Hanson et al., 2014; Molina & Fernandez, 2010; Sultanova et al., 2021). These approaches leverage the engaging and interactive nature of games to address the challenges often associated with teaching abstract and complex chemistry concepts.
Research indicates that gamification in chemistry classrooms fosters a deeper understanding of theoretical and practical aspects by creating a dynamic and participatory learning environment (Janstová et al., 2013; Miranda et al., 2023; Ramos & Condotta, 2024). For instance, incorporating game elements such as challenges, rewards, and storytelling has been shown to enhance students' ability to grasp difficult topics. Similarly, game-based learning environments, which immerse students in problem-solving scenarios, not only improve critical thinking skills but also help them develop strategies for real-world applications of chemistry (López et al., 2015; Monclús et al., 2019; Sugano & Nabua, 2020). Such methodologies also promote collaboration and communication among peers, further enriching the learning experience. These findings highlight the transformative potential of playful and gamified strategies in making chemistry education more effective and engaging for students.
2.4 GAPS, CONTRADICTIONS, AND CONSENSUSES
Despite the growing body of literature supporting playful and gamified learning, several gaps and contradictions remain. While many studies report positive outcomes, others suggest that the effectiveness of these methodologies may vary depending on factors such as the subject matter, student demographics, and implementation quality (Leou et al., 2006; Martín-Fernández et al., 2016; Pizarro, 2018; Wong et al., 2021). Additionally, there is limited research on the application of these strategies in chemistry education, particularly in higher education contexts.
A consensus exists on the potential of digital tools and playful strategies to enhance motivation and engagement. However, there is a need for more rigorous, context-specific studies to examine their impact on academic performance, particularly in STEM fields (Cardenas et al., 2022; Hou, 2013; Kovacs et al., 2019a; Morton & Colbert-Getz, 2017). This research aims to address these gaps by exploring the integration of playful strategies and mobile devices in General Chemistry I courses, contributing to the growing body of knowledge on innovative teaching methodologies.
In summary, the theoretical framework of this study is rooted in constructivist learning theories, gamification, and mobile learning. By leveraging these theoretical foundations, this research seeks to provide empirical evidence on the effectiveness of playful and technology-enhanced learning in improving academic performance in chemistry education.
3 METHODOLOGY
3.1 PARTICIPANTS
This study used a quasi-experimental design to assess the impact of playful strategies combined with digital tools on the academic performance of General Chemistry I students. Conducted during the 2022-2023 academic year at the Central University of Ecuador, the sample consisted of 89 first-semester students from two sections (A and B). Section B (experimental group) and Section A (control group) were randomly selected. The majority of participants were female (65.2%), with males (33.7%) and a small proportion identifying as gender-diverse (1.1%). The average age was 19.7 years (SD = 1.9). This distribution ensured balanced conditions for evaluating the intervention's effectiveness.
3.2 MEASURES
Two instruments were employed:
The methodology section outlines the procedures undertaken in this study, ensuring transparency, replicability, and reliability. This includes the type of study, sample selection, methods of data collection and analysis, ethical considerations, and limitations. Below, the measures applied for data collection and intervention design are described in detail.
The instruments used in this study were selected and developed based on their relevance. To ensure the rigor of the process, all tools underwent expert evaluation and pilot testing with students at the same educational level, focusing on clarity and understanding.
To measure performance in the four units of the General Chemistry I course, two concept questionnaires were used: the pretest and the posttest. Both instruments consisted of 90 items organized according to the course units, assessing theoretical knowledge, technical vocabulary management, and the application of chemical concepts. The pretest evaluated initial knowledge before taking the course, using single-choice, multiple-choice, matching, completion, and true/false questions, while the posttest, applied after completing the course, maintained the same format and included additional questions on sequencing and short-answer responses, focusing on the ability to apply acquired knowledge.
The intervention aimed to improve academic performance in General Chemistry I by integrating playful activities, gamification, and mobile device use. The intervention followed a structured timeline, implemented in three stages: initial (consent and baseline), implementation (application of strategies), and evaluation (posttest and outcome assessment).
3.4 PROCEDURE
In the first stage, the experimental group was randomly selected, and informed consent was obtained. Pre-questionnaires on playful strategies, internet usage, and chemistry concepts were administered to both groups. Playful strategies were designed in collaboration with students, tailored to their characteristics, and aligned with course objectives. In the second stage, playful activities were implemented during the reinforcement phase, focusing on reviewing and consolidating content before assessments, with support from available equipment and materials. The activities were structured in three phases: the first focused on individual work to reinforce concepts; the second promoted collaborative learning through group discussions and problem-solving; and the third involved a gamified tournament to apply learning in a competitive, dynamic setting, using digital tools that provided real-time feedback.
3.5 DATA DESIGN AND ANALYSIS
To assess the effectiveness of the methodological proposal integrated into the chemistry learning process of students enrolled in the General Chemistry I course, a quasi-experimental design with pretest and posttest measurements and a control group was employed. The data analysis was carried out using the General Linear Model (GLM) for repeated measures. For this, the pretest and posttest scores of the evaluated variables were considered as within-subjects factors, while the between-subjects factor was the group assignment, either control or experimental.
The data analysis and graphical representation were conducted using the SPSS v.22 software, licensed to the University of Alicante. This approach allowed for a detailed comparison of the changes in the students' learning outcomes and the evaluation of the impact of the proposed gamified methodology on their understanding of chemistry.
4 RESULTS AND DISCUSSIONS
The objectives set for this research have been achieved, as evidenced by the significant improvement in the academic performance of the experimental group following the methodological intervention. Participants in the experimental group demonstrated notable progress in their performance in General Chemistry I, as reflected in the scores obtained on the posttest knowledge (please, see table 2).
The improvement was significant in two of the four units of the course: Unit III, which focuses on the periodic table, and Unit IV, which covers inorganic chemical nomenclature. Among these, Unit IV stood out for its complexity, as previously noted by students from earlier cohorts. These results underscore the importance of incorporating playful strategies into educational practices, demonstrating their effectiveness in achieving both pedagogical and academic objectives. This was evident even in units traditionally considered more challenging for students.
The quantitative analysis of academic performance provided an objective evaluation of the program's effectiveness, supporting its value as a formal educational approach. Additionally, the findings highlight the potential of rigorous pedagogical interventions when working with adult learners in higher education settings. By expanding the application of playful strategies to a wider age range, this research emphasizes the intrinsic value of playful activities as a universal human quality that can enhance learning at any stage of life.
The findings align with recent scientific literature, suggesting that with careful planning and effective implementation, educational programs incorporating playful strategies and gamification can yield positive learning outcomes (Alwassil et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2024; Ramos & Condotta, 2024; Sultanova et al., 2021). The alignment between the program's implementation and its educational objectives, as well as the adherence to gamification principles, was crucial for the achievement of the set goals.
A clear connection was observed between the learning results and the strength of the playful strategies used. Adjustments made to the strategies in later units, based on feedback from earlier ones, played a significant role in meeting course objectives. These results highlight the importance of a structured and reflective approach when integrating playful activities into education, emphasizing the need for careful planning, precision, and a clear distinction between gamification and other game-based methodologies.
The planning and implementation of playful strategies is an ongoing learning process that improves with experience and reflection. While the first two units showed limited improvements in academic performance, the efforts made during this phase were still valuable in shaping the overall teaching and learning dynamics. This indicates that even early challenges contribute to the learning process, laying the groundwork for the further development of playful teaching methods, in line with other research (Alvarez-Corral et al., 2010; de Souza et al., 2019; Leou et al., 2006; Martín-Fernández et al., 2016; Pizarro, 2018). Continuous reflection and feedback from participants provide crucial insights for refining and enhancing future implementations.
The intervention program also highlights the potential to redefine the learning process itself as an innate human quality that develops naturally through curiosity and exploration. By creating comfortable and engaging environments, the program encourages interaction and collaboration among learners, fostering values such as empathy, solidarity, and friendship. These are just a few of the many benefits that playful learning offers, enhancing both academic and personal growth, in line with other studies (Hanson et al., 2014; Jaramillo et al., 2024; Perminov et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2021).
The program's focus on play and games fosters key cognitive processes such as attention, memory, and creativity, leading to richer, more meaningful learning experiences. It also helps students overcome common obstacles such as anxiety, mental blocks, and feelings of failure, which can impede academic success. Moreover, playful strategies can address broader social challenges, including violence and school disengagement, by offering students constructive outlets for negative emotions, thereby improving their overall performance.
Incorporating ICT tools in the classroom caters to the digital preferences and needs of today's students (Castro & Andrade, 2011; Crivellaro et al., 2015; Pizarro, 2018; Yusuf et al., 2017). This not only makes the learning experience more engaging and relevant but also allows for greater flexibility in teaching. By removing barriers related to time, space, and geography, these tools support personalized and inclusive learning.
The use of Interactive Groups further strengthens the inclusivity of the program, promoting meaningful learning through interaction in equal and diverse settings. This approach enhances cognitive development and values such as tolerance, fostering deeper engagement among students and other educational stakeholders.
Teacher involvement in playful activities nurtures positive relationships with students, as these activities encourage spontaneous expressions of joy and empathy. This connection enhances students' self-esteem, social skills, and academic performance (Kovacs et al., 2019a; Sugano & Nabua, 2020; Sultanova et al., 2021; Yoel & Dori, 2022). It also allows teachers to better understand their students' academic and emotional needs, which may not always be visible in conventional classes.
Collaborating with students to design playful strategies also increases creativity and broadens the use of digital tools, helping bridge generational gaps and enriching the learning process. This collaborative effort benefits both students and teachers, enhancing their digital competencies and fostering a mutually supportive learning environment (de Souza et al., 2019; Monclús et al., 2019; Obada et al., 2023; Ortuzar et al., 2019).
The thoughtful design of playful activities ensures they align with the desired educational outcomes, preventing the inclusion of activities that may be entertaining but lack educational value. Each activity is carefully chosen to serve a pedagogical purpose, contributing to the emotional, intellectual, and social development of students (Alvarez-Corral et al., 2010; Jaña et al., 2015; Kovacs et al., 2019b; Morton & Colbert-Getz, 2017).
Moreover, the program emphasizes intrinsic motivation, recognizing its essential role in fostering meaningful and satisfying learning experiences. While extrinsic motivation is considered, the primary focus is on motivating students to engage with the content in a way that supports both their academic and personal growth.
However, the intervention program had some limitations, including limited impact on the first two units due to the short implementation time and initial design of the activities. Despite this, the groundwork provides valuable insights for future interventions. The reliance on digital tools also posed challenges in schools with limited resources, although their potential for engagement was evident. The small sample size restricted the generalizability of the findings, and future studies should include larger, diverse samples to better assess scalability. Other factors, such as student motivation, were not considered and should be addressed in future research. Additionally, the limited application of playful strategies, primarily in the reinforcement phase, may have hindered their full potential; extending these strategies throughout the entire course could enhance the learning experience. Despite these limitations, the program showed promise, and future research will refine these approaches for greater impact.
5 CONCLUSION
In conclusion, the proposed program demonstrated positive effects on students' academic performance in General Chemistry I, particularly in enhancing the learning process, despite not showing significant results across all units. The integration of playful strategies into higher education underscores the value of play in fostering engagement and learning, confirming that these approaches are beneficial across all educational levels and for individuals of various ages. The versatility of gamification, when combined with other innovative teaching methods, emerged as an effective tool for improving student engagement and learning outcomes. However, the success of these strategies hinges on the dedication, expertise, and adaptability of educators, who play a pivotal role in designing and leading activities aligned with educational objectives. This study highlights the importance of further expanding playful strategies across the curriculum to enhance their effectiveness, suggesting significant potential for future research and application.

From Surface to Deep Learning: Gamified Mobile Education for Subcutaneous and Intramuscular Injection Skills

Author: Tamer, Zeynep1    ; Kavuran, Esin1    1 Atatürk University, Department of Nursing Fundamentals, Faculty of Nursing, Erzurum, Turkey (GRID:grid.411445.1) (ISNI:0000 0001 0775 759X)

Publication info: Tamer, Zeynep; Kavuran, Esin. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/surface-deep-learning-gamified-mobile-education/docview/3259372473/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: The aim of this study was to investigate the effect of a game-based mobile application on nursing students’ skills in administering subcutaneous (SC) and intramuscular (IM) injections. Nursing education traditionally involves both theoretical and practical components. With the advent of digital technologies, innovative methods such as game-based learning have been introduced to enhance practical skills and knowledge retention in nursing education. This study explores the use of a mobile application designed to improve students’ competence in SC and IM drug administration. This was an experimental study conducted during the 2021–2022 academic year. It involved a study group of 64 students who received training through a simulation game system and a control group of 65 students who underwent traditional training methods. Data were collected using the Self-Demonstration Form, the Study Process Questionnaire, and the Skills Performance List for Subcutaneous and Intramuscular Administration. The study focused on assessing the impact of game-based learning on students’ performance and learning approaches. The study group showed significantly greater improvements in learning approaches and medication administration skills compared to the control group. Deep learning scores increased from 31.39 ± 6.23 to 45.05 ± 5.46 in the study group, versus 31.78 ± 5.68 to 37.02 ± 4.17 in the control group ( p  < 0.01). SC and IM administration scores improved significantly in the study group (SC: 22.50 ± 15.46 to 42.45 ± 11.66, p  = 0.015; IM: 27.75 ± 15.98 to 59.45 ± 12.95, p  < 0.001) compared to the control group. Scenario-based analyses also showed significant performance gains in the study group across all scenarios ( p  < 0.05). The HEM-SC-IM game-based mobile application proved effective in improving nursing students’ skills in administering SC and IM injections. The interactive and engaging nature of game-based learning provides a valuable educational experience, promoting deeper understanding and practical skills development. This study supports the integration of educational technology in nursing curricula to enhance learning outcomes.

The Role of Artificial intelligence in Medical training, with its Applicability, Efficiency, Potential, and Challenges among Preclinical Students

Author: Nwe, Tin Moe1; Shamshol, Nur Amni Husna1; Jaafar, Nurul Najwa1; Syahruddin, Syazril Hafiy1; Yusaini, Tariq Ahmad1; Saha'Arif, Tuan Fatma Nadhirah Tuan; Lwin, Soe; Yee, Khin Than; Yi, Myat San; Latt, Swe Swe1 Faculty of Medicine, Royal College of Medicine Perak, Universiti Kuala Lumpur, Ipoh, Per ak, Malaysia

Publication info: Nwe, Tin Moe; Shamshol, Nur Amni Husna; Jaafar, Nurul Najwa; Syahruddin, Syazril Hafiy; Yusaini, Tariq Ahmad; et al. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/role-artificial-intelligence-medical-training/docview/3242363481/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: Introduction: Artificial intelligence (AI) is revolutionizing medical education by enhancing learning experiences, improving knowledge retention, and providing personalized guidance. Through interactive simulations, virtual tutors, and adaptive learning platforms, Al-powered solutions help students in preclinical education grasp difficult ideas. Thus this study aims to examine the impact of Al on preclinical medical education students' academic performance, engagement, and readiness for clinical training among preclinical medical students, examining its applicability, efficacy, potential, and limitations. Which is done by outlining the objectives and evaluating the effectiveness, opportunities, and challenges of integrating artificial intelligence (AI) tools in medical education among Year 1 and Year 2 MBBS students in a private medical university, Malaysia. Methodology: The study involved 300 sample population, including 152 Year 1 and 148 Year 2 students. A cross-sectional questionnaire-based study was conducted, with a sample size of 184 with a 95% confidence level. Data were collected through online surveys and analysis using Microsoft Excel and IBM SPSS version 23.0.Result: All 184 preclinical students used Al tools in their medical education, mainly relying on ChatGPT. About 84.2% are familiar with Al in this context. The effectiveness of Al in improving learning was rated from 1 to 3, with most students scoring Al as 4 or 5 in problem-solving, decision-making, critical thinking, and inspiring new ideas, indicating a high perception of its effectiveness. Many believe AI supports traditional teaching. However, concerns exist about over-reliance on technology (83.2%) and loss of critical thinking skills (77.7%). Also, 42.9% rated their worries about Al's impact on clinical decision-making skills as a 3. Conclusion: Most preclinical students know about Al in medical education and believe it helps improve learning. Al assists students in solving problems, making decisions, encouraging critical thinking, and generating new ideas. However, concerns felt about much dependence on technology and weaken critical thinking skills in medical education. Students believe that AI will not entirely harm clinical decision-making skills. In summary, Al offers both advantages and disadvantages in medical education.

INTRODUCTION:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) nowadays has played a significant role in transforming the way we educate including medical education. AI termed by John McCarthy in 1955, is defined as a machine with intelligent behavior such as reasoning, learning, perception, and ability to perform simple human tasks.1
Several types of generatives Al such as generative text models, generative image models and others, offers a wide array of services that aids in medical education however its integration into medical education and training still remains quite underdeveloped. Technologies like ChatGPT and Google Gemini provide instant access to a vast amount of medical knowledge and can also be used as a study companion that can answer and ask effectively. This enables students to be more personalized in the way that they approach their medical studies which is revolutional for medical education leading to a healthier environment and people's perception surrounding medical education. However, many students, specifically students from a Malaysian medical university, lack necessary training to utilize these tools effectively leading to concerns about overreliance on Al, diminished critical thinking skills, and challenges in addressing ethical issues. Addressing these gaps 1$ critical to preparing future medical professionals to make use of opportunities presented by Al for an Al-guided healthcare system further in their future careers.
The swift progress of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in healthcare has generated both prospects and difficulties for medical education. Although AI tools like ChatGPT and Google Gemini AI present significant opportunities for tailored learning and diagnostic training, their adoption in medical education remains restricted. At schools such as this institution, students frequently miss out on organized training regarding the effective application of these technologies, rendering them illequipped to critically assess Al-generated results or tackle ethical issues like algorithmic bias and data privacy. Additionally, excessive dependence on Al raises worries about the possible decline of critical thinking abilities, while job-related fears arising from AT's increasing impact in various sectors further elevate student stress. The unequal application of specific generative Als leads to a noticeable disparity among students, revealing clear biases from the corresponding generative Als. Recognizing these issues is essential to equip medical students with the skills, knowledge, and foundation required to capitalize on the benefits Al can offer to medical education.
The growing role of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare highlights the importance of equipping medical students with Al-related knowledge and skills. Tools such as ChatGPT, and Google's Gemini AI offer significant potential for enhancing personalized learning and diagnostic training, but their integration into medical education, particularly at this institution, remains inadequate. This study seeks to examine the effectiveness of AI in medical education, address challenges like ethical concerns and unequal access, and provide insights to opportunities presented with integrated Al in medical education.
This study is instrumental in assessing the effectiveness, opportunities, and challenges of integrating artificial intelligence (AI) tools in medical education among students at a private medical university in Malaysia administered through evaluating the level of awareness and knowledge of AI tools among medical students to examine the impact of Al tools on students' academic performance and clinical decision-making skills and identify the ethical, psychological, and technical challenges students face when using AI in medical education and evidenced their hypothetical views through the integration of Al tools significantly improves medical students' academic performance or clinical decision-making skills use of АГ tools significantly enhances students' ability to diagnose and solve clinical problems.
Applications of AI in Medical Education seen with significance:
In the edge of transforming and globalizing world Al offers an encouraging outlook for medical education with tailored learning experiences, improved diagnostic abilities, and simplified curriculum development/ implementation. Addressing the issues of ethics, training, and infrastructure is essential to fully unlock the potential of AI in medical education. It is welldocumented that Artificial intelligence (AI) has significantly impacted medical education, particularly at the preclinical level. Al-powered platforms like ChatGPT and Gemini provide students with readily accessible information, acting as valuable learning and study aids. These tools can answer medical questions, suggest relevant resources, and explain complex concepts in simpler terms, enabling personalized learning experiences tailored to individual needs." For instance, ChatGPT can simulate diagnostic scenarios, allowing students to practice applying their knowledge and receive immediate feedback. Furthermore, Al facilitates personalized education and adaptive learning. By analyzing student performance, Al algorithms can generate customized study plans, quizzes, and content, ensuring that students at different levels receive tailored learning experiences that cater to their specific needs and learning styles? This personalized approach enhances learning outcomes and improves student engagement.
AI also revolutionizes assessment in medical education. Automated quiz systems and Al-powered essay evaluators provide efficient and timely feedback, allowing students to identify and address their weaknesses promptly. This immediate feedback enhances learning and improves overall performance compared to traditional assessment methods." Even one of the previous research reveals the Al includes medical training, as well as Google's search platform? that eases to of gaining advanced knowledge. Al consists of three primary paradigms: symbolic (logic-oriented and knowledge-oriented), statistical (probabilistic techniques and machine learning), and subsymbolic (embodied cognition and search). These frameworks tackle various problem areas (perception, reasoning, knowledge, planning, and communication). Present applications of Al encompass its implementation in automotive industries, finance and economics, healthcare and education."
Finally, Al-powered content recommendation systems guide students towards relevant study materials based on their individual progress and performance. This personalized guidance enhances self-directed learning and improves the overall learning experience.
Effectiveness of Al in Learning Outcomes
AI significantly influences human decision-making in multiple areas by improving efficiency, precision, and the generation of insights. Artificial Intelligence (AT) can revolutionize health care and fundamentally alter the medical field in substantial ways. It has demonstrated significant advancements in areas like diagnostics, data analysis, and precision medicine, and is currently utilized in fields from patient triage to cancer identification. Health care is changing, and along with it comes the necessity to transform medical education. As medicine embraces the era of artificial intelligence (AI), the use of data to enhance clinical decision-making is expected to rise, escalating the demand for proficient interaction between medicine and machines. Al should be smoothly incorporated into various elements of the curriculum. In this paper, we have discussed the current state of medical education and proposed a framework for evolving the medical curriculum to incorporate AL"
AI has demonstrated significant potential in enhancing critical thinking, decision-making, and problem-solving skills among preclinical medical students. Al applications, such as virtual problem sets and case studies, encourage students to apply theoretical knowledge to real-world scenarios. These simulations challenge students' analytical skills by presenting them with incomplete or evolving data, mirroring the complexities of real clinical situations. By requiring students to select appropriate diagnostic tests or treatment plans, these tools enhance their decisionmaking processes and provide valuable feedback."
Furthermore, AI plays a crucial role in developing students' decision-making skills, a critical aspect of medical practice. Al-powered decision-support systems simulate patient interactions and provide real-time guidance, enabling students to make informed clinical decisions based on evolving patient data. This feedback enhances their understanding of treatment protocols, diagnostic reasoning, and clinical judgment. AI also significantly enhances student engagement and knowledge retention. Al-powered gamification in medical learning modules creates interactive and engaging learning environments where students are rewarded for achieving learning milestones. This interactive approach encourages active participation, leading to improved knowledge retention. Gamified Al platforms not only reinforce factual knowledge but also challenge students to apply it in different contexts, solidifying their understanding."
Finally, AI contributes to effective cognitive load management. By presenting information in digestible chunks and providing supplementary explanations, Al tools help students navigate complex subjects like anatomy and physiology. This approach improves student understanding and retention, creating more effective learning environments for students with diverse learning
Opportunities of AI Integration in Medical Education
Artificial Intelligence (Al) is revolutionizing educational practices, especially through its ability to create personalized learning experiences tailored to individual students" needs, preferences, interests, and skill levels. This personalized approach has been available in some form for years, but recent technological advancements have made Al even more effective in offering customized instructional opportunities. This level of personalisation allows students to learn at their own pace, addressing their specific strengths and limitations while keeping them motivated and focused. Al's potential impact on medicine require early exposure and integration into medical education. UME offers unique opportunities for Al training, reaching a broad medical learner population. However, literature shows heterogeneity and poor consensus" Al-powered personalized learning not only enhances educational outcomes but also allows for a more efficient use of time, as students receive the right content at the right time based on their evolving needs. As Al advances, its potential to create educational experiences will grow, making learning more adaptable and accessible to students in a variety of fields, including medical education.
By analyzing students' behavior and identifying areas where they struggle, АГ systems deliver customized explanations, examples, and practice exercises aimed at bridging knowledge gaps. When a student grasps a concept quickly, the system accelerates their leaming by offering more challenging material. Conversely, if a student struggles, the system slows down, providing additional examples and explanations to help them grasp the topic before proceeding. This level of responsiveness ensures that students receive timely feedback and guidance, helping them address challenges early, preventing knowledge gaps from becoming severe, and maintaining steady progress in their learning journey $
Challenges in Adopting AI in Medical Education:
AI tools are widely recognized for their ability to provide instant and precise feedback to students, helping them to identify their mistake quickly. A generative Albased system, such as ChatGPT and Gemini, may detect errors in a diagnostic exercise and treatment plan in real time. However, while the speed of AI feedback is beneficial for the students, it may also come with drawbacks. One of the main concerns is that, instant feedback might reduce opportunities for students to engage in deep reflection about their learning process. Reflection is vital in medical education because it encourages students to think critically, analyse their own reasoning, and learn through experience. Research indicates that interruptions caused by instant Al feedback can diminish the quality and effectiveness of student learning experiences, thus creating a barrier to achieve educational outcomes.
The accessibility of Al and automated problem-solving systems has raised serious concerns about academic integrity. These tools, while powerful, can be misused by students to produce assignments and solve complex problems. This misuse undermines the core values of independent learning and ethical behavior, which are especially critical in medical education. The risk is that students may rely on Al to bypass the reflective and analytical processes essential for developing professional competence and judgment. The uses of Al extend beyond medicine; we should take advantage of the various applications Al offers in medical education and implement necessary adjustments to our curricula, teaching methodologies, and student evaluation by integrating AL?
According to research, while Al can reduce time spent on repetitive tasks and enhance efficiency, 1ts misuse may compromise the authenticity of assessments and evaluations. The intersection of artificial intelligence (AT) and biotechnology has brought about a new wave of innovation in drug development, genomics, and diagnostics. 19
METHODOLOGY:
Study population involved year 1 and year 2 MBBS students in a private Malaysian Medical University from 3'd February 2025 to 13% of February 2025.
The study was conducted using sample population form selected sample year 1 MBBS students is 152, while year 2 has 148 MBBS students. The study included all 300 year 1 and year 2 preclinical MBBS students at this institution, representing.
Study design chosen a cross-sectional descriptive design to gather information from year 1 and year 2 MBBS students. Data were collected through an online survey using google forms. This method allowed us to easily collect responses from all participants. The survey was designed to collect information from the students at a single point in time. The data collection took place over 10 days, from 3rd February 2025 to 13th February 2025.
Sample size and sampling frame the sample size for this study was calculated using a sample size calculator, OpenEpi considering the total population of year 1 and year 2 MBBS students, which 1s 300 students. Based on this, a sample size of 150 students was determined to be sufficient for a 95% confidence level with a 5% margin of error.
The sampling frame consists of all year 1 and year 2 MBBS students enrolled at this institution during the study period. These students were eligible to participate in the study, with selection done through stratified random sampling to ensure proportional representation from both year 1 and year 2.
This study utilized a stratified random sampling method to ensure that year 1 and year 2 MBBS students are appropriately represented. The total student population is 300, with 152 students in year 1 and 148 students in year 2. The sample will be randomly selected from each year group in proportion to their respective sizes, ensuring that both year 1 and year 2 students are equally represented in the study. This method guarantees a more balanced representation of both groups while minimizing selection bias.
This study included their sample population exclusively Year 1 and year 2 MBBS students.
Methods of data collection:
The researchers gathered the data through an online questionnaire using Google Forms. The questionnaire featured a combination of multiple-choice and openended questions to collect data on the demographics of participants and their experiences concerning the study subject. The questionnaire was given to the chosen participants, who were requested to fill it out throughout the study timeframe, from 3'İ February 2025 to 13% February 2025. Every response was automatically captured and securely saved and statistically analysed analysis.
Ethics approval: Ethical approval for this study was obtained from the institutional research ethics committee before data collection began.
RESULTS OF THE STUDY:
The demographic analysis of the respondents processed using SPSS indicate that most respondents are female (68.5%), with an equal distribution of first year and second year students (50% each). The mean age 15 around 20.4 years with standard deviation 1.27, meaning the age variation from the mean is not significant. Almost all respondents (99.5%) have some sort of information about AI. Concerning frequency of Al usage, 72.8% make daily.
All respondents in the study have used Al-based tools or platforms in their medical education. The most commonly used AI application is ChatGPT, utilized by 181 respondents (56.4%). The second most frequently used platform is Gemini, with 87 respondents (27.0%). Copilot ranks third, with 40 respondents (12.5%) using it, followed by Adobe Firefly in fourth place, chosen by 5 respondents (1.6%). Additionally, 2.5% of respondents reported using other Al applications, such as DeepSeek, Google AI Overview, Claude, and MediSearch. The level of familiarity with AI in medical education was assessed on a scale from 1 to 3, where 1 indicates "not familiar," 2 represents "neutral," and 3 signifies "familiar." A majority (84.3%) of respondents reported being highly familiar with AI in medical education. Meanwhile, 14.1% of respondents were neutral, meaning they use Al but are not well-acquainted with its various applications in medical education. Lastly, only 3 respondents (1.6%) reported being unfamiliar with AI in medical education.
Effectiveness of AI based on the respondents:
The effectiveness of Al in medical education, based on respondents" feedback, was measured using four variables: problem-solving, decision-making skills, critical thinking, and the ability to inspire new ideas. Each variable was assessed using three categories, where 1 indicates "Not Effective," 2 indicates "Neutral," and 3 indicates "Effective."
For problem-solving, 140 respondents (76.1%) found Al effective in addressing problems in medical education. 33 respondents (17.9%) rated it as neutral, indicating that AI provides partial assistance in solving clinical problems. Meanwhile, 11 respondents (6.0%) stated that Al is not effective in solving medical education-related problems.
Regarding decision-making skills, 117 respondents (63.6%) considered Al effective, particularly in clinical decision-making. 40 respondents (21.7%) remained neutral, suggesting that Al is not entirely reliable in this area. On the other hand, 27 respondents (14.7%) believed AI is not reliable for decision-making, especially in the medical field.
For critical thinking, 123 respondents (66.8%) stated that AI effectively enhances critical thinking skills. 41 respondents (22.3%) rated it as neutral, meaning Al has some impact but is not highly effective in improving critical thinking. Meanwhile, 20 respondents (10.9%) felt that АГ does not effectively boost critical thinking skills.
Lastly, regarding inspiring new ideas, 161 respondents (87.5%) found AI highly beneficial in stimulating creativity and generating new ideas in medical education. 16 respondents (8.7%) remained neutral, indicating mixed opinions on its effectiveness. Only 7 respondents (3.8%) stated that AI is not effective in generating new ideas.
When asked for specific examples of Al usage in daily life around 78 students responded that АГ helps in simplifying medical concepts for example "Al helps me understand complex topics using simple terms". 65 students respond that AI can help in organising information with example "I ask Al to summarise my lecture slides into key points". Then 52 respondents writes they use Al to answer questions and provide explanations with examples "Al provides in-depth answers to questions from my tutorials and quizzes". Next, 37 answered that Al assists with assignments and presentations while 28 students put AI helps explain diagrams as their response. Around 75% students believes that AI complements traditional teaching methods while 16.8% students are opposed to the idea. Meanwhile 8.2% of students are still unsure on the role of Al in the context of complementing traditional teaching methods.
Table 4 Concerns of the respondents about AL:
The key AI concerns are loss of critical thinking (78.8%) while the lowest concern is put under 'others' (3.3%) which includes false information or inaccurate data, highlighting its impact on cognition, socialization, and security. To reduce Al risks, most people include 31.5% of respondent prefer limiting its use, the lowest suggestion is to emphasize self-reliance which is only 16.3%. This is due to fact that limiting one's access to Al can help them to think and do their own research.
The survey results reveal mixed perceptions of Al's role in clinical decision-making among preclinical students. About 35 students (19.0%) strongly disagree, suggesting concerns about AI hindering independent reasoning.
Around 79 students (43.0%) are neutral, indicating uncertainty, likely due to limited exposure. Meanwhile, 70 students (38.0%) strongly agree, recognizing АГ' 5 benefits in enhancing clinical analysis.
DISCUSSIONS:
The findings of this study provided important insights into the integration of artificial intelligence (AT) in medical education, particularly among preclinical students. The discussion evaluates whether the research questions were answered and whether the study successfully achieved its general objectives. Additionally, the results are compared with existing literature to contextualize the findings within broader academic discourse.
The results indicate that currently Al usage is seen in where Al is widely applied in various aspects of learning. Many students around 84.3% reported being familiar with the concept of AI and has been utilising multiple AI platforms most commonly ChatGPT followed by Gemini with Adobe Firefly being the least chosen AI platform. These platforms offer various services ranging from virtual simulations, automated assessments, and diagnostics tools which can be understood as majority of preclinical students are presently utilising these services. Al-driven technologies such as virtual patients and adaptive learning systems are becoming increasingly common in medical training.!! Furthermore, AI has the potential to bridge knowledge gaps by offering real-time feedback, automating grading, and tailoring educational content based on students" progress.!" These findings confirm that AI plays a significant role in both theoretical and practical aspects of medical education.
In addition to being commonly applied by majority of preclinical students, Al also is found to be effective for medical education. Around 87.5% of respondents answered Al is effective for creating new ideas and 76% of respondents believed that they found AI had been effective in problem solving which shows that the fundamental skills of medical education needed from preclinical students are being nurtured more effectively with AI usage. With 78 students reported that they have found they are able to more effectively simplify lecture notes with AI and 52 students are able to use Al to answer medical questions such as diagnosing diseases with explanations it has made AI effectively improves the medical abilities of these students . Al applications significantly improve students' ability to recognize disease patterns and make informed clinical decisions. Another article further support this, noting that Al-based simulations help students develop critical thinking skills and expose them to realistic patient scenarios without direct clinical risks.!· These findings confirm that AI has a positive impact on medical education, supporting the study's objective of evaluating Al's effectiveness in academic and clinical learning.
The second research question examined the challenges of implementing Al in medical education. The study identified several key obstacles, including ethical concerns, psychological barriers, and technical limitations. Ethical concerns primarily revolved around reduced human interaction in learning and data and privacy security. Around 86 and 48 students reported these concerns respectively showing that they are still challenges to fully integrating Al in medical education. Participants expressed hesitation about the reliability of Al in sensitive medical contexts. Biased training datasets can lead to misleading Al-generated medical advice.!· Also, found that many medical students are wary of Al's decision-making process, fearing possible errors due to biases in AI models.!> From our findings, 154 students reported concerns of becoming overreliance on technology especially Al as they offers many benefits that made the preclinical students education more effective when utilising the Al tools. However, despite these benefits, students expressed concerns about over-reliance on AI, fearing that it might weaken their ability to make independent clinical judgments.'> Thus, it seems there are challenges that are still present in Al role in medical education that is affecting a majority of the students who are applying it in their personal way throughout the preclinical studies.
Psychological challenges were also evident, with some students reporting feelings of uncertainty and anxiety when Al recommendations contradicted traditional clinical teachings. Noted that students often struggle to trust Al-generated diagnoses, particularly when they differ from what they have learned in conventional training.'5 Additionally, technical barriers such as limited access to Al-powered resources, a lack of standardized AI education, and inadequate faculty training in АГ applications were prominent concerns. Emphasised that disparities in AI education and resource availability create unequal opportunities for students, making it difficult for some to fully utilize Al-driven learning tools!" These findings confirm that Al implementation in medical education faces significant ethical, psychological, and technical challenges, successfully addressing the second research question and fulfilling the corresponding study objective.
Despite these challenges, AI presents numerous opportunities to enhance medical education, particularly through adaptive learning platforms, automated assessments, and Al-driven performance analytics. Alpowered systems can personalize learning by adapting educational content to individual students' needs, thereby improving engagement and knowledge retention.!3 However, the preference for traditional teaching methods among some students suggests that a blended learning approach which integrates AI with conventional instructional methods may be the most effective strategy.
To maximize Al's potential in medical education, institutions should focus on developing standardized Al curricula, ensuring ethical AI deployment, and providing faculty with Al training. A structured approach that combines human mentorship with Al-driven learning will enable students to harness Al's benefits while minimizing its risks. Future research should explore the long-term impact of Al-based education on clinical competence and patient care outcomes. Furthermore it can be utilized in medical education in these formats: Virtual Inquiry System, Medical Distance Learning and Management, and Recording instructional videos in medical schools. It can likewise improve the significance of the non-analytical humanistic facets of medicine. '®
The growing incorporation of Al in the field of medicine, particularly over the last few decades, has resulted in a rise in the application of various Al techniques in medical education. Nevertheless, the incorporation of Al into medical education presents both benefits and challenges. The benefits consist of impartial student evaluation, improved organization of clinical simulations, and increased transparency in education. On the other hand, the primary challenges associated with AI integration in education include ethical and legal concerns, limitations in scalability, assessment of the effectiveness of these teaching methods, and technical issues.'
In conclusion, this study successfully addressed both research questions and met its general objectives. The results indicate that AI is widely used in medical education, primarily through personalized learning, diagnostic tools, and simulations, confirming the first research question. Additionally, significant challenges related to ethics, psychological factors, and technical limitations were identified, addressing the second research question. While AI offers immense potential to enhance medical education, its implementation must be carefully managed to ensure ethical, effective, and equitable integration into medical curricula.
LIMITATION AND SUGGESTION:
Time Constraint:
The study was conducted within a short time frame of four weeks, which limited the depth of data collection and analysis. A longer duration could have allowed for more comprehensive insights.
Sampling Bias:
The study focused only on 180 preclinical MBBS students, which may not represent the perspectives of medical students from other institutions or clinical year students. This could affect the generalizability of finding.
Cross-Sectional Nature of the Module:
The study does not take into consideration how students' views of Al in medical education may change as a result of exposure and experience because it collects data at a single occasion. A longer-term investigation would yield more reliable results.
Longitudinal Study Design:
By carrying out a study over a long period of time, it is possible to monitor how students' opinions and experiences with Al in medical education evolve.
Larger and More Diverse Sample:
The results would be more broadly applicable if the study was extended to include students from various universities as well as clinical year students.
Mixed-Method Approach:
Students' experiences and viewpoints on Al in medical education can be better understood by combining quantitative surveys with focus groups or qualitative interviews.
CONCLUSION:
The results of this research indicate that the majority of preclinical students are not only familiar with the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in medical education but also recognize its significant impact on their learning experiences. According to their responses, Al is perceived as highly effective in enhancing learning outcomes by assisting students in solving complex problems related to medical courses, improving decision-making skills, fostering critical thinking, and stimulating innovative ideas. These benefits suggest that Al serves as a valuable tool in medical education, helping students navigate challenging concepts and develop a deeper understanding of medical knowledge. However, despite its numerous advantages, Al also presents potential risks and negative implications that should not be overlooked. Among the primary worries, there certainly is the issues of students turning out completely dependent on AI, which will damage the acquiring of so important cognitive skills as independent solving of a problem or working out a conclusion. This is particularly relevant in medical education, where critical thinking and clinical decision-making are fundamental competencies. If students rely excessively on Al-generated information without engaging in their own critical analysis, they may struggle to develop the necessary skills required for real-world clinical practice. Nevertheless, the findings of this study indicate that while preclinical students acknowledge these potential drawbacks, they do not perceive Al as a direct threat to their clinical decision-making abilities. Instead, they recognize that the impact of Al largely depends on how it is utilized in the learning process. With appropriate use, Al can serve as a powerful supplementary tool rather than a substitute for human reasoning and judgment. Therefore, it is crucial for educators and students to strike a balance between leveraging Al for its benefits while ensuring that it does not compromise essential cognitive and decision-making skills. By using Al responsibly and integrating it effectively into medical education, students can maximize its advantages while minimizing its potential risks, ultimately enhancing their overall learning experience and preparedness for future clinical practice.

No conflict of interest exists among the authors.

From Surface to Deep Learning: Gamified Mobile Education for Subcutaneous and Intramuscular Injection Skills

Author: Tamer, Zeynep1    ; Kavuran, Esin1    1 Department of Nursing Fundamentals, Faculty of Nursing, Atatürk University, Erzurum, Turkey

Publication info: Tamer, Zeynep; Kavuran, Esin. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/surface-deep-learning-gamified-mobile-education/docview/3228023189/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: The aim of this study was to investigate the effect of a game-based mobile application on nursing students' skills in administering subcutaneous (SC) and intramuscular (IM) injections. Nursing education traditionally involves both theoretical and practical components. With the advent of digital technologies, innovative methods such as game-based learning have been introduced to enhance practical skills and knowledge retention in nursing education. This study explores the use of a mobile application designed to improve students' competence in SC and IM drug administration. This was an experimental study conducted during the 2021-2022 academic year. It involved a study group of 64 students who received training through a simulation game system and a control group of 65 students who underwent traditional training methods. Data were collected using the Self-Demonstration Form, the Study Process Questionnaire, and the Skills Performance List for Subcutaneous and Intramuscular Administration. The study focused on assessing the impact of game-based learning on students' performance and learning approaches. The study group showed significantly greater improvements in learning approaches and medication administration skills compared to the control group. Deep learning scores increased from 31.39 ± 6.23 to 45.05 ± 5.46 in the study group, versus 31.78 ± 5.68 to 37.02 ± 4.17 in the control group ( p  < 0.01). SC and IM administration scores improved significantly in the study group (SC: 22.50 ± 15.46 to 42.45 ± 11.66, p  = 0.015; IM: 27.75 ± 15.98 to 59.45 ± 12.95, p  < 0.001) compared to the control group. Scenario-based analyses also showed significant performance gains in the study group across all scenarios ( p  < 0.05). The HEM-SC-IM game-based mobile application proved effective in improving nursing students' skills in administering SC and IM injections. The interactive and engaging nature of game-based learning provides a valuable educational experience, promoting deeper understanding and practical skills development. This study supports the integration of educational technology in nursing curricula to enhance learning outcomes.The aim of this study was to investigate the effect of a game-based mobile application on nursing students' skills in administering subcutaneous (SC) and intramuscular (IM) injections. Navigating the Educational Landscape: The Transformative Power of Smart Classroom Technology

Author: Xu, Lu11 Nantong University, Trade Union, Nantong, China (GRID:grid.260483.b) (ISNI:0000 0000 9530 8833)

Publication info: Xu, Lu. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/navigating-educational-landscape-transformative/docview/3224058370/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: In the rapidly evolving landscape of education, integrating smart classroom technology (SCT) is a transformative force, reshaping traditional paradigms and redefining the dynamics of teaching and learning. The study aims to investigate the transformative impact of SCT on educational practices, focusing on its effectiveness in enhancing student engagement, learning outcomes, and overall educational experience. The study analyzes the implementation of a smart classroom (SMR) system to enhance overall satisfaction and foster positive perceptions among students and faculty concerning the learning environment. The study employed a quantitative methodology and utilized the random sampling technique. The data were collected from 420 college students at different levels from junior level to senior category who received SMR education. The collected data were analyzed by using SPSS software. The findings indicate that incorporation of SCT systems positively impacts student engagement and participation levels in academic activities. The result underscores the role of SCT in fostering a dynamic learning environment that promotes active learning and knowledge retention among students, highlighting its outstanding academic significance in transforming traditional educational practices. The study contributes by examining the transformative potential of SMR systems in education, focusing on enhanced student engagement, collaboration, and digital literacy. Its novelty lies in revealing the positive impact on satisfaction and perceptions, heralding a new era of personalized learning experiences. Practical values of SMR technology include providing data for tailored instruction and enabling personalized learning through interactive whiteboards and digital textbooks. Academically, it enhances understanding and retention with multimedia resources that cater to diverse learning styles.
