Designing Digital Escape Rooms with Generative AI in University Contexts: A Qualitative Study

Author: Rodríguez-Rivera, Paula1    ; Rodríguez-Ferrer, José M2    ; Manzano-León, Ana3    1 Faculty of Education and Social Work, Department of Psychosocioeducational Analysis and Intervention, University of Vigo, 32004 Ourense, Spain; paula.rodriguez.rivera@uvigo.es2 Faculty of Health Sciences, Department of Health Sciences, University of Burgos, 09001 Burgos, Spain; jmrferrer@ubu.es3 Department of Psychology, Health Research Centre, University of Almería, 04120 Almería, Spain

Publication info: Rodríguez-Rivera, Paula; Rodríguez-Ferrer, José M; Manzano-León, Ana. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/designing-digital-escape-rooms-with-generative-ai/docview/3181607395/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: The rapid evolution of technology in education highlights the need for methodologies that enhance student engagement and skill development. This study examines students’ perceptions of designing educational escape rooms using ICT tools and generative AI (GenAI) as a learning methodology. A total of 47 students participated in creating digital escape rooms with GenAI, Genially, and HeroForge in the course “Mediation in Conflicts and Situations of Violence” within a Social Education degree. A qualitative approach was used, analyzing focus group discussions conducted after the activity. Results indicate that students valued the experience, emphasizing its impact on digital competence, creativity, and problem-solving skills. Collaborative learning helped overcome initial technical challenges, and students recognized the practical applicability of escape room design in mediation contexts. However, they identified areas for improvement, such as the need for more initial training, extended development time, and better access to digital tools. This study contributes to game-based learning and AI-enhanced education research, positioning students as active designers rather than passive users. Future research should explore the long-term impact on knowledge retention and transferable skills in professional settings.

Links: https://julac-hkpu.primo.exlibrisgroup.com/openurl/852JULAC_HKPU/852JULAC_HKPU:HKPU?sid=proquest&amp;auinit=Paula&amp;aulast=Rodr%C3%ADguez-Rivera&amp;atitle=Designing+Digital+Escape+Rooms+with+Generative+AI+in+University+Contexts%3A+A+Qualitative+Study&amp;stitle=Multimodal+Technologies+and+Interaction&amp;btitle=&amp;id=doi:10.3390%2Fmti9030020&amp;title=Designing+Digital+Escape+Rooms+with+Generative+AI+in+University+Contexts%3A+A+Qualitative+Study&amp;volume=9&amp;issue=3&amp;date=2025&amp;spage=20&amp;isbn=&amp;genre=article&amp;

https://julac-hkpu.primo.exlibrisgroup.com/openurl/852JULAC_HKPU/852JULAC_HKPU:HKPU?sid=proquest&amp;auinit=Paula&amp;aulast=Rodr%C3%ADguez-Rivera&amp;atitle=Designing+Digital+Escape+Rooms+with+Generative+AI+in+University+Contexts%3A+A+Qualitative+Study&amp;stitle=Multimodal+Technologies+and+Interaction&amp;btitle=&amp;id=doi:10.3390%2Fmti9030020&amp;title=Designing+Digital+Escape+Rooms+with+Generative+AI+in+University+Contexts%3A+A+Qualitative+Study&amp;volume=9&amp;issue=3&amp;date=2025&amp;spage=20&amp;isbn=&amp;genre=article&amp;

Full text: 1. Introduction In recent decades, society has undergone a technological transformation that has profoundly impacted all domains, including education [1,2]. Integrating information and communication technologies (ICT) has radically altered teaching and learning processes, generating a new pedagogical reality that combines physical and digital environments [3].
Acquiring basic digital competencies is essential for students and teachers, regardless of their discipline or educational level [4,5]. In higher education, these competencies facilitate a deeper understanding of content and foster metacognitive skills and autonomous learning, preparing future professionals for an increasingly digitalized labor market [6,7]. However, the effectiveness of ICT in university classrooms critically depends on teachers’ digital competence [8]. While some educators perceive these tools as facilitators of active learning [9], others associate them with additional administrative burdens or technical difficulties [10], limiting their full adoption.
Nevertheless, students’ digital competence is also crucial in this process. Recent studies show that although university students are frequent users of digital tools, their mastery of key competencies such as information management, communication in virtual environments, and digital content creation is uneven [11,12]. The evolution of these competencies has been influenced by various factors, including access to technological resources, prior training, ICT-mediated learning experiences, or social class [13,14]. Current research indicates that while recent generations have developed intuitive skills in using digital devices, this does not automatically translate into advanced digital competence in academic and professional settings [15].
In this context, marked by barriers such as a lack of time, institutional resources, and specialized support for integrating ICT in classrooms [16], the emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in universities has intensified these challenges. ChatGPT, developed by OpenAI, is among the most widely used GenAI technologies in education, recognized for its ability to create new and contextually relevant content based on previously trained data. Its advanced architecture, based on models such as GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, enables the generation of explanations, examples, and materials tailored to the specific needs of students and educators [17].
One of the main challenges is the risk that students may use these tools to avoid completing tasks autonomously. Various studies highlight how these technologies can facilitate the plagiarism of written texts, compromising the development of essential skills such as critical thinking and academic writing [18]. Additionally, reliance on generative tools may limit active learning by reducing the effort required to complete academic tasks [19,20].
Despite these challenges, the potential of generative AI in education warrants critical consideration. Empirical evidence [21,22,23] suggests that these tools can optimize innovative educational processes, such as designing immersive learning experiences or facilitating collaborative dynamics in digital environments. One example of this collaboration is the integration of GenAI into the design of educational escape rooms (EERs). Educational escape rooms (EERs) are defined as immersive game-based learning environments that adapt the structure of recreational escape rooms to educational contexts. These activities challenge participants to solve sequential puzzles, riddles, or tasks linked to curricular content within a narrative framework, fostering critical thinking, collaboration, and knowledge application [24,25,26]. Initially conceived as recreational activities, EERs have been adapted to educational settings due to their ability to promote motivation, active learning, and collaboration through immersive challenges [27]. Recent research highlights how GenAI could further enhance their pedagogical development, enabling everything from the personalization of adaptive narratives to the automated generation of context-based challenges [28,29]. However, as studies emphasize, its adoption must be accompanied by pedagogical strategies that prioritize the development of cognitive skills over the mere automation of tasks.
This duality is reflected in the current uses of EERs across various educational domains. In higher education, for instance, they have been successfully employed in health sciences to reinforce key concepts and practical skills in controlled environments [30,31]. In fields such as the social sciences, EERs have been shown to improve academic performance and student motivation while simultaneously fostering a positive classroom climate and challenge-based learning [10,32,33].
However, EERs’ potential goes beyond their use as passive didactic tools. They reach their fullest expression when students become designers. Creating digital escape rooms integrates narrative elements and playful dynamics that require prior knowledge to be applied, fostering the development of key competencies such as creativity, problem-solving, and decision-making [34].
This active methodology has proven effective in the university setting for acquiring soft skills and digital competencies, particularly in education faculties where technological literacy is essential. For example, at the University of Extremadura, using an escape room via mobile technologies with students in the Social Education degree improved motivation and promoted competencies relevant to their training [35]. Similarly, at Rey Juan Carlos University, implementing a hybrid escape room in the “Informatics and Digital Competence” course enhanced motivation. It facilitated programming instruction for future early childhood and primary education teachers [36]. Planning these activities involves everything from digital tools to structuring pedagogical narratives, simultaneously strengthening digital competence and technological adaptability [37,38].
For this reason, tools like ChatGPT help to streamline these spaces by generating contextualized narratives, personalizing puzzles according to participants’ skill levels, and offering real-time hints, reducing design time by up to 60% [39]. Recent studies highlight that combining language models with specialized databases facilitates the creation of interactive and adaptable scenarios across various disciplines, from engineering to the social sciences [40]. Additionally, adaptive feedback algorithms have been shown to expand the reach of these experiences, decreasing the resources required for implementation by 40% [41]. Experimental research in environments such as Roblox demonstrates that AI-controlled avatars enhance perceived immersion by 30% through contextualized dialogs [42].
Generative AI tools are also adopted in point-and-click games to optimize narrative design, create adaptive puzzles, and enhance interactions with non-playable characters (NPCs). Recent research demonstrates that systems such as PAC-Bot, a conversational agent integrated into development environments for non-expert users, reduce the cognitive load in creating behavioral rules for these games by automatically generating dialogs based on language models [43]. This approach has enabled amateur developers to design personalized experiences with 35% less effort in complex tasks, such as defining contextual events or integrating dynamic feedback mechanics [44]. Additionally, platforms like Adventure Creator and Fungus are incorporating GenAI algorithms to generate non-linear narratives, where NPC dialogs and decisions adapt in real-time to player actions, increasing replayability by 20% according to analyses of public datasets [45].
However, technical and ethical challenges remain. Around 18% of the hints generated by systems like ChatGPT may contain biases or inaccuracies, reinforcing the need for human supervision at key stages of the design process [17]. This duality highlights the importance of hybrid approaches, where GenAI acts as an assistant in EER creation without replacing the pedagogical judgment of designers [46].
In this context, where escape rooms are emerging as a promising strategy for developing key skills, their adaptation to digital environments with GenAI remains underexplored, particularly in the training of social educators. While previous studies focus on their application as pre-designed resources for students [47], this research innovates by positioning future social educators as active designers of their own escape rooms, integrating GenAI. This approach, scarcely explored in the literature, responds to two key findings: first, over 80% of gamified experiences in professional training rely on static tools (such as point-based systems) that do not promote applied creativity [48]; second, other reviews show that the creation of self-developed playful resources significantly enhances the transfer of digital and pedagogical competencies to work contexts [49].
Furthermore, in using GenAI to guide the creation of new narratives and ethical challenges [50] the proposed model develops technical skills and simulates scenarios where participants lead in designing socio-educational interventions. Therefore, this study has the following objectives: - Analyze how creating digital escape rooms mediated by generative artificial intelligence influences learning specific content and the development of teamwork, creativity, and digital competence.

- Explore students’ perceptions regarding integrating digital escape room design activities mediated by generative artificial intelligence.

- Examine how students have incorporated and applied the various technological tools introduced during the activity.

- Identify the challenges associated with the implementation of these activities.


The following sections present the methodology used in a practical activity in which students designed digital escape rooms using digital tools and generative artificial intelligence. Subsequently, the results obtained from student perceptions collected in focus groups are analyzed, followed by a discussion on the competencies developed, the challenges identified, and the pedagogical implications of this strategy. Finally, the study’s conclusions and proposals for future research are presented.
2. Materials and Methods 2.1. Participants This research was conducted with students from the Faculty of Education at Vigo University. A total of 57 students participated in this activity. Upon completing the activity, they were allowed to provide feedback by creating focus groups. Fifty-two students participated in the focus groups (89.4% of the activity participants), including 42 women and 10 men aged 21 to 54 years (M = 22.40; SD = 5.40).
2.2. Procedure This research focused on studying the impact of interactive activities, such as creating educational escape rooms, in the course Mediation in Conflicts and Situations of Violence within the Social Education Degree at Vigo University during the 2024/2025 academic year. This course is a compulsory component of the degree program, as established in the university’s curriculum. Within the course structure is a designated section for group or supervised work, which provides the framework for developing the educational escape room. These activities were mandatory and contributed to students’ final grades, serving as an applied learning strategy to enhance their understanding and practical skills in conflict mediation.
The 52 students were divided into groups of 3 to 4 members to carry out the activity. Each group was presented with several case studies related to different types of mediation: family, school, workplace, and community mediation. These mediation cases and the difficulties encountered were directly linked to the theoretical content of the course. Two examples of mediation cases were a conflict between two students over group assignment responsibilities, requiring mediation to resolve cooperation and communication issues, and a dispute between two sisters over caregiving schedules for their ill mother, necessitating negotiation and agreement.
The activities were conducted over a month and were structured into eight sessions of 90 min each (Table 1).
The activity began with an introductory session, during which the methodology was presented, and students were familiarized with the digital tools to be used: ChatGPT (GPT-4o), Genially ( https://genially.com/es/ (accessed on 26 February 2025)), HeroForge ( www.heroforge.com (accessed on 26 February 2025)), and Pixverse (version 3). This session provided an overview of the project and included practical demonstrations to ensure proper tool handling. Additionally, a detailed evaluation rubric (Appendix A) was introduced, outlining the guidelines and criteria for the structured creation of the escape rooms.
In this context, Generative AI played a fundamental role in this stage, allowing students to design scenarios, generate images, and develop clues that structured the challenges coherently. These images were later animated using Pixverse, adding an interactive component that enhanced immersion in each scenario. To complete the visual design, students used HeroForge to create customized characters representing key actors in the conflicts, integrating them naturally into the mediation case narratives (Figure 1).
Additionally, digital resources such as digital lock generators, timers, and WhatsApp conversation simulators provided functionalities that enriched the challenges.
Finally, all components were assembled in Genially, a platform that unified the narratives, visual elements, and interactive dynamics into a cohesive and functional final product.
The instructor acted as a guide and facilitator, addressing technical questions but refraining from interfering in the creative process. Their role focused on providing support when students had doubts about using digital tools or the feasibility of certain dynamics within the escape rooms.
Below is an example of the work carried out by a team of students whose case was related to school mediation. As Figure 2 shows, one group designed an EER simulating a plane crash scenario in which two students with interpersonal conflicts had to collaborate to solve survival challenges.
This EER required players to decode encrypted messages, share resources under time constraints, and negotiate roles (e.g., medical tasks vs. signal coordination), fostering skills in conflict resolution and cooperative problem-solving. Similarly, family mediation groups designed cases centered on negotiating caregiving responsibilities, while workplace and community groups tackled team collaboration challenges and neighborhood disputes.
In the final sessions, students implemented and evaluated their escape rooms. After conducting pilot tests and adjusting technical and narrative details, each group presented their project to the rest of the class, assuming the role of facilitators.
The experience concluded with a focus group, where students reflected on the challenges faced, the strategies used, and the overall impact of the workshop.
2.3. Instrument This research used a focus group [13] to analyze the students’ experience designing and creating digital escape rooms. Participants were divided into small groups and asked to reflect on their experiences by answering pre-established questions. These questions addressed aspects such as acquired learning, teamwork, the usefulness of the activity to achieve the learning objectives, the difficulties faced and the strategies used to overcome them, and the contribution of the resources used.
The focus group was held at the end of the project, after the implementation of the escape rooms, and was structured around key questions such as: What have we learned during this activity? How would you describe our experience working in a group? What specific aspects of the activity were most helpful for your understanding of the topic? These questions fostered a reflective dialog among the participants, allowing them to identify strengths and areas for improvement in the activity.
The qualitative study included 52 volunteer students organized into 16 focus groups to share their perceptions of the experience. One of the principal investigators moderated each group and guided the discussion following a pre-established script to ensure data comparability. Since the objective was to capture spontaneous and genuine impressions, no audio or video recordings were made. Instead, responses were manually recorded by the moderator, who took note of key ideas, representative phrases, and emerging patterns. To preserve anonymity and facilitate a more fluid analysis, responses were considered units of analysis within the focus group rather than being attributed individually to each student. This approach allowed for the identification of general trends and the assessment of the students’ overall perception of the activity.
2.4. Data Analysis All collected information was organized for analysis and processing using Atlas.ti software (version 9, ATLAS.ti Scientific Software Development GmbH, Berlin, Germany).
The focus group data were analyzed using a qualitative approach based on notes taken during the sessions, as no recordings were available. These notes, recorded by the moderator and an assistant, included key verbatim quotes, recurring ideas, and observations on group dynamics, ensuring a detailed representation of participants’ responses. Subsequently, the notes provided by students during the focus groups were thoroughly reviewed to identify patterns and key concepts related to the questions posed during the activity.
The analysis was conducted through a manual coding process, breaking down responses into units of meaning that reflect recurring themes. These codes were then grouped into thematic categories, supported by representative quotes extracted from the notes, ensuring that the conclusions accurately reflected the experiences shared by the participants.
3. Results The results (Table 2) are shown in response to the first objective.
Students perceive that the activity has significantly impacted their learning, highlighting the development of transversal competencies (knowledge, skills, and attitudes), such as teamwork, creativity, and digital competence, alongside subject-specific learning (communicative mediation).
The results show that all students consider that the cooperative design of digital escape rooms has strengthened their capacity for group work, consolidating this competence as a pillar of experience. The group nature of the activity allowed them to rely on their classmates, facilitating enriching horizontal learning. This is evidenced in testimonies like that of focus group 2: “In activities such as the escape room, key aspects such as communication and collaboration are worked on. It helps to develop social skills related to coexistence, teamwork, and using technologies applied to the academic and professional fields”.
For some students, using digital tools was initially challenging due to a lack of skills in this area. Therefore, the cooperative activity helped overcome the initial frustration experienced by some participants and consolidated teamwork as a fundamental competence for future social educators. This aspect was highlighted in two focus groups: “I felt very comfortable with my work team. Because it was more difficult for me to use AI, I expected help from my colleagues, and I was more dedicated to looking for games or other resources” (FG3), and “I felt comfortable since within the team there is trust, understanding and good teamwork. I feel that the role I acquired was concerning the needs needed in each case, although I needed help from my colleagues to carry out the activities” (FG5).
On the other hand, a considerable number of students (68.75%) highlighted how the activity allowed them to develop their creativity. Designing an escape room encourages creativity because it involves a highly interactive and open process, where students must combine imagination, problem-solving, and originality to create an immersive and challenging experience. This allows participants to explore new ways to apply prior knowledge and generate innovative ideas. This innovative and practical methodology moved away from more traditional approaches, such as revision or repetition, providing greater flexibility and favoring the creative possibilities of the students. This is reflected in comments such as: “What we liked most was the creative opportunity for free expression” (FG13).
Finally, 62.5% of the students directly mentioned their progress in digital competence within the transversal competencies. The experience allowed them to learn how to use or improve their ability to use various ICT tools, something they consider essential for their professional future in an increasingly digitalized society. In the words of focus group 14: “When carrying out the escape room, it was necessary to work as a team. This implied communication, active listening, and agreement, which the escape room participants would need. In addition, it is related to our learning since today’s society is increasingly digitized, and being able to anticipate this event and control these applications from the beginning is a point in favor of our learning”.
About the educational possibilities of escape room creation activities mediated by generative artificial intelligence, the students show a significant consensus on their direct connection with the specific syllabus of their subjects (93.75%). The integration of fictitious cases related to their future professional activity through these dynamics has been perceived as an innovative methodology with great practical applicability, especially in mediation and socio-educational intervention. As focus group 4 points out: “I see it as a very different way of resolving a conflict and seeing that through the analysis of similar situations, we can transfer those behaviors to our situation. We could apply this strategy in subjects such as socio-educational intervention in childhood and adolescence”. This highlights how students value the connection between these activities and the real contexts in which they will develop their professional work, facilitating more meaningful learning.
In addition, these dynamics are seen to make practical learning tangible. According to a student in focus group 9, “It is a good way to learn in the classroom how to carry out professional practice effectively”. This approach allows students to practice skills transferable to their professional performance, consolidating key competencies in their training.
At the same time, the students highlight that digital escape rooms, supported by artificial intelligence, have great potential for their future socio-educational profession (81.25%). They consider this methodology flexible, reusable, and a tool that responds to the demands of an increasingly digitized and technological society. As a student from focus group 16 indicates: “It is also totally related to my learning because we are in a new society where the use of this artificial intelligence will end up being essential; these tools help us to materialize our ideas and improve the quality of the projects, ensuring that they are 100% in line with our expectations”. This testimony highlights the importance of mastering these technologies to create practical, effective, and adaptable resources for various professional situations.
Likewise, escape rooms are specifically mentioned as a valuable tool to address complex situations, such as conflict resolution in school contexts. Focus group 13 emphasizes: “I believe, as I said before, that the escape room is a great tool in resolving conflicts between children, and it also has the advantage of being able to be used several times. I think it would be a great tool in conflicts of coexistence in a school”. This perspective shows how students recognize the pedagogical value of the resource and can identify concrete scenarios where its implementation can generate a positive impact.
The data obtained (Table 3) are shown in response to the second objective of the research.
The results obtained reflect a primarily positive experience on the part of the students, who highly valued the activity as motivating (87.5%) and fun (93.75%). The students argue that the attraction of this educational practice lies mainly in the possibility of designing and creating escape rooms, which allow them to participate actively in their learning process. One focus group expressed satisfaction: “It becomes more dynamic and less boring than a conventional class, in which you only read slides and limit yourself to copying and taking notes” (FG5). Students perceive this educational practice as innovative, especially when moving away from conventional tasks such as delivering reports or taking exams. According to students, this innovation encourages more significant involvement in learning, which can be linked to the pedagogical approaches proposed by Bloom’s Taxonomy [51], highlighting the importance of promoting analysis, evaluation, and creation skills beyond simple knowledge acquisition. Students feel more involved and engaged with the activity by focusing on creativity and problem-solving using digital tools.
Another aspect that was particularly attractive to the students was the possibility of exploring various ICT tools and actively participating in the design of the escape rooms. This playful component, inherent to the dynamics of the escape room, aroused a high level of motivation. One participant in focus group 11 pointed out, “Yes [I liked performing the activity] because we were very motivated to create our own game”. This observation highlights the educational and entertaining activity, suggesting that learning can be effective when combined with playful elements.
However, despite these positive results, the initial experience was marked by difficulties that temporarily reduced the students’ perception of the digital escape room. The participants (43.75%) expressed an initial frustration related to their lack of knowledge of the ICT tools used in the activity. This percentage indicates that almost half of the students experienced a kind of initial block due to their limited digital competence, which led to reduced self-efficacy and, in some cases, even stress. One focus group recounted their experience: “It was a new and also different experience. I had never done an activity like this before, one so heavily based on or supported by the use of digital applications. So, at first, it was quite difficult for me to figure out how to do things. But then, as I explored the application, I started realizing where I could do each task, and somehow, I gained a bit more confidence in creating the escape room”. (FG4). This testimony reflects the learning curve experienced by the students, where the initial fear of the unknown and the lack of digital skills were overcome over time as the participants gained confidence in using the tools. This adaptation process is essential as it shows how supporting technological autonomy through experimentation and self-exploration can lead students to overcome their initial limitations and feel more competent in using new technologies.
Next, the data obtained are shown in response to the third objective of the research (Table 4).
One of the main criticisms that has been made of GenAI is that students tend to use these tools passively, delegating the creation of their work to them without actively participating in the learning process [52]). However, within the framework of this educational activity, the objective was to teach students how to use GenAI ethically and responsibly, showing them how it can become a valuable and complementary tool for their future professional development. In short, the aim was to use GenAI not as a substitute for their intellectual effort but as a resource to enhance their creativity and efficiency in solving problems.
In this sense, the results reveal that most students (93.75%) used GenAI for various purposes, demonstrating its integration in multiple stages of the creative and educational process. Common uses include creating images, assisting in writing scripts for challenges, designing chatbots, creating dialog for non-playable characters (NPCs), consulting, and using other complementary ICT tools.
In addition to GenAI, the students actively used other digital tools to develop the digital escape rooms. Almost half of the students (43.75%) used Genially, a platform known for its ability to create interactive and visual presentations. The students used it to design presentations that linked the different tests and games of the digital escape room, allowing fluid and attractive navigation between the various challenges. In addition, some students used Genially to create interactive games within the same platform. On the other hand, 37.5% of the students used HeroForge, a tool specialized in creating avatars and characters in 3D. The students used it to design custom figures in the escape room.
Finally, the data obtained are shown in response to the fourth objective of the research (Table 5).
It must be recognized that any educational practice has a wide margin for improvement. For this reason, recording the students’ criticisms and suggestions is beneficial to optimize the methodologies and tools used. In this context, the opinions collected in the focus groups provide a valuable perspective for improving educational practice.
Some of the participants (18.75%) in the focus groups specifically mentioned that they would have preferred the design of escape rooms to be face-to-face. This is mainly related to those students whose digital competence was more limited from the beginning of the course. Some indicated: “We would have done better if it were face-to-face because we would have come up with other challenges without needing to use ICTs” (FG3). In addition, some expressed that their preference for face-to-face was due to the consideration that their future users, in a professional context, might not have the necessary digital skills to interact with an online version: “[The escape room] is oriented to the online world and not all people have the skills or access to an online escape room. However, in our professional future, we would carry out an escape room, but physically/face-to-face” (FG1).
Another relevant difficulty, mentioned by 37.5% of the groups, was the limited ICT tools used in the course. Although students worked with free versions of certain apps, these were found to be restricted compared to the paid versions. Because the university could not cover the costs of premium subscriptions for students, many felt limited in terms of the functionalities these tools offered. This technological barrier highlighted one of the difficulties inherent in using digital resources in the classroom, especially when the complete versions of the tools are not available.
Finally, a quarter of the focus groups suggested that having more sessions and more time to use the tools and develop their escape room designs more thoughtfully and leisurely would have been beneficial. Most of these participants agreed that, although learning was generally positive, the time available was insufficient to consolidate the necessary knowledge and skills correctly. “We value learning very positively since we have learned a new way of carrying out mediation. We would rate it with a 9.5 because the app we used gave us quite a few problems, and we would need more time” (FG9). Others, for their part, highlighted the need for greater clarity in the explanations before the activity: “Given the lack of knowledge of the programs, I believe that we would increase the time and the specificity of the explanations prior to the execution of the activity” (FG10).
4. Discussion This study aimed to understand how students perceive the experience of designing educational escape rooms by integrating ICT tools and artificial intelligence as a learning methodology. The results reflect positive perceptions, aligning with recent research in this field [33].
Addressing the first research objective (analyze how creating digital escape rooms mediated by generative artificial intelligence influences learning specific content and the development of teamwork, creativity, and digital competence), the implementation of an EER design activity with GenAI has promoted deep learning of the course content and demonstrated significant development of the valued competencies.
A highly valued aspect was the opportunity to work in groups. Previous studies reinforce that collaborative work promotes horizontal and independent learning while allowing knowledge exchange among peers [53,54].
Another significant aspect is the comprehension required to design educative escape rooms. This process demands that students master the content on which the challenges are based, reinforcing their subject-specific learning [10]. Additionally, it fosters the development of essential transversal skills such as creativity and problem-solving [55], which are key competencies for future professionals in the socio-educational field. In this regard, previous research has demonstrated that integrating technologies with curricular content presents a challenge that promotes the construction of deeper, shared knowledge [56].
The activity also aligns with the experiential and discovery-based learning approach. Designing and participating in escape rooms facilitate the acquisition of specific knowledge, allowing students to practice and consolidate transferable skills such as effective communication, time management, and ICT tools [57]. This methodological approach coincides with the principles of the “learning to learn” competence, which emphasizes student autonomy and their ability to adapt to new learning situations [58].
Regarding creativity, designing an escape room fosters a highly interactive and open environment where students can innovatively apply prior knowledge. The literature suggests that activities like this enhance creativity by integrating problem-solving and generating original ideas in a collaborative context [59]. This aspect is particularly valuable in mediation and socio-educational intervention, where adaptability and critical thinking are required.
Developing digital competencies also stands out as a significant benefit of this methodology. The experience allowed students to improve their ICT skills and better prepare for future professional challenges [60]. The results show how incorporating new technologies, such as generative artificial intelligence and web applications, into the learning methodology has enhanced the acquisition and development of their digital competence. The use of technologies in the classroom has proven to be highly motivating and well-received by students [61].
Addressing the second research objective (explore students’ perceptions regarding integrating digital escape room design activities mediated by generative artificial intelligence), the results indicate that students positively evaluated the activity, highlighting its innovative, motivating, and highly participatory nature.
One of the most frequently mentioned aspects in the focus groups was the positive impact on motivation and engagement with learning. Students emphasized that designing the escape room allowed them to actively engage in knowledge construction, moving away from traditional methodologies centered on passive information reception. The opportunity to design and develop their own challenges within a digital environment fostered experiential and meaningful learning, aligning with previous research on gamification and game-based learning [62].
Additionally, students highlighted that the integration of GenAI facilitated creativity and personalization in constructing activities. Tools such as ChatGPT and Genially were perceived as valuable resources for streamlining the generation of narratives, challenges, and interactive dynamics, allowing for a greater exploration of creative possibilities in escape room design. However, some participants pointed out the need for more structured prior training to maximize the effective use of these tools, preventing a reliance on automated responses without deeper pedagogical reflection [17].
In response to the third research objective, which examines how students have incorporated and applied the technological tools introduced during the activity, the results show that participants actively used various digital tools to design the escape rooms, integrating their functionalities at different stages of the creative process.
The data indicate that generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) was the most widely used tool, with 93.75% of students employing it to generate content within the escape room. Its application focused on creating images, developing interactive challenges, and simulating dialogs with non-playable characters (NPCs), which allowed for optimizing design time and enhancing the narrative coherence of the created dynamics. Additionally, several groups highlighted that they used ChatGPT as a guide to structure the challenges and establish a logical framework for the proposed tasks, thereby facilitating the organization and progression of the game. These findings align with previous research which highlights the potential of generative AI to streamline the design of interactive experiences in educational settings. Previous studies demonstrated that artificial intelligence can enhance creativity and efficiency in the design of gamified activities [9], while recent research has emphasized its ability to generate adaptive content and foster problem-based learning [19,63].
Along with generative AI, the Genially platform was used by 43.75% of students as the primary tool for designing and presenting escape rooms. Its ability to integrate multimedia elements and create accessible interactive experiences was key to materializing the participants’ ideas. Previous studies have highlighted the effectiveness of Genially in educational contexts, noting its capacity to increase student engagement and promote more dynamic and visually appealing learning [64,65]. On the other hand, 37.5% of students used HeroForge to create avatars and customized characters, significantly enriching the visual and narrative dimensions of the designed stories. The visual representation of characters contributed to greater immersion in the experience and promoted a sense of identity and connection with the proposed challenges. In this regard, character customization in digital environments enhances engagement and student motivation in gamification-based activities [66].
These results reflect a significant utilization of technological tools in developing interactive educational experiences, confirming their positive impact on creativity, organization, and the execution of gamified projects in the classroom.
Responding to the fourth research objective (Identify the challenges associated with implementing these activities), the results show that although the experience of designing digital escape rooms mediated by generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) was positively evaluated, students faced various difficulties during its implementation. These findings align with previous studies that have identified similar barriers to adopting technology-based methodologies in educational settings [67].
One of the main challenges highlighted by participants was their preference for in-person experiences over digital ones. A total of 18.75% of students indicated that a physical escape room could have been more effective in specific contexts, particularly in mediation training, where face-to-face interaction is crucial. Previous studies on gamification in education have emphasized that physical presence in these activities enhances immersion and allows for the development of non-verbal communication and real-time conflict resolution [68]. Although digital escape rooms offer accessibility and flexibility, some students perceived that the lack of digital skills among certain users could limit their application in socio-educational environments.
Another identified challenge was the limitation of the digital tools used in the activity. A total of 37.5% of students mentioned restrictions in the free versions of the platforms used, such as Genially and HeroForge, which hindered the customization and expansion of their designs. These technological limitations can affect the learning experience by restricting creative capacity and experimentation with interactive elements. Additionally, the time allocated to the activity was perceived as insufficient by 25% of participants. Students indicated that more sessions would have allowed for better familiarization with technological tools and greater refinement of their projects. Previous studies have shown that time is a determining factor in the effectiveness of active methodologies, as tight planning can generate stress and affect learning quality [69]. In this case, some groups felt pressured to meet deadlines, which may have limited their creativity and ability to delve deeper into the design of their escape rooms.
Finally, a recurring challenge was the initial difficulty in using digital tools, experienced by 43.75% of students. Although most managed to overcome these difficulties through collaborative work, previous studies on digital literacy in higher education have highlighted that a lack of prior training in using technologies can lead to frustration and negatively impact the perceived usefulness of these tools [70]. This research observed that students with less experience in managing digital platforms relied heavily on peer support, reinforcing the importance of implementing initial training strategies before applying these activities.
The identified challenges highlight the need for adjustments in designing and implementing future digital escape room experiences. To optimize the experience, it is recommended to extend the time allocated to the activity and combine digital escape rooms with in-person elements, promoting a more balanced and inclusive learning experience. Addressing these barriers will facilitate consolidating this strategy as an innovative resource for developing key competencies in educational and professional settings.
Several methodological aspects need to be considered as limitations of this study. First, using a single experience based on a qualitative methodology limits the generalizability of the conclusions to other contexts or university student populations. Another limitation pointed out by the students themselves was the duration of the intervention. Future research could design longer interventions that combine qualitative and quantitative methodologies with a larger sample to assess the impact of educational escape room design on students.
Moreover, implementing specific initial training for students could have been beneficial in addressing initial gaps, particularly in digital competencies. Future studies using an educational methodology based on digital escape room design could include this prior training to ensure greater familiarity with technological tools, reduce anxiety associated with digital platform use, and improve students’ autonomy in creating and managing escape room elements.
5. Conclusions The main contribution of this study lies in the innovative use of escape room design as an active learning methodology, where students take on the role of creators rather than participants. This approach requires them to deeply engage with curricular content by designing educational challenges that reflect real-life mediation scenarios. By integrating theoretical knowledge into a structured, immersive experience, this methodology fosters essential skills such as creativity, problem-solving, and teamwork.
Additionally, innovative technologies, such as generative artificial intelligence and web applications, have proven to be key in motivating students and improving their digital competencies. Although the study identifies limitations, such as the limited duration of the intervention and the lack of initial training in technological tools, the results highlight the effectiveness of this methodology in overcoming initial barriers and enhancing meaningful learning.
In conclusion, this experience represented a reflective space where narrative design, character personalization, and the strategic use of digital tools converged to create an immersive educational dynamic.

The data collected were limited to the educational context and pertain solely to classroom activities. No sensitive personal information was gathered and no interventions were performed beyond standard academic practices.

Appendix A
Criteria Excellent Level (4 Points) Good Level (3 Points) Acceptable Level (2 Points) Insufficient Level (1 Point)
Escape Room Design and Structure The sequence of challenges is logical and well-organized. The difficulty is balanced, and the connections between challenges are seamless. The game flows smoothly without interruptions. The escape room is well-structured, although some challenges could be better connected or adjusted in difficulty. The structure is understandable but has minor issues with progression or challenge connections. There is evident disorganization, with no clear sequence of challenges or unrelated tasks.
Variety and Quality of Challenges Various challenges (cognitive, logical, cooperative) are included to challenge players and promote learning. The challenges are varied and appropriate, though some could be more challenging or innovative. The challenges are somewhat repetitive or lack variety but still fit within the escape room dynamic. The challenges are too simple, confusing, or do not contribute to learning.
Integration of Social Skills The escape room dynamics actively promote communication, empathy, teamwork, and decision-making. Social skills are effectively incorporated, although they could be better integrated into some challenges. Social skills are mentioned but not clearly embedded in the game mechanics. Social skills are not evident in the escape room design.
Use of Mediation Strategies The challenges require the use of mediation strategies such as active listening, negotiation, or conflict resolution. Some mediation strategies are present in the dynamics, though their application could be more explicit. Mediation strategies are mentioned, but their integration into the challenges is limited. No mediation strategies are observed within the escape room.
Originality and Innovation The escape room is creative and presents an innovative approach in its design and challenges. There is a clear effort to surprise and motivate participants. Some creative elements are present, though the design follows conventional structures without major innovations. The escape room is functional but not very innovative, using standard mechanics. It lacks creativity, making it monotonous or predictable.
Participant Experience The game dynamics maintain a high level of motivation and engagement. The experience is immersive and meaningful. Most participants engage actively and enjoy the experience. The experience is acceptable, but some elements may hinder immersion or motivation. The activity does not generate interest or engagement among participants.
Materials and Resources Used Generative AI tools (chatbots, image or text generation) are used to enhance challenges or the escape room’s narrative. The materials are appropriate, and generative AI is used, though its implementation could be optimized for a better experience. The materials are basic and functional, with limited or unstrategic use of generative AI. No appropriate materials or generative AI tools were used, or their implementation was confusing or deficient.
Evaluation and Final Reflection A well-structured debriefing phase is included, allowing participants to reflect on their experience and learning. There is a reflection phase, though it is not fully structured. A brief reflection takes place, but it does not deeply explore the learning outcomes. No reflection or evaluation of the activity is included.

Cheese eK-Book: a new web-based medium for capitalising on, structuring and transferring cheesemaking knowledge and know-how

Author: Baudrit, Cédric1    ; Fernandez, Christophe1; Couteaux, Julien2; Buche, Patrice3; Bel, Nadege4; Charles, Cecile4; Notz, Eric51 Univ. Bordeaux, CNRS, INRAE, INP, I2M, UMR 5295, USC 1368, Bordeaux, France2 DOCAMEX, Bordeaux, France3 IATE, INRAE, Institut Agro, Univ Montpellier, Montpellier, France4 ACTALIA, Unité Produits Laitiers, Pôle Technologie Fromagère, Annecy, France5 CTFC, Centre Technique des Fromages Comtois, Poligny, France

Publication info: Baudrit, Cédric; Fernandez, Christophe; Couteaux, Julien; Buche, Patrice; Bel, Nadege; et al. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/cheese-ek-book-new-web-based-medium-capitalising/docview/3172017534/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: Purpose This paper aims to address the challenges faced by the cheese industry, particularly concerning the preservation and transfer of traditional cheesemaking knowledge. It emphasises the need for innovative solutions in sustainably managing knowledge and skills amidst changing demographic and technological landscapes. Design/methodology/approach Our approach consists of developing and implementing a digital tool, the cheese eK-Book, which is designed to capture, structure and disseminate cheesemaking knowledge. This tool is based on a semantic network and is accessible via smartphones and tablets and aims to facilitate continuous learning, knowledge transfer and collaboration across diverse stakeholders in the cheese production sector. Findings The study highlights several critical findings. Traditional cheesemaking knowledge is currently at risk due to a number of factors, including the ageing of skilled workers, a lack of succession planning and pressures from globalisation and industrialisation. The European dairy sector is evolving towards more specialised and automated production, requiring a skilled workforce capable of adapting to these changes. There is a significant gap between traditional cheese makers and research institutions, hindering the adoption of new technologies and best practices. The cheese eK-Book offers a promising solution to these challenges by preserving knowledge, supporting continuous learning and enhancing collaboration between industry stakeholders and educational/research institutions. The tool facilitates access to scientific knowledge, promotes work–life balance by offering a range of flexible learning opportunities and supports tailored training programmes based on individual users’ needs. Originality/value This article contributes original insights by proposing a comprehensive digital solution tailored to the specific, current needs of the cheese industry. By integrating modern technology with traditional knowledge, the cheese eK-Book not only preserves expertise but also fosters innovation and sustainability within the sector. It bridges the gap between practical cheesemaking skills and contemporary scientific understanding, addressing critical challenges such as knowledge retention, succession planning and workforce development in a rapidly evolving industry landscape. The strength of the Cheese eK-Book lies in its capacity to communicate knowledge, traditions and teachings across generations. This transfer of knowledge and skills plays a crucial role in preserving heritage and fostering connections across different generations within a community.
