Full text: Introduction The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) reports that traditional knowledge related to food production is at risk of being lost due to factors such as globalisation, urbanisation and changing dietary preferences (SOFA, 2019). Globally, the turnover rate in the food and beverage industry, which includes cheese production, varies widely depending on factors such as region, company size and job role. However, turnover rates of 20% or higher are not uncommon in some segments of the industry.
In the space of only 30 years, between 1983 and 2013, the number of dairy farms dropped by 81% in the ten largest dairy producers in Europe (Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Poland, the Netherlands, Italy, Spain, Ireland, Denmark and Romania). Dairy plants are struggling not only to attract employees with adequate qualifications but also to attract employees in large numbers. Additionally, dairy plants have difficulty retaining their qualified employees, sometimes due to natural causes such as retirement, but also as younger workers move out of the industry looking for better working conditions and/or higher salaries in other more promising sectors. Many young people aspire to achieve a work–family balance, which does not align with the traditional roles in dairy production plants that operate on 12-h daily shifts, for example. The European dairy production sector is currently undergoing a rapid shift towards more concentrated and specialised productions that increasingly relies on automated processes. In the light of these trends, the industry requires a more skilled workforce if it is going to be able to remain competitive in a market that demands innovative and sustainable solutions, both at the European and at the global levels (Sorensen et al. , 2019).
The cheese industry is not exempt from this general observation. Globally, traditional cheesemaking faces challenges including the ageing of skilled workers, a lack of succession planning and pressure from globalisation and industrialisation. In France, traditional cheesemaking is deeply rooted in cultural heritage, with many regions having their own unique cheesemaking traditions. While specific statistics on knowledge loss and turnover in traditional cheesemaking may not be readily available, reports from agricultural organisations, cheese associations and industry publications often discuss challenges related to succession planning, ageing farmers and preserving traditional practices. For instance, despite remaining the most densely settled mountains in the world, the Alps currently face depopulation and abandonment in the higher-altitude areas, causing a decline in traditional farming lands and occupations as well as a loss of the specific knowledge, skills, traditions, practices and values that shape Alpine Food Heritage (Rinallo, 2021).
Cheese technology (Fox et al. , 2017) is a blend of microbiological, enzymological, biochemical and physical knowledge and practices that require time, extensive educational activities and experience to be fully mastered. Raw milk, the main ingredient, can vary in chemical and microbial composition depending on seasonal variations, animal breeds, transport and storage conditions, etc., all of which significantly impact production processes, especially for raw milk cheeses. In summary, to produce quality cheese, personnel must possess far more knowledge and skills than merely following standardised recipes and operating production equipment. Variations in raw materials, production automation, adherence to food safety standards and the evolution of associated scientific knowledge (milk, proteins, coagulants, lactic acid bacteria, ripening flora, etc.) intensify the complexity of production processes. Processes rely on a diverse array of skills, expertise and experience developed over time. Manufacturers leverage their knowledge and proficiency to adjust their practices in response to changes in raw material properties and the specifications of final products. In the absence of formal tools for transferring knowledge, these manufacturing practices are typically conveyed from experts to novices through observation and imitation. Experts, who accumulate their expertise over many years, often find it challenging to articulate the scientific principles or all the relevant phenomena underlying their skills. Recently, the importance of sharing knowledge between universities and industry has become increasingly evident (Ferreira and Carayannis, 2019; Zimpel-Leal and Fiona, 2021). Traditional cheesemakers are increasingly required to consolidate and document their expertise, particularly by integrating it with contemporary scientific knowledge, to adapt to and mitigate the impacts of future climate change.
Local manufacturers often struggle to connect with research institutions, which limit their ability to adopt new technologies and best practices. This knowledge gap can hinder the sustainability and development of the manufacturing sector. To address this gap, measures should be taken to ensure the transfer of knowledge, including insights into market trends. Research centres offer up-to-date studies and technologies, providing participatory education and peer learning to empower local human capital with innovative techniques aligned with circular economy goals. This knowledge transfer encompasses not only theoretical concepts but also technical and practical support. Facilitated by communication platforms, this bidirectional exchange will close the gap between the remote mountain producers and research institutions (Habli et al. , 2023). The cheesemaking sector must acquire digital tools to structure its knowledge domain and then develop and exploit these knowledge bases. It is absolutely necessary to (1) maintain specific cheese training programmes/degrees, (2) continue to develop work-based learning within dairy schools and universities and (3) pursue continuous training for employees in the cheese production industry and students. The main challenge is to create new media and tools for staff training and development by capturing knowledge and reusing it to create a project history through the collection of expertise and data (Oesterreich and Teuteberg, 2016).
Cheesemakers are organised into sectors associated with schools and technical centres that promote and transmit their knowledge (both theoretical and practical). Cheesemaking knowledge consists of common knowledge related to production and specific knowledge for each sector. This paper presents the implementation of the cheese eK-Book. This is composed of a base cheese eK-Book that then distributes specific books for each sector and the use of them. They are based on a semantic network for collecting, structuring and remobilising the knowledge and know-how for making cheese with French protected designation of origin (PDO) and protected geographical indication (PGI) covering 46 cheeses. The aim of this cheese eK-Book is to (1) ensure the sustainability of knowledge and skills, (2) encourage the sharing of expertise on a daily basis and (3) ensure the reliability of handovers between people. The cheese eK-Book is accessed through smartphones and tablets and useable by all stakeholders via a modern browser in all types of environments and with different levels of accessibility.
Our aim in developing the cheese eK-Book was to meet the recommendations of the industry and to propose a tool capable of:
- Preserving the knowledge of employees who are about to retire;
- Being used and useable for learning and/or improvement in the workplace;
- Providing access to continuous training support that facilitates work–family balance;
- Associating small businesses with relevant educational and research institutions to develop targeted training programmes and thus provide tailored and individualised training based on the users’ level (apprentices, operators, experts, etc.);
- Providing access to scientific knowledge to better understand defects or deviations in the manufacturing processes;
- Being easily updated and upgraded by assisted computer.


Electronic knowledge book (eK-Book) The electronic knowledge book (eK-Book) is a semantic web-driven hypertext platform designed for stakeholders to organise, share and capitalise on knowledge. It utilises concept maps, process diagrams, hypermedia knowledge sheets, web pages and downloadable documents for the effective structuring and dissemination of knowledge. All the previous objects constituting the book are interconnected by hyperlinks. Baudrit et al. (2024) proposed a detailed generic methodology and a web 2.0 tool based on semantic web to build eK-Books. Concept maps (Cmaps) ensure the foundational structure of the eK-Book, featuring a two-level hierarchy that enables users to describe each primary concept based on four types of semantic relationships: taxonomy, synonymy, mereology and domain relation (see section of cmap in Figure 3b and c). Taxonomy is an ontological relation allowing the concepts of a domain to be organised from the specific to the general (Brachman, 1983). The synonymic relation makes it possible to specify equivalent alternative concepts in a given knowledge domain. Mereological relations allow a concept to be connected to the concepts which constitute its parts (Varzi, 2016). Domain relations are specific semantic relationships to the knowledge domain represented including causal, temporal, procedural relations, etc. Baudrit et al. (2024) precisely define in a set of part – whole relations and domain semantic relations (see Tables of S1 File and S2 File in Baudrit et al. , 2024).
Ndiaye et al. (2009) proposed a formalism for representing multistep process. The steps are ordered by unit operations and the number of steps is finite. Each step corresponds to a unit operation defined by a specific set of input state and output state variables. Each unit operation is governed by a set of control variables (see example in Figure 4b). The knowledge sheets are composed of a predefined set of clickable descriptive fields (see detail in Baudrit et al. , 2024 and example in Figure 4c). They correspond to the most detailed information about a concept. Knowledge sheets may integrate a number of different media, including a video, a sound, a photo, a drawing, a graph, a table, an equation, a simulation tool, a decision support system, etc.
Various digital platforms have been developed within the framework of the agri-food sector. For instance, platforms like ClassCentral (https://www.classcentral.com), Coursera (https://www.coursera.org) and EdX (https://www.edx.org) offer e-learning solutions such as Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) and Learning Nuggets, serving as global aggregators of online courses, particularly relevant to the agri-food sector. MOOCs are divided into modules or units that cover various topics, combining video lectures, reading materials and interactive elements like quizzes and discussion forums. Learning Nuggets often focus on specific skills or knowledge areas, both of which could correspond to knowledge sheets in the eK-Book. Industry-specific tools are offered by IT service providers such as Keendoo (https://www.keendoo.com/en/), which covers all stages of product development in the agri-food industry and provides a suite of software tools designed to manage the product lifecycle and data. While Keendoo is a data-centred software solution, the eK-Book is knowledge-centred. Oliveira and Cardoso (2020) and Kommey and Fombad (2024) explore social media platforms like WhatsApp, Telegram and Skype to share knowledge among rice farmers in the Eastern Region of Ghana and for Portuguese traditional food products. Their findings indicate that these tools facilitate knowledge and experience sharing that can lead to innovation; however, the lack of structure in the shared knowledge hinders its reusability. Moreover, many exchanges become private, leading to a lack of broader sharing. These platforms do not enable stakeholders to retain or store know-how for long-term preservation. Xie et al. (2022) highlight the potential of Augmented Reality to revolutionize the food industry, particularly in enhancing the effectiveness of food-related training and learning. Strousopoulos et al. (2023) enhance the power of virtual reality by incorporating gamification principles focused on apiculture education, demonstrating the game's effectiveness in achieving educational goals. However, obstacles to more widespread use include relatively high development costs, potential cognitive load and implementation complexity. More recently, generative AI (GenAI) has emerged as an interesting paradigm for knowledge transfer (Alavi et al. , 2024; Ghobakhloo et al. , 2024; Witkowski and Wodecki, 2024). It enables efficient, real-time retrieval of vast knowledge bases, providing tailored answers and facilitating personalized learning during onboarding. However, GenAI, trained on large datasets that may contain biases, can sometime generate incorrect or inappropriate content that cannot be verified by peers. The use of GenAI for knowledge transfer and problem-solving could potentially undermine critical thinking skills in the long term. Additionally, the “black box” nature of GenAI models complicates the explanation of why certain outputs are generated.
The Electronic Knowledge Book (eK-Book) design process adheres to the framework of knowledge creation defined by Nonaka et al. (1995) reinterpreted in the context of the digital transition by Cerchione et al. (2024). They proposed a dynamic process of knowledge creation, emphasizing the continuous relationship between tacit and explicit knowledge. This process consists of four phases, collectively known as the SECI model: Socialization, Externalization, Combination and Internalization. In the eK-Book design process:
- The Socialization phase (tacit-to-tacit knowledge transfer) corresponds to knowledge elicitation, where tacit know-how is shared through social interactions such as peer-to-peer discussions and brainstorming sessions. This phase could utilize modern tools like virtual reality or augmented reality environments for shared experiences (ref).
- The Externalization phase (tacit-to-explicit knowledge transfer) involves codifying tacit knowledge into explicit formats like concept maps, process diagrams or knowledge sheets (see section Cmaps, Process Maps and Knowledge Sheets).
- The Combination phase (explicit-to-explicit knowledge transfer) merges concept maps and process diagrams to form the foundation of the eK-Book, organized within a semantic network (see section Cheese eK-Book Interface and Homepage).
- The Internalization phase (explicit-to-tacit knowledge transfer) refers to the use of the eK-Book to internalize explicit knowledge, for example by offering interactive tools that simulate practical experiences (see section Evaluation and Usability of the Cheese eK-Book).


The cheese eK-Book has been implemented in the manufacture of French PDO and PGI cheeses using the Cheese_MBK tool (Fernandez et al. , 2021), which is an electronic knowledge book creation environment developed with Web 2.0 tools (HTML5, PHP 7.x MariaDB). Its interface designed for the web enables compatibility with contemporary browsers, ensuring that it operates across multiple platforms and environments. Creating and managing the cheese eK-Book with Cheese_MBK involves authenticated administrators who operate at three levels: (1) project administrator managing all aspects of the cheese eK-Book projects, including documents and user permissions; (2) cheese book administrator handling documents and user permissions but lacking project management rights; and (3) documents administrator managing document-related data without project or user management authority. Administrators may also designate “Readers” who can browse the cheese eK-Book within specified content restrictions.
Cheese eK-Book interface and homepage The cheese eK-Book currently contains a common core describing generalities about cheesemaking and nine specific cheese eK-Book chapters, each with their own homepage. It is currently composed of 1,496 knowledge sheets, 437 Cmaps, 8 process maps and a reasoning engine, based on decision tree structures, that is capable of proposing action levers whose implementation can correct or maintain the quality of the cheese (Buche et al. , 2019, 2022, 2023).
Cheesemaking knowledge and know-how may then be viewed directly by browsing the cheese eK-Book via a modern browser and can be accessed through smartphones and tablets. Users are not obliged to read knowledge in a strict linear sequence. Instead, the interface allows them to freely navigate through hypertext and select different pathways within the content. This freedom enables users to access specific information or to construct their own reading path according to their interests or needs. From a cognitive perspective, the hypertext structure closely resembles human cognitive architecture, facilitating the description of concepts across various contexts. This characteristic enhances cognitive flexibility and promotes the transfer of learned concepts. Figure 1 gives an overview about the different components present in the cheese eK-Book and the interacting network between all its components (some parts of Figure 1 are blurred for privacy reasons).
Figure 2 displays a screenshot of the homepage of the shared core cheese eK-Book with navigational hyperlinks represented by dedicated pictograms (see Table 1). Each of these pictograms is clickable and links to a specific type of resource, such as Cmaps, knowledge sheets, process diagrams, etc.
While navigating, the clickable breadcrumb trail located at the top of the Cmaps keeps track of the user’s navigation path. The left-hand section provides a collapsing menu that points directly to specific cheese eK-Books (such as Comté, Reblochon de Savoie, Beaufort , etc .) or cmaps, process maps and, in a window, displays the cheese eK-Book’s glossary index. Content in the cheese eK-Book may either be found or retrieved through a free search or by using a keyword cloud (see Figure 2).
Cmaps, process maps and knowledge sheet Figure 3 depicts a section of the Cmaps path from a specific PDO cheese homepage (see Figure 3a) to the Cmap for Penicillium Camemberti (see Figure 3b), passing through Cmap for the soft mould cheese ripening process (see Figure 3c). Penicillium Camemberti Cmap explains, for instance, that this mould is, among other things, composed of proteins, magnesium and lipids. It releases proteases and serves to modify the rind texture, aroma, etc . The conceptual map describing the soft mould cheese ripening process explains, for example, that the non-homogeneous Penicillium Camemberti coat distribution is a default.
Figure 4 (on the left) displays, for instance, a path from the previous specific PDO cheese eK-Book homepage to a knowledge sheet (see Figure 4c), passing through a process diagram representing a step in the production of this specific cheese, namely the ripening process. This diagram highlights, for instance, that ripening depends on relative humidity, temperature and the rate of CO 2 /O 2 inside the ripening room. The knowledge sheet in Figure 4 c explains the expert view about the chronological steps involved in ripening for this specific PDO type of cheese.
Evaluation and usability of the cheese eK-Book Transfer capacity evaluation Knowledge transfer is defined as the process through which knowledge is conveyed from a source to a target (e.g. future users, learners). This process involves both the transmission and absorption of knowledge (Davenport and Laurence, 1998; Cheng, 2020), essentially meaning that “transfer” is the combination of “transmission” and “absorption”. Its effectiveness is closely tied to how well the recipient comprehends the transferred knowledge, the cognitive load required and any disorientation caused by the transmission channel.
The capacity of the cheese eK-Book to transfer knowledge is evaluated using three measures: cognitive load, disorientation and understanding. These are assessed through single-selection multiple-choice questions. A lower cognitive load and disorientation indicate easier transfer capacity, while a higher degree of comprehension signifies more effective transfer capacity.
Understanding is measured through two tests: one conducted before (pre-test) and one after (post-test) navigating the cheese eK-Book, using single-select multiple-choice questions (see examples in Table 2). Cognitive load and disorientation are measured using a self-rating technique based on a seven-point mental effort rating scale (Paas et al. , 2003), ranging from 1 (very low) to 7 (very high). This mental effort rating scale is easy to use (non-intrusive) and provides a reliable indication of cognitive load and disorientation. The tests involve assigning ratings to these states, as illustrated in Figure 5.
The test protocol to evaluate the transfer capacity of the cheese eK-Book is detailed in an earlier publication (Baudrit et al. , 2024), which presents the cheese eK-Book and instructions. Participants then complete an information sheet, perform an initial test and navigate the cheese eK-Book freely for 20 min, before undergoing cognitive load and disorientation tests. They then follow a scripted navigation to find information using the eK-Book, take a second test, and complete additional cognitive load and disorientation tests. The purpose of the scenario-based navigation is to search for specific information in the Cheese eK-Book and evaluate the level of difficulty users encountered in finding it (see examples in Figure 5).
Fifteen individuals from diverse backgrounds (including operators, students, trainers, etc.) across three sectors (dairy school and two PDO cheese sectors) participated in testing the cheese eK-book. The participants had never navigated the eK-Book tool and had no prior knowledge of the formalism used in the eK-Book, such as concept maps or process diagrams, to structure and describe knowledge. Each participant self-assessed their level of knowledge about cheesemaking technology and their ease in web navigation at the beginning of the session, using a 7-point Likert scale that strongly correlated with their years of experience. For the Comté sector, the participants included technicians from the Technical Centre for Comté Cheese (https://www.ctfc.fr/) who are experts in cheese technology, particularly Comté. At the training centre, there was a mix of three students and two trainers (one senior and one junior). In the Savoie sector, the sample included four technicians and one project manager with a lower level of expertise in cheesemaking technology. Figure 6 presents their test results, including: (a) the number of correct answers, (b) the average level of disorientation and the mean cognitive load and (c) the average difficulty of scenario-based navigation experienced before and after navigating the cheese eK-book. In Figure 6a, positive feedback on knowledge acquisition is evident: with the exception of individuals 7, 11, 14 and 15, all users improved their scores, reflecting enhanced knowledge levels. Notably, participants like individuals 1 and 2, who were novice students, notably increased their scores. Overall, the average score for knowledge acquisition rose from 11.1 out of 20 before using the cheese eK-book to 13.9 out of 20 after, indicating an improvement of 2.8 points. This suggests effective knowledge identification, understanding, and acquisition during navigation through the cheese eK-book. Following free navigation, average scores for disorientation and cognitive load were 2.2 and 1.95, respectively (Figure 6b). After scripted navigation, these scores improved to 2 for disorientation and 1.85 for cognitive load.
These findings suggest that participants navigated the content with minimal cognitive load, ranging from very low to low levels, and experienced minimal disorientation, averaging from low to slightly low levels. Regarding scenario-based navigation (Figure 6c), the assessment showed minimal difficulty in accessing specific content, with an average score of 1.75.
Evaluation of technological reasoning support The capacity for technological reasoning support was assessed through two questionnaires. One focuses on analytical values and the other on corrective actions. Participants were required to respond to these questionnaires first without the aid of the reasoning engine (Buche et al. , 2019, 2023), then with the aid of the reasoning engine, after which the scores were compared. The objective here was to evaluate the tool’s ability to assist in technological reasoning (e.g. identifying the causes of a defect) and to see to what extent, in a scenario-based situation, the tool will aid technological reasoning. The two selected scenarios, associated with the Reblochon de Savoie production chain, are the surface contamination of cheeses with mucor leading to a crust default and excessive acidification. The participants were questioned on the corrective actions for the crust default and on the analytical values for the excessive acidification default. The participants needed to answer these two questionnaires and then were allowed to freely use the reasoning engine before answering the questionnaires again. In the case of surface contamination of cheeses with Mucor, there are 17 corrective actions to implement, divided into six main categories:
- Contaminated ageing room environment;
- Ageing boards contaminated with Mucor;
- Contamination by personnel;
- Brine contaminated with Mucor;
- Contamination during re-soaking;
- Water splashes on the cheeses;


Participants were asked to list the 17 corrective actions related to these situations of interest to be implemented. Regarding the excessive acidification for the analytical values test, the typical following questions were asked:
- Excessive acidification is said to occur when the pH at demoulding is below what value?
- A lactic starter is considered very acidifying starting from what acidifying power value (in °D)?


Figure 7a depicts the percentage evolution of the good answers about corrective actions before and after using the reasoning engine. The score of 100% means that the user successfully identified the 17 correct actions using the reasoning engine. Figure 7b displays the evolution of scores for the questionnaire on analytical values before and after using the reasoning engine. Regarding the students and the participants in the Reblochon de Savoie sector, their global scores improved after using the reasoning engine (see Figure 7a). The slight improvement for the Comté production chain can be explained by an Internet connection issue that altered the navigation time on the reasoning engine and required reloading of the hierarchies during the tests. The average score obtained for the corrective actions questionnaire without using the tool was 6.7 out of 17, which corresponds to 39% correct responses. This score increased to 11.3 out of 17, or 66.5% correct responses, when using the reasoning engine, representing nearly a 27% improvement. This result suggests a significant improvement in performance when using the reasoning engine. The score obtained for the questionnaire on analytical values without the help of the tool was 18.33% correct answers (see Figure 7b). This score increased to 76.25% correct answers with the help of the tool, representing an improvement of almost 60%. This result suggests a significant improvement in performance when using the reasoning engine. It should be noted that this evaluation was conducted only in the Reblochon de Savoie and Comté production chain because there are no analytical values corresponding to the school, which was more related to schooling.
Use case A cheese manufacturing company is dealing with a problem characterised by the presence of a dark fuzzy layer on the surface of its cheeses, commonly known as “cat hair”. This cheesemaking issue involves the surface development of a Mucor mould. The company aims to correct and, more importantly, understand the origin of the problem. Initially, the use of the reasoning engine will help identify the source of the problem and propose recommendations or corrective actions for addressing this defect (see Figure 8a). The company will select the most appropriate recommendation based on its constraints. For instance, it is identified that this defect is often related to changes in practices or environment which disrupt the balance between “technological flora” and “undesirable flora”. For example, the company may simply need to verify whether the new employee is adhering to all cleaning phases.
The company, due to time constraints or lack of experienced employees, can rely on the content and user-friendliness of the electronic knowledge book to reinforce best practices and train new arrivals. For instance, they can provide access to a knowledge sheet detailing “cheese ageing board hygiene management” (see Figure 8b). By calling the reasoning engine from the cheese eK-Book, employees can gain intuitive access to recommendations, explanations and knowledge. For example, if there is a defect like “cat hair,” possible inadequate cleaning of the ageing board is suggested. At that point, the user can click on “ageing board cleaning”, which opens a cleaning protocol sheet and a best practice video.
Conclusion Given the need for effective knowledge transfer tools in the context of a digital transition, the cheese eK-Books offer an efficient solution to collecting, structuring and mobilising cheesemaking knowledge and expertise. They are designed for both novice and expert operators (technical departments in the cheese sector or cheese companies), as well as trainers and learners (for initial and continuing education). The web navigation from Cmap to Cmap allows for in-depth explanations of specific concepts or the exploration of new ideas. The cheese eK-Books can be easily updated and upgraded without disrupting their overall structure, and access restrictions with identification help control the compartmentalisation of information within each cheese sector. This paper highlights the usability and effectiveness of the cheese eK-Book in transferring knowledge within the cheese sector. Tests have shown that the eK-Book maintains low levels of disorientation and cognitive load. However, caution must be exercised regarding these conclusions, as the tests were conducted on a small sample of users. Larger testing campaigns will be necessary to obtain a representative sample, confirm current trends and examine variability in participant performance. A significant limitation of the cheese eK-Book implementation – and of any approach aimed at efficiently capitalizing on and formalizing knowledge and know-how – is the time and resources that a sector must commit to this endeavour. At a minimum, for the effective operation of the cheese ek-book, at least one person from the sector must dedicate 2 days per month and be capable of mobilizing various stakeholders (such as cheesemakers, other technicians, affineurs, etc.) for collective validation of knowledge models. However, the greater the investment, the more capable the sector becomes of training its new operators more quickly and effectively. Since 2023, the cheese eK-Book has been used and enriched across 16 cheese regions in France ( Comté, Morbier, Mont d’Or, Bleu de Gex, Gruyère IGP, Beaufort, Abondance, Reblochon de Savoie, Emmental de Savoie, Cantal, Salers, Bleu du Vercors-Sassenage, Camembert de Normandie, Saint Nectaire, Ossau-Iraty and Tome des Bauges ). This enrichment has led to the creation of a French association in compliance with the French 1901 law (www.docamex.fr). The cheese eK-Book therefore allows stakeholders in the cheese sector (from novices to experts) to preserve and to have access to the knowledge of cheesemakers who are on the brink retirement. It may be integrated with on-the-job learning, providing access to continuous and customised training support based on user levels that, for instance, facilitate a better work–life balance. It allows cheese production chains to have access to scientific knowledge enabling them to better understand defects or deviations in manufacturing processes.
The implementation of the cheese eK-Book was subsidised by the French Ministry of Agriculture through its CASDAR projects within the DOCaMEx project, the France Relance project “Docamex, an innovative digital tool at the service of cheese knowledge and know-how” (12-363-DNUM-CAAF-003). The funders had no role in study design, data collection and analysis, the decision to publish or the preparation of the manuscript.

Adaptation and validation of a questionnaire for measuring nursing degree lecturers’ perceptions of using active teaching/learning methods in university education

Author: Abselam-Ali, Karima1    ; Capilla-Díaz, Concepción2    ; Puente-Fernández, Daniel2    ; Parra-González, María Elena2    1 Department of Nursing, Faculty of Health Sciences, University of Granada, Instituto de Investigación Biosanitaria (ibs.GRANADA), Granada, Spain2 Department of Research Methods and Diagnosis in Education, University of Granada, Granada, Spain

Publication info: Abselam-Ali, Karima; Capilla-Díaz, Concepción; Puente-Fernández, Daniel; Parra-González, María Elena. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/adaptation-validation-questionnaire-measuring/docview/3171531173/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: The training of nursing professionals has grown increasingly complex due to technological and scientific advancements, demanding higher educational quality and fostering critical thinking. The European Higher Education Area (EHEA) has emphasized active teaching/learning methods (ATLMs), which promote critical thinking, decision-making, group work, motivation, and knowledge retention. ATLMs require teachers to adopt a guiding role and adapt their methodologies. While tools like OPPUMAUGR assess ATLM use in education, validated instruments specific to nursing educators remain unavailable, despite studies highlighting ATLMs’ positive impact on nursing students. This study developed and validated the OPPUMA-NV scale for measuring nursing degree lecturers’ perceptions of the use of active teaching/learning methods nursing degree at the University of Granada. The scale, completed by 381 participants (70.6% women, the largest group aged ‘Between 41 and 50 y. o.’), measures six factors: The institution promotes change (14 items), Range of ATLMs (19 items), Traditional methodology (8 items), Student-centred teaching (4 items), Barriers to implementing ATLMs (9 items) and ATLMs implementation facilitators (5 items). It demonstrated high reliability (α=0.859). Descriptive analysis showed that gender (being a man or a woman) had impact on factor 2 ‘Range of ATLMs’. Within professional categories, had impact factors 3 (‘Traditional methodology’) and 5 (‘Barriers to implementing ATLMs’). This tool indicated effectiveness for determining the factors that influence the nursing degree teachers’ application of ATLMs.

The Virtual Reality in Your Head: How Immersion and Mental Imagery Are Connected to Knowledge Retention

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/virtual-reality-your-head-how-immersion-mental/docview/3159580475/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: Immersive learning is predominantly constrained to technology-based interventions but has the potential for more diverse applications. This study reports on an experiment investigating the learning affordances of psychological immersion evoked by narrative absorption. A total of 228 participants were randomly assigned to one of three forms of media, an image, a word list, and a narrative, all of which contained identical items to be memorized for immediate and delayed free recall memory tests. Other variables measured were immersion, extraneous cognitive load, and mental imagery. ANOVA and correlation analyses showed that the narrative media was found to be significantly more immersive and that it evoked mental imagery in individuals at higher levels than both the list and image media. Importantly, there was more decay in memory recall between immediate and delayed tests for those exposed to the list and the image than for those who read the narrative. This implies the utility of immersive narratives for spontaneous mental image generation, which leads to improved knowledge retention. Other implications for immersive learning theory are discussed, and practical solutions for incorporating narrative immersion in learning are also suggested.

The use of virtual reality in human training: trends and a research agenda

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/use-virtual-reality-human-training-trends/docview/3159007935/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: Traditional classroom training sessions can negatively impact participants’ engagement and knowledge retention. In response, several organisations are moving towards innovative and more engaging approaches, such as virtual reality (VR). By using VR, participants can immerse in a simulated environment, acquiring experiences in rare and hazardous situations that cannot be experienced in the natural environment without risk to the participants. VR has been applied in several areas, and this study aims to understand the applicability and impact of VR simulators on human training and perspectives of this emergent area. Drawn on a rigorous systematic literature review of 82 articles, the study presents findings from the thematic analysis. First, descriptive results outline the VR literature and its applications as an innovative training and learning tool. Second, a prescriptive thematic analysis has identified emerging themes related to behavioural, technological, and organisational benefits. The results also show the VR challenges related to technological limitations, restricted resources, and academic research. This study demonstrates the development of VR in human training, presenting contributions to theory and practice. The study presents some limitations related to the scope and focus of the study, and future pathways to address these limitations are suggested. For instance, the research protocol did not consider conference papers or articles that were not in English, and it was limited to a search period. Furthermore, emergent topics such as artificial intelligence and VR technology's physiological-emotional and sensory aspects in training should be addressed. Therefore, future studies should address these topics and use the research agenda suggested in this study.

Knowledge leakage through social networks: a review of existing gaps, strategies for mitigating potential risk factors and future research direction: Very Informal Newsletter on Library Automation

Author: Adobi, Jessica Timiyo1; Foli, Samuel21 Department of Business Administration, American University of Malta, Bormla, Malta2 Department of Business Administration, Tallinn University of Technology, Tallinn, Estonia

Publication info: Adobi, Jessica Timiyo; Foli, Samuel. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/knowledge-leakage-through-social-networks-review/docview/3157128790/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: Purpose This paper aims to systematically review the literature on knowledge leakage through social networks in the past decade to find existing gaps, identify potential risk factors while, ultimately, proposing ways of mitigating these factors. Design/methodology/approach This study adopted Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analysis as guide for searching relevant scholarly publications. Subject-specific and -related research papers were obtained from three databases, namely, Scopus, Web of Science and EBSCOhost. The review data was generated from the search results while adopting specific criteria to either accept or reject a particular publication during the search process. Findings Technological, operational and human knowledge factors are some of the risks resulting from knowledge leakage. Highlights of the paper include strategies for mitigating these factors, including continuous training, creating awareness, banning social media usage at work and reinforcing nondisclosure policies. This study also found potential gaps from the literature, categorized as topical, geographical, industrial, theoretical, methodological and conceptual gaps while proposing ways of addressing these gaps using specific research questions. These questions set the direction for future studies on knowledge leakage and social networks. Originality/value Implications of the findings are laid out, particularly the idea of developing actionable managerial plans for preventing knowledge leakage from occurring in organizations in the first place. The systematic, rigorous, transparent and methodological procedures used throughout the entire research process strongly suggest that the findings and conclusions are legitimate. While the findings were not drawn arbitrarily, they potentially offer windows of opportunities for bridging the six potential gaps identified in this paper.

Full text: 1. Introduction Despite the many downsides and implementation challenges, technology continues to dominate our daily lives, as individuals both at work and leisure. Like it or not, it is here to stay and will keep defining how work is being performed (Wardynski, 2019). This is more alarming since the boundary between work and leisure is getting quite blurry, thus making it hard for individuals to separate work from leisure. As more employees now work from home than ever before (de Haas et al. , 2020), the work–leisure boundary will keep narrowing down until one runs out of precise definitions of work and leisure. Even growth patterns and trends of business organizations are equally changing at an astronomical pace. Mostly, due to recent events from the global health crisis (coronavirus pandemic), forcing companies to digitalize almost all aspects of their operations, including mundane activities (Soto-Acosta, 2020). However, it is believed that the new work setting is more efficient compared to traditional methods. The evidence could be seen in the many ways technology dehumanizes the boundary between humans and operating machinery in the workplace (Slack and Brandon-Jones, 2018).
Nevertheless, technology poses a threat to businesses and society in general. First, to optimize, businesses must keep pace with the latest technology in their industry while at the same time exploring alternative means of addressing customer satisfaction and firms’ profit maximization objectives. The second challenge is where businesses are expected to communicate effectively with diverse stakeholders using digitalized technologies while at the same time being competitive within their respective industries (Cheah et al. , 2021). Social networks are means for engaging in active communication among organizations’ stakeholder groups. An often-overlooked beneficial aspect of social networks is the tendency of promptly facilitating rapid diffusion and transfer of knowledge among individuals and firms (Jiang and Luo, 2020). In spite of such remarkable benefits to businesses of all types and sizes (Chatterjee and Kar, 2020), if used in an unprotected manner, social networks could possibly violate confidentiality policies of individuals and organizations, thereby infringing on the privacy rights of ordinary people as well as business organizations. Social networks represent widespread medium through which knowledge leakage – the accidental sharing of sensitive information or trade secrets to unintended parties, occurs (Sarigianni et al. , 2015). Transferring knowledge among stakeholders through social networks exposes organizations to risks that could be exploited by rival firms. Knowledge leakage occurs where an individual or organization inadvertently (or intentionally) releases critical information about an organization or other individuals, to unauthorized persons or organizations (Ahmad et al. , 2014; Serna et al. , 2017). What this means is that knowledge leakage can occur accidentally, with no prior motives for such leakage.
For quite some time, knowledge leakage has dominated mainstream dialogue in the knowledge management field, thus presenting contentious viewpoints among scholars (Arias-Pérez et al. , 2020; Durst et al. , 2015a, 2015b; Parker, 2012) and industry practitioners, particularly in the past two decades. Thus, ushering in the dawn of a new approach for managing knowledge as one of the most important intangible assets of an organization. Businesses have realized that how they effectively manage their knowledge base determines, to a large extent, their level of competitiveness within an industry. Indicating a bold move to treat knowledge as a major competitive priority (Agudelo et al. , 2016), as it enhances firms’ ability to create value and secure market dominance in an industry. Hence, it is a highly protected commodity, particularly from imitation and theft by individuals and other firms. Since its emergence in the past few decades (Durst et al. , 2015a), knowledge leakage has attracted enormous research among scholars from different backgrounds even though it is not new within the broader field of knowledge management.
So far, there seems to be a substantial amount of research (Durst et al. , 2015b; Ferenhof, 2016) on knowledge leakage, including empirical and conceptual. But those that have used the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA) approach to investigate knowledge leakage are relatively few. This systematic literature review (SLR) paper adopts the PRISMA research approach to examine knowledge leakage through social networks. Related research publications were sourced from three databases while applying specific search criteria for either accepting or rejecting publications during the search process. Key findings and potential research gaps identified from the review have been highlighted in this paper. This will set the direction for future research with the aim of advancing the discourse on knowledge leakage and social networks.
The paper is divided into six sections. Section 1 deals with general introduction of knowledge leakage and social networks, whereas Section 2 comprises definitions of some key terms that were used in the paper. The methodological approach of the paper is discussed in Section 3, whereas Section 4 presents the thematic classifications of the 26 research publications that provided the analytical data for this paper. This is followed by identifying existing gaps and future research directions in Section 5, and our concluding remarks are presented in Section 6, including theoretical underpinnings and managerial implications of our research findings.
2. Definition of terms Social networks and social networking Changes in work situations, particularly online transitioning, demand employees to make life-changing adjustments to work schedules and personal lifestyles. This has led to unprecedented traffic in online activities, as most websites and online platforms are subjected to intense traffic jams. Social networking thus is now the new normal, as more organizations use it to conduct remote business activities (Anamaria-Mirabela and Monica-Ariana, 2020; Moqbel et al. , 2020). But, what does social network mean? To date, scholars have used social networks and social networking interchangeably, thus disregarding the existence of nuances of both terms. To build consensus, these and other related terminologies are carefully examined and presented in Table 1.
Among the commonly used terms are online social networks (Akkuzu et al. , 2020; Cai et al. , 2020; Wu and Pan, 2021), social network sites (Asuncion and Goodrich, 2010; Nagpure and Jadhav, 2015; Praveena and Smys, 2017), social media (Cho et al. , 2020) and the more generic social networking (DiMicco et al. , 2008; Sophia van Zyl, 2009; Weaver and Morrison, 2008). Though there are no plausible explanations given over the use of different terms, nor why two are used interchangeably, existing research suggests there are differences among these terminologies.
The literature makes use of two main terminologies – social networks and social networking as illustrated in Table 1. Social networks refer to the medium of platforms like Twitter, Facebook, Skype, Instagram, FaceTime and WhatsApp where social interactions occur among individuals in group settings. It is the mechanism through which people interact with each other, whereas social networking describes the interactive process itself. Some of these interactions take place on daily basis, thus are quite frequent; others are not so frequent and take place inadvertently or as occasion demands. Networking, therefore, describes how individuals communicate with each other. This can either be by sending audio messages or engaging in face-to-face video call conversations.
Knowledge and knowledge leakage Some large organizations treat knowledge as a vital resource. Equally, mainstream research (Hajli et al. , 2013; Hitchen et al. , 2017) agrees it is an invaluable scarce commodity that ought to be guarded jealously, as no firm is willing to share it with rival companies. Fundamentally, knowledge is embedded within the culture of an organization and comprises attitudes, values, work processes and rituals of the organisation. It may also be encapsulated in the technology that is used by the organization or, perhaps, the cognitive disposition capability and knowhow of the firm. This latter form of knowledge is often difficult to codify, leading to the two broad classifications of knowledge – tacit and explicit knowledge (Nonaka and Krogh, 2009).
Tacit knowledge includes conceptual models, norms and shared beliefs held by members of an organization (Fawad Sharif et al. , 2022). It is this type of knowledge that exists within an organization’s culture, hence difficult to codify (i.e. copy, replicate or transferred) from one organization to another. Explicit knowledge, on the other hand, can readily be codified, imitated and replicated throughout an organization, which could benefit the organization in many ways, particularly during times of rapid decision-making and implementations. Since it is prone to imitations, explicit knowledge can easily be transmitted from one organization to another (Fawad Sharif et al. , 2022). Both are readily available in almost all forms of organisations, but the challenge facing most organisations is how to protect explicit knowledge from theft, imitations and leakage since it is more likely to be copied by rival firms. Ritala et al. (2015) opines knowledge leakage has negative impact on firms’ competitive position and profitability. Sikka (2018) warned that Fortune-500 firms are estimated to incur losses of about $51.5bn a year due to knowledge leakage, hence necessitating organizations to effectively manage knowledge in ways that secures it from being hijacked by rival firms.
Leakage in tacit knowledge is avoidable and occurs primarily through employees’ personal interactions or close social relations with employees from other companies (Gertler, 2003). Explicit knowledge leakage, on the other, is inevitable and mostly occurs in a well-structured and systematic manner. Both types of knowledge can equally leak through the usage of mobile devices (Agudelo-Serna et al. , 2017) or social networks. Many scholars (Ford and Mason 2013b; Foli, 2022; Leonardi et al. , 2013; Yahav et al. , 2014) have warned that social networks remain the perfect breeding ground for leakages in both types of knowledge.
3. Methods and procedure Drawing insights from the stepwise workflow, as was originally designed by Jesson et al. (2011) (Figure 2), we adopted the PRISMA procedure. This was further modified as the PRISMA Search Framework (PSF) (Figure 1), in accordance with Liberati et al. (2009), to enable us to systematically review studies on knowledge leakage and social network. The PSF was developed to vividly display outcome of our search process drawn from three databases namely Scopus, Web of Science (WoS) and EBSCOhost. PRISMA is increasingly being used in SLR studies for supporting the legitimacy of conducting such studies. The past decade has witnessed frequent use of the PRISMA research protocol among researchers, primarily, for validating the quality of SLR studies. In addition to this, PRISMA helps to address issues of transparency, accuracy and reproducibility of such studies (Nasir et al. , 2020), some of which have also been published in leading academic journals in different fields of study (Abelha et al. , 2020; Booth et al. , 2020; Fukazawa et al. , 2019; Gledhill et al. , 2017; Górska-Warsewicz and Kulykovets, 2020; Mengist et al. , 2020).
In spite of the strength of this research protocol, the burden of proof regarding evidence of SLR studies continue to raise questions. Sometimes, researchers using SLR studies face problems of accessibility and contradictory interpretations of search results. This is because search systems enabling researchers “access to this evidence provide varying levels of precision, recall and reproducibility and also demand different levels of effort” (Gusenbauer and Haddaway, 2020, p. 181). Based on Gusenbauer’s and Haddaway’s (2020) research on academic search systems providing suitable reviews for SLR studies and meta-analyses, evidence identification and synthesis are considered crucial aspects of SLR studies. Both allow researchers to carefully consider the appropriateness of sample size for SLR studies, by providing a pathway for ascertaining the legitimacy of such studies and their corresponding outcomes.
But, if such studies are conducted haphazardly, like the manner with conventional reviews in the past, then the rigor and authenticity of the process could possibly be called into question. Thus, acknowledging that even if SLR studies have come a long way, conducting them arbitrarily will likely undermine their credibility. Over the years, scholars have strongly criticized the results of such arbitrarily conducted studies, arguing that they should not be considered as “genuine pieces of investigatory science” (Tranfield et al. , 2003, p. 207). The above discourse makes the case for evidence-based research and its importance to SLR studies. Doing so will enhance the transparency of the entire research process of SLR studies (Henry et al. , 2017), from conceptualization of research ideas, data collection, analysis to interpretation of findings.
This present SLR study sourced information from three main databases, namely, Scopus, WoS and EBSCOhost using a combination of keywords like “social media AND leakage,” “social networks AND leakage” and “social network sites AND leakages.” As of March 2021, search for keyword combinations produced an initial outcome of 895 research items from all three databases. Among these, 390 were obtained from Scopus, 371 from WoS, whereas 134 were sourced from EBSCOhost.
The 895 research items were further scrutinized to remove articles other than peer-reviewed research papers and conference proceedings thus, further reducing the number to 808. Out of which, 363 were obtained from Scopus, 365 from WoS, whereas 80 were from EBSCOhost. Due to indexing purposes, some research items were found to have been uploaded into more than one database, these were also removed from all three databases by categorizing each research item into separate Microsoft Excel spreadsheets.
Scopus was used as the main point of reference due to its scope and rate of acceptability in academia worldwide, whereas WoS and EBSCOhost formed the basis for comparing research items using either find and/or search commands in excel spreadsheets. A major advantage of doing so was to help speed up the process of selecting the research papers. As a result, 212 research papers were found to have duplicate copies in WoS, whereas 47 were discovered in EBSCOhost. These were excluded from the final selection process. Each research item was then screened through abstracting to eliminate items that were found inconsistent with the objective of this paper.
The abstracting process further reduced the number of research items to 474, out of which, 307 were obtained from Scopus, 137 from WoS and 30 from EBSCOhost. These were also eliminated from the selection process. Each research item was fully text-screened in line with the set standard of inclusion and exclusion criteria. The text screening process produced 26 peer-reviewed research papers, in which 22 were from Scopus, 3 from WoS and 1 from EBSCOhost. These were then merged and entered into a single spreadsheet.
Our research study procedure and process is premised on past studies relating to SLR (Carlbring et al. , 2018; Chu et al. , 2018). We believe our sample size of 26 research papers falls within acceptable range of SLR studies and is therefore considered appropriate, especially as we drew our proposition based on insights from a recent study by Gusenbauer and Haddaway (2020). Finally, the rigorous selection process ended with items on the spreadsheet being meticulously reviewed, one at a time, with respect to four broad themes – yearly number of publications, subject area of publications, research approach used and theoretical framework of the studies. Thus, Section 4 of this paper provides an extensive review of the 26 articles, with respect to the four themes.
4. Thematic classifications of articles Classifications based on yearly number of publications Years 2015 and 2017 saw an unprecedented increase in the number of research papers published on knowledge leakage and social networks (Figure 3). The Global Data Leakage (2016, 2018) registered between 1,505–2,131 leaks in 2015 and 2017 alone. This suggests a 7.8%–36.9% increase compared to the previous two years (i.e. 2014 and 2016), respectively, thereby indicating that knowledge leaks via social networks represent the largest number among all leak channels. In support of Ford and Mason’s (2013a, 2013b) advocacy for more research in this area, many scholars have since responded to the call. The origin of their advocacy can be traced back to the Hawaii International Conferences for Systems Sciences (HICSS) in January 2012, where the authors served as co-chairs of a minitrack on knowledge management and social media. This event may be the reason for the increased interest (particularly between 2014 and 2015 compared to other periods) in the subject matter among scholars largely because of its (HICSS) high recognition.
Classifications based on subject area A summary of the research items based on subject areas is presented next (Figure 4). We found a good number of publications within the fields of business, management and economics. Out of the 26 research items, 9 covered these three disciplines. Computer science was next (i.e. 3 publications out of 26), whereas other fields of study such as interdisciplinary, technology, communication and electronics each had one publication. Ten out of the 26 research items were conference papers; the remaining 16 articles were published in notable journals. These include the Academy of Management Journal , Communications in Computer and Information Science , Computers and Security , Computers in Human Behavior and Contemporary Accounting Research . Others include the Electronics (Switzerland) , Global Strategy Journal , Industrial Management and Data System , Industrial Marketing Management , International Journal of Information Management , International Journal of Knowledge Management, Journal of Business Strategy , Journal of Operations Management , Online Social Networks and Media , Sustainability (Switzerland ) and Technological Forecasting and Social Change . However, it is worth pointing out that even though most of the research items addressed the field of management, only one journal covered the area of knowledge, therefore ostensibly revealing a gap within the knowledge management – social network dyad.
Classifications based on research approach Various research methodologies were adopted by the 26 articles. This information is presented in a tabular form (Table 2). The table highlights in detail the research approaches used in the studies, a synthesis of data collection, as well as analytical procedures used by the authors. The data revealed that the quantitative research approach was the most widely used approach because 11 out of the 26 research publications adopted the quantitative approach in examining the issues addressed in the respective studies. The qualitative research approach ranked the second most widely used approach since 7 out of the 26 articles adopted this approach, whereas 5 of the 26 research publications adopted the mixed methods approach. Two of the publications were conceptual papers, whereas one was mainly a literature review paper. Based on this observation, we conclude that these last three publications did not adopt any particular methodology.
Among other things, Table 2 reveal that there is lack of sufficient research studies exploring knowledge leakage and social networks. The few studies that have explored this dyad appeared to have relied heavily on survey data while making use of either descriptive statistics and/or regression analysis as data collection and analysis tools. In addition to these findings, there are insufficient number of studies that used secondary data in exploring knowledge leakage and social networks, thus undermining the role of secondary data in shaping how researchers build or make advancements on existing knowledge. Lack of secondary data impedes researchers’ ability to develop fresh insights from what is already known in the public domain. In most cases, it is secondary data that reveals the gaps and nuances left unexamined by extant literature.
Classifications based on theoretical framework Finally, our investigation reveals that 18 out of the 26 publications did not adopt any theoretical frameworks. However, those that did, adopted some widely known theories like the agency cost theory, attribution theory, observational learning theory, regulatory theory, transaction cost economics theory, protection motivation theory, social exchange theory, information processing theory, knowledge-based theory and social network theory. We present a summary of the 26 articles used in this SLR paper in a tabular form (Table 3). The table displays the theoretical frameworks, contextual background, underlying aim and key findings of all 26 research publications.
Table 3 reveals two very disturbing yet compelling insights. First, research on knowledge management, generally, focuses on addressing issues and concerns of developed countries, particularly in Europe and the United States of America. Likewise, those addressing knowledge leakage through social networks rely heavily on these countries to gain perspectives regarding the factors driving knowledge leakage in organizations. Therefore, there is need to increase the amount of existing research on developing countries and/or emerging economies. The urgency cannot be overemphasized, as it prepares and equips these countries to better prevent knowledge espionage and other forms of theft from rival firms. Second, the table reveals that only very few studies incorporated relevant theories in examining the knowledge leakage – social networks discourse. Besides, those that used theoretical frameworks were mostly quantitative studies. Those without theories were mainly qualitative in nature, including a few conceptual papers. The next section of the paper addresses gaps in the literature, and thereafter, we propose future research directions on knowledge leakage through social networks.
5. Existing gaps and future research direction Apart from revealing three risk factors, associated with knowledge leakage through social networks, namely, technology, operational and human knowledge, this SLR paper identifies several gaps from existing literature on knowledge leakage and social networks. These are grouped into six broad categories as:
- topical;

- geographical;

- industrial;

- theoretical;

- methodological; and

- conceptual gaps (Table 4).



A summary of the nature of the gaps and potential solutions, which eventually leads to future research directions, have also been presented in Table 4.
Topical category was found to have the largest number of research gaps. It brought to bare the unexploited and unexamined aspects of knowledge leakage and social networks. This literarily suggests that our understanding of knowledge leakage is fragmented. Not only that what is generally known about knowledge leakage from social networks is, at best, circumstantial, it is consistent with previous research (Durst et al. , 2015a) findings. Specifically, there is lack of focus on knowledge management initiatives like formal integration mechanisms for controlling knowledge sharing, with the ultimate purpose of preventing leakages. The mitigation strategies proposed in the literature primarily focused on system management, even though there is need for one to consider strategies arising from knowledge management initiatives. Furthermore, the risk factors we studied are primarily techno-related risk factors (i.e. knowledge leakage risks arising from the use of technology). There is need to examine other types of risks, including operational and human knowledge risk factors.
Another area of research that requires attention is the examination of tacit knowledge leakage through social networks. As opposed to explicit knowledge, which is fluid and easy to transfer, tacit knowledge has a characteristic of “stickiness,” making it difficult to transfer or causing leakages. However, as suggested in Nonaka and Krogh’s (2009) model, tacit knowledge can easily be transferred through personal interactions, which occur via online channels like social networks. Therefore, it is important for researchers to equally investigate the possibility of leaking tacit knowledge, whether intended or unintended, through social networks and its implications on knowledge management systems and capabilities of an organization. Just knowing that this hard-to-copy asset (tacit knowledge) can still be leaked, one way or another, is very concerning and defies any notion of intentionality. This is because tacit knowledge leakages are bound to occur with or without genuine intentions of doing so. Further research directions, therefore, might also include evaluating the pros and cons of unintended leakages of tacit knowledge via social networks.
A comparative analysis can then be conducted between intended and unintended tacit knowledge leakages through social networks, controlling two out of the three risk factors – operational risk and human knowledge. Since such leakages occur via social networks, the technology risk factor can act as the mediator for such future research studies. While these are likely to present very interesting discourse regarding the subject matter, the issue of voluntary disclosure might restrict research efforts, particularly access to data. A synthesis of research studies could be conducted to explore the antecedents of disclosure regarding tacit knowledge leakage via social networks, to develop a conceptual framework that future researchers can draw inferences to support their own studies.
The geographic category presents regions and contexts that lack research on knowledge leakage – social networks. Our review shows that countries in Africa, parts of Europe (like the Baltic region) and South America, are yet to engage in active dialogue on preventing knowledge leakage from occurring, hence are prone to risks associated with such leakages. We identified strategies for mitigating some of these risks at the end of this paper (Section 6.2). Countries in these regions either lack awareness or are apathetic in taking the necessary steps to address the pertinent issues of knowledge management in organizations. Business firms operating in developing world countries lack basic infrastructure like good road, electricity and water. Majority of them cannot boost of state-of-the-art technology needed to take advantage of the risk management strategies proposed in this paper. Instead of adopting Information and Communications Technologies (ICT), most businesses still operate manually in these regions, hence mitigating the threats of knowledge leakage through social networks could pose a daunting effort for these firms.
The most common problems facing firms in Africa in the past decade, in using ICT to aid business operations, were “finance, system downturns, poor network from service providers, epileptic power supply, poor facilities and lack of ICT knowledge and skills” (Tiemo, 2012, p. 322). A major reason is because most public institutions in Africa are not managed digitally. In the same way, knowledge leakage on social networks is yet to make it to the top priority for leaders in Africa. Although recently, some countries in Africa now witness heavy government spending in technology and other social infrastructure, thus gradually showing concern for some of these issues. Since businesses are more prone to knowledge leakage through social networks than government institutions, they ought to be drivers of the change process. The role of government should rather be that of providing the necessary support systems for mitigating risks factors.
The industrial category highlights absence of research studies investigating knowledge leakage via social networks based on different industry background. As earlier mentioned in this paper, while there is considerable number of research on knowledge leakage, those addressing knowledge leakage through social networks are few.
The theoretical category reveals limited number of quantitative studies have, so far, used theoretical frameworks in examining knowledge leakage from social networks. As earlier stated, theoretical frameworks are very relevant to studies adopting quantitative techniques, than those adopting qualitative means. Quantitative research deals primarily with testing variables to determine the nature of relationships existing between the variables. They mostly rely on theoretical underpinnings used to substantiate claims or counterclaims resulting from such studies. Such studies require a critical examination of research questions and/or testing hypothesis, and in this instance, the variables would be knowledge leakage and social networks respectively.
The methodological category reveals an imbalance among different research approaches i.e., qualitative, quantitative and mixed methods, used so far to understand how knowledge leakage occurs through social networks. The most visible approach that seem to be lacking is mixed-methods research on knowledge leakage and social networks. Lastly, conceptual category describes the insufficient number of conceptual papers exploring the subject matter, further contributing to the scanty amount of available information on knowledge leakage. As earlier mentioned, extant research on knowledge leakage on social networks is either skewed or anecdotal, hence present disparaging viewpoints. This begs for answers to the question of how best both concepts can be investigated deeply to provide nuanced understanding and broad applications within the field of management.
6. Conclusion and research implications The past decade did witness a proliferation of research on knowledge leakage, thus making it one of the most substantially explored areas within the broader field of knowledge management. Yet, those addressing knowledge leakage in social networks are limited in scope and breadth. This article suggests that there remains an imbalanced and disproportionate number of research studies dedicated toward addressing knowledge leakage with respect to social networks. As the gap between work and employees’ personal life becomes increasingly blurry, since more employees take to social media to interact with friends, colleagues and relatives even during working hours, the need to pay attention to these issues is undeniable.
Our research is by no means ignoring the numerous research that has been conducted on knowledge leakage; instead, we are emphasizing that leakages occurring via social networks demand renewed attention. We drew our conclusion on the premise that, so far, only one management journal is exclusively dedicated toward research that explores the broader area of knowledge management. Thus, there is need to establish more academic journals for inclusivity and furtherance of evidence-based research on knowledge leakage. Future research directions advocating for research inclusivity on knowledge leakage via social networks is therefore a welcomed idea.
Theoretical implications This paper offers both practical and theoretical implications. First, it provides a comprehensive review of studies on knowledge leakage through social networks within the past decade, primarily to reveal the dearth of research in this area, with respect to theoretical application, methodological approach and contextualization of the studies. Second, the paper contributes to the academic dialogue and limited research examining how knowledge leakage on social networks can best be managed. Our paper serves as gateway for scholars and early career researchers interested in exploring knowledge leakage in organizations.
Early career researchers could benefit extensively from this SLR study by either replicating our study in other academic disciplines or simply advancing it empirically. Due to the rigorous, transparent and scientific approach we adopted throughout the research item selection process, our conclusions and recommendations offer legitimate basis for advancing research on knowledge leakage through social networks.
Managerial implications From a managerial point of view, this paper offers a synthesis of the ideas and research on knowledge leakage through social networks, which further reveals grey areas for managerial actions or inactions. Ultimately, it challenges management thinking to reimagine their organizations’ strategic goals, as well as evaluating viable options for preventing knowledge leakage from occurring in the first place. Nevertheless, in the event of any leakage, the following strategies can be adopted to minimize its effect on the entire organization:
- nondisclosure agreement (Serna et al. , 2017);

- implementation of online social network and security policy (Sarigianni et al. , 2015);

- creating awareness and training staff members;

- restriction access of social networks (Christina et al. , 2016); and

- high performance work practices and human resource management practices (Fawad Sharif et al. , 2022; Timiyo, 2014).
