Summary of articles
S/N Authors Context Theoretical framework Aim/findings
(1) Fang et al. (2021) USA, Canada Agency cost theory Analysing board external network activities’ impact on stock price crash. The findings reveal a significant impact of board’s activities on stock price crash
(2) Ried et al. (2021) Germany, USA Attribution theory Observational learning theory Evaluating spillover effects of opportunistic and information leakage between offender organizations and victims of leakages. Result show significant decline on observer's willingness to share information with offenders
(3) Bouncken and Barwinski (2021) Germany None Contextualizing knowledge ties among global digital businesses, with emphasis on the social context facilitating tacit knowledge transfers likely to reduce risks of unintended knowledge spillover. A notable contribution of the study was the advocacy for shared digital identity
(4) Li et al. (2020) China, USA None Building a model to predict message diffusion in social networks. It successfully developed a framework for predicting message diffusion with high prediction accuracy
(5) Annansingh (2020) USA None Understanding millennials’ habit of using personal devices for work and how this contributes to increased exposure on cyber-attacks, insecurity, and knowledge leakage. The author believes bringing one’s devices to work improves productivity and saves cost for firms
(6) Qiu and Haugland (2019) Norway Regulatory theory Examining the role heterogeneous people play in transferring knowledge within strategic alliances. Findings reveal that tacit knowledge transfer could be achieved through perceived trust among partnered organizations however, knowledge leakage could serve as an impedance to this process
(7) Li and Kang (2019) China, New Zealand Transaction cost theory Economics and social exchange theory Determining firms’ knowledge sharing strategies and factors influencing the strategies. The study identifies knowledge leakage as barrier to knowledge sharing while identifying knowledge relevancy and inference ability as factors affecting knowledge leakage
(8) Gao et al. (2018) China Protection motivation theory Information processing theory Investigating how ubiquitous connectivity, enabled by smartphone-based social networks, lead to privacy concerns and protection motivation, thus resulting in social networks users to discontinue usage intentions. The study provides future research directions, suggesting the use of longitudinal research approach with multiple data sources to examine the causality among the variables
(9) Cascavilla et al. (2018) Italy, Belgium, Denmark None Analyzing the leakage of information in Online Social Networks (OSNs), such as Facebook, by proposing the use of Open-Source Intelligence (OSINT) techniques to extract and infer information from publicly available data sources. The authors successfully developed the OSINT system capable of preventing leakages in social media
(10) Abdul Molok et al. (2018) Malaysia, Australia None Assessing firms’ ability to mitigate risk associated with leaking sensitive information on online social networks. The authors developed a framework for understanding firm-based OSN and leakage mitigation capability of the firm
(11) Choi et al. (2017) Korea None Presenting a method for inferring undisclosed personal attributes of users based on available data on their Facebook public profiles. It was observed that individual differences in matters concerning perception about online security play a crucial role as far as the usage of Single Sign-On services (SSO) is concerned
(12) Serna et al. (2017) Australia None Understanding the occurrence of risk changes using a conceptual framework to explain factors causing knowledge leakage to occur through mobile devices. The findings basically shed light on the various channels, which include social media, cloud computing and mobile devices, that could facilitate leakage of vital organisational information
(13) Kaya and Erkut (2017) Cyprus, Germany Knowledge-based theory Analysing patterns of social media use of financial sector employees to determine the importance of tacit knowledge as a competitive tool for gaining competition over rival firms. Results from the study offer useful suggestions for the financial sector in Cyprus and Germany, by contributing to research on tacit knowledge and recognizing threats that may arise from social media
(14) Leon et al. (2017) Spain Social network theory Identifying factors influencing knowledge sharing processes in internal social networks and forecasting future knowledge flows among the networks. The authors suggest Social Network Analysis (SNA) could potentially serve as tool for analyzing and predicting organisational knowledge flows
(15) Agudelo-Serna et al. (2017) Australia None Analysing knowledge leakage risk among mobile device users by presenting a conceptual framework for explaining the determinants of KLR
(16) Christina et al. (2016) Austria None Identifying knowledge risks among social media users in Austria financial sector
(17) Bokobza et al. (2015) Israel None Assessing the ability of attackers to obtain leaked information using social bots as opposed to wiring individuals’ profiles in organizations’ social network
(18) Sarigianni et al. (2015) Austria None Assessing financial sector risks in Austria so as to identify strategies used by financial institutions in addressing such risks. The findings suggest that further research is required concerning knowledge risks within the financial sector
(19) Cleveland and Ellis (2015) USA None Understanding common social networks technology capacities to propose a framework for explaining their influence on users’ attitudes. The findings reveal SN platforms are avenues for users to easily (with brevity ) share knowledge or information, engage in conversation with other colleagues ( communication/collaboration ) and provides options for users to personalize their account ( source identity ) to attract followers/subscribers ( subscription )
(20) Ilvonen et al. (2015) Sweden, Finland None Extending research on knowledge security, particularly on how to manage security in an organization, by developing the knowledge security risk management model. The study reveals what knowledge is important, how it should be evaluated and shared
(21) Hernandez et al. (2015) USA, Germany None Investigating the way firms protect themselves against knowledge spillover risks among eastern European countries. But the authors could not determine the likelihood of this happening
(22) Li et al. (2015) Singapore None Examining online social networks with respect to privacy leakage and control. The study’s results reveal that current control strategies were unable to safeguard individual personal information. Also, Online Social Network (OSN) platforms lack features to effectively protect user’s privacy
(23) Tse et al. (2014) Korea None Investigating the growing importance of using social media in facilitating business activities. The findings reveal that information risk could be categorized into privacy concerns, leakage of data and human factors
(24) Yahav et al. (2014) Israel None Identifying and quantifying unintentional information leakage issues so as to generate an automated system capable of detecting and preventing knowledge leakage. Results from the study validate the robustness of guided qualitative and text mining techniques, particularly in detecting information leakage though text mining technique, which produces better prediction outcomes than guided qualitative technique
(25) Abdul Molok et al. (2014) Malaysia None Examining the awareness of information security issues on social media among employees of a Malaysian education institution. The findings show that employees’ behaviour towards information leakages is driven mostly by how OSNs functions. The authors then propose mitigation strategies useful for knowledge management scholars to adopt in tackling leakage
(26) Braun and Esswein (2012) Germany None Examining corporate risks within social networks by assessing and measuring risk indicators for operationalization and control purposes. This is among the first studies on corporate risks in social networks, particularly in Germany

Table 4.
Future research directions
Classification of gap Nature of gaps Proposed solutions Proposed research questions
Topical gap Generally, there is an insufficient number of studies on knowledge leakages associated with social networks More research is needed in this grey area (under-researched area)
- What potential risks do firms face if tacit knowledge leakages occur through social networks?

- How might an organization’s knowledge management practices be influenced due to potential risk from knowledge leakage?

- What mitigation strategies should organizations adopt to mitigate knowledge leakages via social networks?

- How effective are these strategies considering the high technologically driven business environment?

- What are the most effective knowledge management initiatives, such as formal integration mechanisms, to control knowledge sharing activities and prevent leaks?

- How do various types of risks (e.g. operational and human knowledge risks) contribute to knowledge leakage through social networks?

- How does tacit knowledge leakage occur through social networks? What are the implications of such leakage?

- What mitigation strategies work best for preventing leakage from knowledge management initiatives?

- What is the role of social network algorithm in driving the knowledge leakage dialogue?

- How does the social network algorithm affect the spread of leaked knowledge? What is the nature and extent of such spread?

- How do demographic factors and individual characteristics influence the occurrence/nonoccurrence of knowledge leakage through social networks?



Geographical gap No studies on knowledge leakages associated with social networks have been conducted so far in Africa, Baltic region and South America Research should be undertaken in African countries, Baltic region (Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania) and countries in the southern part of America due to unique cultural difference
Industrial gap No studies on knowledge leakages via social networks have been conducted across multiple organisational sectors A future work may examine the differences between spread and/or dynamics of information leaked from commercial or governmental organizations and personal information of the OSN users (Bokobza et al. , 2015)
Theoretical gap Inadequate theoretical frameworks The use of theories depends on the type of research approach adopted in the studies
Methodological gap Not enough studies have critically examined, nor questioned the use of particular research designs to explore the concepts Future studies can adopt multilevel analysis or interfirm analysis to evaluate the causality among interacting variables as suggested by Gao et al. (2018)
Conceptual gap There are more empirical research studies on knowledge leakage and social networks than conceptual research papers More research is required for developing a sound and rigor theory

The contribution of technology according to special education teachers working with students with moderate intellectual and developmental disabilities

Author: Garnier, Philippe    

Publication info: Garnier, Philippe. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/contribution-technology-according-special/docview/3177901169/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: While quantitative measures regarding the progress of students with intellectual developmental disorders are important, it is also desirable to understand teachers’ perspectives on the value of these tools, as they are the ones who will design educational activities using them. This research explores the perspectives of special education teachers on the benefits of using technology for students with moderate intellectual and developmental disabilities. Nineteen special education teachers participated in semi-structured interviews, and a thematic analysis was conducted based on the transcripts. The findings indicate that, according to the teachers, technologies are valuable tools for students with moderate intellectual and developmental disabilities offering numerous advantages beyond traditional teaching methods. They are both motivating and engaging for students, as it makes learning more enjoyable and less stressful, particularly when it comes to handling mistakes. By adapting to students’ abilities and offering immediate feedback, it helps develop key skills such as reading, writing, and planning. The study highlights that, according to teacher technologies are essential tools in special education for students with moderate intellectual and developmental disabilities, offering innovative, engaging, and supportive learning experiences that foster motivation, improve skill development, and enhance knowledge retention while addressing the individual needs of each student. Balancing tradition and innovation: rethinking the dichotomy in anatomy teaching

Author: Čavka, Marina; Petanjek, Zdravko; Zanze Beader, Maura; Mathew, Thomas; Brassett, Cecilia; Nagy, András Dávid; Hladnik, Ana11 Ana Hladnik, University of Zagreb School of Medicine, Department of Anatomy and Clinical Anatomy, Šalata 11, 10000 Zagreb, Croatia ana.hladnik@mef.hr

Publication info: Čavka, Marina; Petanjek, Zdravko; Zanze Beader, Maura; Mathew, Thomas; Brassett, Cecilia; et al. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/balancing-tradition-innovation-rethinking/docview/3174460951/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: Medical education has undergone a significant reform in response to evolving health care demands, technological advancements, and emerging research in biomedical and education sciences. The teaching methods in anatomy, a core component of medical education, have notably changed, with traditional cadaveric dissection being increasingly replaced by digital and hybrid alternatives. Despite research indicating no significant difference in short-term knowledge retention between students who engaged in cadaveric dissection and those engaging in alternative methods, dissection uniquely fosters professionalism, empathy, and ethical awareness - traits essential for holistic medical education. This review critically examines the dichotomy between traditional and innovative teaching methods in anatomy education, questioning the assumption that traditional methods hinder progress in modern health care. The findings suggest that changes in medical education are primarily influenced by organizational issues, which frequently results in an incomplete implementation of innovative teaching approaches. The inconsistent application of innovative teaching methods makes it difficult to assess their effectiveness and compare them with traditional methods. Reliable data on their long-term impact can only be generated by randomized controlled trials and longitudinal studies. In the meantime, we need to ensure that current medical students receive high-quality education by incorporating best practices from diverse teaching methods based on valuable insights from experienced educators and current students' learning preferences.Medical education has undergone a significant reform in response to evolving health care demands, technological advancements, and emerging research in biomedical and education sciences. The inconsistent application of innovative teaching methods makes it difficult to assess their effectiveness and compare them with traditional methods. Reliable data on their long-term impact can only be generated by randomized controlled trials and longitudinal studies. In the meantime, we need to ensure that current medical students receive high-quality education by incorporating best practices from diverse teaching methods based on valuable insights from experienced educators and current students' learning preferences.

DEGRADATOR: A Gaming Expedition Into Targeted Protein Degradation Therapies

Author: Szulc, Natalia A; Olchowik, Anna; Jaszczak, Patrycja; Janiak, Bartosz; Cup, Mikołaj; Tomaszewski, Jakub; Pokrzywa, Wojciech

Publication info: Szulc, Natalia A; Olchowik, Anna; Jaszczak, Patrycja; Janiak, Bartosz; Cup, Mikołaj; et al. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/degradator-gaming-expedition-into-targeted/docview/3171879005/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: In an era of rapid scientific advancement, the need for engaging educational tools is critical. DEGRADATOR, a 2D computer game, bridges this gap by immersing players in the ubiquitin-proteasome system, a key pathway in cellular protein degradation. Designed for players aged 12 and above, DEGRADATOR introduces the molecular mechanics of targeted protein degradation, including PROTAC drugs. Through 10 levels of gameplay combined with educational quizzes, it represents the first-ever resource of its kind to make this advanced topic accessible and amusing. The game was evaluated by 97 high school students (age 15–19) during biology classes. Over 75% of students completed the game in under 30 min, and 63% rated it highly (4 or 5 out of 5) for its ability to enhance their understanding of protein degradation. In quizzes, 59% scored 10 or more points out of 12 on the final test, indicating substantial knowledge retention. Teachers highlighted the game's potential for deepening students' comprehension and recommended accompanying materials to maximize educational impact. By blending entertainment with education, DEGRADATOR demystifies complex molecular processes, serving as a tool for popularizing science and addressing the potential misconceptions surrounding new therapeutic technologies. Freely available at https://degradator-game.com, DEGRADATOR is complemented by teacher resources and multimedia materials, ensuring broad applicability. This innovative platform not only supports classroom learning but also fosters curiosity and understanding beyond traditional academic settings.

Exploring the Future of Education: Integrating Metaverse and AI Tools to Enhance Learning Experiences

Author: Svoboda, Petr; Knihová, Ladislava

Publication info: Svoboda, Petr; Knihová, Ladislava. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/exploring-future-education-integrating-metaverse/docview/3206678536/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: The study investigates metaverse technologies, artificial intelligence (AI), AI-enhanced tools, and digital competencies in education to enhance learning. A literature review highlights virtual reality, augmented reality, metaverse, and AI’s role in transforming pedagogy. A comparative analysis of Innovating Pedagogy Reports (2019-2024) identifies the evolution and trends in AI tool utilization and readiness for their practical application. The Key findings demonstrate that metaverse and AI boost student engagement and knowledge retention, yet challenges like high costs and technical requirements persist. A Chi-Square Test links higher AI competency among educators to increased online collaboration, underscoring the need for targeted training.

Emergency management simulation of an unexpected opioid overdose in a rural setting: An innovative use of drone technologies

Author: Niles, Lauren L.1    ; Sullivan, Veronica1; Amiri, Azita1    1 University of Alabama in Huntsville, Huntsville, AL, US lln0004@uah.edu

Publication info: Niles, Lauren L; Sullivan, Veronica; Amiri, Azita. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/emergency-management-simulation-unexpected-opioid/docview/3174447417/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: Background: The utilization of unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) in healthcare presents an innovative and effective approach for the delivery of emergency medical supplies to rural communities. Providing healthcare students with opportunities to work with UAS prepares them to embrace novel technologies in their future careers. Caring for individuals living in rural communities and those with substance abuse disorders are critical components of current healthcare education. Intervention: This simulation ready-to-use describes an innovative simulation learning exercise (SLE) developed using UAS technologies to address an unexpected opioid overdose in a rural setting. Methods: Students received pre-simulation instruction on the concepts of addiction, emergency management of an opioid overdose, and rural healthcare. Students participated in an unfolding, two-part SLE. Results: The first scenario simulated emergency management of the opioid overdose in which a UAS delivered rescue medications. This was followed by a second scenario simulating continuing care after initial stabilization. Debriefing of the simulation and reflection activities were completed. Discussion: The integration of UAS in healthcare education provides a valuable opportunity for students to increase their knowledge of innovative technologies. The UAS provides educators with a novel resource to expand simulation experiences, increase student engagement, and promote knowledge retention of difficult concepts. Instructions for implementation and educational resources provided in the Appendix. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2025 APA, all rights reserved) (Source: journal abstract)

Possibilities of Extended Reality in education

Author: Fernández-Cerero, José1    ; Fernández-Batanero, José María1    ; Montenegro-Rueda, Marta1    1 Department of Teaching and Educational Organization, University of Seville, Sevilla, Spain

Publication info: Fernández-Cerero, José; Fernández-Batanero, José María; Montenegro-Rueda, Marta. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/possibilities-extended-reality-education/docview/3168914005/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: With the constant development of technology and the growing interest of students in its application, Extended Reality (XR) expands the opportunities for students from various disciplines to stimulate their creativity and innovation in innovative ways in education. In this sense, the purpose of this research was to analyse the current scientific literature to assess the opportunities offered by XR, which encompasses Virtual Reality, Augmented Reality and Mixed Reality, in education. The study was developed following the methodology supported by the PRISMA statement, retrieving scientific literature from Web of Science, Scopus, ERIC, PsycINFO, British Education Index and Google Scholar. The analysis of the studies reveals that XR has great potential to enhance teaching and learning in various disciplines. The results indicate that XR can offer immersive and highly interactive learning experiences that can improve understanding of complex concepts and increase knowledge retention. In addition, it has been observed that XR can adapt to different learning styles and provide personalised learning opportunities. However, significant challenges are identified, such as accessibility and costs associated with its implementation in educational settings. Therefore, the need for further research to fully understand the long-term impact of XR on learning and skills development is highlighted.

The virtual reality in your head: How immersion and mental imagery are connected to knowledge retention

Author: Barrett, Alex1    ; Zhang, Nuodi1    ; Wei, Shiyao1    1 Florida State University, College of Education, Health, and Human Sciences, Tallahassee, FL, US abarrett3@fsu.edu; nzhang4@fsu.edu; sw22b@fsu.edu

Publication info: Barrett, Alex; Zhang, Nuodi; Wei, Shiyao. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/virtual-reality-your-head-how-immersion-mental/docview/3163848651/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: Immersive learning is predominantly constrained to technology-based interventions but has the potential for more diverse applications. This study reports on an experiment investigating the learning affordances of psychological immersion evoked by narrative absorption. A total of 228 participants were randomly assigned to one of three forms of media, an image, a word list, and a narrative, all of which contained identical items to be memorized for immediate and delayed free recall memory tests. Other variables measured were immersion, extraneous cognitive load, and mental imagery. ANOVA and correlation analyses showed that the narrative media was found to be significantly more immersive and that it evoked mental imagery in individuals at higher levels than both the list and image media. Importantly, there was more decay in memory recall between immediate and delayed tests for those exposed to the list and the image than for those who read the narrative. This implies the utility of immersive narratives for spontaneous mental image generation, which leads to improved knowledge retention. Other implications for immersive learning theory are discussed, and practical solutions for incorporating narrative immersion in learning are also suggested. Mitigating the impact of tacit knowledge loss in South African explosives manufacturing: A knowledge management perspective

Author: Mouton, Nelda1    ; Henrico, Alfred1    ; Van Wyk, Derick J.1    1 North-West University, Potchefstroom, South Africa nelda.mouton@nwu.ac.za

Publication info: Mouton, Nelda; Henrico, Alfred; Van Wyk, Derick J. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/mitigating-impact-tacit-knowledge-loss-south/docview/3301139118/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: Tacit knowledge loss poses a significant challenge in the South African explosives manufacturing sector, where specialized expertise is critical for operational efficiency and safety. This study examines the role of Knowledge Management (KM) practices in mitigating tacit knowledge loss, employing a quantitative cross-sectional design with data from 350 respondents. Structural equation modeling (SEM) was used to assess the reliability and validity of critical success factors (CSFs) and KM enablers. Findings indicate that human-oriented factors—such as leadership, organizational culture, and mentoring—are essential for effective knowledge transfer, while technology-driven solutions, such as documentation and databases, support knowledge retention. This research provides empirical insights into KM strategies tailored for high-risk industries, contributing to both theory and practice. The study highlights the need for integrated KM approaches to sustain competitive advantage and proposes recommendations for future research on longitudinal KM effectiveness. Augmented reality and embodied learning: effects of embodiment degrees on students' learning achievement, cognitive load, and technology acceptance

Author: Suo, Xiaochen1; Yin, Baoyuan1; Feng, Xiaoyan21 School of Educational Science, Harbin Normal University, Harbin, China2 School of Information Engineering, Henan Institute of Science and Technology, Xinxiang, China

Publication info: Suo, Xiaochen; Yin, Baoyuan; Feng, Xiaoyan. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/augmented-reality-embodied-learning-effects/docview/3297830146/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: Embodiment in augmented reality has attracted increasing attention in educational research. This study investigated how the degree of embodied experience in augmented reality affects high school students' learning achievement, cognitive load, and technology acceptance. Introduction Embodiment in augmented reality has attracted increasing attention in educational research. This study investigated how the degree of embodied experience in augmented reality affects high school students' learning achievement, cognitive load, and technology acceptance.Drawing on embodied cognition and the Cone of Experience, augmented reality learning tasks were designed with different degrees of embodied experience and implemented in biology instruction on cell structure. A total of 122 Chinese high school students participated and were assigned to either low- or high-embodiment augmented reality experiences. Data were analyzed using analyses of covariance, with learners' prior knowledge scores entered as a covariate to control for pre-existing differences in knowledge level. Methods Drawing on embodied cognition and the Cone of Experience, augmented reality learning tasks were designed with different degrees of embodied experience and implemented in biology instruction on cell structure. A total of 122 Chinese high school students participated and were assigned to either low- or high-embodiment augmented reality experiences. Data were analyzed using analyses of covariance, with learners' prior knowledge scores entered as a covariate to control for pre-existing differences in knowledge level.Students who engaged in high-embodiment augmented reality achieved better learning performance in both knowledge retention and transfer, and they also reported significantly lower cognitive load. In terms of technology acceptance, high-embodiment augmented reality enhanced perceived usefulness, while low-embodiment augmented reality was associated with higher perceived ease of use. Results Students who engaged in high-embodiment augmented reality achieved better learning performance in both knowledge retention and transfer, and they also reported significantly lower cognitive load. In terms of technology acceptance, high-embodiment augmented reality enhanced perceived usefulness, while low-embodiment augmented reality was associated with higher perceived ease of use.These findings demonstrate that the degree of embodiment in augmented reality experiences differentially influences learning achievement, cognitive load, and technology acceptance, offering empirical evidence and practical guidance for optimizing embodied augmented reality design in education. Discussion These findings demonstrate that the degree of embodiment in augmented reality experiences differentially influences learning achievement, cognitive load, and technology acceptance, offering empirical evidence and practical guidance for optimizing embodied augmented reality design in education.
