Introduction
In the dynamic and ever-changing realm of higher education, technology assumes an increasingly crucial role in augmenting the educational process. Mentimeter, Google Forms, Socrative, and Kahoot are well recognised educational technologies that have garnered significant attention due to their capacity to actively engage students and foster interactive learning experiences. This article aims to critically evaluate the merits and shortcomings of the four platforms within the higher education setting, therefore providing insights into their efficacy as educational tools for instructors.
Higher education faces the challenge of keeping students engaged, particularly with the increasing use of digital devices (Alenezi, Wardat & Akour, 2023). Playful learning, incorporating fun and interactive methods, is proving to be effective in this context (Heidari-Shahreza, 2024). Digital tools encourage active learning by allowing real-time participation (Wang, Sun, Li, Zhang & Metwally, 2024). Playful learning, combined with technology, enables students to engage through quizzes, polls, and games using their own mobile devices (Junior, 2020). This method transforms passive learning environments into dynamic, participative experiences (Sendra, Lozano-Monterrubio, Prades-Tena & Gonzalo-Iglesia, 2022).
Playful learning involves using game-like elements and interactive activities to engage students in learning. It stimulates creativity, critical thinking, and collaboration while making learning enjoyable. In the digital age, mobile devices provide an opportunity to seamlessly integrate playful learning into the classroom experience (Whitton & Moseley, 2024). Each tool has unique features, but they all aim to enhance engagement by providing real-time interaction and feedback. These tools encourage playful learning while integrating mobile devices into the learning process.
In higher education, maintaining student engagement is a persistent challenge, especially with the increasing use of mobile devices that can serve as distractions in class (Bedenlier, Bond, Buntins, Zawacki-Richter & Kerres, 2020). While technology offers many opportunities for interactive learning, not all digital tools are equally effective in promoting meaningful engagement (Haleem, Javaid, Qadri, & Suman, 2022). Educators face the dilemma of choosing the right tools that encourage productive, playful learning without compromising academic rigor (Chelise, 2024).
This article seeks to address the problem of how interactive tools like Mentimeter, Google Forms, Socrative, and Kahoot can be effectively integrated into the classroom to encourage playful learning and enhance student participation without detracting from deeper learning objectives.
The main aim of this research is to evaluate the effectiveness of interactive digital tools i.e. Mentimeter, Google Forms, Socrative, and Kahoot in enhancing student engagement and promoting playful learning in higher education classrooms. Additionally, it seeks to understand how these tools can encourage productive use of mobile devices during class time.
i. To assess the strengths and weaknesses of Mentimeter, Google Forms, Socrative, and Kahoot in promoting student engagement through playful learning.
ii. To compare the effectiveness of these tools in encouraging active participation and collaboration in the classroom.
iii. To evaluate the accessibility and ease of use of each tool for both students and educators in higher education.
iv. To investigate how the use of these interactive tools supports or hinders the integration of technology for learning purposes in higher education.
To provide recommendations on the optimal use of interactive tools to balance fun, engagement, and learning outcomes.
Literature Review
Strengths of Mentimeter in Higher Education Learning
Mentimeter, an indispensable tool in higher education learning, offers benefits such as increased student engagement. Its interactive features, including quizzes, polls, word clouds, and open-ended questions, captivate students' attention. It was co-founded by Niklas Ingvar and Johnny Warström. The company was established in 2014 in Stockholm, Sweden. Mentimeter has become a popular tool for interactive presentations and is widely used in education, business, and other fields to engage and interact with audiences during live presentations and meetings (De Martino, Tinterri and Dipace, 2023). This interactivity not only aids in keeping students engaged but also renders learning considerably more enthralling. This diversification of teaching methods, wrapped into one singular tool, translates into a more enjoyable learning experience for students.
Another noteworthy strength of Mentimeter is its capacity for real-time feedback. This feature is pivotal for both educators and students. Real-time feedback facilitates instructors' teaching by enabling them to promptly assess the class's comprehension levels, steering them to course-correct their approach when needed. Simultaneously, students get to instantly visualize their learning progress and find effective ways to comprehend complex concepts (Pichardo, López-Medina, Mancha-Cáceres, González-Enríquez, Hernández-Melián, Blázquez-Rodríguez & Borrás-Gené, 2021).
Mentimeter also champions active learning. It prompts students to be an integral part of the learning process rather than just being passive recipients of imparted knowledge. By shifting away from the conventional uni-directional lectures, Mentimeter fosters a dynamic atmosphere and interactive experience (Tay, 2021). Students transition from passive listeners to active contributors, making the learning sessions more inclusive and enriching.
A valuable feature that Mentimeter brings to the table is the option for anonymity in responses. When interacting with this tool, students can express their thoughts and opinions without attaching their names, mitigating the fear of judgment (Ristiniemi, 2019). Especially in higher education atmospheres, where diverse opinions are valued, this anonymity boosts the chances of students participating in class activities more candidly and extensively.
Lastly, the versatility of Mentimeter is unrivaled, solidifying its place in the higher education landscape. It can be adapted for a plethora of purposes, spanning formative assessment, peer collaboration, brainstorming sessions, and seamlessly fits into traditional, virtual, or hybrid learning environments (Nabangi, 2021). Its adaptability renders it suitable across various disciplines, catering to different pedagogical needs and teaching styles, thereby enriching the overall teaching and learning experience.
Weaknesses and solution of using Mentimeter in Higher Education Learning
Many authors (Musliha and Purnawarman, 2020; Nawi, and Na, 2020; Pichardo, López-Medina, Mancha-Cáceres, González-Enríquez, Hernández-Melián, Blázquez-Rodríguez and Borrás-Gené, 2021; Piatnychuk, Boryshkevych, Tomashevska, Hryhoruk and Sala, 2022) have identified the challenges of using Mentimeter. Mentimeter, although proven to be highly effective in enhancing the learning experience in higher education, does have some inherent weaknesses. Undeniably, a significant challenge is its dependence on a steady internet connection and digital devices. Given the disparity in access to such resources among the student population, it could inadvertently lead to uneven engagement and participation. This realization calls for proactive measures to address the potential disparities.
To address the potential disparities caused by connectivity issues, the educators are advised to stay prepared with alternative methodologies. Providing access to offline activities or synchronous sessions can help bridge the gap, ensuring that students are not left out of critical learning experiences due to connectivity issues or lack of suitable devices. However, accessibility isn't the only challenge to address when using tools like Mentimeter.
Another issue to be aware of with Mentimeter pertains to overuse or misuse. Over-reliance on the tool could potentially lead to diminished engagement because students might become desensitized to its interactive elements. Furthermore, deploying the tool incorrectly, such as using it exclusively for trivia, can lessen the educational impact. To counter these challenges, a structured and balanced approach is recommended.
The solution is to use this tool judiciously as part of an entire toolbox of teaching methods. By combining different teaching strategies, educators can maximize student engagement and learning outcomes. Providing sufficient guidance on how best to leverage Mentimeter for educational purposes can help to curb misuse of the tool. However, simply discerning the appropriate usage may not be enough, there's a need to master the technical side too.
The adoption of Mentimeter could entail a technical learning curve for both instructors and students. The process of creating and managing presentations on a new platform may prove challenging for some, and students might take time to become familiar with this new learning method. This realization surfaces the need for the necessary infrastructure to smoothen the transition.
Therefore, it's crucial for institutions to offer training and resources to smoothen the transition to using Mentimeter for both educators and students. Educational resources such as online tutorials or workshops can be beneficial in helping the users to tap into the full potential of this tool. Nevertheless, while navigating the technical aspects, considerations of data privacy must not be overlooked.
Data privacy concerns could arise when using digital platforms like Mentimeter, specifically regarding the storage and use of students' responses. It's imperative to note that these concerns might even be further intensified due to specific data privacy regulations in some institutions that limit the usage of certain interactive features of these platforms. It underscores the critical need for safeguards to proceed ethically.
A viable measure to mitigate such concerns is for educators and institutions to be aware of and stay compliant with data privacy regulations. Clear and transparent communication with students on how their data is being used and safeguarded is key. Educators can also pick and choose interactive features that dovetail with data privacy requirements to ensure ethical handling of student data. However, with these considerations in place, it's also essential to acknowledge the limitations of Mentimeter in a learning context.
One notable weakness of Mentimeter lies in its capability to facilitate more formal assessment processes. Primarily, Mentimeter is known for its prowess in fostering student engagement and immediate feedback. However, in terms of assessing and tracking student performance, it might not be as seamless or comprehensive as more dedicated learning management systems. As a result, it becomes necessary to consider it as a part of a more extensive system of educational tools.
The way forward might be to adopt Mentimeter as a tool for formative assessment, while more robust learning management platforms take charge of summative evaluations. Integration and complementing processes between Mentimeter and Learning Management System platforms can streamline assessment and grading, ensuring a holistic and fruitful learning experience. Ultimately, a blend of different methodologies is the key to an efficient, comprehensive learning program.
Strengths of Google Forms in Higher Education Learning
Google Forms provides a powerful tool for higher education learning due to its accessibility, user-friendly nature, and flexibility. Its widespread accessibility makes it an ideal system for educators and students alike, regardless of their technical proficiency. With no need for installation or special software, users can utilize Google Forms with just a Google account (Jeffery, Rogers, Jeffery and Hobson, 2020). The system's user-friendliness further enhances its appeal as the intuitive interface facilitates educators in creating diverse assessment materials such as surveys, quizzes, or assessments, which students can easily access and navigate.
Offering a high degree of flexibility and customization options, Google Forms elevates educational assessments' quality and adaptability in higher education. Educators have the freedom to devise various question types, extending from multiple-choice to short answer formats, and even incorporating file upload questions (Bhalerao, 2015). The platform's support for question branching proves especially useful for adaptive assessments, allowing the creation of unique, learning objective-focused assessment's.
An essential strength of Google Forms lies in its real-time data collection and analysis capabilities, providing educators with immediate feedback. This instantaneous data insight proves exceptionally valuable in formative assessments where educators need to respond swiftly to student comprehension levels (Bhalerao, 2015). With real-time results, educators can promptly identify struggling students and adjust instructions accordingly, leading to more effective student learning outcomes.
The value of Google Forms is further amplified by its seamless integration with Google Workspace, encompassing tools like Google Docs, Google Sheets, and Google Drive. This integration allows easy exporting, organizing, and sharing of data collected from Google Forms, significantly streamlining the assessment process. By saving educators considerable time when grading or analyzing results, this integration fosters a more efficient learning environment.
One cannot overlook the cost-effectiveness of Google Forms, a free solution for users with a Google account, a major plus point for higher education institutions operating under tight budgets. By allowing powerful assessment tools at no cost, Google Forms enables the strategic allocation of resources to other educational priorities, ensuring higher education institutions can deliver a comprehensive, high-quality learning experience without compromising financial stability.
Weaknesses of Google Forms in Higher Education Learning
Google Forms, while extremely useful, presents a few limitations in the context of higher education. One of the weaknesses is in offering a limited variety of question types. While it supports various question types, Google Forms may fall short in catering to all assessment needs in higher education. For instance, facilitating complex assessments such as essay questions or scientific calculations is not easily achievable through the platform. They also lack advanced features required for effective evaluation of higher-order thinking skills.
To address this key limitation, educators need to adopt a more holistic approach. They should consider using a combination of assessment tools, including traditional assignments, Learning Management Systems (LMS), or specialized quiz platforms that offer a wider array of question types. This strategy would allow educators to use Google Forms for simpler assessments and leverage more specialized tools for complex evaluations, shaping an all-encompassing assessment system.
Another significant weakness of Google Forms is its limited security and anti-cheating measures, making it unsuitable for high-stakes assessments. Given the ease with which students can search for answers or collaborate during online quizzes, the integrity of assessments can potentially be compromised. This issue calls for additional measures to mitigate cheating and secure the evaluation process.
To ensure the integrity of high-stakes assessments, instructors can enhance the security of Google Forms by using it in conjunction with secure browser applications, LMS tools, or proctoring services. These additional layers of security add substantial bulwark against cheating, ensuring a fair and effective evaluation process. However, guarding against cheating isn't the only challenge, as effective learning is also hindered by the lack of user engagement.
A third limitation of Google Forms is its predominantly one-way communication approach. With users mainly responding to questions, interaction or engagement remains limited. This lack of engagement can considerably hamper the active learning process and negatively affect student motivation. It is necessary to remedy this situation with more engaging instructional strategies.
By integrating Google Forms within a broader teaching strategy, educators can foster interactivity and engagement. For instance, Google Forms can be used for pre-assessment. The results can then be discussed in synchronous or asynchronous sessions, followed by another assessment through Google Forms. This blended approach promotes engagement and deeper learning, making the most of what the tool can offer. Yet, while this addresses engagement, there's still room for improving the feedback process.
The feedback customization offered by Google Forms is another critical area of concern. Despite supporting feedback messages for correct and incorrect answers, the feedback tends to be basic and may not provide the depth of information critical for effective formative assessment. Therefore, enhancing the feedback process becomes a crucial objective.
To provide comprehensive feedback that benefits students, educators can integrate Google Forms with Google Docs. This approach allows the creation of detailed feedback documents, complete with explanations, resources, or links to supplementary materials. Encouraging students to ask for clarification or further information after receiving feedback can aid in consolidating the learning process, effectively addressing Google Forms' inherent limitations and maximizing its utility.
Strengths of Socrative in Higher Education Learning
Socrative posits considerable strengths in higher education learning, with its capacity for real-time assessment and feedback representing a standout feature. Educators are empowered to concoct and dispense quizzes, surveys, and polls instantaneously, allowing immediate understanding of student comprehension and offering swift feedback (Aslan and Seker, 2017). The immediacy of this feedback loop proves pivotal in the higher education landscape. By facilitating quick identification and rectification of misconceptions, it bolsters student learning outcomes considerably.
Another significant strength of Socrative lies in its ability to bolster student engagement and interaction (Wang, 2015). The platform boosts active student participation by introducing a range of interactive activities. It supports discussions, encourages debates, and fosters collaborative learning experiences, all integral elements of a vibrant, engaging learning environment. Retaining student interest is made wonderfully feasible through these interactive components, further enhancing the learning process (Wang, 2015)
The power of Socrative also stems from its strong data analytics capabilities. This feature provides instructors with invaluable insights about students' performance and involvement in learning activities (Wahyuningsih, Muchson, Saefi, Muntholib and Suryadharma, 2021). The harvested data serves multiple purposes, including identifying trends, appraising the effectiveness of teaching methods, and customizing future lessons to accommodate students' needs (Jeffery, Rogers, Jeffery and Hobson, 2020). Making data-driven decisions enriches the quality of education and turns Socrative into a significant educational tool.
The accessibility and flexibility offered by Socrative, a web-based platform, maximize its usability and effectiveness. By enabling access from various devices, Socrative underscores the seamless integration of technology into learning. Students have the freedom to engage in activities using a device of their preference, be it smartphones, tablets, or laptops (Buitrago and Díaz, 2018). This high degree of adaptability shines especially in the higher education context, where catering to diverse learning needs and penchants is pivotal.
Weaknesses of Socrative in Higher Education Learning
Socrative, while a potent tool for higher education learning, suffers from a few notable drawbacks The weaknesses / drawbacks have been identified by some scholars (Nawalaniec , 2015; Aslan and Seker, 2017; Conceição, Albuquerque, Soares-Silva and Braule, 2022). One such weakness lies in the susceptibility to technical issues. Given its heavy dependence on internet connectivity and platform stability, Socrative can be affected by technical glitches like server outages or software bugs. Such disruptions are particularly troublesome in higher education, where every moment in class is valuable.
To manage these technical hitches, it is important for instructors to be prepared with backup plans. Preparing offline materials or alternate activities can be effective methods to ensure the continuity of the learning process. Such preparedness aids in mitigating the adverse effects of any potential technical disruptions on the user experience and ensures a smoother teaching-learning process.
Next, Socrative's handling of student data raises some privacy and security concerns. The platform collects and stores student information, which could potentially be targeted in the age of increasing data breaches and cyber attacks. Safeguarding students' personal information, therefore, is crucial and becomes a significant challenge when using a tool like Socrative.
To address these privacy and security concerns, institutions and educators must prioritize data security. Implementing robust data protection measures, such as encryption and secure access controls, can help alleviate potential risks. This approach underscores the importance of data protection and demonstrates a proactive stance against the threat of breaches or cyber attacks.
However, the challenges with Socrative don't end at security. There's a learning curve associated with navigating the Socrative platform, for both instructors and students. Since not all educators are tech-savvy, and some students might find the interface challenging, this could potentially hinder the effectiveness of Socrative's implementation.
Addressing this learning curve requires concerted action by institutions. They should provide adequate training and support for both instructors and students to enable a smooth transition to Socrative. Offering user-friendly guides, conducting workshops, and providing on-demand assistance can all substantially reduce the learning curve and enhance the user experience.
Finally, the risk of overuse presents another obstacle for Socrative. While technology can be a facilitator in education, an overdependence on specific platforms like Socrative can potentially lead to diminished face-to-face interactions and a reduced development of critical thinking skills that traditional teaching methods often used.
To strike a balance, educators should integrate Socrative into their toolkit, along with several other methods. This amalgamation of technology and traditional teaching methods ensures that critical thinking and interaction skills are duly emphasized, thereby maximizing the benefits of Socrative without compromising on essential educational outcomes.
Strengths of Kahoot! in Higher Education Learning
Kahoot!, a popular educational platform, excels in engaging students and elevating their motivation to learn. Its gamified approach, imbued with competitive elements such as leaderboards, quizzes, and timed questions, breathes new life into traditional classroom settings, creating an interactive and exciting learning environment. When students feel enthralled in a game-like atmosphere, they are more likely to participate actively, leading to better retention and comprehension of the subject matter.
The promotion of active learning is another key strength of Kahoot!. Moving away from passive listening, students are encouraged to actively answer questions and solve problems (Stige, 2016). This approach reinforces the learning material while simultaneously enhancing critical thinking skills, preparing students for real-world challenges.
Moreover, Kahoot! serves as an excellent formative assessment tool, equipping instructors with the means to quickly evaluate class understanding and identify struggling areas (Mdlalose, Ramaila and Ramnarain, 2022). With immediate feedback capabilities, educators can fine-tune their teaching approach on the fly, fostering a personalized and responsive learning experience for their students.
In terms of accessibility and convenience, Kahoot! garners high praise for its user-friendly interface and compatibility with various devices, including smartphones, tablets, and computers. Such adaptability promotes flexible learning, allowing students to engage with course materials beyond the classroom and encouraging self-directed learning habits.
Lastly, Kahoot! offers abundant customization options, empowering educators to create tailored quizzes and activities that align with their specific curriculum and learning objectives. By adapting content to the unique needs of their students, educators can provide a targeted and meaningful learning experience that better prepares students for their academic and professional futures.
Weaknesses of Kahoot! in Higher Education Learning
While Kahoot! brings significant value to higher education learning, it's also important to explore its potential weaknesses. One such concern is the encouragement of superficial learning. Because of its game-like nature, students may become more engrossed in winning, which could lead to them prioritizing the memorization of facts over a deeper understanding of the subject matter. This could potentially affect critical thinking and problem-solving skills that are essential in higher education.
Another limitation arises when assessing complex or nuanced concepts. Though Kahoot! is an excellent tool for formative assessment, its multiple-choice format may fall short in capturing comprehensive understanding when it comes to intricate subjects. These often require in-depth analysis and discussion, elements that Kahoot! may struggle to incorporate effectively in its current structure.
Equity in learning also poses a challenge with Kahoot.'s design. Given its dependence on speed, learners with certain disabilities or who need more time to process information may find themselves at a disadvantage. This can inadvertently create an inequitable learning experience, hindering some students from fully benefiting from the tool.
Finally, Kahoot! is primarily designed for objective questions, such as multiple-choice or true-false queries. Its lack of capacity to accommodate essay-style or open-ended questions limits its utility in certain higher education scenarios, where critical thinking and creative responses are often demanded. Overcoming these limitations is essential for Kahoot! to cater to all aspects of higher education learning effectively.
Solutions to Address Kahoot!'s Weaknesses
To tackle the potential trap of superficial learning within Kahoot!, it's important that educators view and implement it as a supplementary tool, rather than being totally reliant on it for instruction. Kahoot! should ideally be used for quick reviews, quizzes, or as a precursor to more intensive discussions and activities. This strategy relegates the platform's game-like aspect to a supplemental role, fostering the potential for deeper, more meaningful learning.
Similarly, the shortcoming of Kahoot! in gauging complex concepts can also be addressed through diversification of assessment methods. Rather than leaning entirely on Kahoot! for this purpose, educators can include other evaluative techniques such as written assignments, group discussions, and oral presentations. This assorted methodology will ensure a well-rounded and comprehensive evaluation of all facets of learning, enabling a more complete appraisal of students' mastery.
In terms of promoting inclusivity within Kahoot!, certain adjustments can be introduced to provide a more equitable learning environment. Educators can, for instance, augment the time limit for questions, offering students of varying processing speeds the opportunity to fully engage. In addition, other alternatives or supplementation should be considered for those with disabilities who might face challenges with Kahoot's! existing setup.
The limited question types offered by Kahoot! can be expanded upon by its developers. By integrating capabilities for different question formats such as short-answer or essay questions, Kahoot! would become a more versatile tool. Consequently, educators could employ the platform more effectively for a wide range of courses and assessments within higher education.
Comparative Analysis - Usability
Mentimeter: Very simple to use with a clean interface, but its advanced features are limited without a paid subscription.
Google Forms: Extremely customizable and free, but its interface is more utilitarian and lacks dynamic interaction.
Socrative: Requires more setup but offers richer feedback and deeper analytics.
Kahoot: Quick and easy to launch, designed for a playful, game-based learning environment.
Comparative Analysis - Engagement
Mentimeter: Encourages participation with live polls and word clouds, but can be less engaging without game-like features.
Google Forms: Collects information efficiently but lacks real-time student interaction during live sessions.
Socrative: Engages students through quizzes, with added excitement from the Space Race game.
Kahoot: Creates a fun, competitive environment, leading to high student engagement, especially in large groups.
Comparative Analysis - Accessibility
Mentimeter: Accessible via any mobile browser, making it easy for students to join sessions.
Google Forms: Works on all devices and browsers, and can be shared via links.
Socrative: Accessible on both web and app platforms, though the app version offers more functionality.
Kahoot: Primarily browser-based, with easy-to-use apps available, offering excellent accessibility for in-class use.
Benefits of Interactive Tools in Playful Learning.
Increased student engagement through active participation:
Interactive tools make learning more dynamic and engaging by allowing students to actively participate in quizzes, polls, and activities rather than passively receiving information. Tools like Kahoot and Mentimeter create a lively classroom environment where students feel more involved in their own learning. This active participation helps keep students focused, especially in large lecture settings, and enhances retention of the material.
Real-time feedback that helps identify learning gaps immediately:
With interactive tools, educators can provide and receive real-time feedback on student understanding. For instance, using Socrative or Google Forms for quick assessments allows instructors to gauge comprehension on the spot and adjust their teaching accordingly. This immediate feedback benefits students as well, helping them recognize areas where they may need additional help, fostering a more responsive learning environment.
Enhanced collaboration among students through group activities and discussions:
Tools like Mentimeter's word clouds or Socrative's Space Race encourage collaborative learning by involving students in group activities. These tools create opportunities for students to work together, share ideas, and learn from one another, which aligns with constructivist principles of learning through social interaction. Collaboration also helps build communication and teamwork skills, which are valuable beyond the classroom.
Gamification of learning that motivates students with fun and competition:
Gamified elements in tools like Kahoot add a layer of excitement to the classroom by introducing points, leaderboards, and competitive activities. This playful approach to learning encourages students to engage more enthusiastically, as they are motivated by the thrill of competition and the rewards of doing well. Gamification can make learning feel less like a chore and more like a challenge or game, increasing student motivation.
Inclusive learning environments where all students can participate via mobile devices:
Interactive tools allow students to participate using their own devices, which reduces barriers to participation, especially for those who may feel hesitant to speak up in class. Tools like Google Forms and Mentimeter enable anonymous input, allowing quieter students to share their thoughts without fear of judgment. This inclusivity ensures that diverse perspectives are heard, creating a more equitable and inclusive learning environment.
Piaget's theory of constructivism linked to playful learning.
Jean Piaget, a Swiss psychologist, developed the theory of constructivism in the 1930s, emphasizing that students learn by building on what they already know through active experiences. His work, particularly in cognitive development, has significantly influenced modern educational practices, highlighting the importance of active, hands-on learning in student's development (Waite-Stupiansky).
Active Learning: Piaget's constructivist theory emphasises that learners actively construct their own understanding through experiences. Interactive tools like Mentimeter and Kahoot provide opportunities for students to engage in active learning by participating in quizzes, polls, and games that require them to apply and reflect on knowledge.
Learning Through Play: Piaget believed that play is essential for cognitive development, as it allows students to explore, experiment, and make sense of the world. Playful learning through tools like Kahoot and Socrative incorporates this concept by turning learning into a fun, interactive experience that encourages deeper understanding through exploration and experimentation.
Collaboration and Social Interaction: Piaget argued that social interaction is crucial for cognitive development. Interactive tools encourage collaboration through group activities, such as the competitive Space Race in Socrative or group discussions in Mentimeter, where students can construct knowledge together.
Constructing New Knowledge: Piaget's theory suggests that learners build on prior knowledge to create new understanding. Interactive tools support this process by providing real-time feedback, helping students recognize misconceptions and refine their understanding, aligning with the constructivist approach of continuous learning.
Conclusion
Each of the aforementioned educational tools, namely Mentimeter, Google Forms, Socrative, and Kahoot, include distinct advantages and disadvantages that may be effectively used in accordance with the particular objectives and preferences of educators, as well as the requirements of learning environments in higher education. An educator should consider their educational objectives, the features of the resource, and their teaching strategies when choosing a teaching tool. The integration of many technologies may be used to effectively cater to the varied requirements of contemporary higher education courses. The ultimate success of integrating these technologies relies on the instructors' capacity to adapt and effectively use technology to augment the learning process.
Interactive tools like Mentimeter, Google Forms, Socrative, and Kahoot provide opportunities for playful learning in higher education. Each tool has distinct strengths and weaknesses, but they all contribute to enhanced student engagement when used thoughtfully. Integrating these tools effectively into the classroom encourages active participation and creative use of technology.
Playful learning can enhance higher education, but it requires balance between fun and educational value.
Recommendation i. Select Tools Aligned with Learning Objectives: Choose interactive tools that directly support your learning goals. For instance, if the objective is to test comprehension, a quiz tool like Kahoot is suitable. Aligning the tool with the goal ensures it enhances learning and remains relevant to the content.
ii. Balance Fun and Academic Rigor: While interactive tools make learning enjoyable, they should also challenge students academically. Strive for a balance that keeps students engaged without sacrificing the depth and rigor of the content, ensuring that fun complements learning rather than overshadowing it.
iii. Encourage Collaborative Learning: Use tools that promote teamwork and group discussions, such as Google Forms for group surveys or Socrative for team-based quizzes. Collaborative elements encourage students to learn from each other and deepen their understanding through shared perspectives.
iv. Providing Real Time Feedback to Support Learning: Interactive tools like Mentimeter and Socrative allow you to give instant feedback, which helps students identify areas of improvement. Real-time feedback keeps students on track and encourages immediate reflection, aiding in more effective learning.
v. Ensure Accessibility and Ease of Use: Ensure that tools are accessible to all students, considering internet connectivity, device compatibility, and user interface. Tools should be straightforward, so students can focus on learning rather than troubleshooting, making the learning experience seamless for everyone.

Application of educational interventions based on gamification in prenatal healthcare: A systematic review of randomized controlled trials

Author: Mehrabi, Rahele1; Tavassoli, Tahereh2; Askari, Fariba31 Department of Medical Information Sciences, School of Allied Medicine, Reproductive Health and Population Research Center, Gonabad University of Medical Sciences, Gonabad, Iran2 Department of Midwifery, School of Medicine, Gonabad University of Medical Sciences, Gonabad, Iran3 Reproductive Health and Population Research Center, Gonabad University of Medical Sciences, Gonabad, Iran

Publication info: Mehrabi, Rahele; Tavassoli, Tahereh; Askari, Fariba. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/application-educational-interventions-based-on/docview/3261800325/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: Gamification takes advantage of game designs to add dynamicity to educational environments and develop students' sociocognitive skills. As technological advances continue to shape many aspects of life, incorporating gamification into prenatal education has emerged as an innovative approach. Therefore, the present study aimed to review the use of educational interventions based on gamification in prenatal care. In the present study, studies indexed in PubMed, Scopus, ScienceDirect, Google Scholar, and Web of Science databases were searched for until March 2023. The main keywords and synonyms of gamification and pregnancy were used to search for studies. The inclusion criteria were English language studies with a gamification intervention and RCT. Abstracts of studies or conferences, book chapters, review articles, and non-randomized studies were excluded from the study. The Jadad scale was used to assess the quality of the studies. Five clinical trials were reviewed. The effects of gamification-based education were divided into four categories: effectiveness of gamification in acquiring knowledge, effectiveness of gamification in increasing prenatal healthcare, emotional and psychological benefits, and compliance with prenatal healthcare advice. Gamification can positively affect pregnancy outcomes through increasing knowledge retention, improving attitudes, promoting healthy behaviors, and reducing stress and anxiety.Gamification takes advantage of game designs to add dynamicity to educational environments and develop students' sociocognitive skills. Digital Learning Platforms in Aircraft Maintenance Technology: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Gamified Learning Approaches

Author: Arthur Dela Peña

Publication info: Arthur Dela Peña. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/digital-learning-platforms-aircraft-maintenance/docview/3257422955/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: Traditional teaching methods in Aircraft Maintenance Technology (AMT) often struggle to maintain student engagement, motivation, and knowledge retention. While gamification has been recognised as a potential solution, its application in AMT education remains underexplored, particularly in bridging theoretical knowledge with practical skill acquisition. This study investigates the effectiveness of Kahoot-based gamification in enhancing student engagement, motivation, knowledge retention, and practical skills development. A mixed-methods approach was employed, integrating quantitative surveys, pre- and post-assessments, and qualitative interviews with students and instructors. The study assessed 120 participants, revealing statistically significant improvements: engagement increased by 43.8%, motivation by 55.2%, knowledge retention by 41.2%, and practical skills by 51.6%. Qualitative findings supported these results, with students reporting higher participation, improved concept recall, and greater enthusiasm. Instructors observed enhanced confidence in applying theoretical knowledge. Despite these benefits, challenges such as internet connectivity issues, time constraints, and question format limitations were identified. The study recommends a blended learning approach integrating gamification with hands-on training, scenario-based exercises, and emerging technologies such as Augmented Reality and Virtual Reality. Beyond AMT, these findings highlight gamification's potential in technical and vocational education, emphasising the need for future research on adaptive gamification models and AI-driven learning platforms.

Virtual Reality Training Programs in Disaster Preparedness: A Systematic Review

Author: Kaggwa, Mark Mohan; Chaimowitz, Gary A; Agboinghale, Precious; Marginean, Diana; Olagunju, Andrew T

Publication info: Kaggwa, Mark Mohan; Chaimowitz, Gary A; Agboinghale, Precious; Marginean, Diana; Olagunju, Andrew T. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/virtual-reality-training-programs-disaster/docview/3257419365/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: Background: The demand for effective disaster preparedness training in hospitals is steadily increasing, as healthcare staff need to handle emergencies efficiently while providing patient care. However, conventional training methods like live drills and tabletop exercises can require significant resources, limit participation, and disrupt hospital operations. In light of these challenges, Virtual Reality (VR) training has emerged as a modern solution, offering an innovative way to improve training efficiency without interfering with routine hospital activities. This study, therefore, examines how VR training compares to traditional methods in preparing hospital personnel for disasters, focusing specifically on effectiveness and cost. Methods: We reviewed studies concerning the effectiveness and economic assessments of VR compared to traditional methods. To answer the research questions, we followed the Canada Drug Agency's guides on conducting a health technology assessment. Articles were identified from both peer-reviewed and gray literature. Results: The review highlights eight pertinent studies demonstrating VR's advantages, including boosting knowledge retention, performance, and overall confidence among healthcare professionals in disaster preparedness. Furthermore, the economic analysis indicates that although the initial costs of VR synchronous training may be higher, the long-term savings from reduced ongoing training and maintenance can lead to greater cost efficiency. In addition, while VR training presents safety benefits, challenges such as cybersickness and accessibility concerns have also been observed. Conclusion: VR training offers considerable advantages over traditional disaster preparedness methods and significantly improves healthcare workers' confidence and skills. Despite the high upfront costs, the potential long-term financial benefits appear promising. To maximize results, funding for VR initiatives must emphasize demonstrated effectiveness alongside ongoing research to explore broader applications and address the challenges posed by these emerging technologies.

Teacher Perceptions of Gamification's Influence on Student Engagement and Learning in Nigerian Primary Schools

Author: Ngeri, Anita Ikpat    

Publication info: Ngeri, Anita Ikpat. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/teacher-perceptions-gamifications-influence-on/docview/3257418161/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: This study investigated teachers' perceptions on the impact of gamification on student engagement and learning outcomes in Nigerian primary schools, aiming to bridge the gap between traditional teaching methods and contemporary learner needs. A mixed-methods approach was utilised, involving quantitative and qualitative data collection through an online survey distributed to 82 primary school teachers. The results revealed that most of the respondents incorporated gamification techniques weekly, with badges and points being the most frequently used elements. Gamification was most commonly applied in Maths, followed by English, Science and other subjects. Teachers perceived significant positive impacts on academic achievement, student participation and knowledge retention, though challenges such as lack of technological resources, curriculum alignment, scepticism from stakeholders, and insufficient teacher training were highlighted. Thematic analysis of qualitative data identified themes related to enhancing problem-solving abilities, catering to diverse learning styles and fostering healthy competition. Despite challenges, the study found unanimous support for gamification, with teachers willing to undergo further professional development. The findings suggest that gamification holds promise for transforming educational environments in Nigerian primary schools by promoting active engagement, motivation, and improved academic performance, although addressing technological and training barriers remains crucial.

Virtual Museum Experience Design and User Behavior Analysis

Author: Chen, Wen1    ; Chen, Yingji11 School of Art, Soochow University, Suzhou, China

Publication info: Chen, Wen; Chen, Yingji. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/virtual-museum-experience-design-user-behavior/docview/3249985283/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: In the evolving landscape of digital cultural heritage, the integration of advanced computational models into immersive virtual environments has become essential for enriching user engagement and fostering more meaningful interpretative experiences. As digital heritage platforms increasingly adopt interactive technologies, there is a growing need to move beyond static presentations and introduce intelligent, responsive systems that adapt to individual users’ interests and behaviors. Traditional virtual museum systems often suffer from rigid content structures, limited adaptability, and a lack of personalized storytelling, all of which constrain user immersion and diminish the potential for impactful learning experiences. To overcome these challenges, our approach integrates semantic-topological modeling with adaptive interaction mechanisms, forming a dynamic and personalized digital museum experience. The proposed framework features a hybrid computational architecture that unites symbolic knowledge representations with algorithmic spatial layout generation. This integration enables the creation of flexible narrative trajectories that are contextually relevant and customized according to each user’s cognitive and behavioral profile. Furthermore, the system incorporates reinforcement-driven semantic planning to interpret and respond to user interactions in real time, ensuring a continuously evolving and coherent interpretative journey. Experimental results reveal substantial improvements in user satisfaction, engagement levels, and knowledge retention when compared to traditional virtual museum platforms. These outcomes highlight the scalability and transformative potential of the model, reinforcing its capacity to enhance accessibility, personalization, and educational value across diverse digital heritage applications.

The Effect of Education 4.0 Tools on 7th Grade Students' Learning Outcomes and Attitudes in the Electrical Circuits Unit

Author: Basgül, Melek    ; Bayram Costu    

Publication info: Basgül, Melek; Bayram Costu. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/effect-education-4-0-tools-on-7th-grade-students/docview/3247451664/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: Education 4.0 represents a visionary approach to the future of education, aiming to enhance teaching and learning through advanced technologies. The aim of this research is to determine student attitudes toward the use of Education 4.0 tools in the 7th-grade Science course Electrical Circuits unit. To achieve this, an attitude test was developed to evaluate the integration of Education 4.0 tools into the Science curriculum, and student attitudes were assessed using this test. A "quasi-experimental design with pre-test and post-test control group," one of the quantitative research methods, was used in the study. The research involved 41 seventh-grade students from one public secondary schools in Turkey, with 21 students in the experimental group and 20 in the control group. The "Attitude Scale toward the Use of Education 4.0 Tools in Science Teaching," developed by the researchers, was used as the data collection instrument. The experimental phase lasted four weeks (16 lesson hours), during which the experimental group engaged in activities involving Education 4.0 tools, while the control group followed the curriculum-prescribed activities. The t-test results of the collected data revealed a statistically significant difference between the post-test scores of the experimental and control groups, with the experimental group showing more favorable outcomes. The research findings reveal that students exhibit a positive attitude toward the use of Education 4.0 tools in science education. These results suggest that the integration of Education 4.0 into science education enhances students' understanding of abstract electrical concepts such as electric current, potential difference, resistance, and Ohm's Law, improves knowledge retention, and transforms the learning process into an interactive and discovery-oriented experience. Furthermore, Education 4.0 tools have contributed to the improvement of learning outcomes by promoting student engagement and make learning processes more efficient by improving students' ability to use technology effectively.

Application of a hybrid virtual-physical teaching model integrating mixed reality and 3D printing in clinical joint orthopedic education

Author: Wang, Honglin1; Xu, Aoshuang2; Hua, Wei1; Ye, Zhewei3; Lu, Lin11 Department of Orthopedics, Renmin Hospital of Wuhan University, Wuhan, China2 Institute of Hematology, Union Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Wuhan, China3 Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Union Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Wuhan, China

Publication info: Wang, Honglin; Xu, Aoshuang; Hua, Wei; Ye, Zhewei; Lu, Lin. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/application-hybrid-virtual-physical-teaching/docview/3247103674/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: The diagnosis and treatment of arthropathic orthopaedic conditions are inherently linked to anatomical structures, necessitating strong spatial visualization abilities in students. Providing intuitively accessible methods for students to master specialized knowledge presents a formidable challenge for educators. This study aims to evaluate the pedagogical value of integrating 3D-printed model with mixed reality (MR) technology in clinical orthopaedic surgery education. Objective The diagnosis and treatment of arthropathic orthopaedic conditions are inherently linked to anatomical structures, necessitating strong spatial visualization abilities in students. Providing intuitively accessible methods for students to master specialized knowledge presents a formidable challenge for educators. This study aims to evaluate the pedagogical value of integrating 3D-printed model with mixed reality (MR) technology in clinical orthopaedic surgery education.Thirty-six senior clinical medical undergraduates were randomized into two groups. The experimental group underwent training using the combined 3D- printed model and mixed reality (MR) technology, while the control group received traditional instruction. Learning outcomes were evaluated through standardized Objective Structured Clinical Examination (OSCE) assessments and questionnaires. Correlation analysis was conducted between total OSCE scores and questionnaire scores. Methods Thirty-six senior clinical medical undergraduates were randomized into two groups. The experimental group underwent training using the combined 3D- printed model and mixed reality (MR) technology, while the control group received traditional instruction. Learning outcomes were evaluated through standardized Objective Structured Clinical Examination (OSCE) assessments and questionnaires. Correlation analysis was conducted between total OSCE scores and questionnaire scores.The experimental group achieved significantly higher OSCE scores compared to the control group ( p    0.8, p    0.8, p < 0.001). The strongest correlation was observed between learning efficiency and OSCE total scores (r = 0.918).Integrating 3D-printed model and MR technology into orthopedic joint surgery clinical teaching significantly boosts student performance, learning efficiency, and overall teaching quality, demonstrating strong potential for wider application. Conclusion Integrating 3D-printed model and MR technology into orthopedic joint surgery clinical teaching significantly boosts student performance, learning efficiency, and overall teaching quality, demonstrating strong potential for wider application.

The Effect of Time Lapse Between Online Lectures and Clinical Practice on Medical Students' Performance in an Orthopedics Hybrid Course

Author: Bvonpanttarananon, Jongdee1; Anusitviwat, Chirathit1; Yuenyongviwat, Araya2; Yuenyongviwat, Varah1    1 Department of Orthopedics, Faculty of Medicine, Prince of Songkla University, Hat Yai, Songkhla, 90110, Thailand2 Department of Pediatrics, Faculty of Medicine, Prince of Songkla University, Hat Yai, Songkhla, 90110, Thailand

Publication info: Bvonpanttarananon, Jongdee; Anusitviwat, Chirathit; Yuenyongviwat, Araya; Yuenyongviwat, Varah. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/effect-time-lapse-between-online-lectures/docview/3246389798/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: The integration of technology in medical education has led to the adoption of hybrid teaching methods, combining online lectures with traditional face-to-face clinical practice. While this approach offers flexibility and safety, it raises questions about the impact of potential time lapses between theoretical learning and hands-on experience. This study aimed to investigate the effect of the time interval between online lectures and on-site clinical practice on medical students' performance in orthopedic rotation. Introduction The integration of technology in medical education has led to the adoption of hybrid teaching methods, combining online lectures with traditional face-to-face clinical practice. While this approach offers flexibility and safety, it raises questions about the impact of potential time lapses between theoretical learning and hands-on experience. This study aimed to investigate the effect of the time interval between online lectures and on-site clinical practice on medical students' performance in orthopedic rotation.A retrospective study was conducted on 116 fifth-year medical students who completed their orthopedic rotation during the 2021/2022 academic year. Students underwent a one-week online course followed by three weeks of on-site clinical practice, with varying time lapses (0-38 weeks) between these periods. Performance was assessed through examinations including key features test (KF), multiple-choice questions (MCQ), multiple-essay questions (MEQ), objective structured clinical examination (OSCE), and long case examination. Spearman's rank correlation was used to analyze the relationship between time lapse and examination scores. Methods A retrospective study was conducted on 116 fifth-year medical students who completed their orthopedic rotation during the 2021/2022 academic year. Students underwent a one-week online course followed by three weeks of on-site clinical practice, with varying time lapses (0-38 weeks) between these periods. Performance was assessed through examinations including key features test (KF), multiple-choice questions (MCQ), multiple-essay questions (MEQ), objective structured clinical examination (OSCE), and long case examination. Spearman's rank correlation was used to analyze the relationship between time lapse and examination scores.The analysis revealed a significant negative correlation between the time lapse duration and KF scores (p 0.05). Results The analysis revealed a significant negative correlation between the time lapse duration and KF scores (p 0.05).This study demonstrates that the time lapse between online lectures and clinical rotation in orthopedic education significantly impacts students' performance in key features tests. However, other examination scores remained unaffected. These findings highlight the need for careful scheduling and potential interventions to mitigate the effects of extended time lapses on specific aspects of medical knowledge retention and application in orthopedic education. Conclusion This study demonstrates that the time lapse between online lectures and clinical rotation in orthopedic education significantly impacts students' performance in key features tests. However, other examination scores remained unaffected. These findings highlight the need for careful scheduling and potential interventions to mitigate the effects of extended time lapses on specific aspects of medical knowledge retention and application in orthopedic education.

Virtual reality in cultural tourism: Optimizing learning and interactive experiences

Author: Chang, Yanan1; Ni, Yujun2; Zhang, Xuwei3    1 Jinzhong University, China2 Philippine Christian University, Philippines3 JinHua QiWuLun Information Technology Co., Ltd., China jhgx_baojia@163.com

Publication info: Chang, Yanan; Ni, Yujun; Zhang, Xuwei. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/virtual-reality-cultural-tourism-optimizing/docview/3242188395/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: This study explored virtual reality (VR) technology to enhance cultural learning in heritage tourism, aligning with a focus on learning systems. Traditional models lack interactivity, but VR digitizes artifacts and historical scenarios. Through surveys (1,200 participants) and data analysis, VR improved student knowledge retention by 45% (F=8.3, p&1t;0.01) and increased visits by 42–75%. While boosting stay time (39%) and consumption (41%), challenges include content stagnation (23% revisit decline) and hardware discomfort (55% dissatisfaction). Proposed solutions are ergonomic headsets (33–50% weight reduction), dynamic content updates, and in-scene augmented-reality commerce (27% online revenue growth in pilots). These innovations position VR as a non-formal learning tool for heritage preservation and digital education. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2025 APA, all rights reserved) (Source: journal abstract)
