Full text: 1. Introduction
The construction sector is dangerous for workers, with alarming injuries and fatality statistics every year (Behm, 2005; Choi et al. , 2019; Haslam et al. , 2005). Recent studies have highlighted that geotechnical works, such as excavation works, continuously expose workers to risks (Liu et al. , 2021). As such, excavation work has been recognised as one of the industry's most dangerous and challenging activities (Wang et al. , 2015). The most common excavation-related hazards are cave-ins and trench collapses, which together caused 332 fatalities from 2011 to 2018 in the US alone (US Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2020). Cave-ins pose a serious safety risk as the walls can collapse without warning and seriously injure, suffocate or even crush anyone nearby. Further, while working at a construction site with on-going excavations, workers are also vulnerable to a wide range of other potential hazards such as working in confined spaces, oxygen deficiency, exposure to flooding, atmospheric hazards, utility sources, heavy machinery, objects falling from high levels and falls from height (Arboleda and Abraham, 2004; Khan et al. , 2019; Lin et al. , 2021; Lu et al. , 2022).
Several strategies and safety standards have been put in place in different countries to reduce the injury and fatality rates on excavation sites. These include establishing guidelines and best practices, safety management procedures and safety training in excavation (Ding et al. , 2014; Khan et al. , 2019). For instance, in the earlier 70s, the US Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) issued its first standard on excavation safety and has since continually amended and improved the standard to further reduce injuries and fatalities (U.S. Department of Labor Occupational Safety and Health Administration, 2015). Additionally, OSHA made trench and excavation safety a priority goal for 2018 with the aim of reducing trench-related accident rates by 10% by 30 September 2019 (Hedmond, 2018).
Existing strategies and safety standards have significantly improved construction's health and safety performance over the last few decades. However, excavation-related accidents continue to plague the industry (Flynn and Sampson, 2012). In the first half of 2022, 22 workers were killed in excavation works in the United States, surpassing 1 in all of 2021 (OSHA, 2022). This situation is due to the lack of proper implementation of safety practices in the industry. Construction workers themselves play a vital role in determining their safety, as they should be capable of identifying, evaluating and responding to hazards (Sacks et al. , 2013). The lack of workers' safety training represents an existing barrier to bringing injury and fatality rates close to zero. Although the lack of safety awareness and misjudgement of hazardous situations cannot be completely eliminated, these errors can be reduced through proper and effective training (Zhao and Lucas, 2015). New technologies, such as virtual reality (VR) combined with gamification, can play a key role in construction safety training.
The use of VR technology is a promising and novel approach to safety training (Buttussi and Chittaro, 2018; Feng et al. , 2018; Lovreglio, 2020). Since the pioneering works by Xie et al. (2006) and Sacks et al . (2013), the literature shows that several VR construction safety training applications have been proposed and tested. Different reviews have analysed the benefits and limitations of using VR for construction training (Bhoir and Esmaeili, 2015; Gao et al. , 2019; Li et al. , 2018; Shamsudin et al. , 2018; Wang et al. , 2018), and these reviews highlight how VR training can play a key role in increasing the safety awareness and risk perception of construction workers and enhance their cognitive learning and critical decision-making skills. However, to the best of our knowledge, no VR application has been developed for comprehensive excavation safety training. Furthermore, as illustrated in Section 2 of this work, only a few studies have compared the effectiveness of VR training and traditional methods for construction safety training.
This study aims to investigate the effectiveness of VR safety training for construction excavation. This is achieved by prototyping an immersive VR training system that enables people to familiarise themselves with the relevant hazards on a construction site and the safety procedures to follow when the site needs to be evacuated. The effectiveness of the proposed VR training system is tested in terms of knowledge acquisition, knowledge retention, self-efficacy and user experience. Finally, the effectiveness of the proposed VR training system is compared with the training provided using a health and safety manual.
2. Background
VR has been playing a key and increasing role in the construction sector in the last few decades due to its ability to immerse users in a virtual construction world. One of the growing trends in its implementation is towards construction health and safety training (Feng et al. , 2022; Zhang et al. , 2020). Virtual reality is located at one of the two extremes of the virtuality continuum proposed by Milgram and Kishino (1994), and it can be classified into non-immersive and immersive, as shown in Figure 1 (Lovreglio, 2020). The former technology relies on the use of displays to show the digital content, while the latter approach uses immersive technologies such as Head Mounted Displays (HMDs) or Cave Automatic Virtual Environments (CAVEs). In the following part of this review section, we will focus only on the existing studies using immersive VR for construction safety training. Readers can refer to existing literature review papers (Bhoir and Esmaeili, 2015; Gao et al. , 2019; Li et al. , 2018; Shamsudin et al. , 2018; Wang et al. , 2018) for non-immersive applications and VR applications for behavioural studies.
One of the first studies to conceptualise the use of immersive VR for construction safety training was conducted by Irizarry and Abraham (2005), while the first case studies to test the efficacy of VR for construction safety training were conducted by Xie et al. (2006) and Sacks et al . (2013). The volume of relevant literature has exponentially increased since then, as shown by the list of works identified in Table 1.
Table 1 highlights that VR applications have been developed and tested for different training objectives, such as hazard recognition and management (Jacobsen et al. , 2021; Jeelani et al. , 2020; Jeon and Cai, 2021; Raimbaud et al. , 2021), fall-from-height avoidance (Gupta and Varghese, 2020; Huang et al. , 2022; Shi et al. , 2019) and scaffolding safety (Gupta and Varghese, 2020; Poshdar et al. , 2021; Xie et al. , 2006). However, the literature also shows that there has been no comprehensive study on VR use for construction excavation safety training. Some excavation hazards have been marginally investigated in a few studies (Hilfert et al. , 2016; Huang et al. , 2020; Isleyen and Duzgun, 2019), but these studies focused on mechanical hazards and confined space hazards.
The type of hardware adopted for immersive VR training has changed over time. The first studies, run in the early 2000s, were carried out with CAVE, while HDM has become the preferred equipment used in the latest applications. Further, several studies have attempted to connect VR with other digital technologies, such as EEG headsets (Huang et al. , 2022; Jeon and Cai, 2021), LiDAR sensors (Jacobsen et al. , 2021) and Digital Twin (Harichandran et al. , 2021).
This review also shows that most of the existing studies did not involve an experiment, or they focused only on the user experience. A comprehensive assessment of the efficacy of VR training for construction safety in terms of knowledge acquisition has been carried out (Gupta and Varghese, 2020; Jeelani et al. , 2020; Joshi et al. , 2021; Sacks et al. , 2013), but among these studies only Sacks et al . (2013) and Poshdar et al . (2021) conducted retention studies to assess how much construction workers remember after the safety training. As such, more research is needed to assess knowledge retention post-VR training.
Finally, only three studies compared the effectiveness of immersive VR training with traditional methods. Sacks et al . (2013) and Poshdar et al . (2021) compared VR training with slide-based presentation training, while Joshi et al . (2021) compared VR training with video training. The results from Sacks et al . (2013) and Joshi et al . (2021) show that VR provides more effective training, while Poshdar et al . (2021) did not observe any difference. More research is required to determine if immersive VR provides more effective training in order to assess and potentially justify its costs to future safety training programs.
Three knowledge gaps emerge from the literature review. First, nowadays, there are commercial immersive VR applications for safety training in the market, such as fire safety (Vobling, 2022) and road safety (StreetWize VR, 2022). These applications are backed by scientific evidence that immersive VR is an effective tool for safety training. In the case of excavation safety, it involves heavy machinery and a set of procedures, which is different from other incidents. However, whether immersive VR effectively delivers excavation safety training is still unknown. Second, there is little scientific evidence showing the long-term impact of immersive VR safety training. This has implications for the actual practice since in reality, safety training is conducted every once in a while (e.g. an evacuation drill is conducted every six months in New Zealand). Retaining the acquired knowledge for a long time after training is essential. However, it is still not clear how the acquired knowledge decays after training through immersive VR. Last, the scientific evidence for comparing immersive VR and traditional safety training is inconclusive. Whether immersive VR is more effective than traditional approaches is not fully understood. This has implications for using immersive VR for safety training in the industry. There is no incentive for the industry to apply immersive VR for safety training if it does the same job as traditional approaches. Therefore, this is another knowledge gap which is worth investigating.
The research in this work aims to bridge these knowledge gaps as we propose the prototype for construction excavation safety training. This work investigates the long-term impact of immersive training by running a retention study four weeks after the training. Finally, the proposed prototype is compared with a safety manual-based training.
3. Immersive VR training system
The training solution presented in this work was an immersive VR application deployed on one of the most popular standalone HMDs: Oculus quest. This section outlines the design, development and deployment of the immersive VR training system. Section 3.1 illustrates the virtual environments and storylines designed for the training system, and Section 3.2 describes users' interaction and navigation. Finally, the training objectives and instructional methods are explained in Sections 3.3 and 3.4, respectively.
3.1 Virtual environments and storylines
The virtual environment was designed and developed to feature three scenarios – an office and two distinct excavation sites (Site A and Site B). The storyline of the immersive VR training system progressed from the office to Site A and ended at Site B. The office scenario offered tutorials for participants to learn and practice interaction and navigation using Oculus Quest's wireless controllers in VR. Site A and B were construction sites consisting of various excavation-related activities. The Site A scenario offered a site to assess pre-training practical performance and deliver actual training content. The Site B scenario was a different excavation site that included similar hazards found in Site A, which allowed for assessing post-training practical performance.
The virtual environments were modelled and rendered using Unity (version 2019.1.10f1). A Unity plugin called ‘Terrain' was used to create site terrains, including the overall representation, location, depth, width and texture of excavation sites. An extensive range of virtual objects was obtained from Unity Asset Store and imported into Unity to model the office room and two excavation sites. For instance, Snaps Art HD – Construction Site was used to develop the construction scenarios (Asset Store Originals, 2022). Figure 2 demonstrates the virtual environments of three scenarios.
3.2 Interaction and navigation
This immersive VR training system features training and assessment; therefore, the interaction with virtual environments was a critical component of the system. The interaction was enabled using two Oculus Quest's wireless controllers. Participants could activate a virtual menu that allowed for four types of actions: grab and position virtual objects, view a safety file, measure spatial distances and tag objects or areas as hazards. Meanwhile, the virtual menu also provided instructions on activating and performing each action. Figure 3 shows the four types of actions provided by the virtual menu in VR.
Thanks to the motion tracking system and sensors embedded in Oculus Quest, navigation in virtual environments was similar to walking and viewing in the real world. Participants could move freely in the real world while maintaining accurate movement translation to virtual environments in VR. The movement area in the real world was confined to a 3 m × 3 m square. Participants could walk within this square to move around at each position associated with the storyline in virtual environments. Participants could stand, crouch, turn around, or view a virtual object in a virtual environment from different angles.
3.3 Training objectives
The training objectives of the immersive VR training system were developed based on two guidelines: Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) Trenching and Excavation Safety (Occupational Safety and Health Administration, 2015) and WorkSafe Excavation Safety (WorkSafe, 2016). These guidelines provide comprehensive safety requirements and recommended practices for excavation work, including procedures for planning, identifying, managing and controlling a wide range of hazards. There are numerous hazards associated with excavation work; however, due to the feasibility of prototyping and testing, only the hazards that require the most critical attention were taken into account as the training objectives of the immersive VR training system. The selection of these critical hazards was made by reviewing the literature on excavation safety and accident types (Arboleda et al. , 2002; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2004; Flynn and Sampson, 2012). As a result, seven critical hazards were selected as the training objectives for the immersive VR training system: - Absence of a safety officer.

- Absence of soil protection.

- Objects or loads near excavation edges.

- Absence of safe access and egress.

- Workers or mobile plants close to dangerous utilities and objects.

- Absence of safety barriers and signage.

- Workers working in an unsafe excavation zone.


3.4 Instructional methods
After the pre-training assessment, actual training sessions took place in Site A. Participants could move to different positions around Site A to learn about the seven critical hazards of an excavation site as identified in Section 3.3. This study adopted questioning as the instructional method for the immersive VR training system. Questioning is a cognitive strategy that has been widely adopted in education at primary, secondary and tertiary levels. Questions can stimulate thinking and enhance engagement (Caram and Davis, 2005; Ramsey et al. , 1990). A systematic review of questioning in different academic and educational fields revealed that it can facilitate learning processes, comprehension, critical thinking and metacognitive skills (Davoudi and Sadeghi, 2015). In the virtual environment, at each position, participants faced a question about a critical hazard that could be present associated with the position on an excavation site (see Figure 4). Participants had to answer the question based on their observation and assessment from the position where they were standing in VR. Multiple choice answers were available to participants relating to the question. After selecting a choice, textual information was offered as immediate feedback for each choice; thus, participants were educated about the procedures in order to identify, evaluate and respond to a hazard associated with an excavation site. In addition, supplementary materials such as photos and videos related to a hazard were also provided for each question. For instance, as shown in Figure 4, participants could assess the excavation site and answer the question about the presence of a safety officer on a site. All the safety information presented in this stage was obtained from the OSHA and WorkSafe's excavation safety guidelines.
4. Pilot study
A pilot study was undertaken to test the proposed immersive VR training system. This pilot study followed a one-group pretest-posttest experimental design. This experimental design involved the same measures to assess participants' practical performance in excavation sites before and after training and thus determined the effect of VR training on a given sample. In addition, participants' user experience was examined immediately after being exposed to the immersive VR training system.
4.1 Participants
A total of 40 participants (16 females, 24 males), who were recruited via posters on the Albany campus of Massey University and through direct contact via emails, participated in the pilot study. The participants consisted of 28 university students and 12 professionals from the construction sector. The ages of participants ranged from 21 to 50, with around two-thirds being between 21 and 30. Eighty per cent (32) of the participants had at least one year of work experience in the construction sector, 45% (18) had experience in excavation work, and 37.5% (15) had received safety training in excavation work. Twenty-five per cent (10) had never played video games, and 27.5% (11) had never experienced VR before.
4.2 Measures
4.2.1 Practical performance
Participants' practical performance was assessed in VR before and immediately after the training. As described in Section 3.1, to conduct a pre-training practical assessment, Site A offered an excavation site where participants were exposed to seven types of hazards. Participants were instructed to walk to the predefined positions around the site and orally identify, evaluate and respond to each hazard in VR within 10 min. In each position, participants were prompted to answer the following questions: - What hazard can you see?

- How did you identify it?

- Why did you identify it as a hazard?

- How will you respond to the hazard?


Participants then received a score ranging from 0 to 3 for their responses to hazards in each position, where 0 means failed to identify, 1 stands for being able to identify, 2 stands for being able to identify and evaluate, and 3 stands for being able to identify, evaluate and respond. As a result, a participant's possible score for pre-training practical performance ranged from 0 to 21. Table 2 shows the full list of hazards and correct responses. After the assessment of pre-training practical performance and receiving training in Site A, participants reached Site B, where post-training practical performance was measured. Site B contained seven similar hazards as to Site A. The same procedure and measures were applied to participants to assess post-training practical performance.
4.2.2 User experience
Participants rated their user experience immediately after being exposed to the immersive VR training system, with their assessments covering three dimensions: realism, ease of use, and ease of learning (Feng et al. , 2020). Realism refers to how credible were the scenarios, animations, simulations and interactions in VR environments. Ease of use means how easy it was for participants to understand and use the immersive VR training system. Ease of learning stands for how easy it was for participants to acquire knowledge and skills from the immersive VR training system. Table 3 lists the dimensions and corresponding statements used to assess user experience. Participants were instructed to provide their levels of agreement with each statement using a 7-point Likert scale (−3 = strongly disagree, +3 = strongly agree).
4.3 Procedures
Massey University Research Ethics Committee granted ethics approval (Southern A, Application 18/21) to conduct this study. Upon arrival at the test facility, participants read participation information sheets and signed consent forms. Following that, they answered a questionnaire which collected demographic information and prior experience in the construction sector, excavation, safety training, video games and VR. Next, participants received instructions and health and safety induction about VR and the use of Oculus Quest and undertook the VR tutorials in the office scenario. When participants were comfortable with VR, they proceeded to Site A where their pre-training practical performance was assessed. Then, participants received training at the same site. After that, participants proceeded to Site B where post-training practical performance was assessed. Finally, participants exited VR and completed another questionnaire about their user experience in VR.
4.4 Results
4.4.1 Practical performance
The boxplots in Figure 5 indicate that participants' practical performance to excavation hazards increased immediately after training (pre-training: M  = 11.3, SD = 4.94; post-training: M  = 17.7, SD = 3.67). Shapiro–Wilk tests confirmed that the sets of scores are non-normal distributed. Therefore, a Wilcoxon signed-rank test was undertaken, which indicated that participants significantly increased their practical performance ( p  < 0.001).
4.4.2 User experience
Three dimensions were measured to assess user experience. Cronbach's alphas suggested that the multiple statements were consistent in each dimension (Realism: 0.735, Ease of use: 0.871, Ease of learning: 0.842). For each participant, the score of each dimension was calculated by averaging the scores of the multiple statements in each dimension. The results of user experience are reported in boxplots (Realism: M  = 2.2, SD = 0.69; Ease of use: M  = 2.5, SD = 0.55; Ease of learning: M  = 2.6, SD = 0.53), as shown in Figure 6. In general, participants acknowledged that VR scenarios were credible, and it was easy for them to use and learn from the immersive VR training system.
5. Comparative study
The pilot study suggested that the immersive VR training system is an effective way to deliver training. However, the performance of the immersive VR training system against traditional training methods was still unclear. Therefore, a comparative study was undertaken to test the proposed immersive VR training system against a traditional training method. This comparative study followed a two-group pretest-posttest experimental design. A treatment group received training from the immersive VR training system. A control group received training via a traditional training method, in this case an excavation health and safety manual. The same measures were used to assess participants' safety knowledge about excavation hazards before, immediately after and four-week after training. In addition, participants' self-efficacy was examined before and immediately after training.
5.1 Participants
A total of 39 participants (16 females, 23 males), who were recruited by direct contacts and referrals, completed the comparative study. None had participated in the previous pilot study. The participants consisted of 9 university students and 30 professionals from the construction sector. Forty-six per cent (18) of the participants had less than two years of work experience in the construction sector, 33.3% (13) had experience in excavation work, and 20.5% (8) had received safety training in excavation work.
5.2 Measures
5.2.1 Safety knowledge
In this comparative study, participants' safety knowledge was measured via a knowledge test, which was applicable to the participants from both groups. This knowledge test included ten multiple-choice questions covering the seven critical hazards identified in Section 3.3. Table 4 displays the full list of questions and correct answers. The knowledge test was administered to both groups before, immediately after and four weeks after training via Google Forms. A correct answer scored 1 point, and a wrong answer contributed to 0 points. As a result, the possible scores of a participant ranged from 0 to 10 for a knowledge test.
5.2.2 Self-efficacy
Self-efficacy is an instrument to indicate an individual's belief in their capability to perform tasks or gain attainments (Bandura, 1978). Based on the general self-efficacy scale (Schwarzer and Jerusalem, 1995), eight self-rated statements were employed to measure participants' self-efficacy: - I can always manage to follow excavation-related health and safety rules.

- I am confident that I could safely deal with hazardous events in excavation work.

- I am confident I can take care of myself and others in excavation work.

- I can remain calm when facing hazardous events in excavation work.

- I can usually find appropriate health and safety solutions when I am confronted with hazardous events in excavation work.

- I know how to protect people from hazardous events in excavation work.

- I can usually find appropriate ways to handle hazardous events in excavation work.

- It is easy for me to comply with health and safety rules to protect myself in excavation work.


Participants' self-efficacy was measured before and immediately after training. According to the general self-efficacy scale (Schwarzer and Jerusalem, 1995), participants were instructed to provide their levels of agreement with each statement using a 5-point Likert scale (1 = Not at all true, 5 = Exactly true). The final score of a participant was the sum of the scores of all statements, so it would be in the range of 8–40.
5.3 Procedures
Massey University Research Ethics Committee granted ethics approval (Southern A, Application 18/21) to conduct this study. Upon arrival at the test facility, participants read participation information sheets and signed consent forms. Then participants were randomly assigned to two groups: a treatment group where the immersive VR training system was implemented and a control group where an excavation health and safety manual was used. Participants answered a pre-training questionnaire that collected demographic information and prior experience in construction, excavation and safety training. Also, the questionnaire measured participants' excavation safety knowledge and self-efficacy.
For the treatment group (VR), participants received instructions and health and safety induction about VR and the use of Oculus Quest and undertook VR tutorials in the office scenario. When participants were comfortable with VR, they proceeded to Site A where training took place. In this case, the pre-training practical assessment at Site A and post-training practical assessment at Site B were skipped. After completing training, participants exited VR and answered a post-training questionnaire about their excavation safety knowledge and self-efficacy.
Participants in the control group (Manual) received health and safety induction based on an excavation health and safety manual. Participants were instructed to study the manual until they felt they understood and remembered the items on it. After completing training, participants answered a post-training questionnaire about their excavation safety knowledge and self-efficacy. For both groups, participants were contacted four weeks after training and asked to complete a retention questionnaire that measured excavation safety knowledge.
5.4 Results
5.4.1 Safety knowledge
The boxplots in Figure 7 indicate that for both groups, participant safety knowledge of excavation hazards had increased immediately after training (Post) as compared to pre-training (Pre) and declined four weeks after training (Retention). Knowledge scores were submitted to a 2 × 3 mixed design ANOVA, where groups (VR and Manual) were served as a between-subject variable and time of measurement (Pre, Post and Retention) was severed as a within-subjects variable. Mauchly's test indicated that the assumption of sphericity was not violated ( χ 2 (2) = 0.637, p  = 0.727). Results reveal a significant main effect of time of measurement ( F (2,74) = 13.763, p  < 0.001, η p 2  = 0.271) and no significant interactions between time and groups ( F (2,74) = 1.598, p  = 0.209, η p 2  = 0.041).
Within each group, a one-way repeated measures ANOVA followed by pairwise comparisons using Bonferroni tests were conducted to test the effects of time of measurement. For the treatment group (VR, see Figure 8), the mean pre-training knowledge score was 5.11 (SD = 1.197), the mean post-training knowledge score was 6.74 (SD = 1.695), and the mean retention knowledge score was 6.47 ( M  = 1.124). ANOVA results suggest that there was a significant main effect of time on knowledge scores ( F (2,36) = 9.343, p  = 0.001, η p 2  = 0.342). Pairwise comparisons with Bonferroni tests indicate significant differences in knowledge scores between pre-training and post-training ( p  = 0.009) and pre-training and retention ( p  = 0.003), but no significant difference between post-training and retention. For the control group (Manual, see Figure 8), the mean pre-training knowledge score was 5.00 (SD = 1.747), the mean post-training knowledge score was 6.80 (SD = 1.508), and the mean retention knowledge score was 5.45 ( M  = 1.669). ANOVA results suggest that there was a significant main effect of time on knowledge scores ( F (2,38) = 6.789, p  = 0.003, η p 2  = 0.263). Pairwise comparisons with Bonferroni tests indicate significant differences in knowledge scores between pre-training and post-training ( p  = 0.006) and post-training and retention ( p  = 0.030), but no significant difference between pre-training and retention.
ANCOVA was performed to test the effects of the groups (VR and Manual) at two levels of time of measurement separately: post-training and retention. Firstly, the analysis controlled for pre-training scores as covariates. Results show that there was no significant difference between groups regarding post-training knowledge scores ( F (1, 36) = 0.017, p  = 0.897, η p 2  < 0.001) but a significant difference regarding retention knowledge scores ( F (1, 36) = 4.829, p  = 0.034, η p 2  = 0.118). Secondly, the analysis controlled for post-training scores as covariates. Results suggest that there was a significant difference between groups regarding retention knowledge scores ( F (1, 36) = 5.176, p  = 0.029, η p 2  = 0.126).
5.4.2 Self-efficacy
The boxplots in Figure 9 demonstrate that participants' self-efficacy about excavation health and safety increased immediately after training. ANCOVA was performed to test the effects of groups (VR and Manual) on self-efficacy scores immediately after training. The analysis controlled for pre-training scores as covariates. Results show that there was a significant difference regarding post-training self-efficacy scores between groups ( F (1, 36) = 7.659, p  = 0.009, η p 2  = 0.175). The treatment group (VR) reported a higher self-efficacy score than the control group (Manual) immediately after training.
Within each group, Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were conducted to examine the increment of self-efficacy scores before and immediately after training. Results suggest that both the treatment groups (VR, pre-training: M  = 21.42, SD = 7.918; post-training M  = 30.42, SD = 4.948) and control group (Manual, pre-training: M  = 19.05, SD = 7.030; post-training: M  = 24.85, SD = 6.683) significantly increased their self-efficacy scores (VR: p  < 0.001, Manual p  = 0.003) immediately after training.
6. Discussion
Excavation safety training is fundamental for construction workers. However, the existing literature highlights that VR-based excavation safety training has been marginally investigated. This study proposes an immersive VR training system designed for excavation safety and tests the training system from multiple perspectives.
First, the pilot study investigated participants' practical performance in immersive VR to assess the effectiveness of the proposed immersive VR training system. Results indicate that participants significantly improved their practical performance in dealing with excavation hazards immediately after training (see Figure 4). This finding is consistent with that of Feng et al . (2020), who reported that immersive VR training effectively delivers safety knowledge. Most prior VR studies in the literature examined the effectiveness of VR training systems by assessing explicit knowledge via paper-based or electronic knowledge tests. However, it remains unclear whether participants can translate acquired knowledge into practical actions. Knowledge translation is a process which involves knowledge creation and knowledge application (Graham et al. , 2006). The knowledge-to-action process is a cycle in which several phases are involved, such as monitoring knowledge use, evaluating outcomes and sustained application of knowledge (Graham et al. , 2006). Manns et al . (2015) conducted a cross-sectional study and discovered a knowledge-to-practice gap. Their results suggest that physical therapy graduates do not use newly acquired knowledge to inform their practice. Similarly, Zeedyk et al . (2001) argued children's road safety knowledge and their behaviour needs to be separated, because knowing more does not necessarily mean behaving more safely on the road. Regarding VR training, many studies tested knowledge acquisition to assess the effectiveness of VR training systems; however, few measured practical performance. Li et al . (2017) tested different training tools to teach self-protection skills in earthquake situations and used various VR scenarios to assess participants' practical performance after training by calculating physical damage received by participants in virtual earthquakes. Their results indicate that participants performed best when trained by VR compared to those trained by other tools. This accords with the results of the pilot study, which suggests that VR training is capable of improving practical performance in dealing with excavation hazards.
Second, the comparative study investigated knowledge acquisition and retention effectiveness. The results indicate that the proposed immersive VR training system effectively delivered excavation safety knowledge to participants and participants retained the safety knowledge four weeks after training (see Figures 7 and 8). For the VR group, safety knowledge improved significantly after training and did not decrease significantly after four weeks. This finding supports the evidence from previous observations that VR training is effective in delivering knowledge and fostering its retention (Chittaro and Buttussi, 2015; Lovreglio et al. , 2021). VR studies for construction safety training often focus on helping people acquire new knowledge and skills (Eiris et al. , 2020; Jeelani et al. , 2020). However, the impact of VR-based construction safety training on knowledge retention is yet to be fully investigated. Knowledge retention is a critical process that transfers new knowledge from short-term to long-term memory (Lindsey et al. , 2014). Newly acquired knowledge is vulnerable because forgetting always occurs, as demonstrated by Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve (Murre and Dros, 2015). In the construction sector, poor safety training and poor safety knowledge retention are known to be contributing factors to the high incidence of injury (Wilkins, 2011). The retention result from the comparative study demonstrates the potential value of VR for construction safety training, because effective knowledge transfer and knowledge retention can be expected. One possible explanation for this could be that VR allows for spatial interaction and the use of interactive instructional methods (Babu et al. , 2018). In our case, participants from the pilot study acknowledged the user experience of the immersive VR training system, where realism, ease of use and ease of learning received high scores (see Figure 6).
Third, the comparative study tested the immersive VR training system against a traditional training method (a safety manual). Results show that both the VR group and the Manual group increased safety knowledge significantly immediately after training. However, four weeks after training, the acquired knowledge decayed significantly for the Manual group but was retained well for the VR group (see Figures 7 and 8). The VR group showed significant and measurable knowledge retention, while the Manual group did not. This finding indicates that VR and safety manuals have a similar capability to deliver construction safety knowledge, but VR outperforms safety manuals in terms of knowledge retention. This finding provides new insights into the existing literature on whether VR training is more effective than traditional training. This finding reflects the results by Sacks et al. (2013) and Joshi et al. (2021), which show that VR provides more effective training for construction safety training. Similar findings were also published by Chittaro and Buttussi (2015) for aviation safety training and Lovreglio et al . (2021) for fire extinguishing training. One possible reason could be that, in their cases, VR provides hands-on operation and achieves learning by doing. Learn-by-doing is one of the most effective processes for acquiring knowledge (Chen et al. , 2020). The results from Li et al . (2017) also show that VR training is superior to safety videos and safety manuals in terms of teaching self-protection skills in earthquake situations. Their participants were trained by VR and learned by doing, where they could engage, explore, evaluate and enrich in a virtual earthquake. When learn-by-doing is applicable in real-world environments, VR training may not beat traditional training. For instance, Murcia-López and Steed (2018) compared virtual and physical training for bimanual assembly tasks. Both training conditions could have hands-on experience in assembling 3D burr puzzles, one virtually and one physically. They did not discover a significant difference between virtual and physical training in both immediate tests and retention tests. Taken together, it is possible that a few factors may determine whether VR is more effective than traditional training, such as instructional methods used in training and types of knowledge or skills delivered.
Finally, the results illustrate that the level of self-efficacy significantly increased for both groups right after the training, but the treatment group (VR) reported a significantly higher self-efficacy score than the control group (Manual) immediately after training. This finding is consistent with the findings reported by Lovreglio et al . (2021). The self-efficacy comparison highlights that VR training is more effective than traditional training in promoting protection motivation; for instance, motivating people to protect themselves from excavation hazards and threats. VR training offers a high level of interaction in virtual environments, which could be one of the contributors to increasing self-efficacy (Merchant et al. , 2012). This is supported by the fact that one of the key influencing factors on self-efficacy is the perceived ability to manipulate and control an event (Bandura, 1993), which is made possible via VR training.
6.1 Limitations and future research
This study has limitations. First, it assesses retention by measuring knowledge test scores. However, whether VR improves long-term practical performance is yet to be investigated. Future research could examine the long-term impact of VR training on whether knowledge can be translated into practical action after a long training period. Second, this study only applies health and safety manuals as a traditional training method. Future research could test VR training against other types of traditional training, such as seminars, videos and health and safety induction meetings. Third, this study uses only questioning as the instructional method for the proposed VR training system, and the VR training system only delivers explicit knowledge to participants. In Section 6, possible explanations for the better performance of VR training are given; however, different instructional methods used and types of knowledge delivered might affect the effectiveness of VR training. This could be the subject of future research. Last, the participants of the pilot study and comparative study consisted of university students and construction professionals. It would be interesting to repeat the study with construction workers on the ground.
7. Conclusion
This study aimed to investigate the effectiveness of immersive VR safety training for construction excavation. A pilot study and a comparative study were conducted to test the proposed immersive VR training system. The pilot study's results suggest that the VR training system is effective in improving participants' practical performance when dealing with excavation hazards. Also, participants acknowledged the realism, ease of use and ease of learning provided by the VR training system. The comparative study's results show that both VR and health and safety manuals can effectively deliver safety knowledge and increase self-efficacy. However, VR is more effective than health and safety manuals with respect to knowledge retention. Overall, the results identify that VR solutions are effective for excavation safety training.
This study makes novel contributions to the extant literature. First, this study provides insights into VR-based excavation safety training. This is an addition to the literature which lacks evidence showing the effectiveness of VR for excavation safety training. Second, this study demonstrates that VR training can improve practical performance. This is different from the literature, where in most cases, VR safety training is assessed by the effect on knowledge acquisition. Last, this study provides extra evidence about comparing VR and traditional training to the literature. This study shows that VR and traditional training may perform similarly in immediate knowledge acquisition. However, VR training outperforms traditional training in the long term because more safety knowledge can be retained following VR training.
These findings have several implications. First, this study demonstrates the effectiveness of VR-based excavation safety training in terms of immediate knowledge acquisition, practical performance and knowledge retention. In addition, VR outperforms traditional approaches in the case of knowledge retention. The construction industry can take from this to test and apply VR solutions into actual practice for excavation safety. By applying a more effective training solution, the construction industry may improve health and safety performance and, ultimately, reduce injuries and casualties in excavation works. Second, this study shows that VR effectively improves practical performance following training. This implies that the knowledge acquired via VR training can inform actual actions. This means that VR safety training could change behaviours, thus, improving practical performance. This implication can be extended to other VR training solutions, where knowledge and practice can be enhanced together. Therefore, it is worth testing the effect of VR on practical performance in different types of training.
The authors would like to thank all participants taking part in this study. Dr Lovreglio would like to thank the College of Science for supporting the research through the Massey University Research Fund (MURF).

Table 2 Practical performance items and criteria
Hazards Identification Evaluation Response
1. Absence of a safety officer Determine whether a safety officer is present on site by viewing a safety file and inspecting excavation sites Accidents may occur as there are no safety officers to identify, evaluate and respond to hazards on site Inform supervisors. Ensure a safety officer is present on site before performing any excavation work
2. Absence of soil protection Determine soil types by viewing a safety file to identify whether the excavation's slope complies with the allowable slope specified in current safety guidelines Measure the depth of excavation sites If the excavation is not properly sloped or shielded, or shored at depths greater than 1.5 m, the soil may potentially collapse Inform supervisors Shore, shield, or slope excavation sites
3. Objects or loads near excavation edges Inspect the area to identify objects or loads near the excavation edge and measure their individual distances to the edge Objects or loads may fall on workers in excavation sites Objects or loads may affect soil stability and cause collapse Move objects or loads 1 m away from the excavation's zone of influence
4. Absence of safe access and egress Inspect the area to identify whether an access system is in place and measure its distance to each worker in excavation sites With the absence of safe access and egress, workers may get injured when entering and exiting excavation sites. Also, workers may not egress safely when there is an emergency Place access systems (e.g. ladders) in excavation sites and ensure access systems are no more than 7.6 m away from workers at all times
5. Workers or mobile plants close to dangerous utilities and objects Determine the types of utilises on site. Inspect the location of utilities and measure their individual distance to each worker Workers may strike utilities and get an electric shock or be exposed to hazardous contaminants Establish adequate working areas by taking into account minimum approach distances to utilities on site
6. Absence of safety barriers and signage Visually inspect excavation sites Objects or loads may fall on workers, or mobile plants may strike workers in excavation sites Place appropriate barriers and safety signages
7. Workers working in an unsafe excavation site Visually inspect excavation sites Accidents may occur due to the aforementioned hazards Stop excavation work immediately and provide means of egress

Test questions Correct answers
1. When does a safety officer need to inspect an excavation site for safety hazards? Before the start of each work shift, during the work, after any circumstance which may affect the stability of the trench and after human-induced or natural events

Lessons learned in developing online violence prevention trainings

Author: Willard, Jessica1    ; Mennicke, Annelise1    ; Coker, Ann L.2    1 School of Social Work, University of North Carolina at Charlotte, Charlotte, NC, US jessdwillard@gmail.com2 Center for Research on Violence Against Women, University of Kentucky, Lexington, KY, US

Publication info: Willard, Jessica; Mennicke, Annelise; Coker, Ann L. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/lessons-learned-developing-online-violence/docview/3088564746/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: PurposeThe proliferation of online learning and digital media has both expanded opportunities for violence prevention programming and presented challenges for replicating the benefits of in-person learning environments. The advent of learning management systems (LMS) and online data collection tools has advanced scientific inquiry and reach, while also requiring mastery of an ever-changing digital landscape.MethodsThis paper provides a framework for developing effective online violence prevention trainings, using tenets of bystander intervention, andragogical learning principles, learning taxonomies, and eLearning instructional design.ResultsOur application of online violence prevention training was selected because evidence-based in-person bystander training models exist and can serve as a content model for online adaptation. Specifically, we review how to design interventions that appeal to adult learners’ needs and motivations (andragogical learning principles), organize learning outcomes according to a range of cognitive processes (learning taxonomies), and create engaging digital learning products (eLearning instructional design). Further, we discuss how to promote knowledge retention and skills acquisition through cognitive and behavioral interactivity, role play demonstrations, real-time assessment, and simulation-based learning. We describe practical components of online training development, including technological considerations, creative elements, and evaluative measures. Lastly, we provide direction on vendor selection; ensuring web content accessibility compliance; and optimizing data capture.ConclusionsBy exploring new directions in online interventions for violence research, we seek to bridge existing gaps in training delivered in-person and in digital settings. The future of virtual reality and education

Author: Feridun, Kamil Bartu1; Bayraktar, Ümmü11 Girne American University, Faculty of Communication, Cyprus bartu.feridun@gmail.com; ummubayraktar@gau.edu.tr

Publication info: Feridun, Kamil Bartu; Bayraktar, Ümmü. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/future-virtual-reality-education/docview/3098790088/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: In today’s world, technology plays a significant role in shaping our daily interactions and how we connect with the world. The rapid advancements in technology have influenced many sectors, particularly education, where integrating technology is now seen as essential rather than just a luxury. As a result, the education field has adapted over time to keep up with innovations and their potential to improve the teaching and learning environment. The incorporation of technology into education has evolved from introducing computer systems in classrooms to the adoption of smartboards, tablets, and e-learning platforms. The rise of Virtual Reality (VR) technology has also opened up possibilities for hands-on learning experiences that allow students to explore and practice skills in ways that traditional teaching methods cannot. VR technology enables students to interact with content in a way that fosters a sense of presence and immersion, which can improve knowledge retention. In fields, like science, engineering, medicine, arts, and language learning, VR applications have shown promise in boosting student engagement and enhancing skills within a controlled learning environment. However, the widespread adoption of VR technology in education faces challenges. One significant obstacle is the cost of acquiring VR equipment and software which can strain budgets. Additionally, the availability of high- quality content for VR platforms poses a barrier for educators seeking to integrate VR into their teaching practices. This article delves into the use of Virtual Reality in education, and how VR can influence student learning outcomes in applications such as medicine, science, arts and language learning. Apart from the advantages of VR, the article also discusses the obstacles that are impeding the use of VR in education including concerns about costs, standardizing content and the necessity for training and support for educators. As VR technology advances and becomes widely available, it stands ready to revolutionize the landscape by offering learning opportunities that were previously beyond imagination. Through this technology, education can introduce a world of possibilities that nurture curiosity, creativity and a lifelong enthusiasm for learning. The Future of Virtual Reality and Education

Author: Kamil Bartu FERIDUN; BAYRAKTAR, Ümmü

Publication info: Kamil Bartu FERIDUN; BAYRAKTAR, Ümmü. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/future-virtual-reality-education/docview/3090230066/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: In today’s world, technology plays a significant role in shaping our daily interactions and how we connect with the world. The rapid advancements in technology have influenced many sectors, particularly education, where integrating technology is now seen as essential rather than just a luxury. As a result, the education field has adapted over time to keep up with innovations and their potential to improve the teaching and learning environment. The incorporation of technology into education has evolved from introducing computer systems in classrooms to the adoption of smartboards, tablets, and e-learning platforms. The rise of Virtual Reality (VR) technology has also opened up possibilities for hands-on learning experiences that allow students to explore and practice skills in ways that traditional teaching methods cannot. VR technology enables students to interact with content in a way that fosters a sense of presence and immersion, which can improve knowledge retention. In fields, like science, engineering, medicine, arts, and language learning, VR applications have shown promise in boosting student engagement and enhancing skills within a controlled learning environment. However, the widespread adoption of VR technology in education faces challenges. One significant obstacle is the cost of acquiring VR equipment and software which can strain budgets. Additionally, the availability of high-quality content for VR platforms poses a barrier for educators seeking to integrate VR into their teaching practices. This article delves into the use of Virtual Reality in education, and how VR can influence student learning outcomes in applications such as medicine, science, arts and language learning. Apart from the advantages of VR, the article also discusses the obstacles that are impeding the use of VR in education including concerns about costs, standardizing content and the necessity for training and support for educators. As VR technology advances and becomes widely available, it stands ready to revolutionize the landscape by offering learning opportunities that were previously beyond imagination. Through this technology, education can introduce a world of possibilities that nurture curiosity, creativity and a lifelong enthusiasm for learning.

AI-enhanced Academic Animations and Chatbots: transforming library learning experiences and user engagement

Author: Bonal, R B11 Central University of Karnataka, Kalaburagi, Karnataka, India

Publication info: Bonal, R B. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/ai-enhanced-academic-animations-chatbots/docview/3168800790/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: The swift advancement of digital and artificial intelligence (AI) technology has offered new avenues for improving library educational experiences. The study discussed in this article examines the efficacy of incorporating Al-powered academic animations and chatbots into library resources to increase user engagement, knowledge retention, and overall learning outcomes. The findings indicate that Al-driven educational animations offer interactive and visually compelling material. This results in substantial enhancement of users' perception of challenging concepts and boosts their curiosity to explore library resources. Additionally, incorporating chatbots as virtual assistants provides individualized support, responding in real-time to users-particular needs and inquiries, promoting a more effective and user-friendly library experience. The study emphasizes how Al-driven academic animations and chatbots can revolutionize library learning spaces, offering users a more engaging, appealing, approachable, and valuable learning environment. The study suggests further research into these technologies and their integration into library systems. They focused on multidisciplinary collaboration and creating standards of excellence to ensure cutting-edge tools, successful deployment, and long-term sustainability.

Full text: Headnote Abstract
The swift advancement of digital and artificial intelligence (AI) technology has offered new avenues for improving library educational experiences. The study discussed in this article examines the efficacy of incorporating Al-powered academic animations and chatbots into library resources to increase user engagement, knowledge retention, and overall learning outcomes. The findings indicate that Al-driven educational animations offer interactive and visually compelling material. This results in substantial enhancement of users' perception of challenging concepts and boosts their curiosity to explore library resources. Additionally, incorporating chatbots as virtual assistants provides individualized support, responding in real-time to users-particular needs and inquiries, promoting a more effective and user-friendly library experience. The study emphasizes how Al-driven academic animations and chatbots can revolutionize library learning spaces, offering users a more engaging, appealing, approachable, and valuable learning environment. The study suggests further research into these technologies and their integration into library systems. They focused on multidisciplinary collaboration and creating standards of excellence to ensure cutting-edge tools, successful deployment, and long-term sustainability.
Keywords: Academic animations, Educational animations, Artificial intelligence, Chatbots, User engagement
Introduction
Commoners to eccentrics, the preset world is surrounded by a digital world filled with multimedia content. The digital world is a vital component of existence for Generation Z and Alpha (Kohnová, Papula, and Salajova 2021) (Çoklar and Tatli 2021). With the rapid advancement of the internet, reliance on online information sources and information-seeking habits have intensified. Progress in information and communications technology (ICT) capabilities with versatile multimedia broadened the bounds of libraries. They are paving the way for an enormous expansion in information, known as the information explosion, which has led to information management assistance for online publication platforms (Barnett 1964; material can cause difficulties for the researchinclined younger generation, which needs improved channeling of online information (Sun and Yuan 2012).
Owing to the simplicity of data/information transfer via communication networks, there may be a rise in the cost or rate of online information production and the risk of data theft (Dewi, Meiliana, Chandra 2019). Programmes designed to reduce data theft have built-in firewalls that reduce this potential risk. These systems have intricate navigation processes built in to filter out unexpected occurrences. This complicated process of reaching the target makes information producers and disseminators feel aggrieved (Alexander, Barrett, Cumming, et al. 2016).
Although information may be secure, it prohibits providing real-time updates to the right users. Fortunately, rapid advancements in ICT have increased the ability to include widely consumed audio-visual information. An example involves scholarly material enhanced with animated elements to aid students in grasping intricate ideas within the syllabus. Teachers may utilize both auditory and visual tools to elucidate topics and strengthen comprehension. Academic Animations
Scholarly animation employs video clips, pictures, and graphical enhancements to communicate ideas, principles, and intellectual discoveries. It aids in diverse fields such as physics, math, engineering, healthcare, and social studies. To illuminate such complex ideas which are approachable and comprehensible (Ismail, Mahazir, Othman, et al. 2017). Many types of academic animation exist, including motion graphics, simulations, 2D and 3D animation, and explainer videos (Smith, McLaughlin, Brown 2012). They often combine music, sound effects, and narration to create multimedia learning experiences that will aid students in understanding and remembering the material. It provides a more engaging learning experience than traditional textbooks and lectures. Academic animation is growing in popularity in the digital age. Educators can give students a visual picture of complicated concepts, theories, and occurrences that can be difficult to comprehend through text alone by using animation (Baglama, Yucesoy, Yikmis, et al. 2018). The software has the ability to create livelier, captivating, and clear graphics accompanied by subtitles and animated : sequences in multiple languages. This surpasses : the static nature of plain text which fails to : capture evolving dynamics and doesn't require : viewers to mentally picture the subject matter, : in contrast to reading a book. This approach of : crafting material using such software is termed : animation. Academic animation refers to : employing animation to enhance educational : experiences.
Designing precise choices proves difficult, : given the wealth of data available. Scholars : acknowledge the enormity of these occurrences. : They prioritize the needs of individuals who : wield authority over their online engagements, : notably on communication platforms, : broadening the scope of available materials. : Animation has gained prominence in education : recently, with science-themed animation : receiving widespread appeal. The benefits : of cuddling animation and some expected : applications in science had been discussed in : previous researches (Nayak, Liu, Hsu, et al. 2021; : Не 2021).
An experimental study carried out amongst : Turkish University students discovered that : utilizing animations in the curriculum favours : academic performance (Bülbül and Kuzu 2021). : Animation as multimedia material can quickly : become popular due to its ability to communicate : complex ideas in brief video clips and various : languages (Ploetzner, Berney, and Bétrancourt : 2021). Astro animation explained the inference : to instructors, students, and the general public in : a study. Designing educational animations could be made simple with the usage of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning. Numerous open source projects support innovative pedagogical techniques for interactive learning (Karavirta and Shaffer 2016). A study on animation design explained how prospective instructors might use technology to develop educational animations as part of their overall pedagogical preparation. The study demonstrated that the technologyenhanced educational system improves contemporary students' educational and cognitive activities (Punchyk, Murodhodjaeva, Averin, et al. 2020).
Academic animations can be used initially in the sciences to teach anatomy and the comprehension of processes, in computer science to prepare flow charts, and in engineering and chemistry to introduce methods and reactions (Lepito 2018). However, there is proof that academic animations have benefited fields outside of science as well (Laksmi, Yasa, and Mirayani 2021). YouTube was used in a case study on scientific procedures involving animations in higher education to determine the impact on learning and the results were encouraging. Research-related animations, in addition to curriculum-based animations, can aid in advancing breakthroughs in science (Agustini, Santyadiputra, and Sugihartini 2020). Ensuring availability of the information sources to the patrons is the responsibility of the libraries. Written material and static graphic images must be encouraging enough to attract new people. The information sources ought to be substituted, usable, and quick to assimilate the information (Kikuchi, Ono, Ito, et al. 2022). Academic animations can draw more visitors and transform a library into a hub for active research, teaching, and learning (Schwarz 2018).

Exploring the Potential of Academic Animations in Digital Libraries
Books of reference in the library encompass diverse entities spanning different historical backgrounds. The content may be general or related to a particular discipline and serve as a primary, secondary, or tertiary source of information. E-books, E-journals, E-thesis/ dissertations, E-newspapers, research databases, manuals, and archives are all commonly used electronic formats. The primary sources began as print and transitioned progressively to electronic, offering new formats to deliver the services to anticipated users.
Online publication is mainly responsible for the exuberance of information available in electronic form. That results in information contamination and undesired information (Meel Vishwakarma 2020). It would be difficult to validate the study's data and determine its accuracy in such a setting (Igbal, Ahmad, and Nawaz 2020). The information sector may use expertly crafted shot animations to address these issues and draw in the desired user (Asyidiq, Oktariani, and Akmal, 2020). The new format for disseminating information may be the universe of pertinent knowledge on a specific subject created by innovators in the form of animation (Sari, Susilo, and Limbong 2021). Therefore, Library and Information Science LIS specialists everywhere must prepare to embrace the hidden world of academic animations (Yin and Chen 2010).
Academics are just beginning to explore the field of academic animation (Tugtekin and Dursun 2022). They are becoming increasingly popular in the sciences since they may depict anatomical phenomena with an immersive experience (Macias and Munino 2021). : According to Hoyek, Collet, Rienzo, et al. : (2014), these animations communicate more : clearly than theoretical briefings. To quickly : communicate in-depth meaning to professionals : and decision-makers, instructional animations : can support academic communities, scientific : literature, knowledge development, and further : research (Sumida and Jefcoat 2018). AI can assist : libraries in producing high-quality academic : animations that are engaging, personalized, : accessible, and correct. AI algorithms can sift : through massive volumes of data to find essential : concepts and ideas. That must be communicated, : and educational materials must be developed, : including animations tailored to individual needs : and learning styles.
Furthermore, Al can personalize animations, : identify learning styles, and adapt to user : feedback apart from providing contextual : information, improve accessibility, and ensure : quality assurance (Zawacki-Richter, Marín, Bond, : et al. 2019). Several libraries worldwide have used : Al-generated academic animations and natural : language processing to provide services to : patrons in different languages (Haffenden, Fano, : Malmsten, et al. 2023). Libraries can translate : their resources and collections into many : languages using Al-powered language translation : services, rendering them readily accessible to : a larger audience (Cox and Mazumdar 2022). : Using Al-generated academic animations : and natural language processing can improve : engagement, comprehension, and learning : effectiveness.
Science-technology-engineering-mathematics (STEM) education much : room for improvement, according to Gagnier, : Holochwost, and Fisher (2022). Game: : academic animations give visual : cues and feedback, reinforcing appealing : and intriguing ideas and abilities (Yin 2022). : Academic animations could merge with : gaming elements, such as animated characters, characters, interactive simulations, and visual challenges, enhance student involvement and enthusiasm in learning. Integrating games with educational animations offers significant benefits, including the enhancement of spatial memory, problemsolving skills, and understanding of real-world scenarios. This approach is a valuable tool for educators aiming to create enjoyable and effective learning environments. The focus and drive to learn by introducing games and animations in the classroom make it less daunting and more entertaining.
The burgeoning demand for access to information in today's fast-paced world has rendered digital libraries indispensable. Integrating academic animations within digital libraries is a promising avenue for augmenting user interactivity and engendering a greater degree of engagement. Particularly in STEM, where visual representation can help understand abstract concepts, these animated graphics can be an excellent tool for learning and comprehending : complex topics (Evagorou, Erduran, and Mäntylä 2015; Wu and Rau 2019). Educational : animations within academia serve to illustrate : library resources such as databases and : research tools. Chatbots and Virtual Assistants
Libraries have the potential to employ chatbots : and virtual helpers to address inquiries from : patrons using advanced language processing promptly. This approach facilitates swift and : effortless access to necessary information without requiring human intervention. Although chatbot utilization is widespread across various sectors, there remains untapped potential within libraries, necessitating further examination. Many libraries have yet to harness the full benefits of chatbot integration to enrich their offerings and cater more effectively to their patrons. However, some libraries have begun implementing chatbots to provide their patrons with faster and more convenient services (Allison 2012; Harisanty, Anna, Putri, et al. 2020). Chatbots are available round-the-clock, every day of the week, enabling users to request aid at any hour, even outside of the library's operating hours (Weigert 2020). This feature proves beneficial for students and scholars in need of information beyond typical library times.
Moreover, automated conversational agents offer consistent responses, ensuring uniform service for all customers, regardless of the time or day. They possess the capability to address numerous inquiries without fatigue or emotional fluctuations. Additionally, they excel in handling repetitive questions and dispensing relevant information while maintaining their composed demeanour. These bots promptly address common queries, suggest books based on user preferences, and gather feedback from patrons. As digital technologies become increasingly integrated, chatbots are poised to become more prevalent in library settings. Their potential to enhance patrons' experiences is vast, providing immediate and tailored assistance. Employing chatbots for routine tasks liberates librarians, allowing them to focus on more complex queries or interactions necessitating human intervention (McNeal and Newyear 2013). Furthermore, chatbots can aid patrons in navigating the physical library space or communicating with staff members more effectively.
A chatbot utilized for library reference services can expeditiously answer commonly asked questions regarding the library, including details about book locations, operational hours, and borrowing policies (Nawaz and Saldeen 2020; Rodriguez and Mune 2022). Chatbots : crafted for suggesting books could aid visitors : in discovering books matching their tastes and : interests. They might ask about preferred authors, : genres, and books and propose similar ones. : Libraries could set up a chatbot to remind users : of upcoming events like book club meetings or : author talks. Additionally, a chatbot could offer : virtual tours of the library, showcasing different : sections and essential resources. Finally, chatbots : could be developed so as to gather feedback : from patrons on library services and suggest : improvements that could enhance services.
Employing a blend of lively virtual : representations and automated conversational : agents might enable libraries to craft a more : persuasive and captivating encounter. For their : patrons while conserving resources and cutting : expenses by reducing the need for human : employees in specific fields (Szarowicz, Amiguet: : Forte, et al. 2001; Li 2021). Given the : inclination towards mechanization and self-aid, : automated conversational systems and digital : representations can assist in enhancing the : operational effectiveness and professionalism of : libraries, all the while catering to the needs of : their patrons.
Conclusion
Libraries ought to offer academic animated : content to their patrons. By providing access : to such materials, libraries enhance the quality : of research and learning experiences for users. : They can procure educational animations : from distributors and animation studios or via : subscription services, either as stand-alone titles : or as part of a package. Additionally, libraries : may enter licensing agreements with animation : creators or vendors to access their collections. : Collaborating with educational institutions and : research centres, libraries can curate academic : animations for their users. They can also explore : open-access repositories like YouTube and Vimeo : to source academic animations. Leveraging : streaming services, libraries could enable users to access these animations on library computers or mobile devices. Furthermore, setting up online archives for remote access ensures the continued availability of academic animations.
Electronic materials reign supreme in the academic realm, which is primarily influenced by the information sector and its innovators. These innovators have also devised the necessary means to enhance the quality and safety of the information they disseminate. Their tools, methods, and rigorous quality evaluations have spurred a significant interest in electronic materials. A similar mobilization of suppliers for educational animations could cater to the needs of prospective clients. Emerging resources, such as electronic ones, are progressively making academic animations an essential element of education.
Furthermore, enhancements in AI and no-cost, application-based programs could simplify the creation of top-notch educational animations for professionals with minimal exertion. The introduction of automated conversational agents in libraries might lead to adverse outcomes. Despite offering library visitors a convenient means to access resources and assistance, concerns regarding privacy should be seriously considered (Adetayo 2023). These agents collect and retain user data on servers, encompassing personal details like names, email addresses, and internet protocol (IP) addresses. Unauthorized parties could potentially access this data, resulting in identity theft or security breaches. Users may become uneasy and dissatisfied if these agents fail to provide accurate or timely responses. Furthermore, they may supplant face-to-face interactions with library staff, diminishing the quality of customer service. Consequently, libraries must carefully evaluate the potential benefits and drawbacks of integrating these agents and deploy them in a manner that enhances rather than diminishes the patron experience. However, it's crucial to acknowledge that animated characters and conversational agents cannot entirely substitute human engagement, particularly in intricate : scenarios requiring empathy and understanding. : Thus, libraries must strike a harmonious balance : between technology and human interaction to : ensure patrons receive optimal service.
Despite numerous global health crises, there : remains ample room for advancing amidst : adversity (Mustafa 2021). While prognosticating : the future is uncertain, individuals can prepare : themselves for it. The recent health crisis : underscored the importance of adeptness in : digital competencies. Learners were compelled : to navigate online realms, procure knowledge, : and effectively interact in virtual settings as : educational landscapes transitioned online. : The aftermath of the pandemic spurred the : assessment of tailored educational aids to : mitigate social seclusion and augment academic : attainment. Through chatbots, forums, and : virtual lecture halls, students could actively : participate, inquire, and collaborate on : group assignments.
A careful and deliberate design of chatbots : is required to keep students' humanism while : learning using emerging technologies (Cerny, : 2023). Educational institutions have valued : massive open online courses and internet : resources. With the rise of online learning, the : prominence of open resources has also grown : within the academic community. Thanks to : smartphones and low-cost mobile networks, : itis now easier to access social media and : tag multimedia content (Wu and Yang 2021). : Unchecked content loading resulted from : that, generating a massive amount of data. It is : essential to choose accurate information first : when considering using a free information : source like this for online education (Razali : and Halim 2021). Resource mobilizers should : consider new avenues in academic animations : to alleviate these circumstances. A tool that : professionals use to illustrate the structure of : ideas. Using AI and machine learning in a natural : language, with subtitles. The general future of : the information society can be guaranteed. One of these hypotheses is that academic animations might be a trustworthy source for incoming patrons. Websites in Asia are already beginning to use animation as a source of information when looking at their content (Brahma and Verma 2022). It is time to focus on exposing library users to fresh materials.
