Full text: Headnote In the dynamic volatile, uncertain, complex, ambiguous (VUCA) landscape, industries like metals and mining face a pressing challenge of skill scarcity due to the struggle to keep up with technological advancements. To revitalize their workforce and appeal to younger generations, integrating gamification into learning and development approaches holds immense potential. Employee motivation and knowledge retention can be elevated by infusing game mechanics such as badges, points, and leaderboards. Gamification fosters engagement, teamwork, and innovation through interactive experiences. This approach can effectively address the skill shortage by enhancing the industry's attractiveness and competitiveness. The paper aims to investigate the skill deficit in the metals and mining sector and explore how gamified learning methods can effectively alleviate this challenge, ultimately aiding in talent acquisition and retention. The study used purposive sampling, and data was gathered through semi-structured interviews with primary stakeholders of learning and development functions. Further, the qualitative data was subjected to thematic analysis using NVivo software. Two significant themes, from eight sub-themes that emerged from thirty codes, were identified. The first theme was issues with the young generation, and the second was the benefits of gamification in learning and development. The study suggests the need for and advantage of gamification in human resource management's learning and development function.
Introduction
There is a shortage of skills and talent in the metal and mining industry. Paucity of qualified and experienced professionals is undeniably a global issue. Around 73% of the companies identified skills gaps in the local labor market as the biggest barrier to the adoption of new technology (ICMM, 2021). The challenges metal and mining companies face in attracting and retaining talent are certainly exacerbated by the industry's perception of them as unattractive and slow to respond to rapid technological changes (Chikatamaria and Prasad, 2019). The metal and mining industry has been through a significant technological transformation. These continuous innovations and technological changes make it more challenging to draw and hold young talented professionals in any sector that is unfashionable to younger generations, perceived as damaging to the environment, and requires hard physical work (Mateus and Martins, 2019).
According to a study conducted by McKinsey and Company (Abenov et al., 2023), 71% of metal and mining leaders find that due to the immense shortage of talented professionals in the company, there is a grievous impact on production targets. It is obstructing the planned objectives of the company as well. Recruiting and retaining talented people in specific fields, such as mining, metallurgy, and process engineering, is more complex than others. According to recent data from Minerals Tertiary Education Council: Key Performance Measures Report 2018, there has been a significant 63% decline in the enrolment ratio for Mining Engineering in Australia since 2014, and a notable 39% decline in courses like mining graduating in the US since 2016. The data demonstrates that the mining and metals industries do not attract young technical experts.
It is extremely disappointing that there is an unprecedented shortage of skills in the metal and mining industry, which will undoubtedly negatively impact the sector's overall productivity and growth. The metal and mining industry has a complete dearth of motivated and trained workforce. Chikatamaria and Prasad (2019) suggested that mining businesses must embrace business risk management practices and integrate change management with developing digital technology to maintain operational sustainability and transparency. The authors also highlighted that one of the major issues in mining industry in India is lack of skill/competent labor. Emerging digital technologies should be incorporated into the training of the next generation of mining professionals to facilitate real-time data collecting, better data analysis, reporting, and process monitoring.
Digital transformation makes businesses more flexible and competitive. There is an urgent need to nurture a learning-friendly culture by introducing different strategies to enhance innovative minds. This learning culture will accelerate the organization's sustainability in digital transformation, raising employee wellbeing and retention (Jain, 2022).
Gamification is one of the most effective and engaging transformations for learning and development. It is a concerted effort to apply different game mechanisms in working environment gaming designs to increase collaborative participation through purposeful and enjoyable interaction. It enables employees to participate wholeheartedly in an interactive experience sharing. It makes learning more enjoyable and inspires and motivates the users to effectively engage with the content. Games incentivize employees to learn and accomplish more skills, which can eventually transform the compelling approach to enjoying and doing approach. It was also reported that a significant number of people are motivated and work more effectively in a competitive environment. Gamification will provide prospects for competitive openings for rewards, incentives, and leaderboard rankings (Mulkeen, 2018).
In this context, one of the major online platforms, Deloitte Leadership Academy, provides a course with multiple components that cover a broad range of themes in consultation. The course aims to simplify several executive training and development initiatives, particularly for those at higher levels. With the aid of Badgeville Game Mechanics, Deloitte adds particular guidelines and incentives like leaderboards, badges, etc., which appear as appropriate gamified features. Trailing leaderboards and status signals is made easier with the app. It also aids in determining how many individuals enroll in, continue, and complete the course. This app aims to generate prompt feedback on the participants progress and eventually guide them toward timely and successful course completion. The prime motive for developing gamification is to boost the senior executives motivation and morale toward completing the training program.
Literature Review
The foremost apprehension in the metal and mining industry today is intrinsically training, motivating, and attracting new talent (Kowalski et al., 2001). The evolving mining workforce has several training issues, like differences between colleagues and their nature of executing job roles. For example, let us compare the newly joined workers who are the youngest (Generation Z) and the existing working population (Boomers) concerning their physiological, mental, social, and cultural characteristics. We can identify a considerable gap. There will also be noticeable differences in their learning modes and job expectations.
Work accomplishments among millennials at the workplace depend on their understanding of work requirements and job roles, which positively influence their learning capacities and motivate them to work more effectively within organizations. According to Jain and Dutta (2019), it is high time to modify the learning contrivances as per millennials preferences and styles. Based on several theoretical studies, the gamification model allows millennials to implement their learning optimally. Adding game elements to the work environment satisfies the needs for immediate satisfaction, accomplishment, and recognition. Researchers recommend that employee gaming platforms should have competitive leaderboards and quick feedback mechanisms.
Gamification in employee training and development is the process of enhancing training and educational exercises with gaming principles, making learning fun, and adding an element of friendly competition to encourage employees to engage with, understand, and retain training content better (Flanagan, 2022). Gamification helps build a learning culture, promoting employee growth and development through fun and engaging training programs (Kaikhosrosh vil i, 2023). It creates a culture that strengthens company culture, builds team spirit, and enhances the training experience. Gamification in training allows employees to see their progress as they learn, which can be very powerful for workplace learning and development. It makes the process more engaging, productive, and enjoyable for employees and improves worker recruitment and retention (Hawley, 2023). Gamification can lead to more engaged, driven, and productive employees. It can also make employees inclined to stay and grow with the company (Flanagan, 2022). Gamification can be incorporated into existing training efforts to make lessons more engaging and successful or build new learning and development initiatives (Hawley, 2023).
Gaonkar et al. (2022) stated that gamification in learning and teaching increases social impact, motivation, and learner engagement. Learners often view gamification as a highly attractive approach to enhance motivation, engagement, and social influence in learning and instruction. Games combine nostalgia, curiosity, visual appeal, and staff involvement to create an emotionally engaging ambience for the player and raise their level of emotional literacy, while inspiring them to explore new avenues and chances. By improving employee engagement and enriching the internal work environment, appropriate gamification makes work enjoyable for staff members. A straightforward example of a game-like tool designed to encourage users to interact with a concept more fully is Linkedln's profile completion tool.
Impact of Gamification on Learning and Development
A study of various research works and journals revealed that the metal and mining industry could revive its attractiveness for young talents with the help of gamification (Kowalski et al., 2001). The benefits of gamification include more adaptive and personalized learning experiences. It provides a clear picture of participants' career growth, increased participation, engagement, and motivation to complete the training through advanced and interesting platforms like VR and online courses. Learners can learn at their own pace, with application-based learning modules at their fingertips and with easy accessibility. Improved retention can help the employees apply the learnings in real-life work scenarios and create a knowledge-sharing environment that provides a platform for interactive peer learning.
Gamification is all about motivating people to achieve their own goals. It is often understood that employees' personal goals are aligned with organizational business goals. If the industries can identify their goals and share them with the employees, then with the help of gamification, employers can encourage employees to achieve their goals, which will eventually help the industries accomplish their targets (Kowalski et al., 2001).
As the global mining industry rebounds from the last downturn, it faces several critical challenges that extend beyond the mining sector. Across various industries, the impending retirement of experienced personnel from the baby boomer generation and the timeintensive nature of developing technical expertise pose significant concerns. This issue is exacerbated by the aging workforce, with alarming statistics revealing that the mining industry's average age is 46.5 years, well above the national average (Ashutosh, 2023).
Furthermore, there is a concerning breakdown in the executive replenishment cycle, with new talent entering the workforce having limited experience compared to the retiring generations of executives. The cyclical nature of boom and bust cycles and traditional cost-saving layoffs during downturns have resulted in a significant loss of middle and lower management, creating a substantial experience gap underneath senior management (Ashutosh, 2023). The industry's struggle to attract young talent further compounds the challenge. Mining engineering enrolments are on a downward trend globally, and the industry's reputation as unstable and its remote work locations make it less appealing to the tech-savvy and convenience-oriented millennial generation (Ashutosh, 2023).
Now, addressing these challenges requires innovative solutions. The impact of gamification on learning and development presents a promising avenue. Studies emphasize that gamification enhances learning experiences and motivates employees to engage actively with training content. Through adaptive and personalized learning modules delivered via advanced platforms like VR and online courses, gamification addresses the slow development of technical expertise by providing accessible and enjoyable training opportunities.
Research Problem: Why is there a skill shortage in the metals and mining industries?
Objective
* To understand the reason behind the skill shortage in the metal and mining industries;
* To know the impact of gamification on learning and development; and
* To examine how gamification can bridge the skill gap and attract young talent to the metal and mining industries.
Data and Methodology
The study adopted thematic analysis as proposed by Barun and Clarke (2006). The objective was to understand skill shortage and the role of gamification in attracting young talent to the metal and mining industry. Thematic analysis helps identify various themes and sub-themes in addressing the research question.
The target population for the study comprised senior officials, HR managers, employees, and job applicants in the metal and mining industry. A purposive sampling technique was adopted to reach out to content-rich participants for the study (Robinson, 2014). Respondents were contacted personally and through snowbowling techniques. All the participants were briefed about the purpose of the study and assured about the confidentiality of their identity. All the respondents signed a consent form to document their personal information and experiences only for research purposes. All the interviews were conducted offline and recorded using audio recording devices. All the recordings were anonymous, and a code was assigned for analysis.
Ten candidates were identified and requested to participate in the present research. The interviewers created 15 open-ended questions (see Appendix). The experts approved the questionnaire. As per experts' feedback, a few sensitive and very personal questions were removed. Some of the questions were reframed for better responses. Respondents were asked to spare 20 to 30 minutes for the interview. The study was conducted in 2023.
Demographic Details of Participants
The average age of the ten respondents was 30.25 years. Reflecting the traditionally maledominated nature of the industry, all respondents were males. 30% of the respondents had a bachelor's degree in engineering or related fields, 40% had a diploma in mining technology, and 20% had advanced degrees in Geology or Metallurgy. Respondents belonged to the following job roles: mining engineer, geologist, equipment operator, safety and environmental officer, and technician. 80% of the respondents had 5-10 years of work experience. All the participants belonged to Jharkhand state. In response to digital literacy, 30% reported having limited digital literacy, 60% of respondents reported moderate digital skills and only 10% reported high tech-savvy.
Data Analysis
For data analysis purposes, Barun and Clarke's (2006) six-step method for thematic analysis was used. The approach is widely accepted and prevalent in thematic analysis (Maguire and Delahunt, 2017). The steps are as follows:
Step 1: Becoming Familiar with the Data: We read and re-read the respondents' transcripts to familiarize ourselves with the data. NVivo 1.5 software was used to create memos.
Step 2: Generating Initial Codes: The data was maintained in two different files: one for the officials, and the other for workers. The data was arranged in Excel files. The Excel files were imported to Nvivo.1.5 software. Each transcription was carefully read, and an initial 31 codes were generated from the data.
Step 3: Searching for Sub-Themes: The next step was to create the sub-themes through the rigorous iterative validation process. In thematic analysis, researchers can identify the themes at two levels: semantic and latent (Boyatzis, 1998). Semantic themes are derived from the explicit and surface meanings of the data. Latent themes aim to capture the underlying ideas, patterns, and assumptions. As our workers were not very knowledgeable and seasoned enough to articulate their motives and experiences in words, the researchers used more interpretative and conceptual orientation towards the data.
Step 4: Reviewing Sub-Themes: All the sub-themes were reviewed through an iterative approach. During the process, similar or overlapping sub-themes were distilled.
Step 5: Defining Themes: Two broad themes emerged, each related to challenges and gamification of L&D. Further, each theme had four sub-themes regarding challenges and the impact of gamification. A brief schema of different themes and sub-themes identified in this process, along with their corresponding representative codes, is shown in Figure 1.
Step 6: Write-Up of Themes: The following section will have a detailed explanation of all the two themes and their sub-themes.
Results
This section elaborates on the two latent themes and their sub-themes, which emerged during the analysis. The first theme is "Issues with the Young Generation" in the metal and mining industry (see Figure 1 ). In today's ever-changing business world, metals and mining industries face a lot of uncertainty and complexity. The industry also deals with the big problem of lack of skilled workers. The first sub-theme that emerged under issues with the young generation is 'Redundant work culture' (Figure 2).
Redundant Work Culture: India's metal and mining industry is regarded as redundant. Many see these jobs as boring, old-fashioned, and environmentally destructive.
"We often get stuck using normal ways of working. When people want to use new technology or make things simpler, they often meet resistance. We often keep methods that may have worked before but might not be the best or long-lasting now" (Participant no. 6).
"Let's think about how we handle data. We still use old software and a lot of hand input. Even though there are fancier tools that could hugely boost work and cut down on mistakes, people do not want to spend the money on these changes" (Participant no. 4).
Redundancy breeds in employees because of fear of job displacement and skepticism of adopting something new. Employees worry that embracing automation or new technologies might lead to job cuts.
Lack of Peer Learning: Although it appears absent in the mining and metals sector, peer learning is essential to professional development. The mining industry employs a diverse workforce of geologists, engineers, and technicians with varying specializations in mining aspects. However, the knowledge exchange between these different roles is minimal. There is a siloed approach where everyone focuses on their tasks without much interaction or collaboration.
"We often work on tight schedule. There is literary no time to discuss anything regarding work. My friends do not want to share much about their work probably because they are also worried about losing their jobs or threat of being replaced" (Participant No. 1).
The traditional hierarchical structure in the industry fosters the culture of information flowfrom the top down, but notas much laterally between peers. Employees have a wealth of knowledge within their workforce, but it is not fully tapped. New employees especially could benefit from the experience of their more seasoned colleagues. It is not just about formal training programs but the informal exchange of insights and lessons learned on the job.
Lack of Career Growth/Opportunity: The industry has a traditional career growth opportunity, and advancement in career follows a predefined path. This can demotivate some employees to diversify their skills or explore different aspects of the industry.
"People with special skills are important, but those who want to grow within the company or do things in new areas do not get the help or encouragement from seniors. Often, it looks like a road that goes just one way" (Participant no. 1).
It can lead to a sense of stagnation. Employees might feel like their professional development is restricted. This not only affects morale but also impacts retention. If individuals do not see a clear path for growth within the organization, they might seek opportunities elsewhere.
Lack of Awareness and Education: The metal and mining sector faces a significant challenge regarding awareness and education. Many employees, especially those in operational roles, might not fully grasp mining activities and the impact of their activities on society and the environment. There is a need for more comprehensive education in the larger context of the industry.
A lack of knowledge and awareness can lead to a disconnect between employees and the broader goals of sustainable and responsible mining. Without a clear understanding of the environmental and social considerations, employees may not be as motivated to adopt practices that align with these goals.
"It is not just about completing the job; it is also about doing so with less carbon footprint. Yes, safety is a very important area. We have safety rules, but we need to keep learning about new ways and tools for staying safe" (Participant no. 10).
Employee activities require improvement in training programs related to new technologies and automation. Many employees might not be fully aware of these advancements' potential benefits and challenges.
The inputs and suggestions from respondents led to the second theme, highlighting the needs and "Advantages of gamification" in learning and development functions (see Figure 3).
Engaging and Real-Time Experiences: Gamification will add an element of excitement. The gamified training programs will instigate active participation among employees in the learning process. This engagement factor is crucial in an industry with high stakes. Gamification offers employees different learning ways that suit their learning styles and preferences. It helps them understand how they can do better in their careers. Using advanced tools like virtual reality (VR) and online courses makes learning more exciting. Gamification also makes things a bit like competition, which makes people want to take part and learn, even if they learn at different speeds.
"Our field is known for being really busy and may be old-fashioned when it comes to learning and growing. Using games can make tasks that might otherwise seem boring more fun and engaging" (Participant no. 7).
A Platform for Interaction: Gamification may turn training and learning into a collaborative experience. Effective communication and teamwork are essential in an industry as collaborative as metal and mining. Gamification may allow employees to practice and enhance these skills dynamically and engagingly. The gamification of learning may create a shared experience for employees across different roles and levels. Employees can navigate these virtual scenarios, overcome challenges, and celebrate successes together.
"Of course. Think about team-building activities as an example. We can work together using games to fix problems, agree on things, and achieve shared goals. Not only is doing well by yourself important, but our ability to team up and talk in a computer-based environment also matters" (Participant no. 7).
Reward Through Badges and Leaderboards: Introducing a system of badges and leaderboards that acknowledges and compensates young workers for their achievements and contributions will be possible with gamification. This element of competition can ignite motivation and positive rivalry, enhancing involvement and skill refinement.
"Of course, the opportunity to receive badges and rewards will take the reward and recognition to a whole new level. It will generate sportsmanship among employees. The badgeswill be considered an obvious symbol of achievement. Leaderboard may clearly state where the employee stands and what he has to do to move upward" (Participant no. 7).
Training Program Through VR: Incorporate virtual reality (VR) training programs that provide immersive and true-to-life encounters. This technology can replicate complex scenarios, creating a secure environment for young workers to cultivate skills and boost self-assurance. Additionally, VR can offer an inventive training approach, capturing the interest of technologically inclined young employees.
"Application of VR in training modules will allow the employees to operate and handle the sophisticated and technical machinery well in advance before they experiment with the real machinery. It will save time, provide on-the-job training and reduce the chance of mishandling or accidents. Employee will receive more than just mere demonstration; he can operate it and learn its functioning as well as troubleshooting" (participant no. 9).
Discussion
The mining industry faces a big problem because there are not enough skilled workers in India. This is causing issues with getting work done and meeting essential goals. Many leaders in the mining industry say that not having enough skilled workers is a big problem. This shortage of skilled workers is terrible in specific areas like planning mines, engineering processes, and working with digital technology. Because there are not enough skilled people, the industry has difficulty developing new ideas and moving forward.
Combining technology and learning is important to deal with the changing skills needed. Changing the way things are done using technology, known as digital transformation, is a big part of making industries more active and competitive. It is crucial to create a culture where learning is encouraged to ensure that employees keep learning and stay in the company. This kind of culture helps to develop new ideas and keeps the company abreast even as technology changes quickly.
One of the strategies that can really change how we learn and grow is gamification. This means adding elements of games to learning situations, making them fun and interactive. The great thing about gamification is that it makes learning enjoyable and motivating. By using things like leaderboards, badges, and other game-like things, employees are encouraged to learn and get better at their skills, which helps solve the problem of not having enough skills. A key part of gamification is that it matches up with what individuals and the company want to achieve. By connecting what employees want with what the company wants, industries can make people want to work harder. Gamification gives a structure for employees to really care about their goals, which can help the industry do well.
In summary, using gamification in learning and development is a good way for the metal and mining industry to deal with the problem of insufficient skilled workers. This approach fixes the skills problem and helps change how people see the industry by making learning interesting, personal, and aligned with big goals. In a changing and uncertain world, gamification is a strong tool to bring in, grow, and keep the talented people needed for the industry to do well and be innovative.
Recommendations: To tackle the issues encountered by the industry in attracting and managing young individuals in the metal mining sectors, here are a few proposals for learning and development programs:
First, provide interactive and immediate learning encounters by developing lively and interactive training modules that provide young workers with engaging and real-time learning experiences. Make use of technology to replicate work situations, enabling them to put their learning into practice. This practical approach helps connect theoretical knowledge with real-world skills.
Second, define transparent career advancement routes by crafting explicit paths for career progression that offer chances for skill enhancement and upward mobility. This framework can give young employees a distinct route for their professional journey, motivating them to dedicate effort to their careers within the field.
Third, provide acknowledgment via badges and leaderboards. Leader boards add an element of healthy competition. Seeing your name on the leaderboard, whether for completing training modules or achieving certain performance metrics, creates a sense of accomplishment. It fosters a bit of friendly rivalry, pushing individuals to strive for excellence, and continuously improves employees' performance.
Finally, implement virtual reality (VR) training. VR gamification transports one to different scenarios, allowing one to experience and respond to challenges as if they were happening in real life. It is an incredibly effective way to prepare for the complexities of employees' work.
Conclusion
The paper focused on the growing practice of gamification, which injects enjoyment and rewards into work to enhance employee loyalty and engagement. By integrating elements of enjoyment and incentives into work routines, gamification can potentially heighten employee engagement and diminish turnover rates. The opportunity for distinctive learning preferences to the younger generation, particularly the millennials, will significantly improve employee engagement.
The proposed model draws from qualitative research methods, outlining how gamification effectively addresses the challenges faced by the metal and mining industry in appealing to the present generation. The model considers the motivating factors for the millennials, like pursuit of immediate rewards, drive for success, and the need for recognition at work. Gamification achieves this by integrating competitive leaderboards, social learning opportunities, and swift feedback mechanisms. These aspects cater to the desire for instant gratification, foster a sense of accomplishment through healthy competition, and offer channels for recognition. By embracing gamification in this manner, the metal and mining industry can reshape itself into an attractive and rewarding workplace for the younger generation.

Exploring the promise of virtual reality in enhancing anatomy education: A focus group study with medical students

Author: Abundez Toledo, Maximiliano1; Ghanem, Ghadi1    ; Fine, Stuart1; Weisman, Daniel1    ; Huang, Yue Ming2; Rouhani, Amir A.31 David Geffen School of Medicine (DGSOM), University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), Los Angeles, CA, US maxbruin17@g.ucla.edu2 UCLA Simulation Center, DGSOM Dean’s Office, Los Angeles, CA, US3 Department of Emergency Medicine, Olive View-UCLA Medical Center, Sylmar, CA, US

Publication info: Abundez Toledo, Maximiliano; Ghanem, Ghadi; Fine, Stuart; Weisman, Daniel; Huang, Yue Ming; et al. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/exploring-promise-virtual-reality-enhancing/docview/3191142570/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: Virtual reality (VR) has the potential to be used as a transformative tool in medical education—offering both interactive models and clinical simulations to enhance training. VR presents a space and cost-effective solution for remote education, combined with prospects of higher efficiency and interactivity than traditional training. This study aimed to explore the potential application and perception of VR in a focus group of medical students as an innovative tool for learning anatomy. Sixteen students underwent a structured VR lesson plan exploring concepts in anatomy. Pre- and post-surveys assessed participants’ exposure to VR, previous exposure to and preparedness in anatomy training, and attitudes toward VR. Results revealed that despite limited prior exposure to VR, participants found the technology both easy to navigate and comfortable to use. Notably, over 90% of students indicated that VR would enhance their anatomy learning experience and help them learn a topic better than traditional models. Furthermore, 94% of participants agreed that this learning modality should be offered to medical students, and if given access to this technology, most would utilize it for learning anatomy and potentially for other subjects as well. This study emphasizes VR’s potential to enhance medical education, particularly in anatomy instruction. VR’s adaptability, user-friendly interface, and positive student perceptions highlight its viability as a supplemental tool. Future research should explore specific anatomy applications, long-term impacts on knowledge retention, and the evolving role of VR in medical education. A cultural, technological, and contextual pedagogy to enhance retention of biology concepts

Author: Onowugbeda, Franklin U1    ; Okebukola, Peter A1    ; Ige, Adeleke M1    ; Lameed, Saladoye N2    ; Agbanimu, Deborah O3    ; Adam, Umar A2    1 Africa Centre of Excellence for Innovative and Transformative STEM Education, Lagos State U niversity, Ojo, Nigeria2 Science and Technology Education, Lagos State University, Ojo, Nigeria3 Science and Technology Education, National Open University of Nigeria, Abuja

Publication info: Onowugbeda, Franklin U; Okebukola, Peter A; Ige, Adeleke M; Lameed, Saladoye N; Agbanimu, Deborah O; et al. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/cultural-technological-contextual-pedagogy/docview/3048300443/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: This study examined the impact of a pedagogy that is culturally influenced and laced with technological and contextual elements known as the culturo-techno-contextual approach (CTCA) on promoting knowledge retention of biology concepts. The research design was mixed methods, and the sample consisted of 88 senior secondary school II students selected from two Lagos State educational district V schools in Nigeria. Quantitative data was collected using the Variation and Evolution Achievement Test with a reliability value of 0.79, while qualitative data was collected using the Students’ Perception of CTCA Interview Guide. All students in the two sample schools used for the experimental and control groups took a pretest before treatment, a posttest at the end of the treatment phase, and a retention test four weeks later. The ANCOVA output demonstrated a statistically significant difference in knowledge retention [F (1,85) = 134.50; p  < .05]. This suggests that experimental students retained more.

Enhancing postgraduate students’ learning outcomes through Flipped Mobile-Based Microlearning

Author: Al-Zahrani, Abdulrahman M.1    1 Educational Technology Department, University of Jeddah, Jeddah, Saudi Arabia ammzahrani@uj.edu.sa

Publication info: Al-Zahrani, Abdulrahman M. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/enhancing-postgraduate-students-learning-outcomes/docview/3034476802/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: This study examines the effects of implementing a Flipped Mobile-Based Microlearning (FMM) approach on postgraduate students’ accessibility, engagement, knowledge retention, overall learning experience and academic achievement. A quantitative multiple methods approach was employed, utilising a two-group quasi-experimental design and a survey questionnaire to gather data. The results suggest that the FMM approach may have positive effects on accessibility, engagement, knowledge retention, overall learning experience and final exam scores when compared to the traditional learning approach. The findings support the efficacy of integrating FMM, highlighting its potential for enhancing the learning process and academic outcomes. These results have implications for educational practice and research, emphasising the value of technology-enhanced learning approaches, active and interactive learning experiences and the promotion of student motivation and attitudes towards learning. This study underscores the broader applicability of FMM and suggests its potential for improving educational outcomes across different educational levels and subject areas. Educational gamification: motivation and engagement strategies

Author: Ma, Junyuan11 School of Civil Engineering and Transportation, WeiFang University, Weifang, Shandong, 261061, China

Publication info: Ma, Junyuan. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/educational-gamification-motivation-engagement/docview/3191227705/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: Gamified learning creates authentic situations for students to solve tasks, provides students with active learning opportunities, and is an effective way to cultivate problem-solving ability, critical thinking, creativity, etc. In this paper, we conduct an in-depth study of gamified learning and learning behavior modeling technology, choose the Hidden Markov Model as the technical support of the study, adopt the Bayesian Information Criterion to select the optimal number of hidden states of the model, and combine the K-means algorithm with the model optimization in model parameter estimation, which to a certain extent improves the speed of convergence in the process of learning behavior modeling. The game elements and learning activity elements have been integrated and migrated, and proposed gamified learning activity elements. Activity theory and self-determination theory were used to design a gamified learning activity process for the educational field. The game-based learning activity process was continuously revised and optimized by iterating the process with actual teaching cases. Subsequently, we merged qualitative and quantitative research to examine students’ gamified learning and the changes in their learning effects. The results showed that gamified learning produced significant facilitation (p<0.001) in all four dimensions of mind-flow experience, intrinsic motivation, knowledge retention, and transfer performance, with effect values of 1.05, 1.65, 1.00, and 1.08, respectively. This indicates that the gamified learning model can enable students to stimulate and maintain good motivation for learning, and further demonstrates that the process of designing gamified learning activities has effectiveness.

Exploration of Virtual Reality Technology Enabling Diversified Teaching Models of Civics and Politics

Author: Lu, Jiang11 School of Marxism, Yellow River Conservancy Technical Institute, Kaifeng, Henan, 475000, China

Publication info: Lu, Jiang. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/exploration-virtual-reality-technology-enabling/docview/3191177330/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: The wide application of virtual reality technology has brought opportunities for teaching ideology and politics, breaking traditional education’s time and space limitations. This paper proposes an automatic three-dimensional modeling technology model, combined with computer vision camera imaging principles, to optimize the amount of data and improve optimization efficiency. And on this basis, it further proposes the Civics virtual scene construction technology, combined with the improved QEM grid simplification algorithm of edge segmentation, to optimize the virtual scene by simplifying the complex three-dimensional grid model. The experimental group’s students have shown good acceptance of this teaching method when teaching Civics in VR venues. In the cognitive and knowledge level of Civics learning, there is a significant difference between the experimental group and the control group in the dimensions of value identity and knowledge retention (P<0.05), and the mean value in the dimension of value identity is as high as 4.55, which is a very significant difference from the control class (P<0.01). And in the experiential feedback of Civics learning, the students in the experimental group have a greater sense of scene realism than the students in the control group (P<0.01), a stronger sense of realism of the interactive experience in learning (P<0.05), a higher degree of concentration in learning (P<0.01), and a more minor degree of interference by the external environment (P<0.01).

Theoretical Model Construction and Path Exploration of Intelligent Party Building Education in Colleges and Universities

Author: Li, Ren11 College of Marxism, Guangxi Arts Institute , Nanning , Guangxi , 530022 , China .

Publication info: Li, Ren. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/theoretical-model-construction-path-exploration/docview/3191175981/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: In the digital transformation era, higher education stands on the cusp of a revolution. This paper dives into the heart of this transformation, presenting a novel model of intelligent party building education that leverages digital technology to forge a new path for learning. Through the lens of ecological construction, we unveil the CFA model and a sophisticated deep knowledge tracking method aimed at enhancing student performance in Civic and Political Sciences. Our journey through empirical analysis and comparative experiments sheds light on the transformative power of digital education techniques. Despite the initial findings suggesting a modest impact of smart party building and teaching methods on knowledge retention (with significance levels of 0.6941 and 0.4963), a deeper exploration reveals a compelling narrative: the synergistic effect of these methods significantly boosts knowledge retention, as demonstrated by an F-value of 5.6941 and a P-value below 0.05. The prowess of Civics teachers, assessed across three dimensions, further narrates the success of this educational innovation, with scores reflecting their deep understanding of the curriculum and a robust theoretical knowledge base. The performance of 32 Civics teachers, with scores ranging from 12 to 24, underscores the efficacy of intelligent party building education in today’s colleges and universities.

Clinical judgment of nursing students and the delivery of virtual health assessment laboratory courses

Author: Naelah Mubarak Ahmed Alsamili; Raad Saud Mehmas Alharthi; Fatimah Makki Alsadiq; Rasmy, Saud Alrashdi; Saleh Ahmed Khormi; Alblewi, Nourah Aaid; Homoud Abdullah Algosheri; Turki Mohammed Hassan Asiri; Ahad Ebrahim Yahiya Asiri; Athba Ebrahim Yahiya Asiri; Ali Mohammed Ali Alghamdi; Ahmed Fahad Alsharari

Publication info: Naelah Mubarak Ahmed Alsamili; Raad Saud Mehmas Alharthi; Fatimah Makki Alsadiq; Rasmy, Saud Alrashdi; Saleh Ahmed Khormi; et al. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/clinical-judgment-nursing-students-delivery/docview/3186336571/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: Background: The education of nursing students faces ongoing challenges in ensuring both high-quality learning and safe clinical practice. Traditional methods have been augmented by advanced simulation technologies, which enhance knowledge and skills in clinical settings. However, limitations such as high costs and space constraints persist. Clinical virtual simulation, an emerging approach, offers an interactive and immersive alternative that may address these challenges, but its impact on student satisfaction, self-efficacy, and knowledge retention remains unclear. Methods: This randomized controlled trial involved second-year nursing students (N=42) enrolled in a course on physiological responses. Participants were randomly assigned to either an experimental group using clinical virtual simulation or a control group using low-fidelity simulation. Assessments were conducted at three time points: pretest (A0), immediately post-intervention (A1), and two months later (A2). Knowledge retention, satisfaction, and self-efficacy were measured using tailored instruments. Data analysis included t-tests, MANOVA, and Cohen’s d for effect size. Results: Significant differences were found between the groups in knowledge retention and learning satisfaction. The experimental group showed superior outcomes in both immediate and long-term knowledge retention (P = .001, P = .02) and higher satisfaction levels (P < .001). MANOVA indicated significant time-related changes influenced by group allocation. No significant differences were observed in self-efficacy between groups (P = .9), although group differences were noted across assessments (P = .003). Conclusion: Clinical virtual simulation significantly enhances knowledge retention and student satisfaction in nursing education. While its impact on self-efficacy was less pronounced, the findings underscore the potential of virtual simulation to improve clinical competence and contribute to safer healthcare training.

Enhancing Team Performance through Mock Drills in Disaster Medicine and Emergency Medical Services

Author: Nofal, Abdullah R; MenahiAlshebani, Meshal; Alanazi, Mohammed Qismi; Alanazi, Abdulrahman Eidhah; Mohammed Abdulrahman Almotlaq; ALdawsari, Faisal Mabkhoot; Abdulaziz Mohammed Almeshari; Alshaibani, Saad Munahi; Mohammed Nasser Almutairi

Publication info: Nofal, Abdullah R; MenahiAlshebani, Meshal; Alanazi, Mohammed Qismi; Alanazi, Abdulrahman Eidhah; Mohammed Abdulrahman Almotlaq; et al. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/enhancing-team-performance-through-mock-drills/docview/3186336021/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: Background: Effective disaster management depends on the well-coordinated performance of teams within disaster medicine and emergency medical services (EMS). Mock drills serve as animportant cornerstone of training for these team members, yet their effectiveness in optimizing team performance remains an area of active investigation. Present narrative review examines the understanding of the applicability of mock drills to further enhance team performance in disaster medicine and EMS. Method:An extensive search of pertinent literature was carried out to identify studies investigating the application of mock drills in disaster preparedness training. The review examines the documented advantages, drawbacks, and prospective research areas for this training method. Results:Mock drills significantly enhance knowledge, communication, and problem-solving skills among disaster medicine and EMS team members. However, transforming these gains into sustained improvements in real-world scenario performance requires further exploration. Merging discussion-based and operation-based drills, customizing scenarios for EMS/paramedic difficulties, and integrating psychological stressors are promising approaches for optimizing drill design. Integrating insights from the learning sciences and conducting longitudinal research studies are necessary for maximizing knowledge retention and establishing the long-term impact of drills on real-world performance. Finally, the potential of virtual reality (VR), artificial intelligence (AI), and serious game-based platforms warrants further investigation for their ability to create immersive and dynamic training simulations. Conclusions: Mock drills offer animportant and variable tools for enhancing team performance in disaster medicine and EMS. By optimizing drill design, maximizing learning and retention, and embracing technological advancements, this training modality can be further refined to ensure optimal preparedness for the complexities of real-world disaster response.

Unlocking Potential: The Transformative Role of Gaming in Rural Higher Learning Institutions of South Africa -- A Systematic Exploration

Author: Mbukanma, Ifeanyi; Manganyi, Madira; Vellem, Bhekithemba; Gqoli, Neliswa

Publication info: Mbukanma, Ifeanyi; Manganyi, Madira; Vellem, Bhekithemba; Gqoli, Neliswa. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/unlocking-potential-transformative-role-gaming/docview/3174442552/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: The aim of this study resonated with the pursuit of achieving enhanced engagement in teaching and learning that informs critical thinking, and knowledge retention among students. Despite the growing trend of technological integration in teaching and learning, however, there exists a lack of empirical evidence and comprehensive studies that investigate the effectiveness of gaming in promoting educational objectives within rural institution of higher learning in South Africa. To investigate this gap, a systematic review method was employed, which provides a comprehensive and logical analysis of existing literature on the significance of gaming in teaching and learning within rural institutions of higher education. Inclusion and exclusion criteria were used in the study to enhance the rigor and transparency of the research process, by providing a solid foundation for synthesizing and interpreting existing literature relevant to the study. The systematic review findings revealed that the significance of gamification in teaching and learning in rural higher education lies in its ability to overcome accessibility challenges, provide personalized learning experiences, address motivation and retention issues, and enhance digital literacy. It was recommended that by incorporating gamified approaches, rural higher educational institutions can create a more inclusive, engaging, and effective learning environment for students within the rural institutions of higher learning in South Africa.

Effects of Classroom Response System on the Achievement and Knowledge Retention of the Students in Mathematics

Author: Jayson Virtucio Alviar    ; Anabel Enriquez Gamorez    

Publication info: Jayson Virtucio Alviar; Anabel Enriquez Gamorez. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/effects-classroom-response-system-on-achievement/docview/3174441284/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: Classroom Response System (CRS) is a promising educational tool that can create an interactive learning space. In high school, less is known about its impact on learning mathematics. Most studies on the integration of CRS in teaching and learning use internet-dependent tool. This paper aimed to determine the effectiveness of the CRS that uses Bluetooth technology in improving the mathematics achievement and knowledge retention of the students. A quasi-experimental design and longitudinal study with post-test and delayed post-test was employed in this study. The assessment and re-administered assessment results of the CRS and Traditional Classroom Instruction (TCI) groups were compared. Data were analyzed using an independent sample t-test and Welch t-test, and the Mean Percentage Scores (MPS) were calculated to determine the achievement level. Findings revealed that there was a significant difference between the assessment of the CRS and the TCI groups. Moreover, the re-administered assessment results suggest that students exposed to CRS have better knowledge retention compared to the TCI. Furthermore, the MPS showed that CRS exhibited higher mastery level of the learning competencies over the TCI group. This study provides valuable insights into the integration of CRS in mathematics teaching and its consequential effect on achievement and retention.

An Interest-Oriented Laboratory Microbial Engineering Course Is Helpful for the Cultivation of Scientific Literacy

Author: Wu, Genfu; Wu, Kejie

Publication info: Wu, Genfu; Wu, Kejie. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/interest-oriented-laboratory-microbial/docview/3174440639/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: Course-based undergraduate research experience (CURE) exposes an entire class of students to scientific research and is thought to increase students' knowledge retention in science, technology, engineering and mathematics education. Microbial engineering is an interdisciplinary subject that combines science and engineering. We transformed a microbial engineering course into a CURE-type course by adopting an interest-oriented case teaching approach. Based on an investigation of the interest of students, which showed that the topics related to food and health were students' favourites, we selected beer brewing, glutamate fermentation and Monascus cultivation as teaching topics. To simulate the reality of industrial fermentation, pilot-scale fermentation equipment was selected and installed. The course focused on fermentation research; most of the time was spent on performing experiments, and theoretical lectures were held at the intervals. To complete the course in 10 days, three series of experiments were alternatively carried out, and students took turns to conduct fermentation control and process analyses in groups. A questionnaire survey showed that students were satisfied with the CURE-type course, their fermentation knowledge and engineering skills were improved, their research abilities were developed, and their scientific attitudes were cultivated. CURE-type courses are worth popularising in biology teaching.

Spatial Ability Predicts Short-Term Retention of Declarative Technical Information in Authentic Engineering Educational Settings: An Original Study with Two Conceptual Replications

Author: Hyland, Tomás    ; Seery, Niall    ; Buckley, Jeffrey    

Publication info: Hyland, Tomás; Seery, Niall; Buckley, Jeffrey. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/spatial-ability-predicts-short-term-retention/docview/3174440079/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: An association between spatial ability, particularly visualisation, and science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) education has been repeatedly demonstrated over the past four decades. Understanding this relationship is of critical importance as substantial evidence illustrates the malleability of spatial ability and that the effects of associated training interventions transfer to desirable STEM outcomes such as improved educational performance and reduced attrition rates. There currently exists a number of theories as to why spatial ability relates to STEM, such as that the nature of STEM activity is inherently spatial. However, there is a need to better understand this relationship from a cognitive perspective. This research examined the hypothesis that spatial ability is predictive of short-term retention for declarative technical information associated with engineering curricula. An original investigation in an authentic educational setting found that visualisation and interest in the lecture material were significant predictors of short-term knowledge retention. This effect was then replicated in two subsequent conceptual replication studies. Based on this predictive finding, it is theorised that increases in spatial ability may support the elongation of the knowledge forgetting curve which would have significant implications for instructional design.

Comparative Effects of Dynamic Geometry System and Physical Manipulatives on Inquiry-Based Math Learning for Students in Junior High School

Author: Guan, Hao; Li, Jing; Rao, Yongsheng    ; Chen, Ruxian; Xu, Zhangtao

Publication info: Guan, Hao; Li, Jing; Rao, Yongsheng; Chen, Ruxian; Xu, Zhangtao. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/comparative-effects-dynamic-geometry-system/docview/3174439863/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: Mathematical inquiry involving hands-on activities has received increasing attention in mathematics education. Besides various customized physical teaching aids, subject-specific information technology, such as Dynamic Geometry System (DGS), finds extensive use in mathematical inquiry activities. However, effects of DGS and physical manipulatives on inquiry-based math learning remain an open question. Hence, by adopting a quasi-experimental research design, this paper aims to empirically compare the immediate learning outcomes, knowledge retention, and learning interest of seventh-grade students who explore with virtual manipulatives (i.e., the DGS) and who explore with physical manipulatives. Specifically, 131 students participated in learning activities centered on exploring pyramids and prisms. During the inquiry process, Group A (n = 33) constructed pyramids and prisms in DGS, Group B (n = 34) observed pre-made virtual models in DGS, Group C (n = 32) observed physical models, and Group D (n = 32) made physical pyramids and prisms with polymer clay and small sticks. Moreover, pretest, post-test, and delayed post-test designed according to the Van Hiele model, as well as an adapted interest questionnaire, were employed to evaluate students' performances; and collected data were analyzed by means of ANCOVA and t-test. Findings of the study revealed that in the context of construction, students employing the DGS exhibited superior immediate learning outcomes and greater knowledge retention compared to their peers who utilized physical manipulatives; while in the case of observation, the virtual and physical manipulatives yielded similar impacts on students' immediate learning outcomes, but students who involved in the DGS demonstrated higher knowledge retention. Furthermore, regarding the DGS environment, students who engaged in constructive manipulation surpassed their peers who engaged in observing manipulation. In terms of interest, the DGS proved to be more effective in both stimulating and maintaining higher interest compared to the physical manipulatives, and constructive manipulation was more effective than observing manipulation. In summary, as compared to the physical manipulatives, DGS, particularly when employed with constructive strategy, has shown to encourage students to more actively engage in task-related cognitive behaviors, thereby supporting and enhancing inquiry-based math learning of students in junior high school.

Virtual, Augmented Reality and Learning Analytics Impact on Learners, and Educators: A Systematic Review

Author: Sakr, Asmaa    ; Abdullah, Tariq    

Publication info: Sakr, Asmaa; Abdullah, Tariq. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/virtual-augmented-reality-learning-analytics/docview/3174439075/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: Virtual and Augmented Reality technologies have emerged as promising tools in the education sector, offering new possibilities for immersive learning experiences. Many researchers have focused their research on examining the potential of these technologies in education from different perspectives. However, it was discovered that there are research gaps in current systematic reviews regarding the examination of the impact of Virtual, Augmented Reality and Learning Analytics utilization on various types of learners and educators across different educational systems, including K-12 Education, Higher Education, Vocational, and Industrial Training, in addition to the educational systems' research tendencies and their adoption of these technologies. Therefore, our study aims to address these gaps by searching various studies in Google Scholar, Scopus, and the IEEE Xplore databases. By following the PRISMA protocol, 150 research papers were selected for analysis, and our findings show that improving motivation and attention, improving learners' understanding & performance, and increasing knowledge retention are the most significant impacts on all types of learners. For educators, we found that these technologies have a prominent effect on assisting educators in teaching and training and reducing the burden. Furthermore, we discovered that Higher Education and Augmented Reality were the dominant educational system and the technology type in the selected studies. We also found that most Virtual and Augmented reality researchers preferred to use questionnaires and online surveys for data collection. We further identified that analyzing learners' traces when interacting with Virtual and Augmented Reality applications can improve learners' performance and learning experience. Our review offers valuable insights into how integrating these technologies with Learning Analytics can benefit learners and educators and how educational institutions and industrial organizations can take advantage of adopting these technologies.

Enhancing Postgraduate Students' Learning Outcomes through Flipped Mobile-Based Microlearning

Author: Al-Zahrani, Abdulrahman M    

Publication info: Al-Zahrani, Abdulrahman M. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/enhancing-postgraduate-students-learning-outcomes/docview/3174408614/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: This study examines the effects of implementing a Flipped Mobile-Based Microlearning (FMM) approach on postgraduate students' accessibility, engagement, knowledge retention, overall learning experience and academic achievement. A quantitative multiple methods approach was employed, utilising a two-group quasi-experimental design and a survey questionnaire to gather data. The results suggest that the FMM approach may have positive effects on accessibility, engagement, knowledge retention, overall learning experience and final exam scores when compared to the traditional learning approach. The findings support the efficacy of integrating FMM, highlighting its potential for enhancing the learning process and academic outcomes. These results have implications for educational practice and research, emphasising the value of technology-enhanced learning approaches, active and interactive learning experiences and the promotion of student motivation and attitudes towards learning. This study underscores the broader applicability of FMM and suggests its potential for improving educational outcomes across different educational levels and subject areas.

The use of AI for Education in Third Age: the role of EU project

Author: Spulber, Diana1; Amoretti, Guido1; Siri, Anna21 University of Genoa, Italy2 Pegaso Telematic University, Naples, Italy

Publication info: Spulber, Diana; Amoretti, Guido; Siri, Anna. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/use-ai-education-third-age-role-eu-project/docview/3159587438/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: Society today is struggling with various challenging phenomena. This manuscript aims to analyse two phenomena, ageing and digitalisation, in the context of education. Both phenomena are an important area of research: the complexity of an ageing population and the intersection of technology and education. In this context, artificial intelligence (AI) offers the opportunity to improve the educational experiences of older adults. AI-driven tools and educational initiatives can be tailored to the different learning preferences and cognitive abilities of this population, promoting engagement and knowledge retention. The adaptability of AI systems enables personalised learning pathways that address individual challenges and promote lifelong learning and cognitive health in older learners. This research will highlight the critical role of AI in reshaping educational paradigms and its potential to facilitate knowledge acquisition and empower an often-marginalised population. Finally, focusing on the role of international projects will allow us to understand the trends in EU research and funding. Understanding the impact of AI on education in the third age and EU funding invites a broader discussion on inclusivity and innovation in the educational landscape.

Effects of classroom response system on the achievement and knowledge retention of the students in mathematics

Author: Jayson Virtucio Alviar1    ; Anabel Enriquez Gamorez2    1 Senior High School Department, Tairan National High School, Lantawan, Philippines; Department of Mathematics and Statistics, Western Mindanao State University, Zamboanga City, Philippines; University of the Philippines Open University, Los Baños, Philippines2 Department of Mathematics and Statistics, Western Mindanao State University, Zamboanga City, Philippines

Publication info: Jayson Virtucio Alviar; Anabel Enriquez Gamorez. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/effects-classroom-response-system-on-achievement/docview/3158522454/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: Classroom Response System (CRS) is a promising educational tool that can create an interactive learning space. In high school, less is known about its impact on learning mathematics. Most studies on the integration of CRS in teaching and learning use internet-dependent tool. This paper aimed to determine the effectiveness of the CRS that uses Bluetooth technology in improving the mathematics achievement and knowledge retention of the students. A quasi-experimental design and longitudinal study with post-test and delayed post-test was employed in this study. The assessment and re-administered assessment results of the CRS and Traditional Classroom Instruction (TCI) groups were compared. Data were analyzed using an independent sample t-test and Welch t-test, and the Mean Percentage Scores (MPS) were calculated to determine the achievement level. Findings revealed that there was a significant difference between the assessment of the CRS and the TCI groups. Moreover, the re-administered assessment results suggest that students exposed to CRS have better knowledge retention compared to the TCI. Furthermore, the MPS showed that CRS exhibited higher mastery level of the learning competencies over the TCI group. This study provides valuable insights into the integration of CRS in mathematics teaching and its consequential effect on achievement and retention.

Learning effectiveness of clinical anatomy and practical spine surgery skills using a new VR-based training platform

Author: Reinhold, Maximilian1; Asal, Can2; Driesen, Tobias1; Roch, Jonathan1; Jäckle, Katharina1; Borgmann, Susanne3; Lehmann, Wolfgang11 Goettingen Medical University, Department of Trauma Surgery, Orthopedics and Plastic Surgery, Robert-Koch-Str. 40, D-37099, Goettingen, Germany2 NonNocere, Sorauer Str. 14, D-10997, Berlin, Germany3 Goettingen Medical University, G1-2 Office of the Dean of Studies/Medical Didactics, Humboldtallee 38, 37073, Goettingen, Germany

Publication info: Reinhold, Maximilian; Asal, Can; Driesen, Tobias; Roch, Jonathan; Jäckle, Katharina; et al. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/learning-effectiveness-clinical-anatomy-practical/docview/3156802152/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: As medical education becomes more complex, the demand for advanced teaching and training methods has grown. Technological advancements have opened up new possibilities, particularly in the realm of virtual reality (VR) simulations for training. Introduction As medical education becomes more complex, the demand for advanced teaching and training methods has grown. Technological advancements have opened up new possibilities, particularly in the realm of virtual reality (VR) simulations for training.Our prospective, randomized pilot study aims to assess whether a novel VR-based 3D training platform can effectively teach the knowledge and skills needed for complex spinal surgery, specifically pedicle screw placement. Material and MethodsWe enrolled 25 participants who received either a traditional lecture (control group, n=11) or a VR lecture with identical content featuring 3D/VR anatomical models (VR group, n=14). The VR group also underwent VR simulation for pedicle screw placement. We evaluated their learning through a quiz, a practical skills test, and selfassessment questionnaires. Research Question Our prospective, randomized pilot study aims to assess whether a novel VR-based 3D training platform can effectively teach the knowledge and skills needed for complex spinal surgery, specifically pedicle screw placement. Material and MethodsWe enrolled 25 participants who received either a traditional lecture (control group, n=11) or a VR lecture with identical content featuring 3D/VR anatomical models (VR group, n=14). The VR group also underwent VR simulation for pedicle screw placement. We evaluated their learning through a quiz, a practical skills test, and selfassessment questionnaires.In the theory multiple-choice test, the contral group scored an average of 69% (range 53-87%, SD 0.10), while the VR group scored 66% (range 47-87%, SD 0.11) (p=0.692, independent sample t-test).For the practical DOPS test (pedicle screw placement), the average score was 2.4 points (n=25; range 1-4). The VR group on average scored 2.9 points compared to the control (2 points) (p=0.134). Discussion and Conclusion Our study indicates that teaching with a new 3D VR training tool yields results comparable to traditional methods in terms of knowledge retention. This research supports the platform's effectiveness as an educational resource. Importantly, trainees can apply VR-acquired knowledge to real surgical procedures, which are well-received. Results In the theory multiple-choice test, the contral group scored an average of 69% (range 53-87%, SD 0.10), while the VR group scored 66% (range 47-87%, SD 0.11) (p=0.692, independent sample t-test).For the practical DOPS test (pedicle screw placement), the average score was 2.4 points (n=25; range 1-4). The VR group on average scored 2.9 points compared to the control (2 points) (p=0.134). Discussion and Conclusion Our study indicates that teaching with a new 3D VR training tool yields results comparable to traditional methods in terms of knowledge retention. This research supports the platform's effectiveness as an educational resource. Importantly, trainees can apply VR-acquired knowledge to real surgical procedures, which are well-received.

THE USE OF TECHNOLOGY IN TEACHING PHYSICS TO STUDENTS WITH DISABILITIES: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW

Author: Pacala, Frank Angelo    

Publication info: Pacala, Frank Angelo. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/use-technology-teaching-physics-students-with/docview/3152079980/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: In recent years, incorporating technology into education for students with disabilities has significantly improved learning experiences and academic achievement. However, there remains a need for a deeper understanding of the most effective methods for using these technologies, particularly in physics education. This systematic review aims to consolidate research on the use of technology to support learning for students with disabilities, assess its effectiveness in improving educational outcomes, and identify areas for further study. The review focuses on the constructs, technological interventions, research gaps, limitations, and key findings from selected articles. The PRISMA framework was used to analyze research from databases, including EBSCO Host, Elsevier Science Direct, Emerald Insight, ProQuest, Google Scholar, ERIC, and Clarivate Analytics Web of Science. Out of 892 articles initially identified, 13 met the inclusion and exclusion criteria and validation from the experts. The most commonly studied disability was visual impairment, followed by intellectual disabilities. Most studies focused on learner achievement, with engagement and participation as secondary themes. The technologies used included assistive tools like web-based platforms, virtual and augmented reality (AR), and interactive learning systems. These adaptive technologies improved student involvement, social integration, and interest in science. Augmented reality, in particular, enhanced academic performance and knowledge retention, making it an effective tool for inclusive physics education. The findings indicate a growing trend towards integrating technology in inclusive education, emphasizing the role of personalized tools in improving accessibility and engagement for students with disabilities in physics. Alternate abstract: В останні роки впровадження технологій в освіту для студентів з обмеженими можливостями значно покращило їх навчання та академічну успішність. Однак залишається потреба ширшому застосуванні найбільш ефективних методів використання технологій, зокрема в навчанні фізики. Цей систематичний огляд має на меті консолідувати дослідження щодо використання технологій для підтримки навчання учнів з обмеженими можливостями, оцінити їхню ефективність з покращення результатів навчання та визначити напрями подальшого дослідження. Огляд зосереджується на конструкціях, впровадженні технологій, прогалинах у дослідженнях, обмеженнях і основних висновках з вибраних статей. Для аналізу досліджень з баз даних, як-от EBSCO Host, Elsevier Science Direct, Emerald Insight, ProQuest, Google Scholar, ERIC та Clarivate Analytics Web of Science був використаний метод PRISMA. З 892 відібраних статей, 13 відповідали критеріям включення та виключення, а також були схвалені експертами. Найбільш часто досліджуваними обмеженнями можливостей учнів були порушення зору та інтелектуальні порушення. Більшість досліджень зосереджувались на результатах навчання учнів, а залучення учнів до навчального процесу та участь їх у ньому були другорядними темами. Використовувані технології мали допоміжні інструменти, такі як вебплатформи, віртуальна і доповнена реальність (AR) та інтерактивні навчальні системи. Ці адаптивні технології сприяли залученню учнів до навчання, їх соціальній інтеграції та підвищенню їх інтересу до науки. Доповнена реальність, зокрема, покращила академічну успішність та сприяла збереженню знань, що робить її ефективним інструментом для інклюзивної освіти з фізики. Отримані результати свідчать про зростаючу тенденцію інтеграції технологій в інклюзивну освіту, завдяки важливій ролі персоналізованих інструментів у підвищенні доступності та залученості учнів з обмеженими можливостями до вивчення фізики.

Use of Interactive Technologies to Increase Motivation in University Online Courses

Author: Guaña-Moya, Javier1    ; Arteaga-Alcívar, Yamileth2    ; Criollo-C, Santiago3    ; Cajamarca-Carrazco, Diego4    1 Carrera Sistemas de Información, Facultad de Ingeniería, Pontificia Universidad Católica del Ecuador, Quito 170523, Ecuador2 Unidad de Investigación y Generación del Conocimiento, Instituto Superior Universitario Japón, Quito 170120, Ecuador; yarteaga@itsjapon.edu.ec3 Carrera de Ingeniería en Ciberseguridad, Facultad de Ingeniería y Ciencias Aplicadas, Universidad de Las Américas, Quito 170125, Ecuador; luis.criollo@udla.edu.ec4 Carrera de Electrónica y Automatización, Facultad de Informática y Electrónica, Escuela Superior Politécnica de Chimborazo, Riobamba 060155, Ecuador; diego.cajamarca@espoch.edu.ec

Publication info: Guaña-Moya, Javier; Arteaga-Alcívar, Yamileth; Criollo-C, Santiago; Cajamarca-Carrazco, Diego. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/use-interactive-technologies-increase-motivation/docview/3149572860/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: This study analyzes the impact of interactive technologies on the motivation and engagement of university students in online courses. Through a systematic literature review and a comparative analysis of existing technologies, 64 articles published between 2020 and 2024 were examined. The results reveal a significant increase in student motivation (23%) and knowledge retention (31%) with the use of these tools. Augmented reality stands out with a mean effect size of 0.67 on academic performance. The bibliometric analysis shows a concentration of research in countries such as Spain, Colombia and China, suggesting the need for more diverse studies. Challenges such as the digital divide and lack of teacher training were identified, with 42% of teachers reporting difficulties in implementation. The findings underline the transformative potential of interactive technologies in online higher education, but emphasize the importance of a holistic approach that considers technical, pedagogical and socioeconomic aspects. It is recommended to invest in teacher professional development, promote equitable access policies and encourage research in diverse educational contexts to maximize the benefits of these technologies.
