ANALYSIS OF THE FEASIBILITY OF IMMERSIVE VIRTUALIZATION IN TECHNICAL TRAINING

Author: Braz, Silvio Marcos1; Winkler, Ingrid2; Catapan, Marcio Fontana31 Master in Manufacturing Engineering. Universidade Federal do Paraná (UFPR). Rua XV de Novembre, 1299, Centro, Curitiba - PR, CEP: 80060-0002 Doctorate in Administration. Centro Universitario Senai Cimatec. Av. Orlando Gomes, 1845, Piata, Salvador - BA, CEP: 41650-0103 Doctorate in Mechanical Engineering. Universidade Federal do Paraná (UFPR). Rua XV de Novembre, 1299, Centro, Curitiba - PR, CEP: 80060-000

Publication info: Braz, Silvio Marcos; Winkler, Ingrid; Catapan, Marcio Fontana. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/analysis-feasibility-immersive-virtualization/docview/3144154666/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: Objetivo: propor um método de capacitaçao em normas regulamentadoras utilizando a virtualizaçâo imersiva, visando a melhora da retençao do conhecimento do aluno se comparada aos modelos online tradicionais. Referencia! teórico: utilizaçâo da literatura por meio de pesquisas de métodos similares já aplicados em treinamentos imersivos, dissertaçoes, artigos e normas nacionais. Método: aplicaçao prática do treinamento em ambiente imersivo em duas industrias de grande porte localizadas na regiâo metropolitana de Curitiba, PR, onde os avahados preencheram um questionário de avaliaçâo de acordo corn o seu grau de satisfaçao, sendo este o principal parámetro utilizado neste trabalho para comprovar a eficiencia do método. Resultados e conclusâo: a aplicaçao prática do treinamento imersivo, compilaçâo dos dados e análise dos resultados, confirmam a viabilidade proposta no método. A medida que o país se desenvolve tecnológicamente, o método terá sua aplicabilidade cada vez mais acessível e comprovada. Implicaçôes da pesquisa: um método de capacitaçao tecnológico desenvolvido como alternativa aos moldes atuais, certamente trará grandes contribuiçôes para a academia, e, ao mesmo tempo, corn a reduęao do tempo de parada de máquinas, deslocamentos, custos logisticos e aglomeraçôes, trarão contribuiçôes deste trabalho para a industria. Originalidade/valor: corn o advento da pandemia por covid-19 vivenciada nos últimos tempos, os métodos tradicionais de capacitaçao profissional precisaram ser rápidamente adaptados, visando minimizar o impacto causado pela restriçao de contato físico entre as pessoas. O método proposto proporciona a possibilidade do mantenimento dos processos de capacitaçao profissional, oferecendo à sociedade a possibilidade de ser capacitada de modo eficaz. Alternate abstract: Objetivo: proponer un método para la formación en normas reglamentarias utilizando la virtualización inmersiva, con el objetivo de mejorar la retención de conocimientos de los estudiantes en comparación con los modelos tradicionales en línea. Marco teórico: utilización de la literatura a través de la investigación sobre métodos similares ya aplicados en la formación inmersiva, disertaciones, artículos y normas nacionales. Método: aplicación práctica de la capacitación en ambiente inmersivo en dos grandes industrias localizadas en el área metropolitana de Curitiba, PR, donde los evaluados rellenaron un cuestionario de evaluación según su grado de satisfacción, siendo este el principal parámetro utilizado en este trabajo para comprobar la eficiencia del método. Resultados y conclusión: la aplicación práctica del entrenamiento inmersivo, la compilación de datos y el análisis de los resultados, confirman la viabilidad propuesta en el método. A medida que el país se desarrolle tecnológicamente, el método tendrá su aplicabilidad cada vez más accesible y comprobada. Implicancias de la investigación: un método de capacitación tecnológica desarrollado como alternativa a los moldes actuales ciertamente traerá grandes contribuciones a la academia y, al mismo tiempo, con la reducción de paradas de máquinas, desplazamientos, costos logisticos y aglomeraciones, este trabajo traerá contribuciones a la industria. Originalidad/valor: con el advenimiento de la pandemia de covid-19 experimentada en los últimos tiempos, los métodos tradicionales de formación profesional necesitaron ser rápidamente adaptados, con el objetivo de minimizar el impacto causado por la restricción del contacto físico entre las personas. El método propuesto proporciona la posibilidad de mantener los procesos de formación profesional, ofreciendo a la sociedad la posibilidad de formarse eficazmente. Alternate abstract: Goal: propose a method of training in regulatory standards using immersive virtualization, aiming at improving student knowledge retention compared to traditional online models. Theoretical Reference: use of literature through research on similar methods already applied in immersive training, dissertations, articles and national standards. Method: practical application of training in an immersive environment in two large industries located in the metropolitan region of Curitiba, PR, where the evaluated ones completed an evaluation questionnaire according to their degree of satisfaction, which is the main parameter used in this work to prove the efficiency of the method. Results and conclusion: the practical application of immersive training, compilation of data and analysis of results confirm the viability proposed in the method. As the country develops technologically, the method will have its applicability increasingly accessible and proven. Research implications: a method of technological training developed as an alternative to the current molds, will certainly bring great contributions to the academy, and, at the same time, with the reduction of machine downtime, displacements, logistical costs and agglomerations, this work will bring contributions to the industry. Originality/Value: with the advent of the covid-19 pandemic experienced in recent times, traditional methods of professional training needed to be quickly adapted, aiming to minimize the impact caused by the restriction of physical contact between people. The proposed method provides the possibility of maintaining professional training processes, offering society the possibility of being trained effectively.

BUILDING AND SUSTAINING CAPACITIES OF HEALTH OFFICIALS IN USE OF DATA FOR DECISION-MAKING: EVIDENCE FROM RAJASTHAN, INDIA

Author: Khanna, Anoop1; Singh, J P2; Tripathi, V B31 Professor, IIHMR University Jaipur, Jaipur, Rajasthan, India. E-mail: anoop@iihmr.edu.in Orcid: https://orcid.org/0000-0001-6421-17102 Professor, IIHMR University Jaipur, Jaipur, Rajasthan, India. E-mail: jpsingh@iihmr.edu.in Orcid: https://orcid.org/0000-0003-0648-490X3 Senior Research Officer, IIHMR University Jaipur, Jaipur, Rajasthan, India. E-mail: vidya@iihmr.edu.in Orcid: https://orcid.org/0000-0002-1218-8237

Publication info: Khanna, Anoop; Singh, J P; Tripathi, V B. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/building-sustaining-capacities-health-officials/docview/3143403171/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: Purpose: This paper critically explores the initiatives that were implemented in Rajasthan during the period of 2018-19 by UNFPA, in collaboration with the Department of Health and Family Welfare, the Government of Rajasthan, and IIHMR University, Jaipur, Rajasthan, India. The main objective of these initiatives was to strengthen the capabilities of health officials and data managers at different levels within the state, enabling them to make evidence-based decisions using data effectively. Theoretical framework: The capacity-building program was designed to reinforce the system for evidence-based planning, monitoring, and data utilization through a comprehensive training approach and continuous support. This study thoroughly investigates the entire process, assesses its effectiveness, and draws policy recommendations based on the outcomes of the capacity-building interventions. An essential aspect underscored by the study is the importance of providing ongoing support and guidance post-training to ensure sustainable development and successful implementation of the acquired knowledge. Methodology: The methodology described in this paragraph involves capacity building approaches for government officials in the health sector. Specifically, the methodology includes the following elements: capacity building approaches; Inhouse Training programme technique; Digital technology enabled process; Training of State, District, and Block Level Health Programme Officials and Data Managers; Mentoring and Hand-Holding Support; Web-Based Learning Method using 'Google Classroom. Findings: The findings of this study emphasize two crucial factors that contributed to the success of the capacity-building initiatives. Firstly, the provision of on-site assistance proved to be highly effective in reinforcing the newly acquired knowledge and skills. Secondly, the utilization of the web-based Google Class platform was found to be instrumental in promoting knowledge retention and enhancing the effective utilization of data. Value: In conclusion, this research sheds light on the significance of capacity-building initiatives in the realm of health and data management. It highlights the positive impact of on-site support and the role of technology, particularly the Google Class platform, in ensuring the lasting benefits of such programs. The paper concludes by underlining the importance of continued support and sustained efforts in maximizing the potential of data-driven decision-making in the healthcare sector in Rajasthan. Alternate abstract: Objectivo: Este artigo explora criticamente as iniciativas que foram implementadas no Rajastão durante o período de 2018-19 pelo UNFPA, em colaboração com o Departamento de Saúde e Bem-Estar Familiar, o Governo do Rajastão e a Universidade IIHMR, Jaipur, Rajastão, Índia. O principal objectivo destas iniciativas era reforçar as capacidades dos funcionários de saúde e gestores de dados a diferentes níveis do estado, permitindo-lhes tomar decisões baseadas em evidências, utilizando dados de forma eficaz. Quadro teórico: O programa de capacitação foi concebido para reforçar o sistema de planeamento, monitorização e utilização de dados baseados em evidências através de uma abordagem de formação abrangente e apoio contínuo. Este estudo investiga minuciosamente todo o processo, avalia a sua eficácia e formula recomendações políticas com base nos resultados das intervenções de capacitação. Um aspecto essencial sublinhado pelo estudo é a importância de fornecer apoio e orientação contínuos após a formação para garantir o desenvolvimento sustentável e a implementação bem sucedida do conhecimento adquirido. Metodologia: A metodologia descrita neste parágrafo envolve abordagens de capacitação para funcionários governamentais no sector da saúde. Especificamente, a metodologia inclui os seguintes elementos: abordagens de capacitação; Técnica do programa de treinamento interno; Processo habilitado para tecnologia digital; Treinamento de Funcionários de Programas de Saúde de Nível Estadual, Distrital e de Bloco e Gerentes de Dados; Mentoria e suporte manual: Método de aprendizagem baseado na Web usando o 'Google Classroom. Constatações: As conclusões deste estudo enfatizam dois factores cruciais que contribuíram para o sucesso das iniciativas de capacitação. Em primeiro lugar, a prestação de assistência no local revelou-se altamente eficaz no reforço dos conhecimentos e competências recentemente adquiridos. Em segundo lugar, a utilização da plataforma Google Class baseada na Web foi considerada fundamental para promover a retenção de conhecimento e melhorar a utilização eficaz dos dados. Valor: Em conclusão, esta investigação esclarece a importância das iniciativas de capacitação no domínio da saúde e da gestão de dados. Destaca o impacto positivo do apoio no local e o papel da tecnologia, especialmente a plataforma Google Class, na garantia dos benefícios duradouros de tais programas. O documento conclui sublinhando a importância do apoio contínuo e dos esforços sustentados para maximizar o potencial da tomada de decisões baseada em dados no sector da saúde no Rajastão. Alternate abstract: Propósito: Este documento explora críticamente las iniciativas que el UNFPA implementó en Rajasthan durante el período 2018-19, en colaboración con el Departamento de Salud y Bienestar Familiar, el Gobierno de Rajasthan y la Universidad IIHMR, Jaipur, Rajasthan, India. El principal objetivo de estas iniciativas fue fortalecer las capacidades de los funcionarios de salud y administradores de datos en diferentes niveles dentro del estado, permitiéndoles tomar decisiones basadas en evidencia utilizando datos de manera efectiva. Marco teórico: El programa de desarrollo de capacidades fue diseñado para reforzar el sistema de planificación, monitoreo y utilización de datos basados en evidencia a través de un enfoque de capacitación integral y apoyo continuo. Este estudio investiga a fondo todo el proceso, evalúa su efectividad y elabora recomendaciones de políticas basadas en los resultados de las intervenciones de desarrollo de capacidades. Un aspecto esencial subrayado por el estudio es la importancia de brindar apoyo y orientación continua después de la capacitación para garantizar el desarrollo sostenible y la implementación exitosa de los conocimientos adquiridos. Metodología: La metodología descrita en este párrafo involucra enfoques de desarrollo de capacidades para funcionarios gubernamentales en el sector de la salud. Específicamente, la metodología incluye los siguientes elementos: enfoques de creación de capacidad; Técnica del programa de formación interna; Proceso habilitado por tecnología digital; Capacitación de funcionarios de programas de salud y administradores de datos a nivel estatal, distrital y de bloque; Mentoría y apoyo de la mano; Método de aprendizaje basado en web utilizando 'Google Classroom. Hallazgos: Los hallazgos de este estudio enfatizan dos factores cruciales que contribuyeron al éxito de las iniciativas de desarrollo de capacidades. En primer lugar, la prestación de asistencia in situ demostró ser muy eficaz para reforzar los conocimientos y habilidades recién adquiridos. En segundo lugar, se descubrió que la utilización de la plataforma Google Class basada en la web era fundamental para promover la retención de conocimientos y mejorar la utilización eficaz de los datos. Valor: En conclusión, esta investigación arroja luz sobre la importancia de las iniciativas de desarrollo de capacidades en el ámbito de la salud y la gestión de datos. Destaca el impacto positivo del soporte in situ y el papel de la tecnología, en particular la plataforma Google Class, para garantizar los beneficios duraderos de dichos programas. El documento concluye subrayando la importancia del apoyo continuo y los esfuerzos sostenidos para maximizar el potencial de la toma de decisiones basada en datos en el sector de la salud en Rajasthan.

Organisational learning and sustainable tourism: The enabling role of digital transformation

Author: Schönherr, Sarah1    ; Eller, Robert2    ; Kallmuenzer, Andreas3    ; Peters, Mike31 Department of Strategic Management, Marketing and Tourism, University of Innsbruck, Innsbruck, Austria sarah.schoenherr@uibk.ac.at2 Excelia Business School, La Rochelle, France3 Department of Strategic Management, Marketing and Tourism, Faculty of Business and Management, University of Innsbruck, Innsbruck, Austria

Publication info: Schönherr, Sarah; Eller, Robert; Kallmuenzer, Andreas; Peters, Mike. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/organisational-learning-sustainable-tourism/docview/3049804837/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: Purpose: Organisational learning drives tourism organisations towards more sustainable tourism. Digital transformation also provides opportunities for sustainable tourism development. This study aims to combine these perspectives and explore how digital transformation enables organisational learning to contribute to sustainable tourism, following organisational learning theory (OLT). Design/methodology/approach: Based on a critical realist paradigm, this study focuses on developing an in-depth understanding of organisational learning in tourism organisations. Thirty qualitative interviews with tourism organisations participating in an executive development programme (EDP) show how tourism organisations create, retain and transfer knowledge. Findings: This study demonstrates that the EDP initiates knowledge creation through content transmission and exchange, triggers knowledge retention through utilisation of digital technologies and reinforces digitalisation through data value creation. Furthermore, this study enables knowledge transformation as implementation, which contributes to the three pillars of sustainable tourism and facilitates the development of networks encouraging sustainable tourism. Originality/value: This study identifies approaches that enable economic, social and environmentally sustainable tourism development by facilitating collaborations via digital transformation, digital technologies that guide guest streams, online mobility offers and online environmental awareness campaigns that reduce environmental impacts. Thus, this study strengthens OLT and has implications for organisational learning and tourism policymakers. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2024 APA, all rights reserved) (Source: journal abstract)

Incorporating Technology in Pharmacy Education: Students' Preferences and Learning Outcomes

Author: Alhur Anas; Remas, Hedesh; Alshehri Mara; Al Qasim Shaima; Alkhaldi Roaa; Bazuhair Walaa; Wafa, Bin Shamlan; Alshahrani Shatha; Shahad, Alshahrani; Alasiri Alaa; Alshalwi Rahaf; Alnefaie Sara; Alotaibi Rana; Aljehani, Ragad K; Alzahrani Laila

Publication info: Alhur Anas; Remas, Hedesh; Alshehri Mara; Al Qasim Shaima; Alkhaldi Roaa; et al. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/incorporating-technology-pharmacy-education/docview/2920587381/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: Introduction The integration of technology in pharmacy education has led to significant changes, making it essential to examine its impact on student learning outcomes. With the rise of emerging technologies, such as game-based learning and augmented reality, new pedagogical approaches have been introduced. However, these technologies also bring challenges that necessitate well-thought-out responses from educational institutions, especially considering the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on learning formats. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted with pharmacy students in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, utilizing stratified random sampling for data collection. The study employed a validated questionnaire to gather information on students' use of technology, their preferences, and their perceived learning outcomes. The analysis was carried out using Statistical Product and Service Solutions (SPSS, version 29) (IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows, Armonk, NY), ensuring adherence to the ethical standards set by the institutional review board. Results The study, involving 508 pharmacy students from Saudi Arabia, revealed that a significant majority regularly use technology in their education, particularly online learning management systems and virtual labs, indicating a shift toward more accessible and efficient learning methods. A notable portion of the students acknowledged the beneficial impact of technology on their learning, with 86.3% reporting improved knowledge retention, 92% noting enhanced skills, and 87.1% observing better academic performance. However, the study also uncovered challenges, with about half of the students facing issues mainly related to distractions while finding technological complexity less problematic. The support from educational institutions in addressing these issues was found to be moderate. These findings underscore the crucial role of technology in enhancing pharmacy education while highlighting the need for more comprehensive institutional support and strategic planning to address the challenges faced by students. Conclusions Technology plays a vital role in the modernization of pharmacy education, significantly aiding in knowledge retention, skill development, and academic performance. Despite the widespread use of technology, the varied experiences and challenges encountered by students underscore the need for increased institutional support and strategic planning. Education must adapt alongside technological advancements to cater to the diverse needs of learners, highlighting the importance of further research into the long-term effects and optimal strategies for technology integration in pharmacy education.

Full text: Introduction
The integration of technology into education has brought about transformative changes in learning methodologies and student engagement, with pharmacy education being no exception. The introduction of digital tools and platforms has catalyzed a shift in the educational paradigm, offering both opportunities and challenges for curriculum development and instructional practices. As the educational landscape progresses, it is critical to understand the integration of these technological advances into pharmacy curricula and their subsequent effects on student learning outcomes.
In pharmacy education, emerging technologies, such as game-based learning (GBL) and augmented reality (AR), are increasingly influential in shaping teaching approaches. These technologies range from complex simulations to basic interactive models, potentially boosting student engagement and facilitating knowledge acquisition [1,2]. Moreover, in 2023, Alhur et al. provided empirical evidence suggesting that the incorporation of health information technology into the pharmacy curriculum is considered essential for the evolving role of pharmacists, as supported by 88% of surveyed pharmacy students [3]. Despite their benefits, adopting these innovations faces challenges, such as financial constraints, technological limitations, and the need for effective assessment methods to gauge learning outcomes in environments rich with technology [1].
Educational modalities notably shifted due to the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic, leading to research on the psychological impacts of transitioning from traditional to online and blended learning environments [4-6]. These studies reveal various student preferences and highlight the significance of accommodating different learning styles in educational strategy development and implementation [7]. Our study aimed to critically assess the current state of technology integration in pharmacy education and its impact on academic performance, emphasizing student preferences and the effectiveness of such technologies.
Materials and methods
Research design
We conducted a cross-sectional study in which data were collected from multiple participants over one week. This design was selected for its effectiveness in efficiently acquiring data from a broad sample and is well-suited for evaluating the present integration of technology in pharmacy education.
Population and sample
The target population for this study comprised pharmacy students from various institutions across the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (KSA). To achieve a representative sample reflective of this diverse group, we employed a stratified random sampling method. This approach was designed to ensure a balanced representation across different academic years, genders, and educational institutions.
Our inclusion criteria were quite specific: the study focused on pharmacy students within KSA who actively engaged with technology in their educational pursuits. This criterion was pivotal in maintaining the relevance and focus of the research, centering on individuals directly involved in technology-enhanced learning within the pharmacy field.
Conversely, the exclusion criteria were set to omit individuals not fitting this profile. This included non-pharmacy students in KSA, pharmacy students who did not actively utilize technology in their education, and those who did not provide informed consent. Additionally, students from academic institutions that fell outside the scope of this study were excluded. This exclusion ensured that the sample remained strictly pertinent to the study's objectives, concentrating solely on pharmacy students immersed in technology-enhanced learning environments.
In total, 508 consenting students formed the sample for this study. This sample size was determined through a statistical power analysis, ensuring adequate representation and validity of the findings.
By adopting this sampling strategy, the study aimed to address the broader challenge of diversity in healthcare research. While focusing on variables such as academic year, gender, and institution, it is crucial to note that diversity in research encompasses additional dimensions, such as socioeconomic backgrounds, cultural and ethnic differences, geographical locations, and individual learning needs, including those with disabilities. Considering these factors is essential for a comprehensive understanding of the impact of technology in pharmacy education and for ensuring that research outcomes are applicable and beneficial to all segments of the student population.
Data collection
We used a validated questionnaire previously established by researchers in 2008 and 2016 [7]. The structured questionnaire included Likert scale items to measure students’ preferences and perceptions of technology in their education, multiple-choice questions to determine the types of technology tools and platforms students are acquainted with, and open-ended questions to elicit further insights or comments from the participants.
The questionnaire was distributed electronically across various social media platforms, with a completion window of one week. Consent was acquired electronically at the survey’s outset, ensuring participants were informed about the study’s aims and their rights.
Data analysis
The data were analyzed with Statistical Products and Service Solutions (SPSS) for Windows, version 29 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY). We employed descriptive statistics such as mean, median, mode, and standard deviation to summarize the findings.
Validity and reliability
To ensure the reliability of the questionnaire domains, we conducted a preliminary analysis to calculate Cronbach’s alpha for each set of items. The domains assessed included the current state of technology integration, student preferences, perceived learning outcomes, and the barriers and challenges to technology use. Cronbach’s alpha for these domains ranged from 0.773 to 0.885, indicating an acceptable to a good level of internal consistency. Details of these reliability statistics are presented in Table 1.
Table 1
Reliability of questionnaire domains assessing pharmacy education technology integration

No Variables Cronbach’s Alpha Number of Items
1 Current State of Technology Integration 0.773 2
2 Student Preferences 0.885 2

4 Barriers and Challenges 0.826 3
Ethical considerations
Participants were informed of the study’s objectives, their rights, and the confidentiality of their responses. Participation was entirely voluntary, and they had the right to withdraw at any time without consequences. The institutional review board of the University of Hail approved the study design (IRB Approval No. H-2023-194).
Results
A total of 508 students (98.10%) consented to partake in the survey. Of the 508 participants, most were women (n=367; 70.80%), while men accounted for 27.20% (n=141). Participants were drawn from a range of institutions, with the majority (n=140) hailing from King Khalid University (27%) and the University of Hail (n=117; 22.6%). The study encompassed individuals across all years of pharmacy education, with the largest group being graduates at 38.4% (n=199) and fifth-year students (n=79), forming 15.3% of the cohort (Table 2).

When exploring the frequency of technology use in pharmacy education, most students frequently utilized technology, with 49.4% (n=256) always incorporating it and 34.7% (n=180) often doing so (Table 3). Discussion
This study provides insight into the incorporation of technology in pharmacy education, revealing its profound impact on students’ learning outcomes and preferences. Here, we discuss these findings within the context of existing literature and explore their broader implications.
Game-based learning
Integrating GBL in pharmacy education appears to enhance student engagement and knowledge retention. Our findings resonate with Huda et al., who report varied sophistication levels in GBL methods, from basic to advanced technological interactions [8]. Like Dabbous et al., our study suggests that GBL can positively influence learning outcomes, fostering a self-motivated and active learning environment [5]. However, financial and technological barriers and a lack of rigorous assessment methods require further attention.
AR in education
Our study aligns with the work of Dhar et al., suggesting that AR offers unique learning advantages, such as remote learning capabilities and interactive simulations, potentially revolutionizing pharmacy education [6]. Despite its potential, the full integration of AR into the curriculum is challenged by the need for continuous innovation and research to overcome existing barriers.
Impact of COVID-19 on education modalities
The COVID-19 pandemic necessitated a pivot to online learning, with mixed reactions from students. Basheti et al. found a preference for traditional learning despite the perceived stress reduction associated with online formats [2]. Additionally, Dabbous et al. identified concerns about the long-term efficacy of online learning on student performance [5]. These findings underscore the need for balanced, flexible learning strategies to adapt to such unprecedented challenges.
Learning preferences and styles
Our study’s indication of a preference for aural and kinesthetic learning styles among pharmacy students suggests a need for educational strategies that cater to these preferences [7]. Understanding these learning styles is crucial for educators to tailor their methods and maximize educational outcomes.
Simulation in education
The application of simulation in pharmacy education offers a safe space for skill practice [9]. McBane et al. highlighted the diverse potential of simulation techniques, yet they also noted limited research on the direct benefits for learning outcomes [10]. This gap suggests an opportunity for future research to validate the effectiveness of simulation-based education.
Students’ technology use and perception
The high percentage of pharmacy students incorporating technology in their education and their comfort in using online learning management systems aligns with that of Medina et al., who highlighted these systems’ benefits for interactive learning [11]. Our findings further suggest that technology has positively impacted knowledge retention and skill acquisition, corroborated by Müller et al. [12] and Cooper et al. [4], who also acknowledge technology’s role in enhancing student performance.
Challenges and institutional support
Despite the benefits, our study revealed a divided opinion on technology integration challenges. The moderate level of institutional support observed indicates substantial room for improvement in this domain. Future research should prioritize identifying and overcoming these hurdles to optimize the benefits of technology in education.
Limitations
This study offers important insights but also presents several limitations. Firstly, its focus on pharmacy colleges within the KSA limits the generalizability of its findings, as these may not be representative of students in different geographic or cultural contexts. Additionally, its cross-sectional nature only provides a snapshot in time, lacking the ability to track changes or establish causality. The reliance on self-reported questionnaires could lead to response bias, with participants potentially providing socially desirable answers or inaccurately recalling their experiences. Furthermore, the study's emphasis on quantitative data might have restricted the depth of exploration into students' experiences, which could have been enriched by qualitative insights such as interviews or open-ended questions. Other factors, such as individual learning styles, technological competencies, or variations in institutional technological infrastructure, may not have been fully explored. Recognizing these limitations is crucial, especially as the study highlights the widespread use of technology in education and its impact on learning outcomes. This underscores the need for educational strategies and institutional support systems that evolve with technological advancements. Future research should aim to understand the long-term effects of technology integration in pharmacy education and develop comprehensive strategies that maximize its potential, catering to the diverse needs of learners for more inclusive and effective educational experiences.
Conclusions
This research highlights the transformative impact of technology in the realm of pharmacy education, notably enhancing learning experiences and fostering improvements in areas such as knowledge retention, skill development, and overall academic performance. The widespread adoption of technology among the student population emphasizes its critical role in the contemporary educational framework. Nonetheless, the variability in student experiences and the obstacles faced in technology integration underscores the necessity for substantial institutional support and strategic planning. As the educational environment continually adapts to technological advancements, it becomes imperative for academic institutions to address these challenges effectively. Doing so ensures that the incorporation of technology into the educational process is seamless, efficient, and attuned to the varied needs of students, thus maintaining the relevance and efficacy of educational methodologies in an increasingly technology-driven landscape.

Tapping into Retirees to Bolster Knowledge Transfer

Author: Ritter, Beth M, CCP1; Clark, Robert L, PhD11 North Carolina State University

Publication info: Ritter, Beth M, CCP; Clark, Robert L, PhD. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/tapping-into-retirees-bolster-knowledge-transfer/docview/2919464239/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: Preservation of knowledge by an organization is critical for ongoing success. The knowledge transfer between retirees and their entity's remaining employees offers a unique opportunity to retain knowledge. Employers that engage with employees prior to their retirement can allow for a longer and more productive knowledge transfer process. The aim of our research has been to learn how to make knowledge exchanges successful by considering methods. Managers should consider new efforts for knowledge-continuity management. Multiple surveys were designed to determine the extent of knowledge-loss risk associated with retirees, the prevalence of informal and formal knowledge-transfer practices and the effectiveness of knowledge transfer for knowledge continuity. Results showed that organizations perceive significant knowledge-loss risk with the impending wave of retirements from an aging workforce and that many are not proactively approaching this opportunity. Organizations are leveraging only a few knowledge-transfer approaches and not leveraging technology for tacit knowledge transfers to occur. The data indicate that there is considerable room for improvement in knowledge-transfer practices - and our research offers practical implications for effective knowledge-transfer activities.

Full text: Headnote "I ran a complex program alone and having time together to go through everything would have been helpful. As it was, we had 3.5 days." - A recent retiree
Preservation of knowledge by an organization is critical for ongoing success. The knowledge transfer between retirees and their entity's remaining employees offers a unique opportunity to retain knowledge. Employers that engage with employees prior to their retirement can allow for a longer and more productive knowledge transfer process. The aim of our research has been to learn how to make knowledge exchanges successful by considering methods. Managers should consider new efforts for knowledge-continuity management. Multiple surveys were designed to determine the extent of knowledge-loss risk associated with retirees, the prevalence of informal and formal knowledge-transfer practices and the effectiveness of knowledge transfer for knowledge continuity. Results showed that organizations perceive significant knowledge-loss risk with the impending wave of retirements from an aging workforce and that many are not proactively approaching this opportunity. Organizations are leveraging only a few knowledge-transfer approaches and not leveraging technology for tacit knowledge transfers to occur. The data indicate that there is considerable room for improvement in knowledge-transfer practices - and our research offers practical implications for effective knowledge-transfer activities.
INTRODUCTION AND CHALLENGE
Most entities have a relatively large group of older workers who are eligible to retire. In the past, many organizations have encouraged older workers to retire to promote upward mobility and allow for the continued introduction of new skills. However, in recent years, given the aging of the global labor force, many organizations are finding it more difficult to recruit and retain enough young and middle-age workers to offset the loss of older workers. The share of the population age 60 and older is projected to increase in nearly every country from 2005 through 2050. Population aging will tend to lower labor-force participation. (Bloom et al. 2010). Add the impacts of the COVID pandemic to that employment dynamic, and organizations could be confronting a substantial loss of knowledge. Each time an employee leaves, an organization risks losing essential knowledge. Without some proactive measures and focus by management, considerable knowledge will continue to leave organizations, eroding their competitive positions. Our research and this paper explore knowledge-continuity management to understand the effectiveness of current institutional knowledge-sharing programs. We study the types and prevalence of knowledge-transfer practices being utilized. We then propose that proactive work, specifically with future retirees, offers a meaningful chance to reduce an organization's knowledge loss. In addition to sharing research, we will offer insights from recent retirees' perspectives and practical advice to minimize the departure of knowledge and experience associated with retirements.
LITERATURE REVIEW OF KNOWLEDGE CONTINUITY
Knowledge management is about finding and developing the right body of knowledge and about using the knowledge to an advantage. According to Durst and Zieba (2019), knowledge loss is a consequence that occurs when an organization loses all or parts of its crucial knowledge from an employee leaving. It can also be from a technical failure, such as a computer breakdown, but our focus will be on departing employees. Knowledge continuity is the efficient and effective transfer of information and knowledge from departing employees to their replacements. Beazley, Boenisch, and Harden (2003) provided a summary of the origins of knowledge management and declared knowledge continuity to be a new management function in their work in 2003. So, managers have been building, and must continue to build, a competency in ensuring knowledge continuity within their departments. Management invests resources to do this because knowledge is a source of competitive advantage for organizations (Beazley, Boenisch, and Harden 2003).
Research indicates two types of knowledge - tacit and explicit. Tacit knowledge is difficult to express, formalize or share, but provides competitive advantage. This is the knowledge that you want to retain and share within your organization, but you do not want it to be shared externally. Roy Lubrit in "Organizational Dynamics" (2001) said that tacit knowledge is the know-how or skills, the ways of solving problems, the mental models or the organizational routines and the knowledge that is embedded in individuals. Alavi and Leidner (2001) summarized more descriptions of knowledge as the "know why," the "know when," and the "know with" knowledge, because it is the ability for one to know why something has or has not happened and what to do at the right time and with whom. Explicit knowledge is documented or codified knowledge, such as job aids and workflows. But one might need the tacit knowledge to interpret the explicit knowledge. Unit performance can depend on the ability to turn knowledge into the right actions.
Effective knowledge sharing or transfer can reduce the learning curve for new hires and internal employees and preserve the knowledge that the organization has invested to develop. This successful transfer of knowledge results in better decision making or fewer operational mistakes for the organization and its customers (Beazley, Boenisch, and Harden, 2003). The two-party process includes those who convey knowledge and those who receive knowledge. Since the process involves people, it can be hampered by motivation, trust, relational competence, common language, culture and the type of knowledge itself (Tangaraja et al. 2016; Alavi and Leidner 2001). We advocate that leaders should be working to create an environment for the effective transfer of knowledge for knowledge continuity and that their support of this effort will be an enabler for it.
DATA AND METHODS
In a series of surveys, we have developed a research methodology that provides an understanding of how both risk managers and recent retirees are thinking about knowledge transfer as a risk - a risk that is increasing with the increase in retirements. We partnered with two organizations to understand perceptions of risk, which tactics or knowledge-transfer approaches are in use in organizations, and what attempts at transferring knowledge between retirees and remaining employees are happening. Because knowledge loss is a risk to organizations, we partnered with the Enterprise Risk Management Initiative at North Carolina State University to survey risk managers about the current knowledge-transfer practices of organizations. The survey had 119 responses, with 34% of respondents coming from private for-profit entities, 31% from publicly traded firms, 19% from nonprofit entities and 16% from government agencies. Our respondents were almost evenly split between international and U.S. entities. Fifty-one percent of respondents were from organizations headquartered in the United States with only U.S. employees. The international perspective is represented by 49% of respondents. Twenty-seven percent of respondents were employed by U.S.-headquartered multinational entities with both global and U.S.-based employees, 13% were employed by internationally headquartered multinational entities with no U.S.-based employees, while 9% were employed by internationally headquartered multinational entities with U.S.-based employees. From a size perspective, 31% percent of respondents employed more than 5,000 employees, while 20% employed from 1,000 to 5,000 employees.
To further confirm or test our findings, we also partnered with Osher Lifelong Learning Institutes (OLLI) to access recent retirees to learn the knowledge-transfer practices they utilized as they attempted to share knowledge. Via survey, we were able to reach a group of 200 OLLI members who retired in the past five years. Osher Institutes deliver non-credit courses and educational activities specifically designed for people who are 50 or older. Nine sites throughout the United States agreed to share the survey with their members, and 205 people responded to the survey request, with only five reporting that they retired outside our five-year timeframe. The breakdown of numbers and percentages of the 200 respondents that met our criteria is evenly distributed with retirees from each of the years from 2016 to 2021. The breakdown by year of retirement was: 2016, 53 respondents or 26.5% of respondents; 2017, 33 or 16.5%; 2018, 43 or 21.5%; 2019, 32 or 16.0%; 2020, 27 or 13.5%; and 2021,12 or 6.0%.
In our surveys, we asked about the extent of knowledge-loss risk perceived with impending retirements, the effectiveness of knowledge-transfer practices, and the approaches used for knowledge transfer with retirees. We also asked retirees for their advice to improve the knowledge-transfer process. Respondents wrote in response to the question, "What, if anything, could the company have done to improve this process?"
RESEARCH RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
Our first finding is that risk managers identify the potential knowledge loss associated with retirees to be a risk in the next three to five years, but the extent of risk varied. Survey respondents were asked "To what extent does your organization face a risk of significant loss of knowledge due to an aging workforce who may leave the organization in the next 3-5 years?" While 43.7% of the overall group found the knowledge-loss risk to be somewhat significant, risk managers from governmental entities indicated this risk as more significant, with 73.7% identifying the risk as "extensive" or "mostly extensive" (see Table 1).
Next, we sought to learn about which methods or approaches entities were using in their efforts to minimize loss of knowledge. We identified 11 potential knowledge-transfer practices that organizations may be using to enable the knowledge-transfer process. We separately asked the risk managers as well as the recent retirees which methods were utilized. The retirees' perspectives confirmed the results. Our findings from both groups are summarized in Table 2, where we list the 11 potential knowledge-transfer practices and how prevalent they were in organizations as ranked by risk managers and recent retirees. Respondents of the surveys were instructed to indicate as many activities as necessary to represent the entirety of activities occurring in their organization to share knowledge between sender and receiver. One interesting finding is that both groups' rankings reinforce that on-the-job training with shadowing and one-to-one mentoring are the most often used approaches.
Another observation is that technology-based knowledge-sharing practices were some of the least utilized by respondents and retirees. For example, collaborative software solutions such as wikis or blogs ranked low in usage on both lists. Artificial intelligence (AI) systems ranked the least used by both groups.
It is important to determine how effective these knowledge-sharing approaches were perceived to be. Responses were quite telling when asked to determine "How effective your organization's processes are for helping transfer critical knowledge from employees as they retire to others in the workforce who will remain." Thirty-seven percent of responding risk managers indicated the processes were "minimally effective," while 42% indicated "somewhat effective."
To continue to learn about current practices, one can consider the number of different activities in use within an entity. Once again, we see consistency in our separate survey responses, where one to four practices were most indicated, and rarely were seven or more different approaches used in one organization. Figure 1 illustrates the data and the decrease in number of methods used after the combined use of three or four knowledge-transfer methods.
To round out this research, we asked how well organizations effectively transfer knowledge. Four out of five (79%) surveyed professionals said their organization's knowledge-transfer efforts are either "somewhat effective" or "minimally effective." This implies that there is room for improvement in the knowledge sharing in most organizations. The other finding is that 25% to 28% of organizations are using just one knowledge-transfer approach. This suggests that improvements to the knowledge-transfer process may occur simply by increasing the number of approaches. Another consideration for improving the transfer would be to consider new approaches. Those approaches that use technology and those that involve groups were some of the least used by all respondents.
Last, when checking this data by retirement year, we found two interesting patterns of responses. First, the use of collaborative software only began in 2018. Second, knowledge transfer appeared to become more formal in 2020, as there were no formal knowledge-transfer processes for retirees.
After considering the knowledge-transfer methods being used by organizations, managers should consider how a unit develops knowledge-transfer policies and programs that will be successful and allow for an orderly knowledge transfer. We offer the following considerations for managers and leverage the open responses of retirees as well as outline further research in our recommendations.
PRACTICAL PROGRAMS AND APPROACHES
First, identify critical knowledge and the knowledge holders
In their work on knowledge-continuity management, Bidian and Evans (2019) suggested that managers should conduct a knowledge audit to identify critical or valuable knowledge and use strategic plans to determine a time horizon for how long this knowledge is needed. Once critical knowledge is identified, then one must consider who holds that knowledge. A manager may know this for their immediate area, but if one is working at an enterprise level, an organization chart or job description database may be the first sources to identify knowledge by role. Another approach is to access HR metrics to predict individuals at risk of leaving and compare that list of employees to the lists of critical knowledge. The metrics can be as simple as the ages of the workforce or could be voluntary turnover rates. In this paper, we advocate that leaders focus efforts to support the knowledge transfer of retirees and that they prioritize this over the knowledge transfer of other departing employees, for two reasons. The first is that under the right conditions, when the retiree feels secure in a job and valued, that employee is more likely to give a longer notice than an employee resigning will provide. Our research confirmed that notice period for retirees to be a mechanism to support effective knowledge transfer. The second reason is that impending retirement is more predictable than other voluntary turnover scenarios and that predictability lends itself to planning and effectiveness. This effort and focus allow an entity to make an assessment for each potential retiree. One can imagine a question similar to this: "Is there critical knowledge that needs to be retained by the organization before this individual retires, and can we begin this process well before they retire?"
Next, make the ask
Once critical knowledge is identified and it is determined that a retiree may be the holder of that information, a leader needs to manage the knowledge-sharing process. Only one-third of retirees we surveyed were asked to share knowledge with others inside the organization. Even acknowledging that some work may not have been worthy of knowledge transfer, it seems that increasing the number of people asked to knowledge-share might help to improve the effectiveness. We propose having a supportive and assuring conversation with the individual who holds the key knowledge to learn about their retirement plans and ask for their advice on a good transfer strategy.
Consider this real-life example. A function leader in an organization was approached by her manager, a person she trusted, and was asked if others knew what she knew. They discussed if there were internal employees who might know the same information. They agreed there was not really anyone who shared her knowledge. This is more than a conversation about successors. It is about learning if others in the entity know the explicit or tacit knowledge that she knew. The manager then asked what her desired retirement date was, indicating that she hoped it was not soon. The employee felt comfortable to share that she was about five years away from retirement. The two then created a formal plan for her to begin a process to share her knowledge with a colleague. The subject-matter expert was to begin knowledge sharing with the other person, and boundaries were set that she should not exceed 50% of the receiver's time. The person was not necessarily her successor. The interviewee shared she may not have revealed her retirement plans to her new leader if there was no trust between them. The new leader expressed the person's value and the organization's vulnerability if she were to leave. Kudos to the manager who first identified critical knowledge the organization needed that was held by one source and then conducted a productive conversation to get the knowledge-transfer process started. A fiveyear plan like the one described may not be workable for most critical knowledge holders, but the model of iterative conversations to identify receivers and a plan is attractive.
Remember, time is of the essence
Our research of open responses from recent retirees tells us that time is often not factored into the knowledge-sharing scenario. Speaking with senior employees early about their timing preferences for retirement allows for a longer time for knowledge transfer compared to the short time that a voluntary resignation and a two-week notice provides. It may mean that work is restructured for both the knowledge conveyer and the knowledge receiver(s) to allow extra time for this activity. There may be an extra expense to having several people learning and observing, but the redundancy may increase the chances of successful knowledge transfer, specifically for tacit knowledge. One retiree's advice was to "start (the) transfer of knowledge and building of relationships early in (the) process" and allocate time up front "instead of working in crisis mode up till the last minute."
Open your mind to potential knowledge receivers
Next, work to identify potential knowledge receivers. Think more broadly than finding a perfect "ready now" successor from the succession charts. Often terms such as "ready now" and "ready in 1-3 years" are used to classify internal employees for succession. One might argue that your "ready-now candidate" has already left or is interviewing, so an organization may be best served to invest in knowledge transfer with more than one person and with those who may seem less ready than you'd like. The advice we learned from recent retirees even highlighted the need for a solid plan for knowledge management when outsourcing. An outsourced activity requires monitoring and management and the knowledge to do that. Consider a knowledge transfer from the retiree to whichever department will become the outsource vendor manager as effective knowledge continuity management of outsourced activities. Also, think about how the knowledge can be shared with more than one person to improve your odds of retaining the knowledge and how that knowledge transfer can be positioned as career enhancing for those who are less experienced.
Research by Fasbender, Gerpott, and Unger (2021) indicated that receivers who are motivated to grow, increase competence and master new skills and knowledge are better receivers. Being an insider, someone who knows the entity, adds an advantage to the successful knowledge transfer. If you must go externally for a candidate, allow for longer-than-expected times to fill the role and expect more of a learning curve as the person learns both the company and the knowledge. A recent retiree said that to improve the knowledge sharing, the organization could have "hired a replacement with some level of institutional and program knowledge - at least a foundation to build upon." If that is not possible, having several employees within the organization who already have some knowledge because of previous successful knowledge-sharing efforts can support new hires more effectively.
Now, consider the type of knowledge and which transfer practices are best suited
As described earlier, organizations are most often using on-the-job training, job shadowing and one-to-one mentoring to attempt their knowledge transfers but are not always satisfied with the effectiveness of the transfers. Research indicates that working with a coach or expert to learn tacit knowledge is most effective when the receiver of the knowledge can problem-solve with the expert or learn their decision-making process experientially. This takes time. In his work on tacit knowledge transfer, Lubrit (2001) offered the idea that structured group discussions are a way to increase the numbers of people who have access to the expert and their expertise. As you consider the list of 11 knowledge-transfer tactics (see Table 2) and the idea that structured group activities may increase access to knowledge, two moderately used options stand out as options to make knowledge transfers more efficient and effective.
Consider the use of communities of practice and after-action reviews. Communities of practice, also called centers of excellence, are groups that regularly convene and share information. They often cross traditional organizational structures, allowing all levels of the entity to participate and learn from others outside their formal departments. These are often set up for a specific discipline or process. If a manager were to direct the center of excellence to focus on critical knowledge that was identified in a knowledge audit, group members can begin the sharing process earlier and add time to what has historically been rushed knowledge-transfer activities. They can also improve the format for the knowledge transfer by allowing topics to be more problem solving in nature and less like forced explicit knowledge exchanges. Greene offered an interesting example in his work on knowledge management (Greene 2020). He told of Xerox repair technicians who created an informal breakfast club where they shared solutions to difficult problems that did not appear in repair manuals. This form of applied learning benefited the company. It would also be beneficial to encourage them to document what they learn.
Next, consider after-action reviews. These have a heritage in the Army, but the concept may also be a way to pivot your current knowledge-transfer approaches to become more effective. A large construction business shared its approach to after-action reviews using the following questions after a planned activity:
| What was supposed to happen? What happened?
| What went well? Why?
| What could be improved? How?
A manager can strategically choose which activities are worth this deliberate expense of time by using the knowledge audit of critical knowledge. The structure of the questions allows experts to unpack their knowledge in a way that shares their logic, which is more effective for tacit knowledge sharing and receiving.
Knowledge-management systems provide another opportunity for knowledge transfer identified from the utilization data in Table 2. Technology or systems are not highly leveraged. Systems can be enablers of knowledge sharing, but we saw collaborative software was not often used and retirees in our survey only reported its use starting in 2018. One might speculate that COVID-related experiences with technology may have increased the usage of these tools, but our data for 2020 and 2021 retirees do not indicate an increase in the use of collaborative tools in the knowledge-transfer process. Collaborative software can facilitate global, remote and other distributed organization interaction. Center of excellence exchanges and after-action reviews can become an even more significant resource for knowledge sharing with many when enabled by collaborative technology.
Consider adding new tricks to your current knowledge-continuity goals to increase the number of approaches your organization utilizes. Once you have identified the critical knowledge, the person who holds that knowledge and the potential receivers, then consider increasing the types of knowledge-transfer approaches. Our research with both organizations and retirees indicates 53% to 56% of organizations are using only one or two approaches. Building a competency for knowledge transfer may involve learning about alternative methods that are available for this work and then expanding the types of approaches. Managers should leverage more critical knowledge-focused group approaches such as communities of practice or centers of excellence. They should implement strategic after-action reviews and support those activities with collaborative software to amplify the reach of these actions to more people. The biggest mind shift for managers may be thinking less about one successor and more about ongoing knowledge sharing to larger groups.
PROVIDE STRUCTURE AND CLARITY TO THE PROCESS
Recent retirees indicate clarity of purpose, documentation and role specification is needed from managers to support effective transfer. Twenty percent of those who wrote comments in our survey discussed these types of topics in their advice to improve knowledge transfers. Hofer-Alfeis (2008) offered a detailed process that can be considered. We highlight a few of the questions from that paper here as ideas in your efforts for more clarity. For example, what are business-critical relationships and knowledge networks that need to be created by the retiree and the unit? What are the knowledge assets needed, the documentation and where will it be stored and by whom and when?
LASTLY, CONSIDER CULTURE
Building a competency for knowledge transfer in an organization will also require a culture that values this work. Measurements, rewards, policies and practices reinforce company values. One way to demonstrate the importance is to measure the completion and effectiveness of this work. One could measure if there is a formal and specific plan with content and knowledge-transfer goals for each critical-knowledge category identified in your audit and for each departing retiree who holds that information. Then ultimately measure and give visibility to whether those goals are achieved. Another way to reinforce a culture of knowledge sharing is to implement new policies or programs that support the effort.
The U.S. government's phased-retirement program is an interesting example. Named the Moving Ahead Program, it allows future retirees to shift to a parttime status where they work reduced hours as they begin retirement. The work schedule shifts to one that is half work and half retirement, but with an important stipulation. The program includes a requirement that 20% of hours worked need to be focused on knowledge-sharing activities. That 20% focus and formalization is the critical knowledge-transfer enabler (Clark and Ritter 2020a). Our surveys and workshops from 2018 to 2020 indicated that most companies were not pursuing phased-retirement plans because of management and cost issues (Clark et al. 2019, Clark and Ritter 2020b). Recent Mercer research findings indicate a shift has occurred and offerings of these programs have doubled since before the pandemic (Tergesen and Weber 2022).
Last, you may also want to consider ending a policy or activity. The use of earlyretirement programs that accelerate the rate of retirements has been a practice for workforce reduction for many years. This practice may no longer be prudent. In fact, we found that 60% of risk managers indicated early-retirement packages were not offered in the past year at their organization. An early-retirement incentive could be sending the signal that there is no knowledge to capture from this group and could be accelerating knowledge loss. Leaders must consider all ways to build a knowledge culture and indicate their support of knowledgesharing activities.
CONCLUSIONS AND IMPLICATIONS FOR MANAGERS
So, what do these findings mean for managers? How can one focus efforts to increase effectiveness of knowledge transfer and minimize knowledge loss? Future retirees can be a potential significant knowledge loss for organizations and, accordingly, this loss is a knowledge-continuity management issue. Our previous research found that orderly retirement of employees is important to business strategy, with 83% of respondents indicating knowledge transfer as a key concern (Clark et al. 2019). We propose that managers focus efforts and resources on future retirees. This offers a more predictable knowledge loss that can be better managed than knowledge loss from other types of employee turnover. We offer practical approaches to be taken to transfer knowledge before it leaves with those retirees.
Recent retiree feedback allows for a view into the knowledge-exchange attempts in the past five years. Their feedback indicates that most efforts were rushed, informal and did not consider the best receivers of the knowledge. Managers hoping for knowledge continuity should conduct a knowledge audit to determine critical information and then consider if potential retirees hold that critical knowledge. They should engage knowledge holders who are potential retirees in a conversation about knowledge sharing of the critical information and develop formal plans with longer time horizons. Those plans should consider knowledge-transfer practices that are problem solving in nature and enable sharing with many instead of with only one person. Efforts should be shifted away from one-to-one, role-based knowledge sharing and succession to efforts that support a culture of knowledge transfer to many people in approaches that better support tacit knowledge transfer and with technology to enable knowledge continuity.
LIMITATIONS AND POTENTIAL AVENUES FOR FUTURE RESEARCH
While our research was novel with the identification of 11 methods for knowledge transfer and the inclusion of recent retirees to learn about recent knowledgetransfer activities, it did not collect demographic data on either the retiree or the knowledge receiver. Future research into the ages and genders of the participants in the knowledge-transfer process should include this data to determine if there is any bias that could inhibit the effective knowledge transfer that may need to be mitigated. While our research indicates a need for more time to support effective knowledge transfer, we did not survey to learn about the ideal time for the knowledge transfer. Future research should explore the time needed for a range of activities from complex to the least complex transfers.

Ritter, CCP, fbmritte2@ncsu.edu) is a professor of practice in the Department of Management, Innovation and Entrepreneurship at North Carolina State University, where she teaches and conducts research about human resources and talent management issues. Prior to joining NC State, Ritter was a senior vice president of human resources at Burt's Bees, which is now a part of Clorox. He received his Ph.D. in economics from Duke University.

Implementation of a Hepatitis-Themed Virtual Escape Room in Pharmacy Education: A Pilot Study

Author: Krishnan, Sunanthiny; Blebil, Ali Qais; Dujaili, Juman Abdulelah; Chuang, Sara; Lim, Angelina

Publication info: Krishnan, Sunanthiny; Blebil, Ali Qais; Dujaili, Juman Abdulelah; Chuang, Sara; Lim, Angelina. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/implementation-hepatitis-themed-virtual-escape/docview/2901459047/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: As we enter a world of blended learning in higher education, an increased need for adaptation of teaching strategies to enhance engagement has been recognised to amplify learning outcomes online. Gamification has been identified as a creative tool to engage the current cohort of learners who are also characteristically tech-savvy. To this end, escape room games have gained considerable traction in medical and pharmacy education to promote learning, critical thinking and teamwork. In this pilot study we describe the implementation of a 60-minute, web-based hepatitis-themed escape room game within a Year 3 Pharmacotherapy unit at Monash University. A total of 418 students participated in this activity. Students' knowledge gain on the topic was assessed through a pre- and post-intervention assessment, whereby a statistically significant improvement was seen in the knowledge score following implementation of the gaming activity (58.66% pre-intervention vs. 72.05% post-intervention, p < 0.05). The innovative learning activity was also well perceived by the students. Virtual escape room game is a viable pedagogical approach to teach and reinforce clinical concepts among pharmacy students. With the evolving landscape of education and learner demographics, investment in technology- enhanced game-based learning is a promising trajectory to support students' growth in a learner-centered environment. A comparison between virtual escape room game and traditional teaching will further inform effectiveness of the gamification on long term knowledge retention.

Clustering of Cities Based on Their Smart Performances: A Comparative Approach of Fuzzy C-Means, K-Means, and K-Medoids

Author: Kenger, Omer N1; Zulal Diri Kenger2; Ozceylan, Eren2; Mrugalska, Beata3    1 Department of Industrial Engineering, Hasan Kalyoncu University, Gaziantep, Turkey2 Department of Industrial Engin eering, Gaziantep University, Gaziantep, Turkey3 Faculty of Engineering Management, Poznań University of Technology, Poznań, Poland

Publication info: Kenger, Omer N; Zulal Diri Kenger; Ozceylan, Eren; Mrugalska, Beata. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/clustering-cities-based-on-their-smart/docview/2899198731/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: Smart City is recognized as a potential approach to address serious urban issues such as traffic, pollution, energy use, and waste management. Therefore, it is vital to evaluate how smart cities are in order to put these methods into practice. To offer advice on these matters, numerous reports are created, and one of which is Smart City Index (SCI). The Institute for Management Development (IMD) and the Singapore University of Technology and Design collaborate on SCI every year (SUTD). The report evaluates how locals view the buildings and technological applications that are available in their towns. Although the study offers a thorough examination of the cities for evaluation, the city clusters should be more sensitive and not be created using strict clustering techniques. In order to address this problem, the clustering algorithms namely K-Medoids, Fuzzy C-Means, and K-Means, which outperform hard clustering approaches in terms of robustness to vagueness and knowledge retention, are used. The main goal of this study is to categorize cities using a scientific manner (clustering algorithms) based on SCI data and to present how the chosen approaches work for dealing with the associated problems. The primary innovation of the present study is the use of clustering techniques in reports where the indexes are used. The results indicate that grouping the cities on the basis of their smart indicators would not be as effective as using the three clustering techniques that are suggested in this paper. These results add to the analysis of the dynamic capacities of smart cities and highlight the sustainability of these tactics.

Organisational learning and sustainable tourism: the enabling role of digital transformation

Author: Schönherr, Sarah1; Eller, Robert1; Kallmuenzer, Andreas2; Peters, Mike11 Department of Strategic Management, Marketing and Tourism, University of Innsbruck, Innsbruck, Austria2 Department of Strategy, Excelia Business School, CERIIM, La Rochelle, France

Publication info: Schönherr, Sarah; Eller, Robert; Kallmuenzer, Andreas; Peters, Mike. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/organisational-learning-sustainable-tourism/docview/2899129317/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: Purpose Organisational learning drives tourism organisations towards more sustainable tourism. Digital transformation also provides opportunities for sustainable tourism development. This study aims to combine these perspectives and explore how digital transformation enables organisational learning to contribute to sustainable tourism, following organisational learning theory (OLT). Design/methodology/approach Based on a critical realist paradigm, this study focuses on developing an in-depth understanding of organisational learning in tourism organisations. Thirty qualitative interviews with tourism organisations participating in an executive development programme (EDP) show how tourism organisations create, retain and transfer knowledge. Findings This study demonstrates that the EDP initiates knowledge creation through content transmission and exchange, triggers knowledge retention through utilisation of digital technologies and reinforces digitalisation through data value creation. Furthermore, this study enables knowledge transformation as implementation, which contributes to the three pillars of sustainable tourism and facilitates the development of networks encouraging sustainable tourism. Originality/value This study identifies approaches that enable economic, social and environmentally sustainable tourism development by facilitating collaborations via digital transformation, digital technologies that guide guest streams, online mobility offers and online environmental awareness campaigns that reduce environmental impacts. Thus, this study strengthens OLT and has implications for organisational learning and tourism policymakers.
