Full text: 1. Introduction
The construction industry operates under an environment that requires high competency levels to prevent catastrophic accidents that may be caused by the surrounding community (Anderson, 2005). Hide et al. (2003) stated that the number and severity of accidents in the construction industry had an increasing trend, which has been much higher than other industries in terms of accident per workforce representation, provided by the Health and Safety Executive (2011). As a general trend, the accidents in the construction industry are associated with human factors such as incompetency, behavioural characteristics and the job requirements that exceed the education level of the worker, which practically impose a risk to construction works (Hide et al. , 2003; Premji and Smith, 2013).
Prior scholars identified hands-on training as an effective method to improve the knowledge of individuals involved in the building and construction industry (Lapinski and Rimal, 2005). However, most of the building utilities and construction training are currently conducted through passive training methods such as lectures, videos or classroom-wide training, focusing mainly on theories with minimal visual aids and feedback in conveying the knowledge (Li et al. , 2018). Somerville and Lloyd (2006) compared the performance of learners who were theoretically trained to work safely with those who learn to work safely in an actual construction workplace. The authors found out that the “codified and structured knowledge practices” ignored the social and physical environments of the construction workplace and resulted in ineffective training. Cherrett et al. (2009) stated that there is a lack of in-depth details, realistic building construction scenarios and information, short attention span and low knowledge retention, resulting in a slow learning curve among learners in passive training. Guo et al. (2012) also suggested that the rapid didactic style of passive training methods results in confusion and misunderstanding among learners. Hence, it is prominent that the passive learning method has drawbacks in terms of knowledge, memory, motivation, engagement and attentional characteristics, which fails to acknowledge the dynamic nature in the current building utility inspection and construction engineering industry.
To overcome the aforementioned limitations in passive building and construction training, researchers started developing active training methods that involve instructional activities to facilitate the learning and thinking process while performing the learning outcome-oriented tasks (Bonwell and Eison, 1991). This active learning method assumes that the learner is actively engaged and self-reflective as a participant in the interactions with the world (Sarason and Banbury, 2004). In this approach, the learning responsibility is placed in the hands of students using informative, summative and instructional activity-based learning methods (Eiris et al. , 2020). In the context of construction training, the involvement of learners in actual construction work is the preferable mode of training, as it enhances the students' engagement and makes connections between the theoretical concepts and actual applications through effective hands-on experiences. However, due to the nature of construction works, building utility and construction education must be carried out in an off-site and hands-off environment as the on-site training is often expensive and time-consuming while it may expose the students to potential hazards.
On the other hand, the advancement of advanced visualisation technologies such as building information modelling (BIM), virtual reality (VR) and serious game made them highly relevant in facilitating active building training. However, there is a lack of integration between these technologies for classroom-wide building training due to the inadequate understanding of effective design principles and influencing factors on learning performance (Pedro et al. , 2016; Price et al. , 2003).
It is highlighted that limited research studies tackled the challenge of integrating these techniques and incorporating them into the existing building utility training curriculum. Therefore, there is an essential need to develop the building utility inspection training using game-based VR (GBVR) and BIM technologies to facilitate active learning and improve the low effectiveness and knowledge retention issues compared to the current passive learning approaches. The study aims to (1) improve traditional passive paper-based building utility training by proposing a framework using BIM + VR for game-based training; (2) compare the performance of the GBVR training system in comparison to passive paper-based training in terms of usability, user-friendliness, speed and effectiveness through user and performance-based evaluations; and (3) evaluate the performance of GBVR training for learners with different demographics and academic performance backgrounds. In this regard, the research questions formulated for this research study are stated as follows: RQ1. What are the design principles of an effective GBVR training platform for improving the capabilities of undergraduate engineering students?
RQ2. What are the influencing factors on learning performance through the GBVR training among multidisciplinary undergraduate students?
RQ3. What are the implications of GBVR training in terms of user experience and training performance compared to conventional paper-based training?

2. Literature review
2.1 Immersive technologies in engineering education
The advancement of visualisation technologies such as BIM, VR and educational game (serious game) have been proven to be beneficial in facilitating active learning in construction education (Wong et al. , 2020). Park and Kim (2013) emphasised that BIM acts as a knowledge repository for effortless reproduction and visualisation of building models. Moreover, the advancement of VR technology allows students to be placed in virtual environments infeasible to simulate in the real world (Le et al. , 2015). Kim et al. (2013) stated that VR is able to simulate an immersive environment with visual tools where users are able to gain valuable insights into how the real-world works. Fogarty et al. (2018) studied the application of VR in assisting students' comprehension of complex spatial arrangements of buckling modes in structural engineering. Behzadan and Kamat (2013) used VR to display live videos of actual construction sites to the classroom, allowing interaction with the objects through the designed interface. However, the authors found that the static VR model lacks the interactive and dynamic components of real-life training.
Serious game received considerable attention from researchers because of its significant impact on various fields, especially education and training. This is mainly attributed to the effectiveness of the educational games in providing a more motivating and engaging learning platform compared to the traditional methods, reinforcement of cognitive skills, emphasis on learning by doing, a more adaptive environment for the users, the reduced time and effort in building realistic virtual environments through the game engine and finally, the highly accurate simulation of real-life scenarios (Trenholme and Smith, 2008; Ibrahim et al. , 2014). Castronovo et al. (2017, 2018) showed evidence that simulative construction educational games can improve the memory retention of replicable problem-solving skills to solve complicated construction issues. Moreover, Nikolic (2011) discovered that virtual construction game increased student's interest and motivation through a more all-rounded view of construction scheduling. To date, most of the research studies on using VR and game-based learning for building utility training are conducted independently on either VR or game-based learning techniques in classroom-wide education (Pedro et al. , 2016; Price et al. , 2003). However, limited research studies tackled the challenge of integrating these techniques and incorporating them into the existing building utility training curriculum. This study posits that the GBVR training environment allows students to learn about building utility inspection more realistic, interactive, engaging and motivating.
2.2 Critical success factors for game-based virtual reality training
Virvou and Katsionis (2008) found system usability and user-friendliness as the two critical factors governing the success of developed GBVR training, while effectiveness, usability and speed were found necessary to gauge its success against traditional paper-based training approaches. System usability is defined as the ease of navigation and control within the virtual environment. The authors categorised system usability into four main groups, namely, the ease of use (ease of navigation within the VR environment), visual output (distractions in VR environment), knowledge retention (degree of knowledge retention after training) and clarity of introduction (understanding of user interface in VR game). As GBVR training aims to facilitate a more understandable and effective learning process than traditional paper-based approaches, it is of great importance to evaluate the system usability of the typical complex serious game (Virvou and Katsionis, 2008). This is because VR games often have a complex user interface to support the narrative, amusement and adventure, resulting in major issues in system usability among different novice-level users. Markopoulos and Bekker (2003) also suggested that system usability may be a significant drawback for students using VR games in learning or enjoyment. However, researchers often neglect the system usability of VR games, whereas the evaluation is purely conducted based on the achievement of educational outcomes (Jones et al. , 1999; Mayes and Fowler, 1999). To ensure that the developed VR environment is sophisticated, attractive and at the same time useable, the expense of student effort for engagement in educational games should be well-defined before VR game development and evaluation (Yacci et al. , 2004). Moreover, the system usability testing of GBVR ensures that the developed game-based experiential learning method does not have an overcomplex user interface and is equipped with realistic building utility objects. Hence, there is a need to evaluate the system usability of developed VR games to determine their effectiveness in training/education among students with diverse gender and VR gaming experience.
User-friendliness is defined as attractiveness, motivation, engagement, interactivity, system response and personalisation. Virvou and Katsionis (2008) suggest that games with excessive educational content may decrease user-friendliness for users familiar with conventional games. This competition and comparison between educational and conventional game takes place unconsciously in participants' minds and greatly affects the frequent game users' perception of the user-friendliness in the developed serious game. Furthermore, Han et al. (2021) showed that excessive number of complex tasks in a VR construction site hazard safety training greatly increases the user's cognitive load, which in turn affects the user's mental well-being, reducing performance, intellectual, analysis and decision-making skills. Due to the variation in human behavioural preferences, user-friendliness (motivation of VR game) also varies according to the preferences of different users. For example, male and female users may have different perceptions of motivations in an educational game (Tsai, 2004). In general, not all users within the targeted group will have a positive experience and likeability towards the VR game. Brody (1993) also stated that integrating educational content into a game results in an unclear boundary between the serious educational component and the motivating learning process. Hence, user-friendliness has been identified as a highly relevant and variable factor towards the success of a developed VR game. However, the user-friendliness of a serious game is often taken for granted and is not evaluated, which is not a healthy practice as it may result in low motivation and attractiveness among the targeted user group (Virvou and Katsionis, 2008).
Speed is defined as the time taken for the students to complete the building utility inspection training. The speed proposition correlates to the efficiency of the proposed training method, as a shorter completion time suggests that more students can be trained in a shorter period of time (Clayton et al. , 1998). Effectiveness is defined as the degree of achievement in expected learning outcomes and deliverables and can be used to evaluate and compare the educational effectiveness of serious game and conventional paper-based methods (Virvou et al. , 2005). Research conducted by Virvou and Katsionis (2008) showed that the efficacy of GBVR training varies according to the students' academic performance, where the poor performers benefited the most, and the high performers benefited the least. This suggests that the effectiveness of GBVR training and conventional paper-based method can be compared between student groups with different academic performance. The degree of task completion in each GBVR training stage referred to the usability has also been identified as a crucial evaluation criterion (Clayton et al. , 1998). This study proposed integrating BIM, VR and game-based learning as a solution to overcome the shortcomings of passive paper-based building utility education, which is through the facilitation of realistic, immersive, engaging and motivating active training. However, there is a lack of knowledge of integrating these three technologies by considering system usability, user-friendliness, effectiveness, usability and speed in the proposed training platform.
System usability and user-friendliness form the internal validity of this study, while effectiveness, speed and usability provide external validity. Hence, this study targeted to test the proposed hypothesis that GBVR building utility inspection training has higher system usability, user-friendliness, speed, effectiveness and usability than traditional paper-based training.
3. Materials and method
This section presents the experimental design (Section 3.2) along with the evaluation methods and parameters (Section 3.3). The population and sample size adopted in comparative evaluation is also justified under Section 3.1.
3.1 Population and sample size
In this study, a group of undergraduate students from the civil, mechanical and electrical engineering discipline of Monash University Malaysia in their fourth year of study was selected as the targeted population. A sample of 15 undergraduate engineering students was selected for each training method (i.e. GBVR and paper-based), making the total number of students in this experiment 30. The study ensured consistency in the two student samples by utilising demographics and background knowledge filtration in terms of gender, academic score and engineering discipline was performed. Each sample consisted of ten civil, three electrical and two mechanical engineering students, with 11 males and four females to study the internal and external validity of GBVR training from a cross-disciplinary perspective,. The total sample size of 30 students was justified as the study conducted by Wang and Dunston (2006) identified that a minimum total sample size of 16 students is required to achieve a significance level of 0.5 and power of 0.95. Pedro et al. (2016) also obtained reliable and consistent VR education system interface evaluation results on a total sample size of 25 students.
3.2 Experimental design
This research adopted a quantitative experimental study with a non-equivalent (pre- and post-test) control-group experimental design for comparative evaluation between paper-based and GBVR training (Creswell, 2013). The 15 participants from the students' sample were individually subjected to either paper-based or GBVR building utility inspection training in a classroom-wide setting to eliminate any post-session knowledge retention. The same building utility training content, evaluation and scoring system were maintained in both training methods to ensure an unbiased and reliable comparison. The paper-based training placed students in a didactic style of passive learning using outcome-oriented PDF PowerPoint slides, which contained two-dimensional (2D) figures of building utility objects. The completion time and assessment score were manually recorded in a paper-based manner. At the same time, the GBVR training facilitated active learning through the virtual walkthrough of BIM of a townhouse with three-dimensional (3D) building utility systems. The completion time and assessment score were recorded within the interface and exported into an MS Excel spreadsheet. Both building utility inspection training consisted of three stages – civil and structural, mechanical, electrical and piping (MEP) and an integrated stage where each stage was tailored with discipline-specific content with the multiple-choice assessment to achieve the specialised learning outcomes.
3.3 Comparative evaluation
The comparative evaluations were performed between paper-based and GBVR training using a user-based survey and Charette test method by Clayton et al. (1998). The embedded survey design is capable of providing a quantitative description of stands, attitudes and opinions for a larger population group based on the study conducted on a smaller sample (Creswell, 2013). A user-based survey was adopted to establish the internal validity (user-friendliness and system usability) of the developed GBVR building utility inspection training through user experience comparison against paper-based training. Two embedded questionnaires, namely, pre-test demographics survey and post-test user-based survey, were used in this study. The pre-test demographics survey collects demographic information, including engineering discipline, gender, academic performance (weighted average mark, WAM) and gaming frequency. Post-test user-based surveys evaluate the user-friendliness and system usability of both training methods through the user experience survey (Butt et al. , 2018) and system usability survey (Brooke, 1996), respectively. Both surveys contain a five-point Likert scale ranging from 5 (strongly agree) to 1 (strongly disagree) for each evaluation criteria (Likert, 1932). The Charette test method (Clayton et al. , 1998) has been adopted to establish the external validity (effectiveness and speed) of the developed GBVR building utility inspection training through performance-based comparison against paper-based training. The independent and dependant variables for each evaluation criteria in comparative evaluation is demonstrated in the adopted research design framework shown in Figure 1.
This research study adopted an internal and external validity validation process for the developed GBVR training (Cook and Campbell, 1979; Feinstein and Cannon, 2002). Internal validity provides representational validity for the GBVR training to accurately simulate the building utility systems in the two-storey townhouse environment necessary for achieving the expected learning outcome (assessed through system usability criterion in this research study) (Wolfe and Jackson, 1989). Moreover, internal validity also provides educational validity for students so that they understand how to play the game (system usability criterion) and ensure that student insights are in line with the intended game design that is to achieve a more user-friendly, insightful and needing training method than paper-based training through the simulated VR townhouse environment (user-friendliness criterion) (Parasuraman, 1981; Cannon and Burns, 1999). External validity was then established through the performance criteria of speed, effectiveness and usability to portray whether the developed GBVR training is better than paper-based training in transferring real-world building utility inspection skills and worth simulating (Cook and Campbell, 1979).
4. Framework for game-based virtual reality (GBVR) building utility education
This study aims to improve traditional passive paper-based building utility inspection training. To achieve the stated objective, a training framework for GBVR training was developed based on the building utility education processes, comprising of two modules: (1) building utility knowledge dissemination (BUKD) to allow the transfer of building utility knowledge and (2) building utility knowledge assessment (BUKA) to gauge the degree of knowledge retention through interactive game-based quizzes. The developed GBVR building utility education framework is summarised in Table 1.
The BUKD module focused on educating and transferring building utility system knowledge through the simulated townhouse environment. The BUKD training module was facilitated using a game-based learning approach, where learners perform a realistic and practical virtual walkthrough and inspection of building utility systems in the townhouse under the guidance of a virtual instructor. Building utility systems were introduced to the learners through VR contents. Learners were expected to understand the key components and working mechanism of building utility systems from civil, structural and MEP engineering point of views.
The BUKA module was formulated to (1) assess the learner's level of knowledge retention after the completion of each game scenario (Section 4.1) and (2) compare the effectiveness of the GBVR training system against the paper-based method through the achieved assessment score. The BUKA module consisted of VR multiple-choice questions related to the presented building utility system content, including component labelling of LSF and roofing system, fire rating specifications and water piping system function. The GBVR interface was utilised to facilitate this module, where learners interact with virtual answer options. Immediate constructive feedback was then provided to allow reinforcement of the presented contents.
4.1 Virtual townhouse modelling and game scenario development (building utility knowledge dissemination module)
The development of GBVR building utility inspection training was initiated with the formulation of virtual townhouse modelling and game scenario for the BUKD module. The two-storey townhouse contents were developed as a BIM-enabled platform in Autodesk ® Revit ® software (Autodesk, 2020). The developed 3D LSF in the BIM environment is a two-storey townhouse (Figure 2) consisting of a living room and kitchen area on the ground floor, the bedroom and toilet area on the first floor and the rooftop area with the roofing and rainwater harvesting systems. The 3D BIM model of the townhouse was imported into Unity ® (Unity Technologies, 2020), a universal and versatile game engine capable of creating 3D VR games and simulations that are widely utilised in architectural, engineering and construction (AEC) education (Axon, 2016). Rigid body physics was assigned to the game objects to increase the realism of the developed townhouse in the VR environment.
A virtual instructor was added to lead the walkthrough of the townhouse and increase the interactivity and engagement of GBVR training. The utilised assets in the Unity platform, including SteamVR ® (movement and interaction), visual scripting (playmaker), animation (rigging), audio effects and environment, were assigned to the building utility objects and were integrated into a scene manager to allow triggering of conditional events, animations and game scenarios. The learners could navigate the virtual townhouse through a changing view of the virtual environment using a frame-based method.
The first game scenario was located at the exterior part of the ground floor level of the townhouse, where learners were exposed to contents related to civil and structural building utility systems, including the manufacturing process and benefits of LSF in terms of material and fire rating of façade system through auditory and visual learning (more significant focus on auditory learning). LSF building system was selected as it has received significant attention in the construction industry because of its lightweight structure with higher ease of assembly and faster construction process. As illustrated in Figure 3a, learners were exposed to an actual full-scale LSFS where the virtual instructor provides an interactive explanation of the components by glowing them with bright white subtitles. The function and fire rating of the façade system was illustrated with the aid of fire animations (Figure 3b). This civil and structural training building utility module aims to allow learners to interact with light steel frames that are not commonly seen due to the enclosure by the façade system in a constructed townhouse.
The second game scenario was situated on the first floor of the townhouse. It is designed to facilitate a virtual walkthrough of the MEP system installed within the ceiling and flooring. Learners were exposed to the working mechanism and function of lighting sensor networks, chilled water system and greywater/blackwater/rainwater piping system in the townhouse through auditory and visual learning (more significant focus on visual learning). The virtual inspector explains the function and working mechanism of MEP building utility systems present in the ceiling and flooring of the townhouse while learners get to observe actual fluid and airflow within those systems (Figure 4). This MEP game scenario allows a high level of visual and audio learning as learners visualise and analyse various types of fluids flowing within a typical townhouse, which is not commonly seen due to the enclosure in building design.
The third and final stage in GBVR training focuses on hands-on training, consisting of the interaction with the light steel roofing system and the maintenance of the rainwater harvesting system (Figure 5).
The learning objectives for each stage of GBVR training are stated in Table 2.
4.2 Virtual assessment development (building utility knowledge assessment module)
Virtual multiple-choice quizzes were formulated based on the expected learning outcomes for each training scenario in training stages (Table 2) and were validated by lecturers, and research investigators specialised in AEC study. The three assessment components (corresponding to each training stage) are mapped to Bloom's taxonomy (Bloom, 1956) domains and levels for both GBVR and paper-based methods, as shown in Table 3 As it can be seen, in GBVR assessment tasks, the trainee will be indirectly assessed for his/her psychomotor skills as well due to the fact that any interaction and responding to the quiz questions needs sufficient level of familiarity with VR gadgets. There are studies in different academic disciplines that approve virtual psychomotor training and assessments that can enhance trainees’ knowledge and understanding (Björn et al. , 2020; Abraham and Connor, 2020).
It is worth mentioning that after each question, the physical or virtual instructor (depends on the training method) provides a constructive feedback to allow further retention and reinforce building utility system knowledge. The time is taken through the designed VR game interface at the GBVR platform or recorded manually in paper-based training. The number of correct answers was concurrently recorded for the pre-designed questions (building utility assessment score) at each game scenario stage. The embedded questions in the VR game environment and paper-based training are shown in Figure 6.
With the well-established BUKD and BUKA modules, the developed GBVR training facilitates active building training for learners with proper post-training assessment.
5. Results and discussion
This section discusses the results obtained from the comparative evaluation between GBVR and paper-based building utility inspection training to validate the developed GBVR training prototype as a proof of concept. The evaluation is categorised into two groups: (1) user experience evaluation and (2) performance-based evaluation.
5.1 User experience evaluation
Learners' user experience – system usability and user-friendliness were identified as essential factors governing the success of the developed GBVR building utility training (Section 2.2). System usability of GBVR ensures that the developed game-based experiential learning method does not have an overcomplex user interface and is equipped with realistic building utility objects. The user-friendliness aspect of the GBVR building utility training gauges whether the training provides a more attractive, motivating, engaging and interactive training method compared to the traditional paper-based training. Upon completing GBVR or paper-based training, learners' system usability and user-friendliness of both training systems were evaluated by learners through a five-point Likert scale user-based survey that contains options varying from 5 (strongly agree) to 1 (strongly disagree) for each evaluation criterion related to system usability and user-friendliness (Likert, 1932). During training observations and post-training, interview sessions were also carried out to obtain descriptive evaluations regarding the system usability and user-friendliness of both training systems.
5.1.1 System usability testing
The system usability of GBVR and paper-based training methods were compared in terms of four main criteria, namely, ease of use, visual output, knowledge retention and clarity of introduction. The results and description for each criterion are tabulated in Table 4.
As tabulated in Table 4, the traditional paper-based training method has higher ease of use than the developed GBVR building inspection training. The majority of the learners commented that navigating within the VR environment was a brand-new experience for them. They felt that performing training in a virtual environment was overwhelming as they were distracted by the virtual environment and unable to focus on the auditory lecture content and tasks conveyed by the virtual inspector. However, navigational functions and game-based lecture contents were said to be well integrated. Students described that the traditional paper-based training system was simple to navigate. As shown in Table 4, the visual output for game-based training is better than the paper-based one. The learners described that the 3D building utility objects looked realistic in the virtual environment compared to the static 2D pictorial representation in traditional paper-based training. GBVR training also better facilitates practical on-site building utility experience through the virtual walkthrough of a townhouse. The low training practicality score in Table 4 is due to the stereotyping for this new training mode.
The GBVR building utility training with higher realism and practicality results in a higher knowledge retention rating than the didactic paper-based training. However, learners' feedback indicated that it was harder to concentrate during GBVR training as the virtual inspector conveyed the lecture contents auditorily. This suggests that auditory content has a short attentional span and the lengthy captions, which were shown for a brief duration are ineffective for knowledge retention compared to paper-based training where learners have the freedom to control their pace of learning. As illustrated in Table 4, learners agreed that the paper-based training introduction is more comprehensive and more straightforward compared to the GBVR training. This is because the GBVR is a more sophisticated and demanding training in terms of functionality and navigational effort compared to the paper-based one. This hypothesis is supported by the higher ease of use in the paper-based training (scored 4.4) compared to GBVR (scored 4.1).
The system usability of GBVR training was also evaluated based on gender, as shown in Figure 7.
As shown in Figure 7, GBVR training has higher system usability among male learners for all four criteria and may be attributed to the higher exposure to VR and game applications. GBVR training has lower ease of use among female learners due to the relatively heavier VR headset and high stress level when subjected to unfamiliar game-based learning platforms.
The effect of learner's gaming frequency on the system usability of GBVR training was studied with the results illustrated in Figure 8.
Based on the system usability comparison of GBVR training against gaming frequency (Figure 8), learners who play games “often” rated the lowest system usability score, supporting the theory that educational content contradicts conventional entertainment games. Learners who play games “sometimes” have higher acceptance toward the education game and rated the highest system usability score for the GBVR training system. As for learners who “rarely” play games, an intermediate system usability score was rated, indicating the acceptance of edutainment games but had a lower familiarity with the game system.
Overall, GBVR training has higher system usability than paper-based training (more useable for males) because of the higher realism and practicality, which results in higher knowledge retention and visual output. The lower ease of use and clarity of the introduction module in GBVR training can be improved by incorporating a more comprehensive, all-rounded introduction module and the transition of auditory content to visual representations and hands-on tasks.
5.1.2 User-friendliness
User-friendliness for both training methods was evaluated based on five criteria – attractiveness, motivation (engagement), interactivity, feedback and personalisation. The results and description for each criterion are tabulated in Table 5.
As tabulated in Table 5, GBVR training has higher user-friendliness than paper-based training in all five criteria. Learners subjected to GBVR training agreed that this training mode has a greater attractiveness than paper-based training because of the incorporated game elements and realistic virtual townhouse environment. Enjoyment of GBVR training is further elevated as learners are able to freely inspect the building utility objects and townhouse environment during the virtual walkthrough. Learners also felt that practising through the GBVR method attracts their attention as it is a new form of training that is more beneficial for their learning and development of practical hands-on experiences. For the traditional paper-based training method, learners critiqued the lack of attractiveness in the dull didactic style of passive learning.
Moreover, learners had higher motivation and engagement factor from the GBVR training. The virtual inspector plays an essential role in motivating and engaging the learner through encouragements and instructions, which allow a better immersion into the game scenario. The game scoring system implicitly encourages learners to improve their score to gain a better game achievement (pleasantly frustrating). Through the replacement of piping for the rainwater harvesting system in the integrated building utility game scenario (Section 4.1), learners are able to perform a hands-on task in the virtual environment, which significantly increases the interactivity of GBVR building utility inspection training. For the paper-based training, only the procedure for piping replacement has been presented, which lacks interaction in this training method. In addition, learners in the GBVR training method interact with the virtual inspector through movements in the designated area before the explanation of building utility systems. Learners agreed that GBVR is a more versatile training system that allows better personalisation according to the user's interests and needs. The BIM can be modified to incorporate the required building utility system content. Paper-based training is often a fixed curriculum with only possible minor modifications due to its structured nature. As shown in Table 5, learners believed that the feedback system in both training methods is quite similar as the actual instructor present in the paper-based training method is replaced by a virtual one in the GBVR method to provide feedback regarding the building utility assessment.
The user-friendliness of GBVR training was also evaluated based on gender, as shown in Figure 9. It was found out that GBVR training has higher user-friendliness among male learners because of their higher familiarity and acceptance towards VR educational game learning method.
Overall, GBVR training has higher user-friendliness than paper-based training in all five criteria (higher user-friendliness among males). This is mainly attributed to the new form of GBVR training, which facilitates a more attractive mode of training through engaging and motivating game-based scoring and learning. Higher interaction is also present due to the movement within the virtual environment upon instructions given by the virtual inspector and the interactive, hands-on tasks. The internal validity of GBVR training was achieved as the user experience evaluation shows higher system usability and user-friendliness than the paper-based training.
5.2 Performance-based evaluation
Performance-based evaluation for both training methods was performed in terms of speed and effectiveness. The completion time and assessment score achieved for each game scenario was recorded within the interface of GBVR training and manually recorded in paper-based training (Section 4.2). This section provides a comprehensive performance-based comparison between training methods.
5.2.1 Speed
The mean completion time for each stage in paper-based and GBVR training along with the total completion time is tabulated under Table 6.
Based on the tabulated completion time (Table 6), paper-based training has a faster total completion time of 13.6 min compared to 24.4 min for GBVR training. Learners are able to control their pace of learning in the didactic style of paper-based training but unable to do so for GBVR training, which adopts an auditory, visual and hands-on mode of delivery.
The distribution of the time taken for each stage in GBVR and paper-based training methods are illustrated in Figures 10(a) and (b), respectively. Due to the discrete manual time record in the paper-based training method, the distribution in Figure 10(b) is not a smooth curve.
As shown in Figure 10, the completion time for each stage of the paper-based building utility inspection training has higher variability than GBVR training due to the freedom in controlling the pace of learning. However, the completion time for Stage 3 of GBVR building utility inspection training (Figure 10a) has a larger variation compared to the other stages. This could be related to the hands-on learning activity (Section 4.1), which may have resulted in variability in completion time among learners due to the difference in their gaming frequencies. Overall, the speed (completion time) of paper-based building utility training is faster than GBVR training. Learners have the freedom in controlling learning pace through the reading of building utility content in a paper-based manner. However, the longer training time in GBVR is justified by having higher system usability and user-friendliness (Section 5.1) by facilitating more realistic and practical building utility inspection training. Future improvements can be made to achieve a faster training speed by transitioning from the auditory content to hands-on tasks.
5.2.2 Effectiveness (accuracy) and usability
The effectiveness of both training methods was compared based on the achieved total building utility assessment score (Table 7). In GBVR training, Stage 1 focuses on auditory learning, and Stage 2 focuses on auditory and visual learning, while Stage 3 adopts a hands-on learning method. Each stage has a total score of 5. The usability of GBVR training is also shown in Table 7, which indicates that all students successfully completed each stage of GBVR training and suggested a very useable training system.
Table 7 shows that paper-based training with a higher total building utility assessment score is a more effective training method than GBVR. This could be attributed to the difference in a delivery mode where the didactic paper-based training is considered a more common and familiar training method among students compared to GBVR training with its relatively new and unfamiliar method. Based on the observation during both training sessions, students subjected to the paper-based training have a better focus due to the absence of distractions by the attractive and realistic virtual townhouse environment in GBVR training. They also get to study the visual contents at their own pace without the interference of the visual inspector. As for the GBVR training method, students have difficulty focusing on the auditory lecture content. They often get distracted by the visual environment and failed to capture the auditory content delivered by the virtual inspector. However, this finding does not prove that GBVR training is the more inferior method with lower effectiveness. The lower performance in Stages 1 and 3 for GBVR training compared to the paper-based method could be attributed to the fact that in these two stages, there are questions that need students to draw on a shown image, while Stage 2 is completely focused on multiple-choice questions. It is possible that conducting such a task in a GBVR environment has been a bit more challenging compared to the paper-based method. As shown in Table 7, Stage 2 in GBVR training achieved a higher score than the paper-based method, confirming that dealing with multiple-choice questions in a VR environment has been easier compared to the paper-based one. This finding highlights the importance of psychomotor skills in such training as insufficient skills may affect the overall learning performance. The mapping of auditory contents presented by the inspector to visual representation effectively overcomes the stated limitation. For example, when the inspector explains the usage of harvested rainwater in toilet flushing, visual animations of fluid flow from the rainwater harvesting tank to the toilet bowl is able to supplement the auditory content through visual representations effectively.
The comparison of effectiveness (building utility assessment score) for GBVR training based on academic performance (academic WAM) is illustrated in Figure 11.
Comparison between the achieved building utility assessment scores for learners with different academic WAM (shown in Figure 11) showed that those with a lower WAM benefited more from the GBVR learning method and achieved a higher building utility assessment score. This indicates the great potential of GBVR training in improving the academic performance of learners, who have a better learning curve through visual and game-based methods compared to the didactic, passive and structured curriculum approach in the traditional paper-based assessment. Although traditional paper-based training achieved higher assessment scores than GBVR training, GBVR training is more effective in facilitating a new mode of training that enhances students' capabilities with lower academic performance (WAM score). The slightly lower effectiveness of GBVR can be enhanced by mapping auditory contents to visual representations and transitioning from auditory to visual and hands-on learning. The external validity of GBVR training is deemed to be achieved as it can be justified by the significantly better system usability and user-friendliness than paper-based training. Improvements can be made to training speed and effectiveness by incorporating more visual and hands-on learning elements.
6. Conclusion
Current passive paper-based building utility training inadequately prepares students to become the competitive future workforce because it fails to acknowledge the dynamic and practical nature of the modern building and construction industry. Moreover, to contribute towards the Industrial Revolution 4.0 and with the current Covid-19 pandemic, there is a need to transform from in-person to technological-based training. Therefore, this study developed a GBVR building utility inspection training for university students through the virtual interactive walkthrough of a BIM-based two-storey townhouse to enhance tertiary building and construction education. The feasibility and applicability of the training were assessed and validated through comparative evaluation against the traditional paper-based method using a user-based survey and Charette test method. The assessment for the developed GBVR training was performed rigorously in terms of internal validity (system usability and user-friendliness) and external validity (effectiveness, speed and usability).
The user-experience and performance-based evaluation of GBVR building utility inspection training demonstrated that: - GBVR training approach effectively supplemented traditional passive paper-based building and construction education, which suffered from low realism and practicality;

- The higher system usability (visual output and knowledge retention) and user-friendliness (attractiveness, engagement and motivational factors) in GBVR training compared to traditional paper-based training were identified as the main drivers;

- GBVR training has higher system usability and user-friendliness among male learners and has higher effectiveness for learners with lower academic performance;

- The lower ease of use, speed and effectiveness of GBVR training can be improved through the transition of auditory contents to hands-on tasks supplemented by visual representations; and

- GBVR training has a lower effectiveness in improving the performance of multiple-choice based evaluation. Hence, to increase the applicability of immersive GBVR training, future studies can consider a more practical scenario-based (hands-on) evaluation method.


This study posits future studies on developing complex training scenarios with more visual representations and hands-on tasks to overcome the low attentional auditory learning span. This study has further potential to be extended in the vocational training platforms for competency development of the construction workforce by using cutting-edge extended reality technologies such as mixed reality (MR) and augmented reality (AR) in the building sector.

Mobile application adjunct to the WHO basic emergency care course: a mixed methods study

Author: Tenner, Andrea G1; Greenberg, Anya L2    ; Nicholaus, Paulina3; Rose, Christian C4    ; Addo, Newton1    ; Shari, Catherine Reuben3; Friedman, Alexandra5; George, Upendo N3; Losak, Michael J4; Mfinanga, Juma A6; Sawe, Hendry R7    1 Department of Emergency Medicine, Univers ity of California San Francisco, San Francisco, California, USA2 School of Medicine, University of California San Francisco, San Francisco, California, USA3 Department of Emergency Medicine, Muhimbili National Hospital, Dar es Salaam, United Republic of Tanzania4 Department of Emergency Medicine, Stanford University School of Medicine, Stanford, California, USA5 Department of Emergency Medicine, Highland Hospital, Oakland, California, USA6 Department of Emergency Medicine, Muhimbili National Hospital, Dar es Salaam, Dar es Salaam, United Republic of Tanzania7 Department of Emergency Medicine, Muhimbili University of Health and Allied Sciences, Dar es Salaam, United Republic of Tanzania

Publication info: Tenner, Andrea G; Greenberg, Anya L; Nicholaus, Paulina; Rose, Christian C; Addo, Newton; et al. 

http://ezproxy.lb.polyu.edu.hk/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/mobile-application-adjunct-who-basic-emergency/docview/2686963476/se-2?accountid=16210

Abstract: Objectives The WHO developed a 5-day basic emergency care (BEC) course using the traditional lecture format. However, adult learning theory suggests that lecture-based courses alone may not promote long-term knowledge retention. We assessed whether a mobile application adjunct (BEC app) can have positive impact on knowledge acquisition and retention compared with the BEC course alone and evaluated perceptions, acceptability and barriers to adoption of such a tool. Design Mixed-methods prospective cohort study. Participants Adult healthcare workers in six health facilities in Tanzania who enrolled in the BEC course and were divided into the control arm (BEC course) or the intervention arm (BEC course plus BEC app). Main outcome measures Changes in knowledge assessment scores, self-efficacy and perceptions of BEC app. Results 92 enrolees, 46 (50%) in each arm, completed the BEC course. 71 (77%) returned for the 4-month follow-up. Mean test scores were not different between the two arms at any time period. Both arms had significantly improved test scores from enrolment (prior to distribution of materials) to day 1 of the BEC course and from day 1 of BEC course to immediately after BEC course completion. The drop-off in mean scores from immediately after BEC course completion to 4 months after course completion was not significant for either arm. No differences were observed between the two arms for any self-efficacy question at any time point. Focus groups revealed five major themes related to BEC app adoption: educational utility, clinical utility, user experience, barriers to access and barriers to use. Conclusion The BEC app was well received, but no differences in knowledge retention and self-efficacy were observed between the two arms and only a very small number of participants reported using the app. Technologic-based, linguistic-based and content-based barriers likely limited its impact.

Strengths and limitations of this study
- Mixed-methods study design enables both quantitative and qualitative assessment of outcome measures of interest.

- Two-armed intervention-based prospective cohort study with relatively large number of participants and high follow-up rate provides a solid ground for drawing conclusions.

- Significant difficulties were encountered in both installation and subsequent usage of the app, despite attempts to mitigate issues. This limited the study’s ability to assess impact of the app on knowledge retention.

- Study was limited to a single country in Eastern Sub-Saharan Africa, thus limiting generalisability of results.


Introduction
Well-organised emergency care systems play an important role in the delivery of emergency services and health outcomes of patients in low-resource settings. 1–6 However, healthcare workers in low and middle-income countries (LMICs) often lack basic training to recognise and treat life-threatening conditions, 7 8 and access to adequate emergency care in low-resource settings is limited. 9 Although over half the deaths in LMICs are potentially addressable by prehospital emergency care, 10 the burden of acute diseases, coupled with the lack of emergency care training in LMICs, leads to unnecessary deaths. Additionally, staff working in LMICs frequently site lack of training in emergencies as a frustration, leading to lack of satisfaction with their work and desire to work in other parts of the hospital. 11
To give countries the tools to reduce mortality from emergency conditions, the WHO, in collaboration with the International Committee of the Red Cross and with endorsement by the International Federation for Emergency Medicine, developed a 5-day, open-access basic emergency care (BEC) course to provide standardised training in basic assessment and life-saving techniques using a traditional lecture format. The BEC course materials focus on the primary survey, or airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure (ABCDE) approach to emergencies. The course was developed using a robust consensus process, and initial pilot studies showed that the course was both effective in knowledge transfer and locally acceptable in varied communities of Tanzania, Uganda and Zambia. 12
Given the unprecedented increase in mobile phone and internet users as well as a decline in the price of devices and services in LMICs, 13 supplementing the BEC course with technology-based, ‘just-in-time’ content that can be used at the patient bedside was suggested by end users. Indeed, adult learning theory suggests that lecture-based courses alone may not promote long-term knowledge retention and that just-in-time training might be preferable. 14 Just-in-time training, defined as training that is done immediately prior to the procedure, has been shown to improve provider performance in a variety of surgical and non-surgical procedures across multiple specialties and practice settings. 15 However, it is unknown if these newer techniques are acceptable to, or useful for, healthcare workers in LMICs who are presented with medical emergencies.
In response to this request for additional support, a mobile application was developed as an adjunct to the BEC course in 2017. The application walked the user through a decision-making process and is based on the principles of the BEC course. It was intended to enable learners to access content before the course through simple links as well as basic yes/no html pathways through primary survey (ie, ABCDE) elements, which could serve as a real-time clinical, bedside reference after course completion. We conducted a small pilot study in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania in 2017 to compare knowledge acquisition and retention between participants who received the standard BEC course alone and participants who received the course with educational adjuncts (a suite of clinical cases to simulate patient care and the mobile application). Preliminary findings were promising, indicating that such tactics may improve knowledge and retention. However, the study was small, results did not reach statistical significance, and the study had several limitations. 16
The purpose of this study was to assess if a mobile application adjunct to the BEC course, specifically, can impact knowledge acquisition, knowledge retention and work experience compared with the BEC course alone. We hypothesised that the application would improve knowledge retention, knowledge acquisition and work experience. In addition, we aimed to evaluate perceptions, acceptability and barriers to adoption of such a tool.
Methods
Development of second-generation mobile BEC application
A second-generation mobile application adjunct to the BEC course (BEC app) was developed for this study. Similar to the first-generation application that was used in the 2017 pilot, the second-generation BEC app was designed to be a point-of-care reference tool that guides healthcare workers through the ABCDE approach and the evaluation and treatment of seriously ill patients at the bedside (online supplemental appendix A). The second-generation BEC app incorporated extensive feedback from the first-generation application and addressed reported limitations with that version, including the ability to function without internet access and track application use centrally. 17 The second-generation BEC app was designed as an expanding logic framework that could be deployed within a self-contained app on any mobile operating system or accessed through chatbot services across multiple platforms like WhatsApp or Facebook Messenger as well as short message service (SMS) for the greatest possible reach. Additionally, a chat-based approach was believed to allow for broader translation from English to other languages as it does not always require completely rewriting the app software, but rather may allow for common translational services to be employed.
The second-generation BEC app was developed through a collaboration between study investigators and a software engineer. It underwent extensive prerelease testing with emergency medicine doctors and nurses across the world, including Tanzania, Rwanda, Cameroon, Sierra Leon, South Africa, United Arab Emirates and the USA. Reviewers were asked to recall their last five emergency cases, run them through the app and provide feedback on the algorithm and application interface based on this process. Updates to the application were made accordingly.
Study design
We conducted a prospective, cohort study with adult (over 17 years of age) healthcare workers without prior formal emergency care training in six health facilities in Tanzania. The six facilities include Mt. Meru Regional Hospital in Arusha Region; Mbagala Rangi Tatu Health Center in Temeke, Dar es Salaam; Sinza Health Centre in Kinondoni, Dar es Salaam; Vijibweni Health Center in Kigamboni Dar es Salaam; Mkuranga District Hospital in Coastal Region and Mbeya Zonal Referral Hospital in Mbeya. These are considered busy hospitals with high-acuity patients who currently receive evaluation and care by providers who have not undergone emergency care training.
The onboarding, courses and follow-up—including all associated assessments and focus groups (FGs)—were delivered at or near these six facilities. Courses at Sinza Health Center; Mbagala Rangi Tatu Health Center and Mbeya Zonal Referral Hospital consisted of participants from these sites only, while the courses at Mt. Meru Regional Hospital; Vijibweni Health Center and Mkuranga District Hospital were comprised of participants from multiple sites within the district.
The study consisted of two arms. The first arm was the control arm with participants in this arm undergoing the traditional BEC course, but without access to the mobile application. The second arm was the intervention arm. Participants in this arm were given access to the BEC app in addition to completing the BEC course. Mkuranga District Hospital, Mbagala Zakheim and Mt. Meru Hospital were arbitrarily assigned to be in the control arm (arm 1, non-app arm) and Sinza Health Center; Mbeya Zonal Referral Hospital and Vijibweni Health Centre to be in the intervention arm (arm 2, app arm).
Participants from each site were selected from a convenience sample from these six hospitals based on voluntary enrolment in July 2019. Participants were initially approached and offered the opportunity to volunteer by Medical Officers Incharge at each site. There were no exclusion criteria. Prior to enrolment in the course, informed consent to participate in the study was obtained from all participants (online supplemental appendix B). Participants received no financial incentives for participating in the course or enrolling in the study. Ninety-seven participants were enrolled across the six sites 1.5–2 weeks prior to course initiation.
On enrolment in the study (T1), participants were given a multiple-choice knowledge assessment to assess baseline knowledge, Likert scale self-efficacy survey (online supplemental appendix C) and BEC course materials. Knowledge assessments used at all phases of the study were developed by WHO and are a standard part of the BEC course. Recognising the inherent knowledge acquisition through test-enhanced learning, 18 the same knowledge assessments were given to participants in both arms at the same time points. In the absence of existing tools with validity evidence in our study population, the self-efficacy survey was designed by our team to assess key aspects of the workplace experience, including participants’ comfort with, satisfaction with and enjoyment of their work.
Basic information about demographics (including age, sex) and professional background (including role, years of experience) were gathered at enrolment. Participants in the app arm who had smart phones compatible with the mobile application were given the opportunity to download the BEC app with moderator support.
Basic emergency care
BEC courses were held at each healthcare site over a 2-week period, with three courses running simultaneously during the first week and the second week. Courses at non-app arm facilities ran during the first week, while courses at app arm facilities ran during the second week.
Of the 97 participants who enrolled, 92 participants (46 in each arm) presented on the first day of the course (T2). Participants who were not present for the initial enrolment were not permitted to join the course. All participants were given a second multiple-choice knowledge assessment on the first day of the course prior to any course instruction. Participants in the app arm who were not able to successfully access the BEC app during the initial onboarding were given another opportunity to download the BEC app during the course. Of the 46 participants within the app arm, 42 had smartphones. These participants were assisted with BEC app downloading and troubleshooting of technical issues, with no discussion of course content. Of these participants, 29 were able to download and use the mobile application.
Swahili is participants’ native language and English is spoken as a second language. Each of the BEC courses was taught by local instructors fluent in both English and Swahili. Each course had at least four instructors, with two instructors from the site at which the course was held and the rest from an outside site. At the end of the course (T3), participants completed a third multiple-choice knowledge assessment and the same Likert-scale self-efficacy survey they filled out at onboarding. All 92 participants who initiated the course completed the postcourse assessment.
Written course materials, the BEC app, course assessments and self-efficacy surveys were provided in English. If a participant did not meet the 75% passing threshold for the final examination, questions answered incorrectly were translated to Swahili to address language barriers. The new score was used as the basis for successful completion of the course, but the initial score was used for study purposes. All data were collected at the location of training at each site.
Focus groups
After completion of the BEC courses, participants were invited to participate in FGs to elicit perspectives of accessibility, applicability and opportunity for improvement of the BEC course and BEC app without course instructors or study moderators. Each 1-hour FG was moderated by two Swahili-speaking facilitators, who were male or female doctors (MD) or nurses (RN) at the Muhimbili National Hospital Emergency Medicine Department and who underwent training on how to facilitate FGs led by an experienced FG facilitator. FGs were conducted in Swahili with a written facilitator guide (online supplemental appendix D). Field notes were taken during the FG by one of the FG facilitators. In order to minimise potential bias, participants had no prior relationship with FG facilitators and understood them to be external parties (outside of the course structure) present only to facilitate the FGs. FGs were audio recorded, content was transcribed and translated into English, and identifying information was redacted by the FG facilitators. Original recordings were subsequently deleted.
Study follow-up
Approximately 4 months after completion of the BEC courses (T4), participants in both arms were reassessed with a fourth multiple-choice knowledge test and another Likert-scale self-efficacy survey. Participants were also invited to participate in another FG discussion (online supplemental appendix E) that was structured similarly to the initial. Seventy-one out of the 92 enrolees participated in the follow-up. US$25-equivalent stipend was provided for their participation in the follow-up. As with the initial pilot, following the conclusion of the study, access to the BEC app was made freely available to participants in the non-app arm.
Data analysis
Outcomes of interest in this study were participant scores on the knowledge assessments at four time points; scores from the Likert-scale self-efficacy survey at three time points and qualitative FG data on user perspectives of the BEC app. An intention-to-treat analysis was performed to compare the two arms.
Descriptive statistics were used to compare demographic and professional characteristics between the two arms. We used ANOVA models to compare mean knowledge assessment scores by time point and further analysed differences by site using analysis of variance (ANOVA)-based mixed-effect models, accounting for repeated measures within the same individual. Responses to the self-efficacy survey in the group of study completers were compared at three time points with either χ 2 or Fisher exact tests, as appropriate. All analyses were performed using R V.3.6 (R Project for Statistical Computing).
Two investigators (ALG and AF) conducted thematic analysis of the FG transcripts. 19 Transcripts were independently read by both investigators and codes were identified using an inductive approach. The investigators then came to a consensus on the codebook based on joint discussion and recoded all transcripts accordingly. Codes were reviewed to generate themes and subthemes through iterative discussion and refinement by the two investigators. The process was repeated for the follow-up FGs. Codes generated from the initial phase, as well as emerging codes, were applied. Themes and subthemes were identified. One investigator used the qualitative analysis software Atlas.ti V.8, whereas the other used Microsoft Word.
Results
A total of 92 healthcare workers (table 1) from the six participating sites, 46 (50%) in each arm, completed the BEC course and the first phase of the study, including a knowledge assessment and self-efficacy survey at onboarding (T1), a second knowledge assessment on the first day of the course (T2) and a third knowledge assessment and second self-efficacy survey on completion of the course (T3) (figure 1). Per intention to treat analysis, participants were compared according to their initial arm allocation; all 46 participants in arm 1 were compared against all 46 participants in arm 2 (including those who were unable to download the app).

No significant differences in demographic or professional characteristics were observed between the two arms. While compared with the non-app arm, participants in the app arm had a lower absolute mean age (32.8 years vs 36.1 years), this difference did not reach statistical significance (p=0.71). Participants in both arms were more likely to be woman (61%) and more likely to be nurses (61%), with no difference in proportion of women (p=0.83) or nurses (p=0.29) between the two arms. A trend towards statistical significance was seen in years of experience, where compared with the non-app arm, participants in the app arm were more likely to have less than 5 years of experience (p=0.09).
Knowledge assessments
Knowledge assessments were administered at all four time points, T1–T4. Mean knowledge assessment scores at T1 (prior to any exposure to BEC course materials or the BEC app) were not statistically different between the two arms (62.9% arm 1, 61.5% arm 2) (table 2). Mean scores at T2 (after the distribution of BEC course materials for all enrolees and download of the BEC app for a small minority of participants in arm 2), were significantly higher than T1 (p<0.001) for both arms, but no difference was observed in the mean scores at T2 between the two arms. Mean knowledge assessment scores at T3 (after completion of the BEC course) were significantly higher than T1 (p<0.001) and T2 (p<0.001) for both arms, but again no difference was observed in the mean scores at T3 between the two arms.

Of the 92 enrolees who completed the BEC course and assessments in the first phase (P1), 71 (77%) returned for the second phase (P2) while 21 (23%) were lost to follow-up. The trends in knowledge assessments during P1 for this subgroup are consistent with those seen for the overall group of enrolees who completed the BEC course. For this subgroup, mean scores at T2 were significantly higher than those at T1 (p<0.001) and mean scores at T3 were significantly higher than those at T1 and those at T2 (p<0.001) for both arms.
While there was some drop-off in mean scores from T3 to T4 for both arms, this change was not significant for either arm (p=0.78 arm 1, p=0.60 arm 2) and mean scores for both arms at T4 remained significantly higher than those at T2 (p<0.001) and T1 (p<0.001). No difference in mean scores was observed between the two arms at any of the four time periods (figure 2).

Four-point Likert scale self-efficacy surveys were administered at three time points: at onboarding (T1), at completion of the BEC course (T3) and at the 4-month follow-up (T4). The self-efficacy survey was not administered at T2. Responses were compared among the 71 participants who completed the surveys at all three time points and are seen in table 3.

Significant decreases from T1 to T3 in the proportion of responses of ‘1’ or ‘2’ were observed for question 2 (‘very uncomfortable’ or ‘somewhat uncomfortable’ taking care of patients with emergency conditions; p=0.015) and question 4 (‘very uncomfortable’ or ‘somewhat uncomfortable’ with knowledge of emergency conditions; p=<0.001). A decrease from T1 to T3 in the proportion of responses of ‘1’ or ‘2’ for question 5 (‘unsatisfied’ or ‘somewhat unsatisfied’ with ability to do work well) was also observed, but it did not reach significance (p=0.16). Significant differences in the proportion of responses of ‘1’ or ‘2’ between T3 and T4 were not observed for question 2 (p=0.54), question 4 (p=0.47) or question 5 (p>0.99).
There was a significant increase from T1 to T3 in the proportion of responses of ‘4’ for question 1 (‘frequently’ see patients who present with emergency conditions; p=0.03), question 2 (‘very comfortable’ taking care of patients with emergency conditions; p<0.001), question 4 (‘very comfortable’ with knowledge of emergency conditions; p<0.001), question 5 (‘very satisfied’ with ability to do work well; p=0.004), and question 7 (‘frequently’ able to make a difference in patient’s lives; p=0.004). The proportion of responses of ‘4’ decreased significantly from T3 to T4 for these questions, returning to T1 levels for question 1, 2, 5 and 7 but to a level still significantly higher than T1 for question 4 (p=0.02).
The same trends were observed for each individual arm, with no differences in responses between the two arms for any question at any time point (table 4).

FG discussions
Two FGs were held at each study site; the first immediately after completion of the BEC course (T3) and the second at the 4-month follow-up (T4). Comparison of recurrent codes across app sites and both time periods revealed five major emerging themes related to the perceptions, acceptability and barriers to adoption: educational utility, clinical utility, user experience, barriers to access and barriers to use (table 5).
